Kindergarten · Science

Kindergarten Science: What We Are Learning

Our plan for the year, unit by unit, and the Islamic connection running through it | 2026 to 2027

PLEASE READ FIRST: THIS IS A PLAN, NOT A PROMISE

  • The content and the timing will change. This page is what we are aiming to teach and roughly when. Units move, investigations get swapped, and some take longer than planned. The overall goal does not change: that your child leaves Kindergarten able to notice something, ask a question about it, and find out.
  • The months are approximate on purpose. No exact dates are given here because they would be wrong by October. Your teacher confirms what is actually happening on Class Dojo.
  • How the subject runs. Science is taught twice a week for about 40 minutes, and every session has children doing something rather than listening. There is no homework. Two things run outside the lesson all year: a weather chart read every morning at Morning Meeting, and a Change Journal in which each child draws the same thing in the schoolyard six times across the year. Both are read back in June, and the journal comes home after the showcase.
Late August to early SeptemberUnit 1

What your child is learning about

Thinking Like a Scientist

A scientist is not a person in a white coat. Your child learns to ask a question about something they noticed, look closely, predict, sort, compare, and record what they found. Every session has children doing something, never just listening.

New words: scientist, observe, question, predict, sort, compare, record,

hand lens, evidence

By the end of the unit: Ask a question about something they notice, look closely with a hand lens, make a prediction, and record what they found in a drawing.

Sample question: What is in this bag? Feel it, but do not look, and tell me what you notice.A strong answer: It is hard and smooth and round on one side. It has a bumpy part. I predict it is a shell. Takes it out to check. It is a shell!

Watch for: Drawing a tidy picture instead of what is really there. Praise a drawing that shows the true details, like a leaf with a hole in it.

Try this at home

When your child notices something odd, resist explaining it. Ask what they think, and how we could find out.

SeptemberUnit 2

What your child is learning about

My Five Senses

Five senses, five body parts, a job for each. After this unit no observation is asked for without naming the sense doing the work: which sense will tell us? That question then runs for the rest of the year.

New words: senses, sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch, rough, smooth, loud,

sweet, sour, salty, bitter

By the end of the month: Name the five senses and the body part for each, and say which sense gave them each piece of information.

Sample question: How did you know the fire alarm went off? Did you have to touch it?A strong answer: No, I heard it with my ears. That is hearing. I did not touch it, but I still knew.

Watch for: Thinking only touch and taste are real senses because you feel them. Ask how they know it is raining without going outside.

Try this at home

At dinner, ask which sense told them the food was ready. More than one answer is right.

OctoberUnit 3

What your child is learning about

Sun, Light, and Shadows

The sun lights what it reaches and warms what it touches, and anything it cannot reach is cooler and has a shadow behind it. The class builds a shadow clock outside and watches one shadow move across a whole day.

New words: sun, sunlight, light, block, shadow, shade, warmer, cooler,

longer, shorter

By the end of the month: Explain that the sun warms what it reaches, that a shadow forms where light is blocked, and that shadows move and change during the day.

Sample question: Why was your shadow longer in the afternoon than at lunchtime?A strong answer: At lunch the sun is high, so my shadow is short. In the afternoon the sun is low, so my shadow gets long. The sun moved in the sky.

Watch for: Thinking a shadow is always the same size and shape as the object. Look at the same shadow in the morning and afternoon together.

Try this at home

Stand in the same spot in the morning and again in the afternoon, and look at what the shadow did.

Late October to late NovemberUnit 4

What your child is learning about

Pushes and Pulls

A push or a pull is the only reason anything ever starts moving, stops moving or turns a corner. Children test strong and gentle pushes, then build something with a ramp, find it wanting, and change it.

New words: push, pull, force, motion, direction, strength, speed, start, stop,

faster, farther, ramp

By the end of the unit: Show that a push or pull can start, stop or turn something, and that a stronger push makes it go faster and farther.

Sample question: Why does a ball roll farther on the smooth floor than on the carpet?A strong answer: The carpet rubs on the ball and slows it down faster. The smooth floor does not rub as much, so the ball keeps going.

Watch for: Thinking you have to keep pushing to keep something moving. Roll a ball and ask what made it stop, since nobody pulled it back.

Try this at home

At the playground, ask whether that was a push or a pull, and whether it was strong or gentle.

December and early JanuaryUnit 5

What your child is learning about

Looking Closely: Properties of Objects

Everything can be described, by color, by shape and form, by how it feels, by how big and how heavy. Children sort a set of objects by one property, say the rule out loud, then sort the very same set a different way.

New words: property, color, shape, form, sphere, cube, texture, bumpy,

size, weight, heavier, lighter, group, rule

By the end of the unit: Describe objects by color, shape, texture, size and weight, and sort the same set of objects in two different ways.

Sample question: Can you sort these buttons one way, and then a different way?A strong answer: First I sort by color: blue ones and red ones. Now I sort by size: big ones and small ones. The same button can be blue and small.

Watch for: Thinking bigger always means heavier. Hold a balloon and an apple and ask which is bigger and which is heavier.

Try this at home

Empty the silverware drawer and sort it together. Then ask for a different rule and sort it again.

Mid January to late FebruaryUnit 6

What your child is learning about

Wonderful Water

Water is what everything alive depends on. It is in more places than children expect, it is hard or runny depending on how warm it is, and it always runs downhill. The class agrees its own wudu water rule and posts it at the sinks.

New words: water, liquid, solid, ice, melt, freeze, heat, cool, flow, downhill,

stream, river, lake, ocean, puddle

By the end of the unit: Show that water can be liquid or solid depending on how warm it is, and that water always flows downhill.

Sample question: Where will an ice cube melt faster, on a sunny windowsill or in the fridge? Why?A strong answer: On the sunny windowsill, because it is warmer there. The warm makes the ice turn into runny water. In the fridge it is cold, so it stays ice longer.

Watch for: Thinking ice is something different from water. Melt an ice cube in a cup, then put the water back in the freezer and look the next day.

Try this at home

Put one ice cube somewhere warm and one somewhere cool, and let your child predict which goes first.

Mid March to early AprilUnit 7

What your child is learning about

Living and Nonliving

Some things are alive, some were never alive, and telling them apart is harder than it looks, because a seed looks like a stone and a plastic plant looks like a plant.

New words: living, nonliving, alive, grow, offspring, respond, model, real,

organism

By the end of the unit: Sort things into living and nonliving, and explain that living things grow, need food and water, and make young.

Sample question: Is a seed alive? How can we find out?A strong answer: It looks like a stone, but if we plant it and give it water it will grow. Stones do not grow. So the seed is alive.

Watch for: Thinking anything that moves is alive. Ask about a car, a river or a flag. Moving is not the same as living.

Try this at home

On a walk, ask alive or not alive. The hard ones are the useful ones: a seed, a feather, a plastic flower.

The second half of AprilUnit 8

What your child is learning about

Caring for Our Earth

What we throw away does not disappear. The class hunts the trash, works out what could be reused or recycled, and writes a waste plan that goes to the principal for a real answer rather than onto a poster.

New words: resource, reuse, recycle, trash, waste, landfill, material,

cardboard, care

By the end of the month: Sort trash into reuse, recycle and trash, and explain that what we throw away goes to a landfill and stays there.

Sample question: Where does our trash go after the truck takes it away?A strong answer: It goes to a landfill, a big place where trash is buried. It does not disappear. It stays there a long time, so we should reuse and recycle.

Watch for: Thinking everything can be recycled. Check what Prince William County accepts, and sort your own bin against that list together.

Try this at home

Let your child sort the recycling, and say out loud why each thing goes where it does.

May and early JuneUnit 9

What your child is learning about

Plants and Animals: Needs and Life Cycles

Living things need certain things or they die, they change as they grow, and their young look like them without being copies. Four cups were planted in April, two of them deliberately given no light or no water, so the class can see what happens. Caterpillars arrive in May and are released at the end of the month.

New words: needs, shelter, air, space, survive, life cycle, seed, sprout, root,

stem, leaf, egg, larva, adult, parent

By the end of the unit: Explain what plants and animals need to live, and describe how a living thing changes as it grows.

Sample question: Our plant with no light did not grow. Why not?A strong answer: Plants need light and water to live and grow. That plant had water but no light, so it got weak and did not grow.

Watch for: Thinking plants grow by eating soil. Ask what was different between the plant that grew and the one with no light, since both had soil.

Try this at home

Grow something on a windowsill and make your child the one responsible for watering it.

The last two weeks of schoolUnit 10

What your child is learning about

Patterns and Change: Reading Our Year

Four sessions to read ten months of work. Children read the class weather chart they have built every morning since August, then lay their six Change Journal drawings of the same object side by side and say what changed, and whether it was fast or slow.

New words: weather, season, spring, summer, fall, winter, day, night,

pattern, change, fast, slow, over time

By the end of the month: Read the class weather chart to find patterns across the seasons, and tell how an object changed over the year, fast or slow.

Sample question: Look at your Change Journal drawings. What changed, and was it fast or slow?A strong answer: In fall the tree had orange leaves. In winter it had no leaves. Now it has green leaves again. That change was slow. It took months.

Watch for: Thinking every winter day is cold and every summer day is hot. Ask them to find a warm day in the winter part of the weather chart.

Try this at home

The Change Journal comes home after the June showcase. Look at the six drawings and let your child talk you through the year.

OVERALL ISLAMIC CONNECTION

Integration here means the Islamic content and the science content are the same observation, not two things stapled together. Where a connection would be forced, we do not invent one.

  • Ilm, knowledge. Rabbi zidni ilma, my Lord increase me in knowledge (Quran 20:114), is said at the opening of every new unit. From the first week, looking closely at creation is framed as worship rather than as a school subject.
  • Adab, gratitude for the senses. He gave you hearing and sight and hearts, that you might be grateful (Quran 16:78). Every station in the senses unit closes with the children naming the sense they used and saying Alhamdulillah for it.
  • Hikmah, wisdom in what we see. Have you not considered your Lord, how He extends the shadow? (Quran 25:45). This is read outdoors on the day of the shadow clock, standing in front of the very shadow the ayah describes. The science lesson and the ayah are the same observation.
  • Amanah, stewardship of water. We made from water every living thing (Quran 21:30), alongside Eat and drink, but do not waste (Quran 7:31), and the practice of the Prophet, peace be upon him, who made wudu with a very small amount of water (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). The class agrees its own wudu water rule, posts it at the sinks, and checks in April whether it actually held.
  • Khidmah, service. There is a reward for serving any living creature. The watering schedule for the class plants is set as service rather than as a chore, and the hadith is said aloud when it is set.
  • Adab, strength under control. The strong person is not the one who overpowers others, but the one who controls himself. This is where the gentle hands rule comes from when the class builds and tests, not from a teacher telling them to be careful.

Aligned to the Virginia Science Standards of Learning 2018, Kindergarten K.1 to K.11, taught from WIS-created workbooks. Amplify CKLA covers much of the science through its read-alouds, so the workbooks are supplementary. This plan is tentative and will be adjusted during the year. | Woodbridge Islamic School | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org

Kindergarten · Social Studies

Kindergarten Social Studies: What We Are Learning

Our plan for the year, unit by unit, and the Islamic values running through it | 2026 to 2027

PLEASE READ FIRST: THIS IS A PLAN, NOT A PROMISE

  • The content and the timing will change. This page is what we are aiming to teach and roughly when. Units move, activities get swapped, and some weeks take longer than planned. What will not change is the overall goal below: that your child finishes Kindergarten understanding what a community is and how to be a good member of one.
  • The months are approximate on purpose. No exact dates are given here because they would be wrong by October. Your teacher confirms what is actually happening on Class Dojo.
  • How the subject runs. Social Studies is taught twice a week for about 35 minutes. It is taught from WIS-created workbooks. Amplify CKLA covers much of the social studies through its read-alouds, so the workbooks are supplementary. Most of it is talking, looking at real photographs and maps, and doing something, and almost all of it is assessed by watching and listening rather than by tests.
Late August to late SeptemberUnit 1 · Civics

What your child is learning about

Citizenship in Our Classroom

How does a responsible citizen help a community? What it means to belong to a group and to act like it: following rules, telling the truth, caring for things that are not yours, and taking turns. The class writes its own Class Promise and it stays on the wall all year.

New words: citizen, community, rule, responsibility, honesty, kindness,

property, fair, respect, belong

By the end of the unit: Explain what a good citizen does in the classroom, such as following rules, telling the truth and taking turns.

Sample question: Why do we have rules in our classroom?A strong answer: Rules keep everyone safe and make things fair. If we take turns, everyone gets a chance. Our Class Promise helps us remember.

Watch for: Thinking rules only matter when a grown up is watching. Ask what a good citizen does when no one is looking.

Try this at home

Give your child one small job at home that is genuinely theirs, and let them own it.

Late September to late OctoberUnit 2 · Geography

What your child is learning about

Near and Far: Where Things Are

How can I tell someone exactly where something is? The language of location, and why being precise matters. The unit ends with a classroom treasure hunt where the only clue is a description of where something is.

New words: location, position, near, far, above, below, left, right, behind, in

front, next to, between

By the end of the unit: Use position words such as above, below, left, right, behind and between to describe exactly where something is.

Sample question: Where is your shoe? Tell me without pointing.A strong answer: My shoe is under the bed, next to the blue basket, on the left side.

Watch for: Mixing up left and right. Have them hold up their left hand, which makes an L shape, before giving directions.

Try this at home

Hide something and give directions using position words only. No pointing allowed.

Late October to late NovemberUnit 3 · Civics

What your child is learning about

Symbols of Our Country

What is a symbol, and what do these ones stand for? The flag, the bald eagle, the Pledge of Allegiance and the national anthem, plus Virginia’s dogwood and cardinal. The class builds a Symbols Museum.

New words: symbol, flag, stars, stripes, bald eagle, dogwood, cardinal,

president, leader, vote, country, state

By the end of the unit: Name the American flag, bald eagle, Pledge of Allegiance and national anthem, plus the Virginia dogwood and cardinal, and tell what a symbol is.

Sample question: Why are there 50 stars on the American flag?A strong answer: There is one star for each of the 50 states. Virginia is one of those stars. The 13 stripes are for the first 13 colonies.

Watch for: Mixing up the national symbols with the Virginia ones. Ask which bird is for our whole country and which is for Virginia.

Try this at home

Spot the flag on the way to school and ask your child what it stands for.

December and early JanuaryUnit 4 · Civics

What your child is learning about

Holidays and Traditions

Why do communities celebrate holidays, and how are our traditions alike and different? Children build a Class Holiday Calendar on which Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha sit alongside the civic holidays, and learn to describe a tradition unlike their own accurately and respectfully.

New words: holiday, tradition, celebrate, honor, remember, calendar, month,

past, present, veteran, freedom, gratitude

By the end of the unit: Explain why communities celebrate holidays, and describe a tradition different from their own kindly and accurately.

Sample question: Why do people celebrate holidays like Veterans Day or Eid?A strong answer: Holidays help us remember and celebrate something important. On Veterans Day we thank people who served our country. On Eid we celebrate with family and give gifts.

Watch for: Describing other traditions as weird or wrong. Ask how that tradition is alike or different from one your family has.

Try this at home

Tell your child about one tradition from your own childhood, and why it mattered.

Mid January to late FebruaryUnit 5 · Geography

What your child is learning about

Maps and Globes

How do maps and globes help us find where things are? Land and water, continents, countries and states, and what a map key is for. Children find the United States, Virginia and Woodbridge, and draw a map of their own neighborhood.

New words: map, globe, Earth, land, water, ocean, continent, country, state,

map key, United States, Virginia, Woodbridge

By the end of the unit: Tell the difference between a map and a globe, find land and water, and point to the United States and Virginia.

Sample question: What is the difference between a map and a globe?A strong answer: A globe is round like the Earth. A map is flat, so you can fold it. On both, blue shows water and the other colors show land.

Watch for: Thinking Virginia and the United States are the same thing. Ask them to find Virginia, then show how it is one part of the whole country.

Try this at home

Find where we live on a map or a phone, then find somewhere family lives.

Mid March to early AprilUnit 6 · History

What your child is learning about

Our Community Long Ago

Who lived here before us, and how has our community changed? The class builds a Then and Now timeline on the wall and buries a class time capsule.

New words: history, long ago, past, present, change, Indigenous, tribe,

settler, artifact, time capsule

By the end of the unit: Compare life long ago with life today, and explain that people lived in this area before us.

Sample question: How was life in our area long ago different from today?A strong answer: Long ago the Indigenous people lived here. They did not have cars or electricity. They walked or used canoes. Now we have cars and roads.

Watch for: Thinking long ago means when their parents were little and nothing older. Use a family photo and a much older picture to compare.

Try this at home

Show your child a photograph of you as a child and talk about what is different now.

Mid April to early MayUnit 7 · History

What your child is learning about

Community Helpers and Changemakers

Who does the work that keeps our community going, and how can I help? First responders, medical staff, teachers, farmers, business owners and volunteers. A guest comes in for Community Helper Day, and the class chooses one act of service to actually carry out.

New words: community helper, job, role, first responder, medical personnel,

volunteer, service, contribute

By the end of the unit: Name community helpers, tell how each one helps, and suggest a way they can help their community.

Sample question: What would happen if there were no firefighters in our community?A strong answer: If a house caught on fire, no one would come to put it out. Firefighters keep people safe. I can help too, by being careful and calling for help.

Watch for: Thinking only people in uniforms are community helpers. Ask about a farmer, a store owner or a volunteer.

Try this at home

When you see someone doing a job, name it out loud and ask what would happen without them.

Mid May to early JuneUnit 8 · Economics

What your child is learning about

Needs, Wants, and Choices

How do people decide what to buy, what to save for, and what to give? The difference between a need and a want, what coins and dollars are, and what earning, saving, spending and giving mean. Children earn tokens over four weeks and spend them at a Classroom Market, where giving to sadaqah is one of the choices.

New words: need, want, money, coin, dollar, earn, save, spend, give,

choice, goods, services, sadaqah

By the end of the unit: Tell the difference between a need and a want, name coins and dollars, and explain earning, saving, spending and giving.

Sample question: Are new sneakers a need or a want?A strong answer: If my shoes are too small, new shoes are a need, because I need shoes to walk. But fancy light up sneakers are a want.

Watch for: Calling everything they like a need. Ask what would happen if they did not have it. If they would be fine, it is a want.

Try this at home

At the store, ask whether something is a need or a want. Accept the answer, then ask why.

The last two weeks of schoolUnit 9 · All strands

What your child is learning about

Our Community Showcase

What do I now know about my community, my state and my country? Children choose work from across the year and explain it, using the word wall they have been adding to since August. Families are invited.

New words: no new words; the whole year’s word wall is reviewed

By the end of the month: Choose work from across the year and explain it, using the year's word wall words correctly.

Sample question: Pick three words from this year and tell me what they mean.A strong answer: A citizen is someone who belongs to a community and helps. A symbol stands for something, like the flag. A need is something you must have to live.

Watch for: Saying a word but explaining it with the word itself. Ask them to give an example from home or school.

Try this at home

Ask your child to pick three words from the year and explain them to you.

OVERALL ISLAMIC CONNECTION

Five WIS values run through the year. A connection is made only where it genuinely belongs to the content, never bolted on at the end of a lesson, and where it would be forced we leave it out.

  • Adab, manners. How we speak, listen and take turns. The Class Promise is framed as an ahd, a promise we keep. In the holidays unit it is what lets a child describe a tradition unlike their own accurately and without mockery.
  • Amanah, trust. Being reliable with what is not yours. It starts with a classmate’s pencil and grows into the idea that land and place are handed to us by those before and owed to those after.
  • Ilm, knowledge. Position words are how we find the qiblah, and children locate it in their own classroom. In the maps unit they meet Muslim geographers such as al Idrisi, whose twelfth century world map was among the most accurate of its age.
  • Khidmah, service. Service to others is worship. The community helpers unit connects volunteering to sadaqah, and the class carries out one act of service rather than only talking about it.
  • Hikmah, wisdom. Choosing well and being able to say why. In the economics unit that means moderation and avoiding waste, israf, and a sadaqah jar that funds a real class project.
  • One thing we are careful about. When we teach the flag and the anthem, respect for national symbols is taught as civic courtesy and is clearly distinguished from worship, which belongs to Allah alone. Both adults in the room answer that question the same way.

Aligned to the Virginia History and Social Science Standards of Learning 2023, Kindergarten: Community. This plan is tentative and will be adjusted during the year. | Woodbridge Islamic School | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org

Kindergarten · Quran

Kindergarten Quran

A family guide to the year, month by month

THIS PLAN IS TENTATIVE

This is a plan, not a promise. Quran is taught four times a week, and the class moves at about one or two ayahs a week on purpose. A surah may take longer than the month shown here, and short weeks and holidays shift things along. What does not change is where your child lands in June. Anything that changes is emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Your child's teacher confirms what is being memorized each week, and the teacher's version is always the one to go by.

Children work at the pace that suits them, so some are further along the Arabic alphabet and the Qaidah than others. The surahs below are the same for everyone. Alongside the Quran, the class uses the Mini Tafseer e-Workbooks for Juz Amma from Ad-Duha Institute and the Surahs and Duas packs from Primary Ilm, so you may see pages from these come home. Islamic Studies has its own guide.

Late August and SeptemberSurah Al-Fatiha

What your child is learning

  • Surah Al-Fatiha, The Opening, learned a line or two at a time and finished by the end of September.
  • How we sit, listen and recite, and the manners of handling the Quran.
  • The Arabic alphabet begins: hearing the letters, then tracing Alif and Baa.
  • Surah An-Nas, Mankind, is introduced in the last week of the month.

Words to know: surah, ayah, recite, Al-Fatiha, An-Nas, Alif, Baa

Try this at home

Recite Surah Al-Fatiha together in your own salah. Hearing it in the place it belongs is what makes it stick.

OctoberSurah An-Nas

What your child is learning

  • Surah An-Nas, Mankind, ayahs 1 to 6, two ayahs at a time.
  • Arabic alphabet practice every week.
  • A review of everything so far in the week Quarter 1 ends, October 23.
  • Surah Al-Falaq, The Daybreak, begins in the last week of the month.

Words to know: An-Nas, Al-Falaq, review, letter, sound

Try this at home

Ask your child to recite to a grandparent or on a call. An audience they want to impress is worth ten reminders from you.

NovemberSurah Al-Falaq

What your child is learning

  • Surah Al-Falaq, The Daybreak, ayahs 1 to 5, then a review week.
  • Arabic alphabet practice continues.
  • Several short weeks this month, so new ayahs come slowly and review matters more.

Words to know: Al-Falaq, protection, review, alphabet

Try this at home

Al-Falaq and An-Nas are said together for protection at bedtime. Make that the habit and the memorizing takes care of itself.

DecemberSurah Al-Ikhlas

What your child is learning

  • Surah Al-Ikhlas, Sincerity, ayahs 1 to 4, then a review before the winter break.
  • Arabic alphabet practice continues.

Words to know: Al-Ikhlas, One, sincerity, review

Try this at home

Ask what Surah Al-Ikhlas is about, not only how it sounds. A five year old can tell you that it is about Allah being One.

JanuarySurah Al-Masad

What your child is learning

  • Surah Al-Masad, The Palm Fiber, ayahs 1 to 5.
  • Arabic letter practice moves toward joining sounds together.
  • Quarter 2 ends January 15 and Quarter 3 begins January 19.

Words to know: Al-Masad, joining sounds, review

Try this at home

Five minutes of listening every day beats twenty minutes on a Sunday. Little and often is how memorizing works.

FebruarySurah An-Nasr, and Ramadan

What your child is learning

  • A review of Surah Al-Masad, then Surah An-Nasr, The Help, one ayah at a time.
  • The Qaidah is introduced alongside the alphabet.
  • Ramadan falls across this month, so routines change and review carries the weeks.

Words to know: An-Nasr, Qaidah, review

Try this at home

Ramadan is the easiest month of the year for this. Recite together at iftar and your child will not think of it as homework.

MarchSurah Al-Kafirun begins

What your child is learning

  • School is closed March 1 to 12 for Eid al-Fitr.
  • A review of Surah An-Nasr in the first week back.
  • Surah Al-Kafirun, The Disbelievers, ayahs 1 to 3.
  • Qaidah and alphabet practice each week.

Words to know: Al-Kafirun, Qaidah, review

Try this at home

Two weeks away from school will cost some of it. A few minutes over the break saves two weeks of catching up.

AprilSurah Al-Kafirun

What your child is learning

  • Surah Al-Kafirun, ayahs 4, 5 and 6.
  • One full week given to the Qaidah and the Arabic alphabet.
  • Quarter 3 ends April 9 and Quarter 4 begins.

Words to know: Al-Kafirun, Qaidah, letter, sound

Try this at home

Ask your child to teach you one Arabic letter. Explaining it is what proves they know it.

MayReview of the year begins

What your child is learning

  • A review of Surah Al-Kafirun, then back through Al-Fatiha, Al-Ikhlas and An-Nas.
  • Qaidah review every week.
  • If the class finishes early: it begins Al-Kawthar, Al-Ma’un and Quraish, surahs Grade 1 covers later in the year.
  • School is closed May 17 to 19 for Eid al-Adha.

Words to know: review, recite from memory, Qaidah

Try this at home

Go back to the earliest surahs now and again. The first ones learned are the first ones forgotten.

JuneFinishing the year

What your child is learning

  • A review of Surah An-Nasr and Surah Al-Masad.
  • Qaidah review, and writing the Arabic alphabet.
  • If the class finishes early: it continues with Al-Kawthar, Al-Ma’un and Quraish. These are not required in Kindergarten; every child meets them again in Grade 1.
  • The last day of school is June 17.

Words to know: review, write, Arabic alphabet

Try this at home

Keep it going through the summer. A surah left alone for ten weeks has to be learned twice.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Recite Surah Al-Fatiha from memory, correctly and without prompting.
  • Recite six short surahs from memory: An-Nas, Al-Falaq, Al-Ikhlas, Al-Masad, An-Nasr and Al-Kafirun.
  • Recognize the letters of the Arabic alphabet, and write many of them.
  • Read simple letter sounds from the Qaidah.
  • Keep the earlier surahs, not only the most recent one.

Classroom lessons alone will not get your child there. The children who can do all five are the ones who practiced at home.

SO HERE IS WHAT HELPS MOST AT HOME

  • Listen to your child recite once a day. Five minutes is enough.
  • Play the surah of the month in the car until the sound is familiar.
  • Recite together in your own salah, so memorizing has a purpose.
  • Praise the effort to get the sounds right, not only a perfect run through.
  • Do not push ahead of the class. One or two ayahs a week is deliberate.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Memorizing the Quran is the oldest way our tradition has carried knowledge, and in Kindergarten it is where ilm begins: your child holds something now that no one can take away later. We go slowly and we return to what is already learned, because hifz is amanah, a trust to be kept rather than a race to be won. The surahs chosen this year are the ones recited in salah and at bedtime, so what is memorized is put straight to use. And reciting aloud to a teacher, then to a family at home, is how this has always been passed on, Inshallah.

Questions are always welcome. Please reach out through Class Dojo or the office.

Kindergarten · Islamic Studies

Kindergarten Islamic Studies

A family guide to the year, month by month

THIS PLAN IS TENTATIVE

This is a plan, not a promise. These are the topics planned for each month, and the order and timing will change as the year goes on. A topic may run longer when a class needs it, and short weeks and holidays shift things along. The goals for June stay the same. Anything that changes is emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Your child's teacher confirms what is being taught each week, and the teacher's version is always the one to go by.

The year alternates between a topic and a prophet's story, so your child meets an idea and then sees it lived out in a life. Quran memorization has its own guide.

Late August and SeptemberStarting well, and keeping clean

What your child is learning

  • Classroom rules, and the manners of reciting the Quran.
  • A short check in the first week to see where each child is starting from.
  • We are Muslims: who we are, and what that means in a school day.
  • Keeping clean, and using the toilet properly. This is where taharah begins.

Words to know: Muslim, manners, clean, taharah

Try this at home

Let your child tell you one classroom rule and why it exists. Reasons stick where rules alone do not.

OctoberThe five pillars, and Prophet Adam

What your child is learning

  • Paradise and hell, told gently and at five year old level.
  • The story of Prophet Adam, peace be upon him, over two weeks.
  • The five pillars of Islam, named and counted.
  • The names of the five daily prayers.

Words to know: Jannah, Jahannam, pillar, Shahadah, salah, zakah, sawm, Hajj

Try this at home

Count the five pillars on five fingers at bedtime. Then the five prayers on the other hand.

NovemberPrayer times, wudu, and two prophets

What your child is learning

  • The story of Prophet Nuh, peace be upon him.
  • The times of the five daily prayers, and what is happening in the sky at each one.
  • The story of Prophet Ibrahim, peace be upon him.
  • How to make wudu, in order.

Words to know: Fajr, Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib, Isha, wudu

Try this at home

Let your child lead wudu and talk you through it. Correcting you is how they remember the order.

DecemberSalah itself, and the Shahadah

What your child is learning

  • The story of Prophet Ibrahim, peace be upon him, continues.
  • The basic positions of salah, practiced properly.
  • The Shahadah: what we say, and what it means.
  • The story of Prophet Yunus, peace be upon him.

Words to know: qiyam, ruku, sujud, Shahadah

Try this at home

Pray one prayer together where your child can see you, and let them copy the positions. Watching teaches more than telling.

JanuaryFasting, giving, and Prophet Musa

What your child is learning

  • Fasting, and why Muslims fast.
  • The story of Prophet Musa, peace be upon him, over two weeks.
  • Zakah and sadaqah: giving that is owed, and giving that is chosen.

Words to know: sawm, Ramadan, zakah, sadaqah

Try this at home

Give something away together and let your child choose what. Sadaqah understood once is worth a semester of explaining.

FebruaryThe articles of faith, and two prophets

What your child is learning

  • The six articles of faith, introduced together.
  • The story of Prophet Isa, peace be upon him.
  • Belief in Allah, taken on its own and unhurried.
  • The story of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, begins.

Words to know: iman, belief, article of faith

Try this at home

Ask what your child believes and why. At five the answers are short, and they are the foundation of everything after.

MarchAngels, and the Prophet Muhammad

What your child is learning

  • School is closed March 1 to 12 for the end of Ramadan and Eid al-Fitr (Eid is expected around March 9 or 10, depending on moon sighting).
  • Belief in angels: what they are, and what they are not.
  • The story of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, continues.
  • Four angels and what each one does, including the Angel of Death, Malak al-Mawt.

Words to know: angel, Jibril, Mikail, Israfil, Malak al-Mawt

Try this at home

Ask your child to name the four angels and what each one does. Four facts is a good week's work at this age.

AprilBooks, messengers, and the Day of Judgment

What your child is learning

  • The story of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, concludes.
  • Belief in the books Allah sent.
  • Belief in the messengers Allah sent.
  • Belief in the Day of Judgment, told gently.

Words to know: book, messenger, Day of Judgment

Try this at home

When your child does something kind without being asked, name it. Talk about how Allah sees every good deed.

MayThe Islamic year, and Hajj

What your child is learning

  • The Islamic months, and how the Islamic year works.
  • The story of Prophet Ibrahim, peace be upon him, revisited alongside Hajj.
  • Hajj: what it is, and who goes.
  • That all good and all hardship come from Allah.
  • School is closed May 17 to 19 for Eid al-Adha.

Words to know: Islamic months, Hajj, Kaaba, qadr

Try this at home

Eid al-Adha lands in this month. Tell your child why we sacrifice, and connect it back to Prophet Ibrahim.

JuneLooking back over the year

What your child is learning

  • The Islamic months revisited.
  • A review of the year: the pillars, the articles of faith, and the prophets met along the way.
  • The last day of school is June 17.

Words to know: review, pillar, article of faith, prophet

Try this at home

Ask your child to tell you the whole year as five things they learned. What they choose will tell you what landed.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Say the Shahadah, and say what it means in their own words.
  • Name the five pillars of Islam, and the five daily prayers.
  • Make wudu in the right order, and take the basic positions of salah.
  • Name the six articles of faith.
  • Tell the story of a prophet they have learned, in their own words.

Practice at home makes a real difference. Children who practice a little each week usually find these goals much easier.

SO HERE IS WHAT HELPS MOST AT HOME

  • Ask for the story of the week at dinner. Retelling is what fixes it.
  • Let your child lead wudu for you, and correct gently.
  • Name the prayer when you hear the adhan, so the five become real.
  • Tie a topic to something in the day: cleaning up, sharing, giving.
  • Answer the questions, even the hard ones. At five they ask better than we answer.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Islamic Studies in Kindergarten is where belief becomes a set of habits. A five year old learns the five pillars as things a family does, not as a list to recite, so ilm here is knowledge that shows up in how a day is lived, which is adab. The prophets' stories carry most of the year because character is learned from people rather than from rules, and every prophet your child meets kept a trust under pressure, which is amanah. And teaching wudu, salah and giving early means the first time they matter is not the first time they are met, Inshallah.

Questions are always welcome. Please reach out through Class Dojo or the office.

Grade 1 · English · Reading and Spelling

Grade 1 Reading and Spelling

How your child learns to read this year, month by month

PLEASE READ THIS FIRST

This guide covers the phonics, spelling and writing half of Grade 1 English. The other half, where your child is read to and learns about the world, is taught daily alongside it and has its own guide. A spelling list of ten words comes home most weeks and is tested on Friday. The first list goes home the week of September 7. The months here are approximate and dates shift for holidays and topics that need more time.

Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Spelling test and assessment dates live there, not on this sheet.

Late Aug & SeptGetting the sounds back

What your child is learning

  • Reviewing every letter sound learned in Kindergarten
  • Reading and writing three letter words like cat, bed and pig
  • Two letters that make one sound: sh, ch, th
  • Words that do not follow the rules and are learned by heart, like a, I, said

Spelling words like: off · miss · buzz · ship · chip · this

By the end of the unit: Read and spell three-letter words by sounding them out, read words with sh, ch and th, and know a, I and said by sight.

Sample question: How do you read the word ship?A strong answer: The s and h are a team, and together they say /sh/. Then I say /i/ and /p/. Sh, i, p. Ship.

Watch for: Reading s and h as two separate sounds, so ship comes out as s-hip. Ask them to circle the two letters that work together as one sound.

Try this at home

Ask them to sound out a word on a sign or a package. Sounding out is the whole skill right now.

OctoberThe silent ‘e’

What your child is learning

  • The magic ‘e’ that changes a vowel: cap becomes cape
  • Long vowel words: time, home, cute, name
  • Naming words, and which ones take a capital letter
  • Heart words to spell: they, their, my, by, you, your

Spelling words like: feet · cake · time · bike · home · nose · cute · mule

By the end of the month: Read and spell long vowel words with a silent e, like cape and bike, and start the names of people and places with a capital letter.

Sample question: What happens when you add an e to the end of kit?A strong answer: The e is silent, but it makes the i say its name. So kit becomes kite. The e is quiet, but it does a big job.

Watch for: Leaving off the silent e when spelling, so time becomes tim and home becomes hom. Have them read the word back exactly as written; they will hear the short vowel.

Try this at home

Write cap on paper, add an e, and let them read the new word. It is the best trick of the year.

NovemberVowels made of two letters

What your child is learning

  • Two letters working together: oo, ou, oi, aw
  • Words like book, shout, coin and saw
  • Doing words, and telling past from present
  • Planning, writing and sharing a whole story of their own

Spelling words like: look · book · good · foot · spoon · moon · because

By the end of the month: Read and spell words with oo, ou, oi and aw, use past and present doing words, and write a short story of their own.

Sample question: Which letters make the sound in the middle of coin? Can you think of another word with it?A strong answer: The o and the i work together to make /oi/, like in coin. Another word with that sound is join, or boil.

Watch for: Reading every oo the same way, so book rhymes with moon. Remind them oo has two sounds, as in book and as in moon. If the word sounds wrong, try the other one.

Try this at home

When they finish writing something, ask them to read it back to you. Reading it aloud catches the errors.

DecemberReading longer words

What your child is learning

  • Putting all the vowel sounds together in longer words
  • Reading a whole page without stopping at every word
  • Writing a book report about something they have read
  • The Unit 3 test, covering everything so far

Spelling words like: proud · room · shout · join · draw · down · out

By the end of the month: Read longer words by breaking them into parts, read a whole page smoothly, and tell what a book was about in a short book report.

Sample question: Tell me about the book you read. Who was in it, and what happened?A strong answer: The book was about a girl who lost her dog. First she looked in the park. Then she asked her neighbors. At the end she found him asleep under the porch.

Watch for: Guessing a long word from its first letter, like reading shout as shot. Cover part of the word with a finger and have them read one part at a time.

Try this at home

Let them read to you, and wait when they stick. Count to five before helping.

JanuaryWhen ‘r’ changes the vowel

What your child is learning

  • The sounds in her, car, corn and fern
  • Words with two parts: sun-set, pic-nic, nap-kin
  • Contractions, where two words squeeze into one
  • Past, present and future: walked, walks, will walk

Spelling words like: sharp · start · fern · fork · corn · sister · sunset

By the end of the month: Read and spell words with ar, or and er, split two-part words like sunset, and use contractions and past, present and future verbs correctly.

Sample question: How would you spell sunset? How many parts does it have?A strong answer: It has two parts, sun and set. Sun is s, u, n. Set is s, e, t. I put them together and get sunset.

Watch for: Dropping the vowel before the r, writing frn for fern or sistr for sister. Ask them to say the word slowly and listen for the vowel and r working together.

Try this at home

Clap the parts of long words together. Sun-set, pic-nic. Hearing the parts is how they read them.

FebruaryOne sound, several spellings

What your child is learning

  • The same sound written more than one way: c, k and ck
  • Double letters at the end: hopping, robbed, kitten
  • Describing words, and how they make writing better
  • Writing a paragraph that says what they think and why

Spelling words like: hopping · hopped · robin · pepper · horn · park

By the end of the month: Choose c, k or ck, double the last letter before adding ing or ed, and write a paragraph giving an opinion and a reason.

Sample question: Why does hop need two p's when you write hopping?A strong answer: Hop has a short o. If I just add ing, it spells hoping, which is a different word. Doubling the p keeps the o short, so it says hopping.

Watch for: Writing an opinion with no reason, like I like summer, and stopping there. Ask why, then have them add a sentence that starts with because.

Try this at home

Ask for an opinion about anything, then ask why. The reason is the part being taught.

MarchMore spelling choices

What your child is learning

  • When ‘g’ says /g/ and when it says /j/
  • Sounds written with two letters: tch, dge, ff, ll
  • Planning and writing an opinion paragraph on their own
  • Reviewing everything before the unit test

Spelling words like: gem · magic · germ · page · fringe · chips · fetch

By the end of the month: Tell when g says /g/ and when it says /j/, spell words with tch, dge, ff and ll, and write an opinion paragraph on their own.

Sample question: Why does the g in gem sound like /j/, but the g in game does not?A strong answer: When g comes before e, i or y, it often says /j/, like gem and magic. When it comes before a, o or u, it says /g/, like game and go.

Watch for: Spelling the end of fetch or catch with just ch, so it becomes fech. A handy tip: right after a short vowel, the /ch/ sound is usually spelled tch.

Try this at home

When they are unsure of a spelling, ask them to write it two ways and pick the one that looks right.

AprilSilent letters and pronouns

What your child is learning

  • When ‘c’ says /s/: ice, nice, city, pencil
  • Silent letters: kn in knee and know, wh in when
  • Pronouns, the words that stand in for names
  • Writing a true story about something that happened to them

Spelling words like: ice · rice · place · dance · city · knot · knee

By the end of the month: Read words where c says /s/, spot silent letters like the k in knee, and use pronouns like he, she and they in a true story.

Sample question: Which letter is silent in knee, and how do you know?A strong answer: The k is silent. When I say knee, I only hear /n/ at the start, not /k/. But the k is still written there.

Watch for: Using a pronoun before saying who it is, so a story starts with She went to the park and no one knows who she is. Ask: who is she?

Try this at home

Point out silent letters when you see them. Children find them genuinely interesting.

MayLong vowels spelled new ways

What your child is learning

  • The /ae/ sound as ai and ay: rain, wait, day, play
  • Joining two ideas with and, but and so
  • Commas in a list

Spelling words like: rain · mail · day · play · wait · tail

By the end of the month: Read and spell words with ai and ay, join two ideas with and, but or so, and put commas between items in a list.

Sample question: Why is rain spelled with ai, but day is spelled with ay?A strong answer: Ai usually comes in the middle of a word, like rain and wait. Ay usually comes at the end, like day and play.

Watch for: Putting ay in the middle of a word, like rayn, or ai at the end, like dai. Remind them: ai in the middle, ay at the end.

Try this at home

Read a page and hunt for one spelling pattern together. Finding it themselves is what makes it stick.

JuneShowing how far they have come

What your child is learning

  • The /oe/ sound as oa: boat, soap, float
  • Writing instructions with the steps in the right order
  • Reading a passage silently and answering questions about it
  • Reading aloud smoothly, at a steady speed
  • A final check on reading, writing and spelling

Spelling words like: snail · sail · soap · float · mailbox · raincoat

By the end of the month: Write instructions with steps in order, read a passage silently and answer questions about it, and read aloud smoothly at a steady pace.

Sample question: Tell me how to brush your teeth, step by step, using first, next, then and last.A strong answer: First, I put toothpaste on my brush. Next, I brush the top and bottom teeth. Then I spit and rinse with water. Last, I rinse the brush and put it away.

Watch for: Reading fast and skipping small words like the, a or of, which changes the meaning. Ask them to reread the sentence slowly, pointing at each word.

Try this at home

Keep reading together every day through the summer. This is the year reading is built.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

School alone will not get your child here. Ten to fifteen minutes of reading together every day is what turns a sounded out word into a read one.

  • Read a simple book aloud without stopping at every word
  • Sound out a word they have never seen before
  • Spell most one syllable words correctly
  • Read longer words by breaking them into parts
  • Write several sentences that belong together
  • Use capital letters, periods and question marks
  • Read silently and answer questions about what they read

WHICH IS WHY THESE SIX THINGS MATTER

  • Read together every day. Ten minutes is enough if it is every day.
  • When they stick on a word, wait. Count to five before helping.
  • Let them sound it out, even slowly. Telling them the word skips the learning.
  • Practice the spelling list a little each night, not all on Thursday.
  • Praise the effort of sounding out, not just the correct answer.
  • If reading is getting hard, tell the teacher in October, not April.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

The first word revealed to the Prophet, peace be upon him, was Iqra, meaning read. This is the year your child actually learns to do it, sound by sound, and it is slow and effortful work. Sabr, patience, is being asked of them every time they stop at a hard word and try again, and of us every time we wait instead of saying the word for them. Ilm begins here, one word at a time.

Questions are always welcome. Please speak to your child’s teacher or the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org

Grade 1 · English · Stories and Subjects

Grade 1 English

The stories and subjects we read about, month by month

PLEASE READ THIS FIRST

This guide covers the reading and listening half of Grade 1 English, where your child is read to and learns about the world. The other half, phonics and spelling, is taught daily alongside it and has its own guide. The months here are approximate and dates shift for holidays and topics that need more time. The final weeks of the year review everything read aloud since August.

Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Test and showcase dates live there, not on this sheet.

Late Aug & SeptFables and tales

What your child is learning

  • Famous fables and the lesson each one teaches
  • What a character does, and why it matters
  • Retelling a story with the events in the right order
  • Listening carefully to a long story read aloud

Words and stories: The Boy Who Cried Wolf · The Fox and the Grapes · moral · fable

By the end of the unit: Retell a fable with the events in order and explain its lesson, called the moral, in their own words.

Sample question: In The Boy Who Cried Wolf, why did no one come when the wolf really came?A strong answer: He lied and said there was a wolf when there wasn't, more than once. So when the wolf really came, nobody believed him. The lesson is that if you lie, people stop trusting you.

Watch for: Telling what happened instead of the lesson. If you ask for the moral and hear the wolf ate the sheep, ask: so what should we learn from that?

Try this at home

Read a fable at bedtime and ask what the lesson was. Then ask if they agree with it.

OctoberHow your body works

What your child is learning

  • Bones, muscles and what holds us up
  • How food travels through the body
  • The brain, and the nerves that carry messages
  • Five keys to staying healthy

Words and stories: skeleton · muscle · digestion · brain · nerves · healthy

By the end of the month: Explain what bones, muscles, the stomach and the brain do, and name ways to keep the body healthy.

Sample question: How does your brain tell your hand to move?A strong answer: My brain sends a message along my nerves to the muscles in my hand. The muscles pull on the bones, and my hand moves. It happens really fast.

Watch for: Thinking food stops in the stomach. Ask where it goes next; they should say it keeps moving through the intestines, where the body takes in what it needs.

Try this at home

Ask them to name a bone or a muscle while you are getting dressed or cooking. Bodies are always close at hand.

NovemberSimilar stories from different lands

What your child is learning

  • Cinderella stories told in many different countries
  • How the same story changes when a different people tells it
  • Comparing two versions and finding what stayed the same
  • Writing and sharing a story of their own

Words and stories: version · compare · culture · tradition · narrative

By the end of the month: Compare two versions of the same story and tell what stayed the same and what changed, including where each version comes from.

Sample question: How are two Cinderella stories from different countries alike, and how are they different?A strong answer: In both stories a kind girl is treated badly and ends up happy, and she loses a shoe. But the helper is different. In one it is a fairy godmother, and in Yeh-Shen from China it is a magic fish.

Watch for: Listing only differences and missing what stayed the same. Ask: what happens in both stories? The shared parts are what make them the same story.

Try this at home

If your family knows a version of any of these tales, tell it to them. That is exactly what this unit is about.

DecemberAstronomy

What your child is learning

  • The sun, the moon and the stars
  • Why we have day and night, and constellations in the sky
  • The planets of the solar system
  • Astronauts, and how people first reached the moon

Words and stories: sun · moon · star · planet · constellation · astronaut

Also taught in: Science in January, where your child tracks the sun across the sky and how it warms the land.

By the end of the month: Explain that Earth spins to make day and night, that the sun is a star, and name some planets and a constellation.

Sample question: Why does it get dark at night?A strong answer: The Earth is always spinning. When our side turns away from the sun, it gets dark and it is night. When our side turns back toward the sun, it is day.

Watch for: Thinking the sun goes to sleep or moves away at night. Ask where the sun is when it is dark here. It is still shining on the other side of the Earth.

Try this at home

Look at the night sky together, even for two minutes. Ask what they can name.

JanuaryGeography

What your child is learning

  • Using an atlas, and the four cardinal directions
  • Landforms: mountains, rivers, valleys and plains
  • Cities, towns, and the difference between rural and suburban
  • Drawing a map of their own neighborhood

Words and stories: atlas · north · south · east · west · landform · city

Also taught in: Social Studies in December and January, which ends with a make-a-map project.

By the end of the month: Use the four cardinal directions and an atlas, name landforms like mountains, rivers, valleys and plains, and tell a city from a rural or suburban place.

Sample question: How is a rural place different from a city?A strong answer: A city has lots of people, tall buildings and busy streets close together. A rural place has farms and open land, and the houses are far apart.

Watch for: Thinking north always means straight ahead or up. On a map north is at the top, but outside it is one fixed direction. The sun rises in the east, which helps them find it.

Try this at home

Ask which direction you are driving. Then ask them to draw the route home from memory.

FebruaryAnimals and habitats

What your child is learning

  • What a habitat is, and why animals live where they do
  • The Arctic, the desert, the forest and the grasslands
  • How animals are suited to the place they live
  • Animals in danger, and why habitats matter

Words and stories: habitat · Arctic · desert · forest · endangered · survive

Also taught in: Science in December, which looks at what animals need and how their bodies help them survive.

By the end of the month: Explain what a habitat is and how an animal's body helps it live in the Arctic, the desert, the forest or the grasslands.

Sample question: Why can a polar bear live in the Arctic but not in the desert?A strong answer: A polar bear has thick fur and a layer of fat to stay warm in the cold. In the hot desert it would get much too hot, and it could not find the food it eats.

Watch for: Saying an animal lives somewhere because it likes it there. Steer them to its body: what does this animal have that helps it survive in that place?

Try this at home

Pick any animal and ask where it lives and why that place suits it. Works with any animal, anywhere.

MarchHabitats, then a new nation

What your child is learning

  • Freshwater and saltwater habitats
  • Habitat destruction and endangered animals
  • The thirteen colonies, and the Boston Tea Party
  • Why the colonies wanted to be free

Words and stories: freshwater · saltwater · colony · protest · independence

By the end of the month: Tell freshwater from saltwater habitats, and explain why the thirteen colonies thought British rule was unfair and held the Boston Tea Party.

Sample question: Why did the colonists throw tea into Boston Harbor?A strong answer: The British government made them pay a tax on tea, and they had no say in making the rules. They thought that was unfair, so they dumped the tea into the water to protest.

Watch for: Thinking freshwater means clean and saltwater means dirty. Freshwater is in most lakes, rivers and ponds, and saltwater is in the ocean. Both can be clean or dirty.

Try this at home

Ask what they would do if a rule felt unfair. That is the question this unit is really asking.

AprilAmerican independence

What your child is learning

  • Declaring independence, and what that meant
  • George Washington, and the story of Betsy Ross and the flag
  • How a long war finally ended
  • Building a new country once the fighting stopped

Words and stories: declaration · liberty · flag · commander · nation

By the end of the month: Retell the story of American independence in order, from declaring independence through the war to building a new nation.

Sample question: Why is George Washington important in the story of American independence?A strong answer: He led the colonists' army in the war against Britain. After the Americans won, he became the first president of the new country.

Watch for: Getting the order mixed up, like saying Washington was president during the war. Ask: what came first, the war or the new country with a president?

Try this at home

Ask them to tell the story from start to finish. Getting the order right is the skill being built.

MayThe history of the Earth

What your child is learning

  • What the Earth is made of, layer by layer
  • Rocks and minerals, and the three kinds of rock
  • Fossils, and what they tell us about long ago
  • Dinosaurs, and how we know they were here

Words and stories: layer · mineral · rock · fossil · dinosaur · ancient

By the end of the month: Name the layers of the Earth and the three kinds of rock, and explain how fossils tell us about dinosaurs and life long ago.

Sample question: How do we know dinosaurs were real if no person ever saw one?A strong answer: Scientists find fossils, like bones and footprints, inside rock. They are very old and come from animals that are not alive today. So we know dinosaurs lived long ago.

Watch for: Thinking people and dinosaurs lived at the same time, often from cartoons. Ask: were there people when dinosaurs were alive? Dinosaurs died out long before people.

Try this at home

Collect a few rocks on a walk and sort them. Ask how they think each one was made.

Late May and JuneYear-end review

What your child is learning

  • A review of the year’s read-aloud topics, from fables to the history of the Earth.
  • It builds on the listening, thinking and writing done since August.

By the end of the unit: Listen to longer stories, retell them in order, and use new words from the year when talking and writing.

Sample question: What was your favorite topic this year, and what did you learn from it?A strong answer: My favorite was astronomy. I learned that the sun is a star and that the Earth spins, which is why we have day and night. I want to learn more about the planets.

Watch for: Short answers like it was good. Ask one follow-up question, like what happened or why, so they practice explaining with details.

Try this at home

Keep reading aloud through the summer. Being read to is what builds the vocabulary for next year.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

School alone will not get your child here. Being read to and talked with at home is what turns a heard word into one they can use.

  • Sit and listen to a long story read aloud, then answer questions about it
  • Retell a story with the events in the right order
  • Say what a story was teaching, and whether they agree
  • Use new words from a subject in their own talk
  • Explain something true they have learned, in their own words
  • Compare two versions of the same story
  • Ask a question about something they want to know

WHICH IS WHY THESE SIX THINGS MATTER

  • Read aloud to your child every day, above the level they can read alone.
  • Talk about what you read. One question is enough.
  • Use the new words yourself in ordinary conversation.
  • Let them explain something to you, even badly. Explaining is how it sticks.
  • Each unit ends with a showcase. Come if you can, and ask about it if you cannot.
  • If it is getting hard, tell the teacher in October, not April.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

A first grader cannot yet read most of what this year teaches, so they learn it by listening. That is how knowledge has always traveled, and it asks something of them: adab, the manners of listening well while someone else speaks. The subjects themselves, the body, the stars, habitats, the Earth, are the ones the Quran returns to again and again when it asks people to look and to reflect. Ilm begins here, in a child sitting still and paying attention.

Questions are always welcome. Please speak to your child’s teacher or the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org

Grade 1 · English · Every Spelling List

Grade 1 Spelling Words

Every weekly list for the year · ten words a week

THIS LIST IS TENTATIVE. IT IS NOT YET FINAL.

The teacher will confirm the actual ten words each week, and the weekly list she sends home is the one that counts. Words may be swapped, reordered, or moved to a different week as the class moves faster or slower through the program. Do not treat the dates below as fixed.

BUT EVERY WORD ON THIS SHEET IS ESSENTIAL AND MUST BE TAUGHT.

These words are not a suggestion. Each one carries a letter pattern or a heart word that Grade 1 has to master before Grade 2, and the year is built so that every pattern is covered in order. A word may move to a different week. A word may not be dropped. If a week is lost to a closure, the words from that week are folded into the next list rather than skipped.

EXPECT SOME WORDS TO BE DIFFERENT. When the weekly homework packet comes home, compare it against this sheet and look for the changes. Practice the words in the packet, not the words here. The packet is always the correct list.

The confirmed weekly list is also emailed home or posted on Class Dojo. Use this sheet for what is coming, and the packet for what to practice.

HOW THE WEEK RUNS

Ten words go home on the first school day of the week and are tested on the last school day of that same week, normally Monday to Friday. Spelling begins the week of September 7; the first two weeks of the year have no list. Five weeks in the year carry no list at all: winter break, the two Eid al-Fitr weeks, the two day Eid al-Adha week, and the two day week before winter break.

PRACTICE AT HOME, AND WHY IT MATTERS

Two or three words a night, not ten on Thursday. Say the word, cover it, write it from memory, then check. Say each sound as they write it, because Grade 1 spelling is built on sounds. Praise a sensible wrong attempt: sounding it out is the skill. Each list teaches one letter pattern, not a random set of words. Some words are there because they break the rules and must be learned by heart. The patterns build in order, so a missed week makes the next one harder, and Grade 2 begins assuming every pattern on this sheet is known.

Grade 1 · Mathematics

Grade 1 Mathematics

What your child will learn this year, month by month

PLEASE READ THIS FIRST

This guide is a plan, not a promise. The months are approximate and dates shift for holidays, snow days, and topics that need more time. There is a topic test roughly every two to three weeks, always with a review day the day before. The timing and some detail will change. Where your child is going by June will not.

Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Test dates live there, not on this sheet.

Late Aug & SeptPatterns, and what adding means

What your child is learning

  • Finding, continuing and making patterns
  • What adding and taking away actually mean
  • Solving a story problem by drawing it
  • Adding and subtracting within 10

Words to know: pattern · add · subtract · sum · difference · equal

By the end of the unit: Continue and make patterns, and add and subtract within 10 by drawing or acting out a story problem.

Sample question: You have 6 crackers and eat 2. How many are left?A strong answer: I drew 6 circles and crossed out 2. Then I counted the ones left: 4. So 6 minus 2 is 4. I can check: 4 plus 2 is 6.

Watch for: Adding when the story means take away, because they see two numbers and add them. Ask them to draw it first; the picture shows whether the group gets bigger or smaller.

Try this at home

Make a pattern with spoons or socks and ask what comes next. Patterns are everywhere at home.

OctoberKnowing the facts by heart

What your child is learning

  • Adding and subtracting within 10 quickly, without counting
  • Doubles, and making a ten
  • Addition facts up to 20 using strategies
  • Two days on patterns and symmetry in Islamic art

Words to know: doubles · make a ten · strategy · fact · symmetry

By the end of the month: Add and subtract within 10 quickly, and use doubles and make a ten to solve addition facts up to 20.

Sample question: What is 8 + 5? Can you make a ten to help?A strong answer: 8 needs 2 more to make 10. I take 2 from the 5, so 3 are left. 10 plus 3 is 13. So 8 + 5 = 13.

Watch for: Counting on fingers for every fact, even 5 + 5. Practice doubles first, then near doubles: if 6 + 6 = 12, then 6 + 7 is one more, 13.

Try this at home

Two minutes of quick facts while walking or in the car. Ask out loud, do not write.

NovemberSubtraction facts to 20

What your child is learning

  • Taking away from numbers up to 20
  • Using addition to work out a subtraction
  • Choosing a strategy that fits the numbers
  • Explaining how they got the answer

Words to know: take away · count back · related facts · strategy

By the end of the month: Subtract within 20 by counting back or by using a related addition fact, and explain which strategy they used.

Sample question: What is 14 minus 6? How did you work it out?A strong answer: I thought, 6 plus what makes 14? 6 plus 4 is 10, and 4 more is 14. I added 4 and 4, so that is 8. So 14 minus 6 is 8. Check: 8 plus 6 is 14.

Watch for: Counting the starting number when counting back, so 12 minus 3 becomes 12, 11, 10 and the answer is 10 instead of 9. Have them count only the jumps: 11, 10, 9.

Try this at home

Ask how they worked it out, not just what the answer is. The method is what is being taught.

DecemberNumber sentences

What your child is learning

  • The equals sign, and what it really means
  • Finding the missing number in a sentence like 6 + __ = 10
  • Writing a number sentence to match a story
  • Two days on sadaqah and counting good deeds

Words to know: equation · equals · missing number · number sentence

By the end of the month: Explain that the equals sign means both sides are the same amount, and find the missing number in a sentence like 6 + __ = 10.

Sample question: What number goes in the blank: 7 + __ = 12?A strong answer: I count up from 7 to 12: 8, 9, 10, 11, 12. That is 5 more. So 7 + 5 = 12. Check: 12 minus 7 is 5.

Watch for: Thinking the equals sign means write the answer next, so 6 + __ = 10 gets 16 in the blank. Ask: is 6 plus 16 the same as 10? Both sides must match.

Try this at home

Say a number sentence with a gap and let them fill it. Six plus what makes ten.

JanuaryGraphs, and counting to 120

What your child is learning

  • Asking a question that needs counting to answer
  • Making and reading a simple graph
  • Counting all the way to 120
  • Counting by 2s, 5s and 10s

Words to know: data · graph · tally · count on · more than

By the end of the month: Count to 120 starting from any number, skip count by 2s, 5s and 10s, and make and read a picture graph or tally chart.

Sample question: A graph shows 7 people like apples and 4 like bananas. How many more like apples?A strong answer: 7 is more than 4. I count up from 4 to 7: 5, 6, 7. That is 3. So 3 more people like apples. Check: 4 plus 3 is 7.

Watch for: Losing their place after 100, so 109 is followed by 200, or 101 is written 1001. Practice counting aloud from 95 to 120 a few times a week.

Try this at home

Count something real together and make a picture graph of it. Socks, shoes, anything.

FebruaryTens and ones

What your child is learning

  • What the two digits in a number each mean
  • Building numbers from tens and ones
  • Comparing two numbers and saying which is larger
  • Two days on Ramadan counting and fair shares

Words to know: tens · ones · digit · greater than · less than

By the end of the month: Tell how many tens and ones are in a two-digit number, build numbers from tens and ones, and compare two numbers.

Sample question: Which is greater, 47 or 74? How do you know?A strong answer: 74 has 7 tens and 47 has only 4 tens. 7 tens is more than 4 tens, so 74 is greater than 47.

Watch for: Reading the digits as two separate numbers, so 47 is just a four and a seven. Ask them to show it as 4 groups of ten and 7 ones with spoons, sticks or coins.

Try this at home

Ask how many tens and how many ones are in a number you see. House numbers work well.

MarchAdding tens and ones

What your child is learning

  • Adding a two digit number and a one digit number
  • Adding tens onto a number: 34 and 20
  • Using what they know about tens to work faster
  • Checking whether an answer is sensible

Words to know: add tens · add ones · regroup · estimate

By the end of the month: Add a two-digit number and a one-digit number, add tens to a number, and check that the answer makes sense.

Sample question: What is 34 + 20? What is 34 + 8?A strong answer: For 34 + 20, I add 2 tens to 3 tens, so 5 tens and 4 ones is 54. For 34 + 8, 4 and 8 make 12, so I get 1 more ten. 30 plus 12 is 42.

Watch for: Adding the tens to the ones, so 34 + 20 becomes 36. Ask: are you adding 2 or 20? Then count on by tens: 34, 44, 54.

Try this at home

Ask what ten more than a number is. Then ten less. Quick, out loud, often.

AprilSubtracting tens, and measuring

What your child is learning

  • Taking tens away from a two digit number
  • Measuring how long something is
  • Comparing weight, and how much a container holds
  • Estimating a measurement before checking it

Words to know: subtract tens · longer · shorter · heavier · holds more

By the end of the month: Subtract tens from a two-digit number, measure length with units, and compare objects by weight and by how much they hold.

Sample question: What is 65 minus 30? How did you do it?A strong answer: I take away 3 tens from 6 tens, so 3 tens are left. The 5 ones stay the same. 3 tens and 5 ones is 35. Check: 35 plus 30 is 65.

Watch for: Leaving gaps or overlaps when measuring with paper clips or hands, which makes the count wrong. Look for each unit touching the next, end to end, starting right at the edge.

Try this at home

Measure things with a ruler or with hands and feet. Ask for a guess before you measure.

MayTime, the calendar, and shapes

What your child is learning

  • Telling time to the hour and the half hour
  • Counting coins, and the days and months of the year
  • Naming flat shapes and solid shapes
  • Putting shapes together to make new ones

Words to know: hour · half past · coin · month · square · cube

By the end of the month: Tell time to the hour and half hour, count a group of pennies, nickels or dimes, name the months, and name flat and solid shapes.

Sample question: You have 4 dimes. How much money is that?A strong answer: Each dime is worth 10 cents. I count by tens: 10, 20, 30, 40. So 4 dimes is 40 cents.

Watch for: Reading the wrong hour at half past. At 3:30 the short hand sits between 3 and 4, and children often say 4:30. The hour is the number the short hand has just passed.

Try this at home

Ask the time from a real clock with hands, not a phone. Count coins at the store.

JuneEqual parts

What your child is learning

  • Splitting a shape into halves and fourths
  • Sharing a group fairly between people
  • Two days on geometry in the masjid and prayer times
  • A final look back over the whole year

Words to know: half · fourth · equal parts · fair share

By the end of the month: Split shapes into halves and fourths, share a group fairly, and show what they have learned across the whole year.

Sample question: If you cut a pizza into 4 equal pieces and eat 1, what part did you eat?A strong answer: The pizza has 4 equal parts, so each part is one fourth. I ate 1 part, so I ate one fourth. If I ate 2 parts, that would be one half.

Watch for: Calling any two pieces halves, even when one is bigger. Ask: are the two parts the same size? Halves and fourths must be equal parts.

Try this at home

Cut food into equal parts and name them. Halves and fourths at the table beat any worksheet.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

School lessons alone will not get your child here. A few minutes of number talk at home every day is what makes the rest possible.

  • Add and subtract within 20 without counting on fingers
  • Count to 120, and by 2s, 5s and 10s
  • Say how many tens and ones are in a two digit number
  • Compare two numbers and say which is larger
  • Tell time to the hour and half hour, and count coins
  • Measure and compare length, weight and how much something holds
  • Split a shape into halves and fourths

WHICH IS WHY THESE SIX THINGS MATTER

  • Two to five minutes of quick facts every single day. This is the one that matters most.
  • Ask out loud rather than setting written work.
  • Ask how they worked it out, not just the answer.
  • Count real things together, often.
  • Let them handle coins, a ruler and a clock with hands.
  • If it is getting hard, tell the teacher in October, not April.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Four times this year the class spends two days on where the mathematics meets our faith. In October, the patterns and symmetry of Islamic art, and the order Allah placed in creation. In December, sadaqah, and counting the good deeds that every small kindness adds up to. In February, counting the days of Ramadan and counting Zakat al-Fitr for each person in the family. In June, the geometry of the masjid and telling the time of each prayer. These are not decoration around the math. They are the same math, in the place your child already lives.

Questions are always welcome. Please speak to your child’s teacher or the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org
