Grade 1 · Science

Grade 1 Science

What your child will learn this year, month by month

PLEASE READ THIS FIRST

This guide is a plan, not a promise. Science meets twice a week for about forty minutes, so a single closure costs a whole lesson and the months are approximate. Several units run an investigation that takes several weeks, such as growing a plant or keeping a weather chart. The timing and some detail will change. Where your child is going by June will not.

Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Assessment dates live there, not on this sheet.

Late Aug & SeptHow things move

What your child is learning

  • Asking questions a scientist can actually answer
  • Movement: straight, circular, spinning, back and forth
  • How something shaking makes a sound
  • Building a device that moves an object, then improving it

Words to know: observe · predict · motion · vibration · sound

By the end of the unit: Describe how objects move (straight, circular, spinning or back and forth) and explain that vibrating things make sound.

Sample question: How does a drum make a sound when you hit it?A strong answer: When I hit the drum, the top shakes back and forth really fast. That shaking is called vibration, and it makes the sound. When the shaking stops, the sound stops.

Watch for: Thinking the hit itself is the sound. Have them hum with a hand on their throat; feeling the buzz shows that sound comes from vibration.

Try this at home

Ask how something is moving, not just that it is. Straight, round, or back and forth.

OctoberWhat things are made of

What your child is learning

  • Describing a material: color, texture, smell, weight, size
  • Why a thing is made of the material it is made of
  • Materials that let all, some, or no light through
  • Designing a screen or covering that blocks light

Words to know: material · property · texture · weight · light

By the end of the month: Describe materials by color, texture, smell, weight and size, explain why an object is made of its material, and sort materials by how much light passes through.

Sample question: Why is a window made of glass and not wood?A strong answer: Glass lets light through, so we can see outside and the room is bright. Wood blocks the light. So glass is the right material for a window.

Watch for: Thinking a small piece of a material is a different material from a big piece. Cut foil in half and ask if it is still foil; most properties stay the same.

Try this at home

Ask why a window is glass and a coat is not. Properties and uses go together.

NovemberPlants

What your child is learning

  • What a plant needs to stay alive
  • Roots, stems, leaves, flowers and seeds, and what each does
  • Growing a plant and measuring it over several weeks
  • Sorting plants by what you can see

Words to know: roots · stem · leaf · seed · grow · measure

By the end of the month: Name what plants need (water, air, light, nutrients and space) and explain what roots, stems, leaves, flowers and seeds do.

Sample question: Why does a plant need roots?A strong answer: Roots hold the plant in the soil so it does not fall over. They also take in water from the soil, and the stem carries the water up to the leaves.

Watch for: Thinking soil is the plant's food. Plants take water and nutrients from soil, but their leaves need light to make food. Ask what happens to a plant kept in the dark.

Try this at home

Grow something on a windowsill and check it together each week. Seeds, beans, anything.

DecemberAnimals

What your child is learning

  • What animals need, including us
  • How legs, wings, fins, fur and feathers help an animal survive
  • Why an animal can live in one place and not another
  • Sorting animals by what you can see

Words to know: needs · survive · covering · environment · classify

Also taught in: English (Stories and Subjects) in February, through read-alouds about animals and their habitats.

By the end of the month: Explain what animals, including people, need to survive and how wings, fins, fur and feathers help an animal live where it does.

Sample question: How do a duck's webbed feet help it survive?A strong answer: Webbed feet work like paddles. The duck pushes the water with them so it can swim and find food in ponds. A chicken does not have webbed feet, so it does not swim like a duck.

Watch for: Naming only food and water as needs. Ask: what else does an animal need? Air, shelter and space count too.

Try this at home

Pick any animal and ask what its body helps it do. Works at the zoo, in a book, or out the window.

JanuaryComparing, then the sun

What your child is learning

  • Putting plants and animals side by side
  • How sunlight warms the land, the air and the water
  • Where the sun is in the sky at different times of day
  • A mid-year check on everything since August

Words to know: compare · sunlight · warm · shadow · pattern

Also taught in: English (Stories and Subjects) in December, through read-alouds about the sun, moon and stars.

By the end of the month: Compare the needs and parts of plants and animals, explain that sunlight warms land, air and water, and describe where the sun appears during the day.

Sample question: Why is a sidewalk in the sun hotter than grass in the shade?A strong answer: The sidewalk is in the sun, and sunlight warms it up. The grass is in the shade of the tree, so less sunlight reaches it and it stays cooler.

Watch for: Saying the sun travels across the sky. It only looks that way from Earth. Ask where they see the sun in the morning and where in the late afternoon.

Try this at home

Notice which side of the house is warm in the morning and which in the afternoon. Ask why.

FebruaryThe sun, then weather

What your child is learning

  • Keeping a safe sun diary and spotting the pattern
  • Designing something that keeps a place cooler
  • Describing weather: light, temperature and rain
  • Building a class weather chart

Words to know: temperature · shade · weather · record · graph

By the end of the month: Record the sun's position and find the pattern, design something that keeps a place cooler, and describe weather by light, temperature and rain.

Sample question: How could you keep a toy on a sunny windowsill from getting hot?A strong answer: I would make a little roof out of cardboard to make shade. The shade blocks the sunlight, so the toy does not warm up as much. I can touch it to test if it worked.

Watch for: Thinking a sun diary means looking at the sun. They should never look straight at it; they note where it is by a tree or roof, or watch where shadows fall.

Try this at home

Check the weather together each morning and say it out loud. Thirty seconds, every day.

MarchWeather and seasons

What your child is learning

  • Reading the class weather chart and finding the pattern
  • How temperature, light and rain change with the seasons
  • Working out the season from the evidence
  • What the seasons do to plants, animals and people

Words to know: season · pattern · evidence · change · graph

Also taught in: Social Studies in February, which looks at how the seasons change daily life in Virginia.

By the end of the month: Read a weather chart to find patterns, use temperature, light and rain or snow to name the season, and explain how seasons change living things.

Sample question: It is cold, the days are short, and trees have no leaves. What season is it? How do you know?A strong answer: It is winter. In winter it is colder and there is less daylight. Many trees drop their leaves in the fall, so in winter their branches are bare.

Watch for: Naming the season from one clue, like rain means spring. Rain falls in every season. Ask for two or three pieces of evidence, such as temperature and what the trees look like.

Try this at home

Ask what has changed outside since last month. Trees, light, clothes, all of it counts.

AprilNatural resources

What your child is learning

  • Where the things we use actually come from
  • Why many resources are limited
  • How our choices affect what is left
  • Reducing, reusing and recycling, and telling them apart

Words to know: resource · limited · reduce · reuse · recycle · conserve

By the end of the month: Name natural resources and what we make from them, explain why many are limited, and tell reducing, reusing and recycling apart.

Sample question: What is the difference between reusing and recycling a plastic bottle?A strong answer: Reusing means using the same bottle again, like filling it with water. Recycling means it goes to a factory, gets broken down and is made into something new.

Watch for: Calling every good choice recycling. Ask which one it is: using less is reduce, using again is reuse, and making it into something new is recycle.

Try this at home

Pick one thing to waste less of at home for a week. Then ask whether it worked.

MayPutting it into practice

What your child is learning

  • Running a real conservation project and measuring the result
  • Explaining what they found and why they think it
  • A task that links two units together
  • Reviewing the science journal from the whole year

Words to know: plan · result · claim · explain · journal

By the end of the month: Carry out a conservation project, measure the result, and explain what they found with a claim and evidence.

Sample question: What did your class project find out, and how do you know?A strong answer: We tried to throw away less paper. The first week we filled 3 trash bags, and the next week only 1. So our plan worked, because we made less trash.

Watch for: Giving a claim with no evidence, like it worked. Ask: how do you know? Listen for a number, a drawing or something they saw.

Try this at home

Ask them to tell you what their project found. Explaining it out loud is where it lands.

JuneLooking back

What your child is learning

  • A final check across everything from August to June
  • Looking through the science journal from the start of the year
  • Reflecting on what they can do now that they could not then
  • Sharing their favorite work

Words to know: review · reflect · portfolio · evidence

By the end of the month: Look back through their science journal and explain what they learned this year, using evidence from their own work.

Sample question: Pick a page from your science journal. What did you find out, and how?A strong answer: This is my plant page. We grew one bean plant in the sun and one in a dark closet. The one in the sun stayed green and strong, and the dark one turned pale and weak. Plants need light.

Watch for: Remembering the activity but not the science, like we planted beans. Ask: what did that teach you? The idea behind the activity is what counts.

Try this at home

Ask what they will remember most from science this year, and why that one.

THE SCIENCE JOURNAL

Your child keeps one science journal from the first week of school to the last. Drawings, measurements, predictions and what actually happened all go in it, and it is reviewed at mid-year and again in June so they can see their own progress. If your child shows you a page from it, ask what they drew and what they found out rather than whether it is neat. In Grade 1 science, recording what you really saw matters more than how neat the page looks.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

School alone will not get your child here. Twice a week for forty minutes is very little time, so noticing science outside the classroom matters more here than almost anywhere.

  • Describe how something is moving, and connect shaking to sound
  • Describe a material and say why it suits its job
  • Name what plants and animals need to live
  • Say what a root, a leaf, a wing or a fur coat is for
  • Explain how sunlight warms things, and read a weather chart
  • Name a natural resource and say why it is limited
  • Record what they observed, and say what it shows

WHICH IS WHY THESE FIVE THINGS MATTER

  • Ask what they learned in science this week.
  • Ask how they know. Every time.
  • Let them explain something to you. Explaining it out loud is how it sticks.
  • Say you do not know when you do not, then find out together.
  • Notice science outside: puddles drying, shadows moving, seeds sprouting.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

The Quran asks people again and again to look at the world and reflect: at the rain, the plants, the animals, the sun and its shadow. That is exactly what a six year old does in this subject, with a journal and a windowsill plant. The April unit adds a second idea, that the things we use are limited and we answer for how we treat them. Ilm begins with noticing, and a child who looks carefully and records honestly is already doing it.

Questions are always welcome. Please speak to your child’s teacher or the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org

Grade 1 · Social Studies

Grade 1 Social Studies

The Commonwealth of Virginia, month by month

PLEASE READ THIS FIRST

This guide is a plan, not a promise. Grade 1 Social Studies is about Virginia, our own state, and meets twice a week on Mondays and Fridays for 40 minutes, so a single closure costs a whole lesson and the months are approximate. Mondays and Fridays fall on more holidays and teacher work days than any other days, so about one lesson in five is lost to closures. Please expect a slower pace than in subjects that meet on other days. There is a short checkpoint about every three weeks, given orally. The timing and some detail will change. Where your child is going by June will not.

Your child reads from Our World: Our State Virginia (Five Ponds Press) all year. Every unit has its own chapter in the book, from citizenship in September to Virginia changemakers in May.

Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Assessment dates live there, not on this sheet.

Late Aug & SeptHistorians and good citizens

What your child is learning

  • What a historian does: asking questions and looking at evidence
  • Classroom rules, taking turns, and voting together
  • Why communities set aside special days to remember people
  • The first of twelve holidays we study across the year, starting with Labor Day

Words to know: historian · evidence · citizen · rule · vote · holiday

By the end of the unit: Explain that historians ask questions and look at evidence, follow class rules, take turns, and take part in a class vote.

Sample question: How can a historian find out what life was like long ago?A strong answer: A historian asks questions and looks at evidence, like old photos, letters, tools and buildings. Things left from long ago help us learn what people did back then.

Watch for: Thinking a vote means everyone gets what they want. Explain that the choice with the most votes wins, and good citizens accept it even when their pick loses.

Try this at home

Ask how they know something, not just what they know. That question is the whole subject.

OctoberHolidays we honor

What your child is learning

  • Holidays that remember people, and holidays that remember events
  • Why different communities honor different days
  • Columbus Day and Indigenous Peoples’ Day, and Yorktown Victory Day
  • Listening respectfully when a tradition is not our own

Words to know: tradition · honor · remember · community · celebrate

By the end of the month: Explain that some holidays remember people and some remember events, and tell what holidays like Columbus Day and Yorktown Victory Day honor.

Sample question: Why do we remember Yorktown Victory Day?A strong answer: It remembers the battle at Yorktown, Virginia, in 1781. The Americans and their French allies won, and it was the last big battle of the American Revolution.

Watch for: Knowing a holiday only as a day off from school. Ask: who or what does this day remember? Every holiday they study has an answer.

Try this at home

When a holiday comes up, ask what it remembers and why people mark it. One question is enough.

NovemberSymbols and what they stand for

What your child is learning

  • The American flag and the Virginia flag
  • The bald eagle, the Capitol, and other national symbols
  • The Pledge of Allegiance and the national anthem
  • Election Day and Veterans Day, in the month they fall

Words to know: symbol · flag · pledge · anthem · patriotism

By the end of the month: Explain what the American flag, the Virginia flag and other symbols stand for, and explain that the Pledge of Allegiance is a promise.

Sample question: Why does the American flag have 50 stars and 13 stripes?A strong answer: The 50 stars stand for the 50 states. The 13 stripes stand for the first 13 colonies. So the flag shows our whole country, then and now.

Watch for: Saying the Pledge or the anthem without knowing what the words mean. Ask: what is a pledge? A pledge is a promise, and that word unlocks the rest.

Try this at home

Spot a flag or a symbol on a coin and ask what it stands for. They are everywhere once you look.

DecemberMaps and globes

What your child is learning

  • What a map is for, and how a globe is different
  • Using a map key and the four directions
  • Finding Virginia, and finding where we live on it
  • Drawing a map of a place they know

Words to know: map · globe · key · north · south · east · west

Also taught in: English (Stories and Subjects) in January, where your child draws a map of their own neighborhood.

By the end of the month: Use a map key and the four cardinal directions, explain how a map and a globe are different, and find Virginia on a map.

Sample question: How is a globe different from a map?A strong answer: A globe is round like the Earth, so it shows the whole world in its real shape. A map is flat, so it can fold up and show one small place up close.

Watch for: Guessing what a map symbol means instead of checking the key. Ask them to point to the key first, find the symbol there, then find it on the map.

Try this at home

Look at a map before you drive somewhere. Ask which direction you are heading.

JanuaryMaps, then Virginia’s land

What your child is learning

  • Finishing the map unit with a make-a-map project
  • Virginia’s mountains, valleys, rivers and coast
  • Where the water is, and why it matters
  • How the land shapes the way people live and work

Words to know: landform · mountain · valley · river · coast · region

Also taught in: English (Stories and Subjects) in January, where your child draws a map of their own neighborhood.

By the end of the month: Make a map with a title, key and compass rose, and name Virginia's mountains, valleys, rivers and coast and how they shape people's lives.

Sample question: How does living near the Chesapeake Bay change the work people do?A strong answer: People near the bay can catch fish, crabs and oysters, or work on boats. People in the mountains might farm or work in the forests. The land and water shape the jobs.

Watch for: Mixing up landform and water words. A river is moving water, a bay is ocean water partly surrounded by land, and a valley is low land between hills or mountains.

Try this at home

Ask what the land looks like where we live, and how it is different somewhere else in Virginia.

FebruaryVirginia’s seasons

What your child is learning

  • The four seasons and how each one changes daily life
  • What people wear, grow and do in each season here
  • Comparing our part of Virginia with another part
  • The longest unit of the year, finishing before the Eid break

Words to know: season · weather · climate · crops · compare

Also taught in: Science in March, which looks at weather and the seasons from the science side.

By the end of the month: Describe Virginia's four seasons and how each changes what people wear, grow and do, and compare our area with another part of Virginia.

Sample question: How do the seasons change what people here wear and do?A strong answer: In winter it is cold, so we wear coats and hats, and sometimes it snows. In summer it is hot, so we wear shorts and play outside longer. Farmers plant in spring and harvest in summer and fall.

Watch for: Mixing up weather and season. Weather is what it is like today, like rainy or windy. A season is a part of the year with a usual pattern, so one cold spring day is not winter.

Try this at home

Talk about what changes at home with the seasons. Clothes, food, daylight, all of it counts.

MarchVirginia long ago

What your child is learning

  • The Indigenous people who lived in Virginia first
  • Werowocomoco, and life before the English arrived
  • Jamestown, the first permanent English settlement
  • How Virginia’s communities have changed over time

Words to know: Indigenous · Werowocomoco · Jamestown · settlement ·

change

By the end of the month: Explain that Indigenous people lived in Virginia first, describe Werowocomoco, and tell that Jamestown, from 1607, was the first permanent English settlement.

Sample question: Who lived in Virginia before the English came to Jamestown?A strong answer: Indigenous people lived here first, for thousands of years. The Powhatan people had an important town called Werowocomoco near the York River. The English came much later, in 1607.

Watch for: Thinking Virginia's story begins with Jamestown, or that the land was empty. Ask who was already living there when the English ships arrived.

Try this at home

Ask what surprised them. Most children assume the story starts with Jamestown, and it does not.

AprilNeeds, wants and money

What your child is learning

  • The difference between goods and services
  • What we need versus what we want
  • Earning money, spending it, and saving it
  • The unit ends with a class Market Day

Words to know: goods · services · needs · wants · earn · save · choice

By the end of the month: Tell goods from services and needs from wants, explain how people earn, spend and save money, and show it at Market Day.

Sample question: Is a haircut a good or a service? How do you know?A strong answer: A haircut is a service. Someone does a job for you, but you do not take home a thing you can hold. A comb would be a good.

Watch for: Calling anything they really want a need. Ask: could you live without it? Food, water, clothes and a home are needs; toys and treats are wants.

Try this at home

At the store, ask whether something is a need or a want. Best five second lesson of the year.

MayVirginians who changed things

What your child is learning

  • Fourteen Virginians who shaped the Commonwealth
  • How one person’s idea can change a whole community
  • People from many backgrounds and many times
  • What made each of them worth remembering

Words to know: changemaker · contribution · community · courage

By the end of the month: Name several Virginia changemakers and explain one thing each person did that changed their community.

Sample question: How did Maggie L. Walker help her community?A strong answer: Maggie L. Walker started a bank in Richmond. She was the first African American woman to found a bank, and her bank helped Black families save money and buy homes.

Watch for: Remembering a name but not what the person did. Ask: what did this person do that made things better? The action is what the unit is about.

Try this at home

Ask which changemaker they would want to meet, and why. The reason matters more than the name.

JuneOur Commonwealth showcase

What your child is learning

  • Putting together a portfolio built up across the whole year
  • Presenting what they have learned out loud
  • Looking back over everything since August
  • The year ends with the Commonwealth Showcase

Words to know: Commonwealth · portfolio · showcase · present

By the end of the month: Choose their best work for a portfolio and present what they learned about Virginia out loud, clearly and in order.

Sample question: What is one piece in your portfolio you are proud of, and what does it show?A strong answer: I am proud of my Virginia map. It has a title, a key and a compass rose, and it shows the mountains, the Chesapeake Bay and Richmond, our capital.

Watch for: Reading notes word for word instead of explaining. Ask them to tell you about one piece without looking; explaining in their own words is the skill being shown.

Try this at home

Let them practice their showcase presentation on you. Saying it out loud twice beats saying it once.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

School alone will not get your child here. Twice a week for 40 minutes is very little time, so talking about it at home matters more in this subject than in almost any other.

  • Say what a good citizen does, and why rules matter
  • Name national and Virginia symbols and what they stand for
  • Read a simple map using a key and the four directions
  • Describe Virginia’s land, water and four seasons
  • Say who lived in Virginia first, and what Jamestown was
  • Tell a need from a want, and a good from a service
  • Name Virginians who changed their community, and how

WHICH IS WHY THESE SIX THINGS MATTER

  • Ask what they learned in Social Studies. Monday or Friday evening is the moment.
  • Ask how they know, not just what happened.
  • Look at maps together. Any map, any time.
  • Talk about needs and wants when you go shopping.
  • Take them somewhere in Virginia and name what you see.
  • If it is getting hard, tell the teacher in October, not April.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Five values run through this course, and each one has a plain meaning here. Ilm is studying the evidence and asking good questions, which is what a historian does. Amanah is being honest and accurate about what we find. Adab is showing respect for people, places and traditions, including the ones that are not our own, and this year asks that of your child repeatedly. Hikmah is thinking before choosing. Khidmah is using what we learn to help the community we live in.

Questions are always welcome. Please speak to your child’s teacher or the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org

Grade 2 · English · Reading and Spelling

Grade 2 English

What your child will learn this year, month by month

PLEASE READ THIS FIRST

This guide is a plan, not a promise. The months are approximate and dates shift for holidays, snow days, and topics that need more time. The timing and some detail will change. Where your child is going by June will not.

Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Spelling test and assessment dates live there, not on this sheet.

Late Aug & SeptThe Cat Bandit

What your child is learning

  • Getting back the sounds and letters from Grade 1
  • Blending letters together: stop, crunch, shelf
  • Two letters, one sound: sh, ch, th
  • Adding –ing, and when the last letter doubles

Spelling: blends and digraphs · compound words · short vowels · the –ing ending

By the end of the unit: Read and spell short vowel words with blends and the digraphs sh, ch and th, and add -ing, doubling the last letter when needed.

Sample question: How do you spell running? Why does it have two n's?A strong answer: Run has one short vowel and ends in one consonant, so I double the n before I add ing. If I only used one n, it would look like it rhymes with tuning.

Watch for: Reading sh, ch or th as two separate sounds, so ship becomes s, h, ip. Ask them to point to the two letters and say the one sound together.

Try this at home

Have your child read the sign, the label, the menu. Short and often beats long and rare.

OctoberBedtime Tales

What your child is learning

  • The silent ‘e’ that changes a vowel: cap → cape
  • When ‘r’ changes the vowel: her, for, car
  • Quotation marks, and where they go when someone speaks
  • Their first full piece of writing: plan, draft, correct, copy out

Spelling: the –ed and –ing endings · contractions

By the end of the month: Read words with a silent e and with r-controlled vowels, and put quotation marks around only the exact words a character says.

Sample question: Why does adding an e to the end of cap change how we say it?A strong answer: The e at the end is silent, but it makes the a say its name. So cap with a short a becomes cape with a long a. Kit and kite work the same way.

Watch for: Putting quotation marks around the whole sentence, including Mom said, instead of only the spoken words. Check that the marks hug just what the character said.

Try this at home

When you read together, stop where a character speaks and find the quotation marks.

NovemberKids Excel

What your child is learning

  • One sound spelled several ways, and how to choose
  • Words that could be read two ways, and testing which fits
  • Naming words, and which ones take a capital letter
  • Opposites, and words that mean nearly the same

Spelling: the /ae/ and /oe/ spellings · er, or, ar · soft g and c

By the end of the month: Choose the right spelling when one sound has several, like ai, ay and a with silent e, and capitalize names of people, places and days.

Sample question: The long a sound can be spelled ai or ay. Which one goes in the word play, and why?A strong answer: Play is spelled with ay, because ay usually comes at the end of a word. Ai usually comes in the middle, like in rain. So it is p, l, a, y.

Watch for: Spelling a sound the first way they learned it, like rain as rayn or boat as bote. Ask which spellings could make that sound, then which one looks right.

Try this at home

When they stick on a word, let them try a sound and test it. Try not to say it for them.

DecemberKids Excel → The Job Hunt

What your child is learning

  • Silent letters at the start: knee, write, whale
  • Describing words, and what they add to writing
  • Writing a true story about something that happened to them

Spelling: silent letters · long vowel review · oi, oy, au, aw, oo

By the end of the month: Read words with silent letters like kn, wr and wh, and write a true story about themselves with a clear beginning, middle and end.

Sample question: In the word knee, which letter is silent? Can you think of another word that starts the same way?A strong answer: The k is silent, so we just say nee. Knife and knock start the same way. The k is written there, but we do not say it.

Watch for: Writing a true story as a long list joined by and then, and then. Ask which part mattered most, and whether the story has a real ending.

Try this at home

Ask about their day with a beginning, middle and end. That is the writing skill.

JanuaryThe Job Hunt

What your child is learning

  • One sound, four spellings: her, bird, hurt, doctor
  • The four jobs of ‘y’: yes, gym, try, funny
  • Making words plural, including the ones that change first
  • Writing a letter that tries to persuade somebody

Spelling: the /er/ spellings · tricky ‘e’ · ‘ow’ as two sounds · /ee/

By the end of the month: Spell the er sound as er, ir, ur or or, make plurals including words that change like baby to babies, and write a letter that gives reasons.

Sample question: How do you make the word baby mean more than one? Why does it change?A strong answer: Baby ends with a consonant and then y, so I change the y to i and add es, which makes babies. Boy ends with o and y, so it just gets an s, boys.

Watch for: Adding s to every plural, which gives babys, foxs or mans. Ask whether the word ends in y, x, s, ch or sh, or is a word like man that changes to men.

Try this at home

Let them write the shopping list or a note home. Real writing for a real reader.

FebruarySir Gus

What your child is learning

  • The /u/ sound hiding in son, come, touch
  • Word endings –y and –ly: happy, quickly
  • Reading longer words by breaking them into parts

Spelling: suffixes –y and –ly · /ie/ as igh and y · the –ies plural

By the end of the month: Read longer words by breaking them into syllables, and add the -y and -ly endings, as in happy and quickly.

Sample question: How would you read the word fantastic if you did not know it?A strong answer: I break it into parts with one vowel sound each: fan, tas, tic. I read each part, then put them together fast. Fantastic.

Watch for: Reading son and come so they rhyme with on and home. Remind them the o in these words makes the sound in cup, and to check that the word makes sense.

Try this at home

Take turns, a page each. Hearing you read with expression teaches more than correction.

MarchSir Gus

What your child is learning

  • Letters read more than one way, and using the sentence to decide
  • The quiet vowel in longer words: tab-le, pen-cil
  • Word endings –le, –el and –tion
  • Reading aloud smoothly, with the voice rising and falling

Spelling: the four sounds of ‘y’ · the quiet vowel · –le, –el, –tion

By the end of the month: Read words ending in -le, -el and -tion, use the sentence to decide how a letter sounds, and read aloud smoothly with expression.

Sample question: How do you say the ending of the word station, and how is it spelled?A strong answer: The ending is spelled t, i, o, n, and it says shun. So station is sta and shun. Lots of words end that way, like action and nation.

Watch for: Spelling the tion ending the way it sounds, so station becomes stashun. If you see shun at the end of a word in their writing, ask how that ending is usually spelled.

Try this at home

Read the same short passage twice. The second time is smoother, and they hear it.

AprilThe War of 1812

What your child is learning

  • Story books versus books of real information
  • Using a contents page, glossary, caption and timeline
  • ‘ph’ that says /f/: phone, dolphin, graph
  • Their first non-fiction book of the year

Spelling: review · ‘ph’ · silent letters · /er/ · the –tion ending

By the end of the month: Tell a story book from an information book, and use a contents page, glossary, caption and timeline to find facts.

Sample question: If you wanted to know what a hard word in your book means, where would you look?A strong answer: I would look in the glossary at the back. It lists the hard words in ABC order and says what each one means. The contents page at the front only shows where each chapter starts.

Watch for: Reading only the main text and skipping captions, timelines and pictures. Ask what the caption under a picture says, because a lot of the information lives there.

Try this at home

Read something true together: a recipe, a museum label, a page about an animal.

MayThe War of 1812

What your child is learning

  • Taking notes on what they read, chapter by chapter
  • Words that say how something is done: quickly, carefully
  • Past, present and future
  • Working out an answer that is not written down directly

Spelling: history vocabulary · tricky ‘a’ after w and qu

By the end of the month: Take short notes on each chapter, use past, present and future tense correctly, and work out answers the book does not state directly.

Sample question: Why do you think Americans were so proud after the battle at Fort McHenry? How do you know?A strong answer: In the morning the flag was still flying, so the British had not taken the fort. The book does not say they were proud, but Francis Scott Key wrote a song about it, so it must have mattered a lot.

Watch for: Copying whole sentences from the book as notes. Ask them to close the book, tell you the fact in their own words, and write that instead.

Try this at home

Ask one thing they learned from their reading. Then ask how they know it.

JuneThe War of 1812

What your child is learning

  • Finishing the book and the class timeline
  • Reading a whole page without stopping at every word
  • Looking back at how far they have come since September

Spelling: final history vocabulary

By the end of the month: Read a whole page smoothly without stopping at every word, and retell the main events of the War of 1812 in order using the class timeline.

Sample question: What happened first, next and last in the War of 1812?A strong answer: First, British ships were taking American sailors. Next, the British burned Washington, D.C. Then Fort McHenry held out, and Francis Scott Key wrote The Star-Spangled Banner. Last, both sides signed a peace treaty.

Watch for: Stopping to sound out words they already know, which makes reading slow and hard to follow. Have them reread a familiar page and listen for phrases, not single words.

Try this at home

Keep reading through the summer. Twenty minutes a day holds on to the whole year.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

School lessons alone will not get your child here. Reading at home is what turns a taught skill into an easy one.

  • Read a page of a chapter book smoothly
  • Work out a new word by trying a sound and testing it
  • Spell most common words, and make a sensible attempt at the rest
  • Write a piece that was planned, drafted, corrected and copied out
  • Use capitals, periods, apostrophes and quotation marks correctly
  • Point to the part of the page that proves their answer
  • Use a story book and an information book differently

WHICH IS WHY THESE SIX THINGS MATTER

  • Twenty minutes of reading a day. Regular beats long.
  • They read to you, and you read to them. Both matter.
  • When they stick, count to five before helping. The learning is in that pause.
  • Practice spelling a little each night, not all the night before.
  • Ask what happened, or what they found out. Then ask how they know.
  • If it is getting hard, tell the teacher in October, not April.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Ilm, the pursuit of knowledge, begins with reading. The very first word revealed to the Prophet, peace be upon him, was Iqra, meaning read. When your child sits down with a book at home, that is not separate from their Islamic education. It is the foundation of it.

Questions are always welcome. Please speak to your child’s teacher or the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School · 703-910-7029

Grade 2 · English · Stories and Subjects

Grade 2 English: Stories and Knowledge

Stories, knowledge and writing, month by month

PLEASE READ THIS FIRST

This guide is a plan, not a promise. The months are approximate and dates shift for holidays, snow days, and topics that need more time. The timing and some detail will change. Where your child is going by June will not.

Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Test and assessment dates live there, not on this sheet.

Late Aug & SeptFairy Tales and Tall Tales

What your child is learning

  • What makes a story a fairy tale, and how it differs from a true story
  • Characters, setting and the order events happen in
  • Listening closely to a story read aloud, then answering questions about it
  • Retelling a story with one thing changed, and explaining what that changes

New words and names: The Fisherman and His Wife · The Emperor’s New Clothes · Paul Bunyan

By the end of the unit: Tell what makes a fairy tale or tall tale different from a true story, and retell one in order with its characters and setting.

Sample question: In Paul Bunyan, what parts could never really happen? How do you know it is a tall tale?A strong answer: Paul Bunyan is taller than the trees and his footprints make lakes. No real person could do that. A tall tale stretches the truth to be funny, so it is not a true story.

Watch for: Retelling every detail in a jumble instead of beginning, middle and end. Ask what happened first, what the problem was, and how it ended.

Try this at home

Read a story aloud at home and ask what would change if the ending were different.

OctoberAncient Greece

What your child is learning

  • What makes a people a civilization: work, leaders, beliefs, cities
  • How mountains and sea shaped the way the Greeks lived
  • Where the Olympic Games came from, and what is left of them today
  • Joining two ideas into one sentence with and, but, because and so

New words and names: The Olympic Games · Greek city states · the first democracy

By the end of the month: Explain how mountains and the sea shaped Greek life, name things the Greeks gave us like the Olympics, and join ideas with and, but, because and so.

Sample question: Why did the ancient Greeks become such good sailors?A strong answer: Greece has lots of mountains, so farming and traveling over land were hard. But the sea was all around them, so they built boats to fish, trade and visit other city states.

Watch for: Thinking ancient Greece was one country with one ruler. Listen for this; Greece was many city states, like Athens and Sparta, each with its own rules.

Try this at home

Ask your child to tell you one thing the Greeks did that we still do now.

Late Oct & early NovFables from the Islamic World

What your child is learning

  • What makes a story a fable, and how a fable teaches a lesson
  • Mapping a story: who is in it, where it happens, the problem, the solution
  • Working out the moral, and saying what the character should have done
  • The unit ends with the class performing for Kindergarten and Grade 1

New words and names: The Blessed Bananas · The Wise Fool · traditional fables

By the end of the unit: Map a fable's characters, setting, problem and solution, and state its moral in their own words.

Sample question: How is a fable different from a fairy tale, and how do you find the moral?A strong answer: A fable is short, often has animals or simple characters, and teaches one lesson. I look at the character's mistake and what happened because of it. The moral tells us what to do instead.

Watch for: Retelling the plot when asked for the moral. A moral is a lesson for anyone, like be honest, not a summary. Ask what the story wants all of us to learn.

Try this at home

Ask what lesson the story taught, then ask whether they agree with it.

NovemberCycles in Nature

What your child is learning

  • Why we have day and night, and what the Earth is doing while we sleep
  • Why the seasons change, and what is different about each one
  • Reading to find out a fact, rather than reading a story
  • Compound words, where two words join to make a new one

New words and names: day and night · the seasons · the water cycle

By the end of the month: Explain that the Earth's spin makes day and night, describe the four seasons, and read to find a fact rather than a story.

Sample question: Why is it dark at night? Where does the sun go?A strong answer: The sun does not go anywhere. The Earth spins all the way around once a day. When our side faces the sun it is day, and when our side turns away it is night.

Watch for: Saying the sun moves around the Earth or hides behind the hills at night. Ask what the Earth is doing; it spins, and the sun stays put.

Try this at home

Look at the sky together in the morning and the evening, and talk about what changed.

DecemberInsects

What your child is learning

  • What makes an insect an insect, and where different insects live
  • How an insect changes shape as it grows, from egg to adult
  • Insects that live together in huge groups, like bees and ants
  • Writing an opinion, and giving a reason for it

New words and names: habitat · life cycle · exoskeleton · colony

By the end of the month: Name the three body parts and six legs that make an insect, describe an insect's life cycle, and write an opinion with a reason.

Sample question: Is a spider an insect? How can you tell?A strong answer: No. An insect has six legs and three body parts: the head, thorax and abdomen. A spider has eight legs and only two body parts, so it is not an insect.

Watch for: Writing an opinion with no reason, like bees are the best insect, and stopping there. Ask because why, and look for the word because in their writing.

Try this at home

Ask your child for an opinion about anything, then ask for the reason. The reason is the skill.

JanuaryInsects, then The Civil War

What your child is learning

  • Finishing the insect research and writing it up
  • Who Harriet Tubman was, and what she did
  • What slavery was, and why it was wrong
  • Writing real facts down clearly, rather than making up a story

New words and names: Harriet Tubman · Abraham Lincoln · freedom · fact

By the end of the month: Write up their insect research using real facts, and explain who Harriet Tubman was and why slavery was wrong.

Sample question: Why do people say Harriet Tubman was so brave?A strong answer: She escaped slavery herself, and then she went back many times to lead other people to freedom on the Underground Railroad. She could have been caught every time, but she kept going.

Watch for: Thinking the Underground Railroad was a real train under the ground. Ask what it was; it was a secret network of people and safe houses that helped people escape.

Try this at home

This unit covers difficult history honestly. Ask what they learned and talk about it together.

FebruaryThe Civil War, then Poetry

What your child is learning

  • Why the country divided, and how the war ended
  • People who helped others during the war, like Clara Barton
  • What a poem is, and how it is different from a story
  • Rhyme and rhythm, and why poets use them

New words and names: Gettysburg · rhyme · rhythm · line · stanza

By the end of the month: Explain why the country split and how the Civil War ended slavery, and tell how a poem is different from a story.

Sample question: Why did the North and South go to war?A strong answer: The states disagreed about slavery. Many Southern states wanted to keep it and broke away from the country. President Lincoln wanted to keep the country together, and when the North won, slavery ended.

Watch for: Mixing up rhyme and rhythm. Rhyme is words that end with the same sound, like cat and hat; rhythm is the beat. Ask them to clap a line, then find the rhymes.

Try this at home

Read a short poem twice: once for what it says, once for how it sounds.

MarchPoetry

What your child is learning

  • Giving something not alive a human action: the wind whispered
  • Words in a row that start with the same sound
  • Planning, writing and then performing a poem of their own
  • Reading aloud to an audience, with expression

New words and names: personification · alliteration · verse · poet

By the end of the month: Use personification and alliteration in a poem of their own, and perform it aloud with expression.

Sample question: In the line the wind whispered through the trees, what is the poet doing?A strong answer: That is personification. Wind cannot really whisper, only people can. The poet gives the wind a human action so we can hear how soft and quiet it is.

Watch for: Thinking alliteration means rhyming. Alliteration is words close together that start with the same sound, like silly snakes slide. Ask them to point to the first letters.

Try this at home

Let your child perform their poem at home before they perform it at school. Twice beats once.

AprilJourneys: Immigration

What your child is learning

  • What an immigrant is, and why people leave one country for another
  • The reasons that push people away, and the ones that pull them somewhere new
  • What it means to be a citizen, and how many peoples built one country
  • Writing a story about a journey, using facts they have researched

New words and names: immigrant · ancestors · citizenship · opportunity

By the end of the month: Explain what an immigrant is, give push and pull reasons people move, and write a journey story using facts they researched.

Sample question: Why might a family leave their home country to come to America?A strong answer: Something might push them away, like war or not enough work or food. Something else pulls them here, like jobs, school, safety or family already living here. Often it is both.

Watch for: Using immigrant and citizen as if they mean the same thing. An immigrant moved here from another country; a citizen is a member of the country, and many immigrants become citizens.

Try this at home

Tell your child the story of your own family’s journey. It is the best possible homework for this unit.

May and JuneStill being planned

What your child is learning

  • The final weeks of the year are still being planned
  • They will build on the reading, research and writing done since August
  • We will confirm the plan with families in the spring

New words and names: to be confirmed

By the end of the unit: Use the reading, research and writing skills built this year in the final units, which will be shared with families in the spring.

Sample question: What was your favorite unit this year, and what is one thing you learned from it?A strong answer: My favorite was Insects. I learned that an insect has six legs and three body parts, and that a spider is not an insect because it has eight legs.

Watch for: Reading less as the year winds down. Daily reading that slips in May and June is a main reason skills fade over the summer, so keep twenty minutes a day going.

Try this at home

Keep the daily reading going. It is what holds on to everything gained this year.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

School lessons alone will not get your child here. Talking and reading at home is what turns a taught skill into an easy one.

  • Listen to a long read-aloud and answer questions about it
  • Retell a story with the events in the right order
  • Explain what a story was teaching, and whether they agree
  • Find a fact in an information book and use it in their writing
  • Write an opinion and give a real reason for it
  • Write about something true, clearly and in order
  • Read a poem aloud to other people

WHICH IS WHY THESE SIX THINGS MATTER

  • Read aloud to your child, even now they can read themselves.
  • Talk about what you read. One question is enough: what happened, or what did you find out.
  • Ask for the reason behind an opinion, every time.
  • Let them tell you about their day in order, beginning to end.
  • Visit a library, a museum, or just read a page about something real.
  • If it is getting hard, tell the teacher in October, not April.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Much of this year asks your child to look carefully at the world and think about what they see: why the seasons turn, how an insect grows, why people leave one home for another. The Quran asks the same of us again and again, to look and to reflect. Ilm, the pursuit of knowledge, is not only what happens in Islamic Studies. It is the habit of paying attention, and it is what these lessons are building.

Questions are always welcome. Please speak to your child’s teacher or the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School · 703-910-7029

HELPING AT HOME

LOOK, SAY, COVER, WRITE, CHECK. Look at the word, say it aloud, cover it, write it from memory, then uncover and check.

FIVE TO TEN MINUTES A NIGHT beats one long session the night before the test.

SAY THE RULE ALOUD together. A child who can say why a word is spelled that way remembers it far longer than one who has only copied it.

SOME WORDS FOLLOW NO RULE and simply have to be learned by heart. Those are worth extra practice across the week.

Questions are always welcome. Please contact the school office or message through Class Dojo. Jazakallahu Khairan for practicing with your child.

Grade 2 · Mathematics

Grade 2 Mathematics

What your child will learn this year, month by month

PLEASE READ THIS FIRST

This guide is a plan, not a promise. The months are approximate and dates shift for holidays, snow days, and topics that need more time. The timing and some detail will change. Where your child is going by June will not.

Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Test and assessment dates live there, not on this sheet.

Late Aug & SeptFacts, counting and patterns

What your child is learning

  • Adding and subtracting within 20 quickly, without counting on fingers
  • Doubles, near doubles, and making a ten
  • Skip counting by 2s, 5s, 10s and 25s, and counting back by 10s
  • Even and odd numbers, and repeating and growing patterns

Words to know: sum · difference · even · odd · pattern · skip count

By the end of the unit: Add and subtract within 20 without fingers using doubles and making a ten, skip count by 2s, 5s, 10s and 25s, and tell even from odd.

Sample question: What is 8 + 7? Show me a quick way.A strong answer: I know 7 + 7 is 14, and 8 is one more than 7, so 8 + 7 is 15. Or I make a ten: 8 + 2 is 10, and 5 more is 15. Both ways give 15.

Watch for: Counting on fingers from the bigger number for every fact, which is slow and easy to miscount. Ask for doubles first, then near doubles like 6 + 7.

Try this at home

Two minutes of quick facts in the car. Ask, not write. Speed only comes from being asked often.

OctoberAdding within 100

What your child is learning

  • Adding two digit numbers using tens and ones, not counting on
  • Adding on a hundred chart and an open number line
  • Estimating the answer before working it out
  • One step and two step word problems

Words to know: estimate · tens · ones · strategy · reasonable

By the end of the month: Add two-digit numbers using tens and ones on a hundred chart or open number line, and estimate first to check the answer is reasonable.

Sample question: What is 34 + 25? Estimate first.A strong answer: Estimate: 30 + 30 is about 60. Tens: 30 + 20 is 50. Ones: 4 + 5 is 9. 50 + 9 is 59. That is close to 60, so it makes sense.

Watch for: Adding every digit as ones, so 34 + 25 becomes 3 + 4 + 2 + 5 = 14. The estimate of about 60 shows 14 is far too small.

Try this at home

Before they add, ask roughly how big the answer will be. Estimating first is the habit Virginia asks for.

NovemberFluent adding, then subtracting

What your child is learning

  • Adding within 100 quickly and accurately, including regrouping
  • Adding in more than one way, and explaining which way was chosen
  • Taking away two digit numbers using tens and ones
  • Checking whether an answer is sensible

Words to know: regroup · subtract · strategy · reasonable

By the end of the month: Add within 100 with regrouping quickly and accurately, explain the strategy they chose, and begin subtracting two-digit numbers using tens and ones.

Sample question: What is 47 + 38?A strong answer: Ones: 7 + 8 is 15, which is 1 ten and 5 ones. Tens: 40 + 30 is 70, plus the extra ten is 80. 80 + 5 is 85. Estimate: 50 + 40 is 90, so 85 is close.

Watch for: Writing both digits of the ones sum, so 47 + 38 becomes 715. Ask how many tens and ones are in 15, and where that extra ten goes.

Try this at home

Ask for one sum and one difference at dinner, and ask how they worked each one out.

DecemberSubtracting within 100

What your child is learning

  • Subtracting within 100 quickly and accurately
  • Regrouping, sometimes called borrowing
  • Checking a subtraction by adding the answer back
  • Deciding whether a word problem needs adding or subtracting

Words to know: subtract · regroup · check · inverse

By the end of the month: Subtract within 100 with regrouping, check each answer by adding back, and decide whether a word problem needs adding or subtracting.

Sample question: What is 62 minus 27? Check it by adding.A strong answer: I can't take 7 from 2, so I regroup: 62 is 5 tens and 12 ones. 12 minus 7 is 5. 5 tens minus 2 tens is 3 tens. So it is 35. Check: 35 + 27 = 62.

Watch for: Taking the smaller digit from the bigger one in each column, so 62 minus 27 gives 45. Adding back catches it: 45 + 27 is 72, not 62.

Try this at home

When they finish a subtraction, ask them to add it back to check. That one habit catches most errors.

JanuaryProblem solving and equations, then money

What your child is learning

  • Two step word problems, where one answer feeds the next
  • Writing an equation to match a story
  • The equals sign and the not equal sign, and what they really mean
  • Coins and bills, and counting by 25s for quarters

Words to know: equation · equals · not equal · two step · quarter

By the end of the month: Solve two-step word problems, write an equation to match a story, and explain that the equals sign means both sides have the same value.

Sample question: Is 9 + 6 = 10 + 5 true or false?A strong answer: True. 9 + 6 is 15, and 10 + 5 is also 15. The equals sign means both sides are worth the same amount, not that the answer comes next.

Watch for: Treating the equals sign as the answer comes next, and writing chains like 9 + 6 = 15 + 5 = 20. Ask whether the two sides of each equals sign really match.

Try this at home

Turn a real situation into a number sentence out loud. We had 12, we used 5, how many left.

FebruaryMoney and time, then place value to 999

What your child is learning

  • Counting amounts up to two dollars, and telling time to the nearest five minutes
  • Minutes in an hour, hours in a day, and which unit fits an activity
  • What the hundreds, tens and ones digits each mean
  • Reading, writing, comparing and ordering numbers up to 999

Words to know: dollar · cents · minute · hundreds · tens · ones · compare

By the end of the month: Count coins and bills up to two dollars, tell time to the nearest five minutes, and read, compare and order numbers up to 999.

Sample question: You have 3 quarters, 2 dimes and 1 nickel. How much money is that?A strong answer: I count the biggest coins first. Quarters: 25, 50, 75. Dimes: 85, 95. Nickel: 100. That is 100 cents, which is one dollar.

Watch for: Thinking a bigger coin is worth more, like saying a nickel is worth more than a dime. Have them sort coins by value, not size, before counting.

Try this at home

Let your child pay with coins and count the change. Read house numbers aloud as hundreds, tens and ones.

MarchEid break, mid year check, then measuring

What your child is learning

  • Two review days after the Eid al-Fitr break, then the mid year benchmark test
  • Measuring length in inches, feet and yards with a ruler
  • Weighing things in pounds, and measuring liquid in cups
  • Estimating a measurement before checking it

Words to know: benchmark · inch · foot · pound · cup · length

By the end of the month: Measure length in inches, feet and yards, weight in pounds and liquid in cups, estimating first and then checking.

Sample question: Would you measure the length of the classroom in inches or yards? Why?A strong answer: Yards, because the room is long. An inch is small, so I would need a huge number of them. A yard is 3 feet, so it fits big things better.

Watch for: Starting a measurement at the 1 on the ruler instead of the 0 mark, which adds an extra inch. Watch where the end of the object lines up.

Try this at home

Keep five minutes of facts going over the Eid break. Then measure things at home with a ruler or a measuring cup, guess first, then check.

AprilShapes, symmetry, and equal parts

What your child is learning

  • Flat shapes and solid shapes, and the difference
  • Faces, edges and vertices on a solid shape
  • Lines of symmetry, where a shape folds in half exactly
  • Splitting a shape into equal parts

Words to know: symmetry · face · edge · vertex · equal parts

By the end of the month: Name flat and solid shapes, count faces, edges and vertices, find lines of symmetry, and split a shape into equal parts.

Sample question: How many faces, edges and vertices does a cube have?A strong answer: A cube has 6 faces, and they are all squares. It has 12 edges, where two faces meet. It has 8 vertices, the corners. I counted 4 on top and 4 on the bottom.

Watch for: Calling a cube a square or a ball a circle. Squares and circles are flat. Ask whether the shape is flat like paper or solid like a box or ball.

Try this at home

Fold paper in half and look for the line of symmetry. Cut food into equal parts and name them.

MayFractions, then data

What your child is learning

  • Halves, thirds, fourths, sixths and eighths, and counting in fractions
  • Asking a question that needs data, then collecting it
  • Reading and making pictographs and bar graphs
  • The year end review begins on May 21

Words to know: half · third · fourth · eighth · graph · data

By the end of the month: Name and count halves, thirds, fourths, sixths and eighths, and collect data to make and read pictographs and bar graphs.

Sample question: A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices and you eat 3. What fraction did you eat?A strong answer: The pizza has 8 equal parts, so each slice is one eighth. I ate 3 of them, so I ate 3/8. That leaves 5/8, and 3/8 + 5/8 is the whole pizza.

Watch for: Thinking 1/8 is bigger than 1/4 because 8 is bigger than 4. Cut two same size slices of bread into 4 and 8 parts and compare one piece from each.

Try this at home

Share food into equal parts and name the fraction out loud. Count a collection at home and graph it.

JuneReview and the year end benchmark

What your child is learning

  • Six review days, one for each strand of the year
  • The end of year benchmark test
  • Enrichment work for children who are ready for it
  • Looking back at how much has changed since September

Words to know: review · benchmark · strategy

By the end of the month: Show the year's skills in every strand: facts, adding and subtracting within 100, money, time, measuring, shapes, fractions and graphs.

Sample question: It is 3:45. What time will it be in 15 minutes?A strong answer: 15 minutes after 3:45 moves the minute hand from the 9 to the 12. That starts a new hour, so it will be 4:00.

Watch for: Skipping the estimate and the add back check when rushing through review. Ask them to say an estimate out loud before each answer, and to add back after every subtraction.

Try this at home

Keep the daily facts going through the summer. Five minutes a day protects the whole year.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

School lessons alone will not get your child here. Five minutes of facts a day at home is what makes the rest possible.

  • Recall addition and subtraction facts within 20 without counting
  • Read, write and compare numbers up to 999
  • Add and subtract within 100 and explain the method used
  • Estimate an answer before working it out
  • Count money to two dollars and tell time to five minutes
  • Measure length, weight and liquid volume
  • Name equal parts of a whole and read a bar graph

WHICH IS WHY THESE SIX THINGS MATTER

  • Five minutes of quick facts every single day. This is the one that matters most.
  • Ask questions out loud rather than setting written work.
  • Ask how they worked it out, not just what the answer is.
  • Ask for an estimate before the real answer, every time.
  • Let them handle real money, a ruler and a measuring cup.
  • If it is getting hard, tell the teacher in October, not April.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Two of our core values sit right inside a math lesson. Hikmah, wisdom, is choosing the strategy that fits the numbers in front of you rather than the one you always use. Amanah, trust, is checking your work carefully and honestly, and being willing to find your own mistake. A child who does both of those in mathematics is practicing them everywhere else too.

Questions are always welcome. Please speak to your child’s teacher or the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School · 703-910-7029

Grade 2 · Science

Grade 2 Science

What your child is learning this year • 2026 to 2027

PLEASE READ FIRST

This is a tentative plan for Grade 2 Science. The order of the topics and the timing of each one may change during the year as we see what the class needs, and as school closures and school events move things along. Please treat every date here as approximate. What will not change is what your child is working toward by June, which is listed at the end of this guide. Your child's teacher will send the real dates for tests and projects through Class Dojo and email as they come.

Science meets twice a week for 40 minutes, and lessons begin the week of September 14. We use Five Ponds Press, Exploring Science All Around Us, Level 2, and we follow the Virginia Science Standards of Learning for Grade 2. There is a science worksheet once every two weeks, which comes home inside the weekly packet. There is one test at the end of each unit, and your child will have a review sheet and a review lesson before every one of them.

Mid September to late October

What your child is learning

Forces and Motion, and Thinking Like a Scientist

The unit opens with Five Ponds Chapter 1, All About Moving, where the class meets push, pull, gravity and magnetism. Then the class investigates those ideas properly: predicting before testing, measuring how far a toy car travels in inches after a gentle push and after a hard one, sorting which materials a magnet pulls toward it, and showing that gravity and magnets both work without touching. The unit ends with each child designing a small tool that uses a push, a pull or a magnet to solve a classroom problem. Alongside the science, this is where the science notebook starts, where the ruler and thermometer are taught, and where two routines begin that run right through June: a Daily Weather Watch chart, and a Seasonal Change Journal in which the class draws the same tree at school six times between September and June.

New words: force, push, pull, magnet, attract, gravity, observe, measure

By the end of the unit: Explain that pushes and pulls change how things move, predict and measure how far a toy car rolls, and sort what a magnet attracts.

Sample question: Why did the toy car go farther when you pushed it harder?A strong answer: A harder push is a bigger force, so the car starts out faster and keeps rolling longer before it stops. We measured both pushes with a ruler, and the hard push went much farther.

Watch for: Thinking magnets pull any metal, or anything shiny. Test foil, a coin and a paper clip at home; only the paper clip, which has iron in it, is pulled.

Try this at home

Look at your fridge magnets together. Ask what else in the house a magnet would stick to, then test a few and see who was right.

Late October to late November

What your child is learning

Matter: Solids, Liquids and Gases

Matter is anything that has weight and takes up space, and that includes air. Solids keep their own shape, liquids take the shape of the container, gases fill the whole container. Heating and cooling change water between ice, liquid water and water vapor, and it stays water the whole time.

New words: matter, solid, liquid, gas, melt, freeze

By the end of the unit: Describe solids, liquids and gases, explain that air is matter, and show how heating and cooling change water between ice, water and water vapor.

Sample question: Is air matter? How do you know?A strong answer: Yes. Matter is anything that has weight and takes up space. When I blow up a balloon, the air fills it and makes it bigger, so air takes up space.

Watch for: Thinking water poured into a tall thin glass is more water. Pour the same cup into two shapes and ask; the amount stays the same, only the shape changes.

Try this at home

Pour the same cup of water into three differently shaped containers. Ask whether there is more, less or the same amount each time.

Early December to mid January

What your child is learning

Weather on Earth

The four things we measure: temperature, cloud cover, precipitation and wind. The class builds a simple rain gauge and a wind vane, then graphs the weather data it has been collecting since September and finds the pattern. Storms follow, then drought and flooding. The unit closes with each child writing a forecast and saying what people should do to get ready for it.

New words: thermometer, rain gauge, precipitation, forecast, drought, flood

By the end of the unit: Measure and record temperature, cloud cover, precipitation and wind, read the class weather graph, and say how people should prepare for a forecast.

Sample question: How does a rain gauge tell us how much it rained?A strong answer: A rain gauge is a container with numbers marked on the side. Rain falls in and collects. Afterward we read the line the water reaches, like one inch, so we know how much fell.

Watch for: Calling any cloudy day rainy, or mixing up clouds with precipitation. Precipitation is water falling: rain, snow, sleet or hail. Ask whether anything actually fell.

Try this at home

Watch a weather forecast together. Ask your child what people should do to get ready for it.

Mid January to late February

What your child is learning

Seasons and the Changing Land

How plants rest through winter and grow again in spring, and how animals get through it. Some migrate, some hibernate, and some stay and grow thicker fur or use camouflage. Then how wind and water slowly break rock into smaller pieces and carry soil away, and why plant roots hold soil in place.

New words: season, dormant, migrate, hibernate, camouflage, erosion

By the end of the unit: Explain how plants and animals get through winter by resting, migrating, hibernating or adapting, and how wind and water wear down rock and carry soil away.

Sample question: Why do some birds fly south for the winter?A strong answer: In winter it gets cold and there are fewer insects, seeds and berries to eat. So some birds migrate to warmer places where they can find food, then come back in spring.

Watch for: Thinking erosion only happens fast, in a flood. Most erosion is slow, a little wind and rain every day. Look together for soil washed away near a downspout after rain.

Try this at home

Pick a tree near your home in January and look at it again in April. Talk about everything that changed.

Mid March to early April

What your child is learning

Life Cycles of Plants and Animals

Every living thing is born, grows, makes new living things and dies. Some baby animals look like their parents and some do not at all. The butterfly and the frog life cycles, then the plant life cycle from seed to flower to new seed. Each child plants bean seeds in class at the start of the unit and measures them as it goes on.

New words: life cycle, egg, larva, pupa, tadpole, seed, germinate

By the end of the unit: Describe the life cycles of a butterfly, a frog and a bean plant, and explain why some young look like their parents and some do not.

Sample question: What are the stages in a butterfly's life cycle?A strong answer: First an egg. A caterpillar, called a larva, hatches and eats a lot. Then it makes a chrysalis, the pupa stage. A butterfly comes out, lays eggs, and the cycle starts again.

Watch for: Talking about a tadpole or a caterpillar as if it were a different animal. Ask what it grows into; it is the same animal at a younger stage.

Try this at home

Save a seed from fruit at home. Ask your child to name the stages the plant would go through.

Mid April to early May

What your child is learning

Habitats and Living Things

The five things a habitat has to give an animal: food, water, air, shelter and space, and what happens to the animal if even one is missing. How plants and animals depend on each other. How habitats change, both through storms and seasons and through people building roads and houses. Each child builds a labeled model of a habitat.

New words: habitat, living, nonliving, shelter, depend

By the end of the unit: Name the five things a habitat gives an animal, explain how plants and animals depend on each other, and build a labeled habitat model.

Sample question: What would happen to a frog if its pond dried up?A strong answer: A frog needs water to keep its skin wet and to lay its eggs. Without the pond it loses its water and some of its food, so it would have to move somewhere else or it could die.

Watch for: Naming only food, water and shelter, and forgetting air and space. Ask what else the animal needs; all five must be there for it to survive.

Try this at home

Look under a stone or a leaf outside together. Talk about what that small creature finds in the place where it lives.

Mid May to early June

What your child is learning

Plants as Natural Resources

How much comes to us from plants: paper, cotton, wood, rubber, spices and some medicines. Which crops grow well in Virginia and why the soil and the weather decide it. How plants feed and shelter animals, put oxygen into the air we breathe, and hold the soil against wind and water.

New words: natural resource, crop, oxygen, windbreak

By the end of the unit: Name things that come from plants, explain why some crops grow well in Virginia, and describe how plants give oxygen and hold soil in place.

Sample question: Why are plants important even if you never eat them?A strong answer: Plants put oxygen into the air we breathe. Their roots hold the soil so wind and rain do not carry it away. They also give us wood, paper and cotton for clothes.

Watch for: Thinking paper, cotton shirts or rubber just come from a factory. Ask what each one was made from at the very start; the answer is a plant.

Try this at home

Open a kitchen cupboard together and find three things that came from a plant. Some will surprise you both.

June

What your child is learning

A Year of Change, and the Science Showcase

The class looks back over the whole year, and each child prepares one investigation to present, alongside the Daily Weather Watch graph running from September to June. The year closes with a Grade 2 Science Showcase.

New words: investigation, showcase

By the end of the month: Present one investigation from the year, explaining the question, the prediction, what was tested and what was found.

Sample question: What was your investigation, and how did you find out the answer?A strong answer: I asked which soil holds water best. I predicted clay. We poured the same amount of water on each soil and measured what drained out. Clay held the most, so my prediction was right.

Watch for: Telling only what happened and leaving out the prediction or the evidence. Ask what they thought would happen first, and how they know their result is true.

Try this at home

Ask your child to teach you one thing they found out this year, and to tell you how they found it out.

BY JUNE, INSHALLAH, YOUR CHILD SHOULD BE ABLE TO

Describe a push, a pull, gravity and magnetism, and give an everyday example of each. Sort things into solids, liquids and gases, and explain how heating and cooling change them. Read a thermometer, describe the weather in four ways, and explain a pattern in weather data. Explain how plants and animals respond when the seasons change, and how wind and water change the land. Describe the life cycle of a plant and the life cycle of an animal, and say what they have in common. Name the five things a habitat gives an animal, and say what happens when a habitat changes. Explain why plants matter, to people and to animals.

FIVE THINGS THAT HELP MOST AT HOME

1. Ask how do you know whenever your child tells you something. That one question is most of science. 2. Let your child measure real things. Cooking, height on a door frame, how far the ball went. 3. Step outside and notice the weather and the trees, even for two minutes. It takes no preparation and it is exactly what the class is doing. 4. When the science worksheet comes home, read the questions aloud if your child needs it, but let your child write the answers. 5. Let your child be wrong first and then find out. Guessing, testing and correcting is how science is actually done, and it is not a mistake.

OUR ISLAMIC CONNECTION THIS YEAR

The theme of Grade 2 science is that change happens all around us. Water changes, the weather changes, the seasons turn, living things grow and pass on, and all of it happens in an order we can notice and rely on. We want the children to look closely and then to feel gratitude for what they have seen. Three of our school values run through the year: Ilm, in seeking knowledge carefully and honestly; Amanah, because the natural world is a trust we are asked to look after; and Khidmah, in using what we know to serve the people and the places around us.

Questions about Grade 2 Science are always welcome. Please contact the school office or message through Class Dojo. Jazakallahu Khairan for reading this with your child.
