Grade 2 · Social Studies

Grade 2 Social Studies

The United States of America, month by month

PLEASE READ THIS FIRST

This guide is a plan, not a promise. Social Studies meets twice a week, on Wednesdays and Thursdays, so a single closure costs a whole lesson and the months are approximate. The timing and some detail will change. Where your child is going by June will not.

Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Test and assessment dates live there, not on this sheet.

Late Aug & SeptBeing a good citizen

What your child is learning

  • How families lived long ago and how they live now
  • Rules and laws, and why we have them
  • What a good citizen does, and what rights everyone has
  • How our government works and who leads it

Words to know: citizen · rights · responsibility · law · government · vote

By the end of the unit: Explain why we have rules and laws, describe what a good citizen does, and name rights and responsibilities everyone has.

Sample question: Why do we need laws?A strong answer: Laws keep people safe and help things be fair. A speed limit near a school keeps cars from going too fast. Without laws, people could get hurt and nobody would know what is fair.

Watch for: Thinking rules exist only to stop kids from having fun. Ask who a rule protects; most rules keep people safe or make things fair.

Try this at home

Give your child one real responsibility at home and let them own it. That is citizenship in miniature.

OctoberMaps and the land

What your child is learning

  • Reading a map, and using a key and a compass rose
  • The continents and oceans, and where we live on them
  • Mountains, rivers, lakes and plains across North America
  • How the land shapes the way people live

Words to know: map · key · compass rose · continent · ocean · region

By the end of the month: Use a map key and compass rose, name the seven continents and five oceans, and find where we live in North America.

Sample question: How do you know which way is north on a map?A strong answer: I look for the compass rose. It shows N for north, S for south, E for east and W for west. North is usually at the top, but I check the compass rose to be sure.

Watch for: Mixing up continents and countries, like calling the United States a continent. Ask which continent the United States is on; the answer is North America.

Try this at home

Look at a map together before a car trip. Ask which way is north and what you will pass.

NovemberIndigenous peoples of North America

What your child is learning

  • The first peoples of this land, and that they are still here today
  • Nations of the Eastern Woodlands, the Plains and the Southwest
  • How the land and the weather shaped how each group lived
  • What these nations have given to the country, past and present

Words to know: Indigenous · nation · tribe · sovereignty · tradition

By the end of the month: Describe how Eastern Woodlands, Plains and Southwest nations lived, explain how land and weather shaped their homes and food, and know they are still here today.

Sample question: Why did many Plains peoples live in tipis instead of longhouses?A strong answer: Many Plains peoples followed the buffalo herds, so they moved often. A tipi could be taken down and carried quickly. Eastern Woodlands peoples stayed in one place and had trees to build longhouses.

Watch for: Talking about Indigenous peoples only in the past tense, as if they disappeared. Ask whether these nations are here today; they are, with their own governments and traditions.

Try this at home

Ask what surprised them this month. This unit changes what most children assume about American history.

DecemberExplorers, and the thirteen colonies

What your child is learning

  • Explorers who sailed to North America, and why they came
  • What happened to the peoples already living here
  • The thirteen colonies and what life was like in them
  • The Declaration of Independence, and what it said

Words to know: explorer · voyage · colony · settler · declaration ·

independence

By the end of the month: Explain why explorers came, what changed for the people already living here, what colonial life was like, and what the Declaration of Independence said.

Sample question: Why did the colonists write the Declaration of Independence?A strong answer: The colonists felt the British king was treating them unfairly, like making them pay taxes without a say. So in 1776 they wrote that they would be a free country of their own.

Watch for: Saying explorers discovered an empty land. Ask who was already living here; millions of Indigenous people were.

Try this at home

Ask them to tell you the story of the colonies in order. Sequence is half the skill in history.

JanuaryPeople who fought for freedom

What your child is learning

  • George Washington, and why he was chosen to lead
  • Paul Revere, and the night ride that warned the colonies
  • Ordinary people who took great risks for freedom
  • What courage looks like when the outcome is not certain

Words to know: revolution · liberty · patriot · courage · leader

By the end of the month: Explain who George Washington and Paul Revere were, what each did in the fight for independence, and what courage looks like.

Sample question: Why was Paul Revere's ride so important?A strong answer: He rode at night to warn the colonists that British soldiers were coming. Because of the warning, the colonists were ready the next morning, and the fight for independence began.

Watch for: Thinking Washington was already president during the war. He led the army first and became the first president years later. Ask what job he had in each part of the story.

Try this at home

Ask who they would have been in that story, and why. The answer tells you what they understood.

FebruaryA new nation grows

What your child is learning

  • How Washington, D.C. became the capital city
  • The Louisiana Purchase, and how the country doubled in size
  • Lewis and Clark, and what they found on the journey west
  • Why a country needs a capital at all

Words to know: capital · purchase · territory · expedition · frontier

By the end of the month: Explain why a country needs a capital, how the Louisiana Purchase doubled the country, and what Lewis and Clark found on their journey west.

Sample question: What did Lewis and Clark do, and why?A strong answer: President Jefferson bought a huge piece of land called the Louisiana Purchase and sent Lewis and Clark to explore it. With help from Sacagawea, they mapped rivers, wrote about new plants and animals, and reached the Pacific Ocean.

Watch for: Mixing up Washington, D.C., the capital city, with Washington State. Find both on a map; the capital is right next door to Virginia.

Try this at home

Find Washington, D.C. on a map with them. It is close enough to be real rather than abstract.

MarchSymbols and landmarks

What your child is learning

  • The flag, the eagle, the Liberty Bell and what each one stands for
  • The Statue of Liberty and Mount Rushmore
  • The words of the Pledge of Allegiance and what they mean
  • Why a country chooses symbols in the first place

Words to know: symbol · landmark · monument · pledge · liberty

By the end of the month: Tell what the flag, bald eagle, Liberty Bell, Statue of Liberty and Mount Rushmore stand for, and explain the words of the Pledge of Allegiance.

Sample question: Why are there 50 stars and 13 stripes on the American flag?A strong answer: Each star stands for one of the 50 states we have now. The 13 stripes stand for the first 13 colonies that started the country.

Watch for: Saying the Pledge by sound without knowing the words. Ask what one word means; allegiance means loyalty, and indivisible means it cannot be split apart.

Try this at home

Point out a flag or a landmark on a coin and ask what it stands for. Symbols are everywhere once you look.

AprilAmerican changemakers

What your child is learning

  • Scholars and inventors who changed how people live
  • Explorers and adventurers who went first
  • Reformers who worked to make life fairer
  • The unit ends with a Living Wax Museum the children perform

Words to know: inventor · reformer · contribution · justice · changemaker

By the end of the month: Explain how one changemaker made life better for others, and present that person in the Living Wax Museum using researched facts.

Sample question: Who is your changemaker, and how did that person make life better for others?A strong answer: Mine is George Washington Carver. He was a scientist who found hundreds of uses for peanuts and taught farmers to switch crops so their soil stayed healthy. That helped farmers grow more food.

Watch for: Listing facts about the person, like where they were born, without saying what they changed. Ask what was different in the world after this person's work.

Try this at home

Ask which changemaker they chose and why. Let them practice their wax museum part on you.

MayNeeds, wants and money

What your child is learning

  • The difference between what we need and what we want
  • Natural, human and capital resources
  • Trading by barter, and why money makes trading easier
  • Why we cannot have everything, and how choices get made

Words to know: needs · wants · resources · barter · scarcity · choice

By the end of the month: Tell needs from wants, name natural, human and capital resources, and explain how barter works and why scarcity means making choices.

Sample question: Why is money easier than trading by barter?A strong answer: With barter, I have to find someone who wants my thing and also has what I want. That is hard. With money, I can sell to anyone and buy from anyone, so trading is much easier.

Watch for: Mixing up natural and capital resources. A tree is a natural resource; a saw that people made to cut it is a capital resource. Ask whether people made it or nature did.

Try this at home

At the store, ask whether something is a need or a want, then talk about the choice. Best lesson of the year.

JuneOne nation, many people

What your child is learning

  • The many cultures that make up this country
  • National holidays and what each one remembers
  • Looking back over the whole year of American history
  • What it means to belong to a community

Words to know: culture · celebration · community · heritage

By the end of the month: Explain how many cultures make up one country, tell what national holidays remember, and describe what it means to belong to a community.

Sample question: Why do we celebrate Independence Day on July 4?A strong answer: On July 4, 1776, the colonies said they were free from Britain in the Declaration of Independence. We celebrate that day as the birthday of our country.

Watch for: Thinking holidays are only about days off or fireworks. Ask whom or what the holiday remembers, like Martin Luther King Jr. Day honoring his work for fairness.

Try this at home

Ask what they will remember most from the year. Then tell them your own family’s story of coming here.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

School alone will not get your child here. Twice a week for 35 minutes is not much time, so talking about it at home matters more in this subject than in most.

  • Read a map using a key and a compass rose
  • Explain what a citizen’s rights and responsibilities are
  • Name Indigenous nations and where they lived
  • Tell the story of the colonies and independence in order
  • Recognize the national symbols and say what they stand for
  • Name changemakers and what each one contributed
  • Tell the difference between a need and a want, and explain a choice

WHICH IS WHY THESE SIX THINGS MATTER

  • Ask what they learned in Social Studies this week. Wednesday or Thursday evening is the moment.
  • Ask how they know, not just what happened.
  • Look at maps together. Any map, any time.
  • Talk about needs and wants when you go shopping.
  • Tell them your own family’s story. It belongs in this subject.
  • If it is getting hard, tell the teacher in October, not April.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

History is told by someone, and how it is told is a matter of adab. This year your child learns that Indigenous nations were here first and are here still, that explorers arrived into places already full of people, and that people of many backgrounds built this country. Telling that story fairly to every people in it is part of the honesty we ask of them everywhere else. Amanah runs alongside it: leadership is a trust, not a prize, and the leaders they study are judged by what they did with it.

Questions are always welcome. Please speak to your child’s teacher or the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School · 703-910-7029

Grade 3 · English

Grade 3 English

What your child will read and write this year, month by month

PLEASE READ THIS FIRST

This guide is a plan, not a promise. In Grade 3, reading and phonics join into one subject, so spelling is taught inside the reading units rather than as a separate strand; the weekly lists are in the Every Spelling List guide. Every unit ends with a finished piece of writing the class publishes and shares. The months are approximate and the timing will change. Where your child is going by June will not.

Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Test and showcase dates live there, not on this sheet.

Late Aug & SeptClassic stories

What your child is learning

  • Classic tales from around the world
  • Characters, theme, and who is telling the story
  • Finding proof in the text for what you say about it
  • Writing and publishing an opinion paragraph

Words to know: character · theme · point of view · evidence · opinion

By the end of the unit: Retell a classic tale, name its theme and who is telling it, and back up an opinion about it with evidence from the text.

Sample question: What lesson does The Tortoise and the Hare teach, and what part of the story shows it?A strong answer: The theme is that slow and steady wins the race. The hare brags and takes a nap, but the tortoise keeps going and wins. That part shows the lesson.

Watch for: Retelling the whole plot when asked for the theme. A theme is the lesson in one sentence, like keep trying, not a list of what happened.

Try this at home

Read together and ask what the story was really about. Then ask what in the story shows that.

OctoberAnimals, and how they are sorted

What your child is learning

  • How scientists classify animals with backbones
  • Reading to find facts rather than to follow a story
  • Prefixes, and how they change a word’s meaning
  • Writing an informative paragraph with real evidence

Words to know: classify · vertebrate · mammal · reptile · prefix · evidence

By the end of the month: Sort animals with backbones into groups, use prefixes to work out new words, and write an informative paragraph with real facts.

Sample question: Is a whale a fish or a mammal, and how can you tell?A strong answer: A whale is a mammal. It breathes air with lungs, is warm-blooded, and feeds its babies milk. Fish breathe with gills, so a whale is not a fish even though it swims.

Watch for: Sorting by where an animal lives instead of its body, such as calling a whale a fish. Ask which body clue they used to decide.

Try this at home

Pick an animal and ask which group it belongs to and how they can tell. Works at the zoo or on a screen.

NovemberPoetry

What your child is learning

  • What makes a poem different from a story
  • Rhyme, rhythm, imagery and other tools poets use
  • Reading a poem closely and saying what it means
  • Writing an original poem and reading it aloud to the class

Words to know: stanza · rhyme · rhythm · imagery · verse · poet

By the end of the month: Read a poem closely, point out rhyme, rhythm and imagery, explain what it means, and read an original poem aloud.

Sample question: How is a poem different from a story, and what is imagery?A strong answer: A poem is written in lines and stanzas instead of paragraphs, and it often has a beat. Imagery is when words make a picture. If a poem says the moon is a silver coin, I can see it.

Watch for: Thinking every poem has to rhyme. Many strong poems do not, so praise the pictures and rhythm in their poem, not just the rhyming words.

Try this at home

Let them read their poem to you before they read it in class. Twice out loud beats once.

DecemberAncient Rome

What your child is learning

  • How Rome rose, and why it eventually fell
  • Roman myths, and the figures behind them
  • Verb tenses and suffixes in their own writing
  • An opinion essay on Rome’s most important contribution

Words to know: empire · myth · contribution · suffix · essay

By the end of the month: Explain how Rome grew and why it fell, retell a Roman myth, and write an opinion essay with clear reasons for Rome's most important contribution.

Sample question: Which Roman contribution was most important, and what is your best reason?A strong answer: I think roads were most important. Romans built thousands of miles of roads, so armies, traders and news could travel fast. That held the empire together, and we still use roads today.

Watch for: Switching verb tenses inside one paragraph, such as the Romans build roads and they used them. Writing about history should stay in the past tense.

Try this at home

Ask which Roman contribution they chose and why. The reason is the graded part, not the choice.

JanuaryAstronomy

What your child is learning

  • The solar system, gravity, and how we learned about space
  • People who studied the sky and what they found
  • Taking notes from an informational text
  • A project: a day in the life of an astronaut

Words to know: solar system · gravity · orbit · astronaut · notes

By the end of the month: Explain how gravity keeps the planets in orbit around the sun, and take short notes from an informational text in their own words.

Sample question: Why does Earth go around the sun instead of flying off into space?A strong answer: The sun's gravity pulls on Earth. Earth is also moving very fast, so the pull keeps bending its path into a loop around the sun. That path is an orbit, and one trip takes a year.

Watch for: Copying whole sentences when taking notes. Good notes are a few key words in their own words, so look for long copied lines in their notebook.

Try this at home

Look at the night sky for two minutes and ask what they can name. They will know more than you expect.

FebruaryRegions and cultures

What your child is learning

  • Native American communities across different regions
  • How the land shaped the way each community lived
  • Researching from more than one source
  • Writing a newspaper article based on that research

Words to know: region · culture · adapt · research · source · article

By the end of the month: Explain how the land shaped the way a Native American community lived, using facts gathered from more than one source.

Sample question: How did the land shape the way people lived in a Native American community you studied?A strong answer: The Lakota lived on the Great Plains, where huge herds of buffalo roamed. They used buffalo for food, clothing and tipis, and tipis could be packed up to follow the herds.

Watch for: Treating all Native Americans as one group who lived the same way. Ask how two communities were different, and listen for land, food and homes.

Try this at home

Ask what surprised them. This unit changes a lot of what a child assumes about American history.

MarchCharlotte’s Web

What your child is learning

  • Reading a whole novel together across several weeks
  • Why characters do what they do, and how the mood changes
  • Figurative language: what the words mean underneath
  • Writing an original story inspired by the novel

Words to know: novel · motivation · mood · figurative · narrative

By the end of the month: Explain why a character in Charlotte's Web acts the way they do, describe how the mood changes, and explain what figurative language really means.

Sample question: Why does Charlotte work so hard to save Wilbur?A strong answer: Charlotte is Wilbur's true friend. When she learns he will be killed, she spins words like Some Pig in her web so people think he is special. She does it because she cares about him.

Watch for: Taking figurative language word for word, such as thinking someone who is over the moon is in space. Ask what the words mean underneath.

Try this at home

Read a chapter together or ask them to catch you up. A novel is the best thing to talk about all year.

AprilLight and sound

What your child is learning

  • How light travels, and how sound is made
  • Inventors who worked with light and sound
  • Researching a topic and organizing what you find
  • Publishing a newspaper article for a real audience

Words to know: reflect · vibration · inventor · research · headline

By the end of the month: Explain that light travels in straight lines and reflects, that sound is made by vibrations, and organize research into a newspaper article.

Sample question: How does the sound of a drum get from the drum to your ear?A strong answer: When I hit the drum, the top vibrates back and forth. That shakes the air next to it, and the vibrations travel through the air to my ear. Then my eardrum vibrates and I hear it.

Watch for: Thinking sound can travel through empty space. Sound needs something to move through, like air, water or a wall, which is why space is silent.

Try this at home

Ask them to explain how sound reaches your ear. Explaining it is where the learning lands.

MayPulling the year together

What your child is learning

  • Finishing and publishing the newspaper article
  • Reviewing reading and writing across the whole year
  • Building a portfolio of work from September on
  • A reading check to see how ready they are for Grade 4

Words to know: portfolio · revise · publish · review

By the end of the month: Revise and publish their newspaper article, and choose portfolio pieces that show how their reading and writing have grown.

Sample question: Which piece in your portfolio are you proudest of, and what did you change when you revised it?A strong answer: I am proudest of my newspaper article. My first draft had no headline and the facts were out of order. When I revised, I added a headline and put the most important facts first.

Watch for: Thinking revising means recopying neatly. Revising means changing ideas, order or words, so ask what they added, cut or moved.

Try this at home

Look through the portfolio with them and ask which piece they are proudest of, and why.

JuneThe showcase

What your child is learning

  • Presenting finished work to an audience
  • Comparing September writing with May writing
  • Reading and writing checks for the end of the year
  • Looking back at how much has changed

Words to know: showcase · present · compare · progress

By the end of the month: Present finished work clearly to an audience and explain how their writing has changed from September to May.

Sample question: What is different between your September writing and your May writing?A strong answer: In September I wrote a few short sentences with no proof. Now my paragraphs have a clear claim, evidence from the text, and reasoning that explains it. My spelling and punctuation are better too.

Watch for: Reading a presentation straight off the page with their head down. Practice once at home and ask them to look up at the end of each sentence.

Try this at home

Keep reading together through the summer. Twenty minutes a day holds on to the whole year.

CURSIVE: THIS IS THE YEAR

Grade 3 is when Virginia asks children to learn cursive, and it runs quietly through every unit rather than sitting in a separate lesson. Lowercase letters and joins come first, then slant and spacing, then capitals, then writing a whole paragraph in cursive without a model. Three dated samples are kept, in September, January and May, and your child compares their own three at the end of the year. If you write them a note in cursive at home, they will read it, and that is worth more than a page of practice.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

School alone will not get your child here. Twenty minutes of reading together a day, and talking about it, is what turns a taught skill into an easy one.

  • Read a chapter book and talk about what happened and why
  • Back up what they say about a text by pointing to the words
  • Read informational text and take notes from it
  • Write an opinion, an informative piece and a story
  • Plan, draft, revise and publish a finished piece
  • Research a topic using more than one source
  • Write legibly in cursive

WHICH IS WHY THESE FIVE THINGS MATTER

  • Read together every day, even now they can read alone.
  • Ask what happened and why, then ask what in the book shows it.
  • Let them explain something they read to you. Explaining is how it sticks.
  • Ask to see the published piece at the end of each unit.
  • If it is getting hard, tell the teacher in October, not April.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Almost everything this year asks your child to say what they think and then show where it came from. That habit has a name in our tradition: a claim without evidence carries no weight, and knowledge is traced back to its source. Ilm is the pursuit of that knowledge, and amanah is being honest about where it came from rather than passing off what we wish were true. A nine year old learning to point at the line in the book that proves their answer is practicing both.

Questions are always welcome. Please speak to your child’s teacher or the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School · 703-910-7029

Grade 3 · English · Every Spelling List

Grade 3 Spelling Words

Every weekly list for the year · fifteen words a week

THIS LIST IS TENTATIVE. IT IS NOT YET FINAL.

The teacher will confirm the actual fifteen words each week, and the weekly list she sends home is the one that counts. Words may be swapped, reordered, or moved to a different week as the class moves faster or slower through the program. Do not treat the dates below as fixed.

BUT EVERY WORD ON THIS SHEET IS ESSENTIAL AND MUST BE TAUGHT.

These words are not a suggestion. Each one carries a spelling pattern, a unit word or a tricky homophone that Grade 3 has to master before Grade 4, and the year is built so that every pattern is covered in order. A word may move to a different week. A word may not be dropped. If a week is lost to a closure, the words from that week are folded into the next list rather than skipped.

EXPECT SOME WORDS TO BE DIFFERENT. When the weekly homework packet comes home, compare it against this sheet and look for the changes. Practice the words in the packet, not the words here. The packet is always the correct list.

The confirmed weekly list is also emailed home or posted on Class Dojo. Use this sheet for what is coming, and the packet for what to practice.

HOW THE WEEK RUNS

Fifteen words go home on Monday and are tested on Friday. The first list opens Wednesday September 9 and is tested Friday September 18. Every list is tied to the unit being taught that week, so the spelling words are also words your child is reading and writing in class. Some weeks carry no new list, such as the first weeks of school and short weeks; those are marked no list below.

PRACTICE AT HOME, AND WHY IT MATTERS

Three or four words a night, not fifteen on Thursday. Say the word, cover it, write it from memory, then check. Use the word in a spoken sentence as well as writing it, because several lists this year are homophones where only the sentence shows which spelling is right. Each list teaches one spelling pattern or one set of unit words, not a random group. The patterns build in order, so a missed week makes the next one harder, and Grade 4 begins assuming every pattern on this sheet is known.

Grade 3 · Mathematics

Grade 3 Mathematics

What your child will learn this year, month by month

PLEASE READ THIS FIRST

This guide is a plan, not a promise. The months are approximate and dates shift for holidays, snow days, and topics that need more time. A homework packet comes home every week with five days of about twenty minutes each. The timing and some detail will change. Where your child is going by June will not.

Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Test dates live there, not on this sheet.

SeptemberPlace value to six digits

What your child is learning

  • Reading, writing and building numbers up to 999,999
  • Seeing a number in more than one way: 256 as 25 tens and 6 ones
  • Comparing and ordering numbers up to 9,999
  • Rounding, and saying which numbers a number sits between

Words to know: place value · digit · compare · order · round · compose

By the end of the month: Read, write and build numbers up to 999,999, show a number in more than one way, and compare and round numbers using place value.

Sample question: Round 4,682 to the nearest hundred. Which two hundreds does it sit between?A strong answer: 4,682 sits between 4,600 and 4,700. To round to the nearest hundred I look at the tens digit. It is 8, which is 5 or more, so 4,682 rounds up to 4,700.

Watch for: Looking at the wrong digit when rounding. To round to the nearest hundred, check only the tens digit. If they say 4,682 rounds to 4,600, they missed it.

Try this at home

Read big numbers aloud from prices, signs and odometers. Ask how many hundreds are in it.

OctoberAdding, subtracting, and money

What your child is learning

  • Adding and subtracting numbers up to 1,000
  • Estimating the answer before working it out
  • Regrouping, and choosing a strategy that fits the numbers
  • Counting money and making change up to five dollars

Words to know: estimate · regroup · strategy · change · reasonable

By the end of the month: Add and subtract numbers up to 1,000 with regrouping, estimate first to check the answer, and make change from five dollars.

Sample question: You pay $5.00 for something that costs $3.65. How much change should you get?A strong answer: I count up. $3.65 plus 35 cents makes $4.00, and one more dollar makes $5.00. So the change is $1.35. Check: $3.65 plus $1.35 is $5.00.

Watch for: Subtracting the smaller digit from the bigger one in every column, so 503 minus 278 becomes 375 instead of 225. The estimate, 500 minus 300, shows 375 is too big.

Try this at home

Let them pay and count the change. Then ask whether the change looks about right before counting it.

NovemberWhat multiplication means

What your child is learning

  • Multiplication as equal groups, arrays and repeated addition
  • How multiplication and division are connected
  • Writing a number sentence to match a story
  • Starting the multiplication facts

Words to know: multiply · divide · equal groups · array · product

By the end of the month: Show multiplication as equal groups, arrays and repeated addition, and write a multiplication or division sentence that matches a story.

Sample question: There are 4 plates with 3 cookies on each. Write a number sentence and solve it.A strong answer: That is 4 equal groups of 3, so 4 × 3 = 12. I can check by adding: 3 plus 3 plus 3 plus 3 is 12. There are 12 cookies.

Watch for: Adding the numbers in a story instead of multiplying, so 4 plates of 3 becomes 4 plus 3 equals 7. Ask them to draw the groups and count.

Try this at home

Count things in groups at home. Six eggs in a row, five rows. That is multiplication before it is a fact.

DecemberMultiplication facts

What your child is learning

  • Learning the facts in order: 0, 1, 2, 5, 10, then 9
  • Patterns that make some facts easy to remember
  • Using facts you know to work out facts you do not
  • Five minutes of fact practice every single day

Words to know: factor · product · pattern · fact family · fluent

By the end of the month: Recall the 0, 1, 2, 5, 10 and 9 facts quickly, and use a fact they know to work out one they do not.

Sample question: What is 9 × 7, and how can a fact you already know help?A strong answer: I know 10 × 7 is 70. Nine sevens is one seven less, so 70 minus 7 is 63. Check: 6 plus 3 is 9, and the digits of nines facts like this always add to 9.

Watch for: Mixing up times zero and times one, such as saying 8 × 0 is 8. Zero groups of anything is zero, and one group of 8 is 8.

Try this at home

Five minutes of facts a night in the order the class is learning them. Not random, and not all at once.

JanuaryThe rest of the facts, and dividing

What your child is learning

  • The harder facts: 3, 4, 6, 7 and 8
  • Using multiplication to work out a division
  • Dividing within 100 quickly and accurately
  • Related facts, and what they tell you

Words to know: divide · quotient · related facts · inverse · fluency

By the end of the month: Recall the 3, 4, 6, 7 and 8 facts and use a related multiplication fact to divide within 100.

Sample question: What is 56 ÷ 8, and what multiplication fact helps?A strong answer: I think, 8 times what makes 56? I know 8 × 7 = 56, so 56 ÷ 8 = 7. The fact family is 7 × 8, 8 × 7, 56 ÷ 7 and 56 ÷ 8.

Watch for: Writing a division backward, like 8 ÷ 56 for 56 shared into 8 groups. The total being shared always comes first, so ask which number is being split up.

Try this at home

Ask a multiplication fact, then ask the division that goes with it. Six times seven, then forty two divided by seven.

FebruaryFluent multiplying and dividing

What your child is learning

  • Multiplying and dividing within 100 without stopping to work it out
  • Solving word problems that need more than one step
  • Choosing whether to multiply or divide
  • Checking whether an answer makes sense

Words to know: fluent · two step · operation · check

By the end of the month: Multiply and divide within 100 without stopping to count, and solve two-step word problems by choosing the right operations.

Sample question: You buy 3 packs of 6 pencils and give away 5. How many pencils are left?A strong answer: First I multiply: 3 × 6 = 18 pencils. Then I subtract the 5 I gave away: 18 minus 5 = 13. Check: 13 plus 5 is 18. There are 13 pencils left.

Watch for: Stopping after the first step and answering 18. Ask them to reread the question and say what it is really asking for before they finish.

Try this at home

Keep the daily facts going. This is the month it either clicks or does not, and home practice decides which.

MarchArea and perimeter

What your child is learning

  • What area is, and why it connects to multiplication
  • Finding the area of a shape by counting and by multiplying
  • Perimeter, the distance all the way around
  • Working in both inches and centimeters

Words to know: area · perimeter · square unit · length · width

By the end of the month: Find area by counting square units and by multiplying length by width, and find perimeter by adding all the sides.

Sample question: A table is 5 feet long and 3 feet wide. What are its area and its perimeter?A strong answer: Area is 5 × 3 = 15 square feet, the space covering the top. Perimeter is 5 plus 3 plus 5 plus 3 = 16 feet, the distance all the way around.

Watch for: Adding only two sides for perimeter, which gives 8 feet instead of 16. Also check units: area is in square feet, perimeter in plain feet.

Try this at home

Measure a room or a table. Ask for the area and the perimeter, and which one you would need for a carpet.

AprilFractions

What your child is learning

  • What a fraction is, and reading it on a number line
  • Halves, thirds, fourths, fifths, sixths, eighths and tenths
  • Fractions that are equal to each other
  • Comparing a fraction to zero, to a half and to one

Words to know: fraction · numerator · denominator · equivalent · compare

By the end of the month: Name fractions, place them on a number line, find equivalent fractions, and compare a fraction to 0, 1/2 and 1.

Sample question: Which is bigger, 2/8 or 2/4? How do you know?A strong answer: 2/4 is bigger. Both have 2 pieces, but fourths are bigger pieces than eighths because the whole is cut into fewer parts. 2/4 is one half, and 2/8 is less than one half.

Watch for: Thinking a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction, so 1/8 seems bigger than 1/4. Ask them to draw both on the same size rectangle and compare.

Try this at home

Cut food into equal parts and name them. Ask which is bigger, two eighths or two fourths, and why.

MayGraphs, measuring and time

What your child is learning

  • Asking a question, collecting data and graphing it
  • Reading pictographs and bar graphs
  • Measuring length, weight and how much a container holds
  • Telling time and working out how long something took

Words to know: data · pictograph · bar graph · scale · elapsed time

By the end of the month: Collect data and graph it in a pictograph or bar graph, measure length, weight and liquid volume, and find elapsed time.

Sample question: A game started at 3:20 and ended at 4:05. How long did it last?A strong answer: From 3:20 to 4:00 is 40 minutes. From 4:00 to 4:05 is 5 more minutes. 40 plus 5 is 45 minutes. Check: 3:20 plus 45 minutes is 4:05.

Watch for: Subtracting times like regular numbers: 405 minus 320 gives 85, but an hour has 60 minutes, not 100. Counting up to the next hour avoids it.

Try this at home

Ask how long something took. Started at 3:20, finished at 4:05, how long was that.

JuneShapes, patterns and review

What your child is learning

  • Naming polygons and describing their sides and angles
  • Putting shapes together and cutting them apart
  • Finding and continuing number patterns
  • A final review across everything since September

Words to know: polygon · angle · side · pattern · rule

By the end of the month: Name polygons by their sides and angles, combine and split shapes, and find the rule that continues a number pattern.

Sample question: What comes next in 4, 9, 14, 19, and what is the rule?A strong answer: Each number is 5 more than the one before, so the rule is add 5. 19 plus 5 is 24, so 24 comes next, then 29.

Watch for: Naming shapes by how they look instead of their sides, such as calling a tilted square a diamond. Ask how many sides and angles it has, since that decides the name.

Try this at home

Keep the facts going through the summer. Five minutes a day protects everything gained this year.

THE MULTIPLICATION FACTS, IN THE ORDER WE TEACH THEM

The class does not learn the times tables in order from one to twelve. They learn them in the order that makes each one easier than the last: 0, 1, 2, 5 and 10 first, then 9, then the harder ones, 3, 4, 6, 7 and 8. If you practice at home, please follow the same order. Working on the 7s in December, before the easy facts are secure, makes it harder rather than faster. Five minutes a day, every day, from November on is the single most useful thing you can do for Grade 3 math.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

School lessons alone will not get your child here. Five minutes of fact practice a day at home is what makes the rest of Grade 3 possible.

  • Read, write and compare numbers up to six digits
  • Add and subtract within 1,000, and estimate first
  • Know the multiplication and division facts within 100
  • Find the area and perimeter of a shape
  • Name and compare fractions, and place them on a number line
  • Read a bar graph, measure, and work out elapsed time
  • Explain which strategy they chose and why

WHICH IS WHY THESE FIVE THINGS MATTER

  • Five minutes of facts every single day, in the order the class is learning them.
  • Ask out loud rather than setting extra written work.
  • Ask how they worked it out, not just the answer.
  • Ask for an estimate before the real answer.
  • If it is getting hard, tell the teacher in October, not April.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Three of our core values sit inside an ordinary math lesson. Amanah, trust, is honest work: checking your own answer and owning a mistake rather than quietly changing it. Hikmah, wisdom, is choosing the strategy that fits the numbers in front of you, and knowing when an estimate is enough. Adab, good manners, is listening to how a classmate solved it before saying how you did. A child who practices those three in mathematics is practicing them everywhere.

Questions are always welcome. Please speak to your child’s teacher or the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School · 703-910-7029

Grade 3 · Science

Grade 3 Science

What your child will learn this year, month by month

PLEASE READ THIS FIRST

This guide is a plan, not a promise. The months are approximate and dates shift for holidays, snow days, and investigations that need more time. Each unit ends with a test or a project. The timing and some detail will change. Where your child is going by June will not.

Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Test dates live there, not on this sheet.

SeptemberSimple and compound machines

What your child is learning

  • The six simple machines, and how each one makes work easier
  • Levers and pulleys, ramps, wedges and screws
  • The wheel and axle, and machines made of other machines
  • Building a machine of their own for the Build Challenge

Words to know: lever · pulley · inclined plane · wedge · screw · wheel and

axle

By the end of the month: Name the six simple machines, find them in everyday objects, and explain how a machine makes work easier.

Sample question: How does a ramp make it easier to get a heavy box onto a truck?A strong answer: A ramp is an inclined plane. Instead of lifting the box straight up, you push it a longer distance up the slope. That takes less force, so it feels easier even though it takes longer.

Watch for: Thinking a machine makes the work disappear. A simple machine trades less force for a longer distance, or changes the direction you push or pull.

Try this at home

Hunt for simple machines around the house. Scissors, a doorknob, a bottle opener, stairs.

OctoberMaterials and water

What your child is learning

  • Why water dissolves some things and not others
  • What sinks, what floats, and what mixes
  • Getting the salt back out of salt water
  • Measuring carefully, and planning a fair test

Words to know: dissolve · mixture · solution · fair test · measure

By the end of the month: Test which materials dissolve, sink or float in water, separate salt from salt water, and plan a fair test that changes only one thing.

Sample question: How can you get the salt back out of salt water?A strong answer: Put the salt water in a shallow dish in a warm, sunny place. The water evaporates into the air, but the salt does not, so salt crystals are left behind in the dish.

Watch for: Thinking dissolved salt is gone because they cannot see it. Letting the water evaporate shows the salt was there the whole time.

Try this at home

Stir salt, sugar, sand and oil into water and ask what happened to each. Kitchen science, five minutes.

NovemberAdaptations and survival

What your child is learning

  • How a body or a behavior helps an animal survive
  • Why some animals survive alone and others in groups
  • What happens when an environment changes
  • Fossils, how they form, and what they tell us

Words to know: adaptation · survive · environment · fossil · evidence

By the end of the month: Explain how a body part or behavior helps an animal survive, and tell what a fossil shows about life and environments long ago.

Sample question: How does a polar bear's body help it survive in the Arctic?A strong answer: A polar bear has thick fur and a layer of fat called blubber that keep it warm. Its white fur blends in with the snow, so it can sneak up on seals to hunt.

Watch for: Saying an animal grew a feature because it needed it, like a giraffe stretching its neck. Adaptations are passed down over many generations, not grown on purpose.

Try this at home

Pick any animal and ask what about it helps it survive where it lives. Works anywhere, anytime.

DecemberLife cycles and traits

What your child is learning

  • How living things grow and change through a life cycle
  • Traits passed down from parents to their young
  • Traits that come from the environment instead
  • Comparing life cycles of different animals

Words to know: life cycle · trait · inherited · offspring · pattern

By the end of the month: Describe the stages of a life cycle and tell which traits are inherited from parents and which come from the environment.

Sample question: Is a scar an inherited trait? How do you know?A strong answer: No. A scar comes from getting hurt, so it comes from the environment. Inherited traits come from your parents, like eye color or the shape of your ears.

Watch for: Calling every trait inherited, including a haircut or a skill like riding a bike. Ask whether a baby is born with it or gets it later.

Try this at home

Look at family photos and talk about which traits were passed down and which were not.

JanuaryEcosystems, food chains and soil

What your child is learning

  • What an ecosystem is and how living things depend on each other
  • Producers, consumers and decomposers in a food chain
  • What soil is actually made of
  • Comparing sand, silt and clay, and planting seeds

Words to know: ecosystem · food chain · producer · consumer ·

decomposer · soil

By the end of the month: Build a food chain from producer to consumers to decomposers, and describe what soil is made of, comparing sand, silt and clay.

Sample question: Why does every food chain start with a plant?A strong answer: A plant is a producer. It makes its own food using sunlight, and animals cannot. A rabbit eats the plant and a fox eats the rabbit, so the energy starts with the sun and the plant.

Watch for: Drawing food chain arrows backward, from the eater to the food. The arrow shows where the energy goes, so it points from the grass to the rabbit.

Try this at home

Dig up a little soil and look at it closely. Ask what they can see in it.

FebruarySoil, then the water cycle

What your child is learning

  • Soil layers, and how soil helps plants grow
  • Running their own plant investigation and reporting the results
  • Where all of Earth’s water actually is
  • How the sun powers the whole water cycle

Words to know: humus · layer · investigation · evaporation · water cycle

By the end of the month: Name the layers of soil, explain how humus helps plants grow, report on their plant investigation, and explain that the sun powers the water cycle.

Sample question: Where is most of Earth's water, and can we drink it?A strong answer: Most of Earth's water is in the ocean, and it is salt water, so we cannot drink it. Only a small part is fresh water, and a lot of that is frozen in ice.

Watch for: Changing more than one thing in the plant investigation, like the soil and the amount of water. Then they cannot tell which change made the difference.

Try this at home

Ask them to explain their plant investigation to you. Explaining it is where the learning lands.

MarchThe water cycle

What your child is learning

  • Evaporation, condensation and precipitation
  • How clouds form, and where rain goes afterward
  • Building a working model of the water cycle
  • A unit test at the end of the water cycle work

Words to know: evaporation · condensation · precipitation · runoff · model

By the end of the month: Explain evaporation, condensation and precipitation, describe how clouds form, and use a model to show the water cycle.

Sample question: Why do water drops form on the outside of a cold glass?A strong answer: The air has water vapor in it that we cannot see. When the vapor touches the cold glass, it cools and turns back into liquid drops. That is condensation, the same way clouds form.

Watch for: Thinking the water leaked through the glass. Ask where the drops came from, and listen for the answer: the air, not the cup.

Try this at home

Point out condensation on a cold glass or a bathroom mirror and ask what is happening.

AprilPeople and the environment

What your child is learning

  • How people affect the air, the water and animal habitats
  • Why fresh water is a limited resource
  • Natural events: fire, flood, disease and erosion
  • Making a plan to protect a resource, and a final unit test

Words to know: resource · pollution · erosion · habitat · stewardship

By the end of the month: Describe how people affect air, water and habitats, explain why fresh water is limited, and make a plan to protect a resource.

Sample question: Why should we save fresh water if most of Earth is covered in water?A strong answer: Most of Earth's water is salty ocean water or frozen ice. Only a tiny part is fresh water we can use, and people, plants and animals all need it. If we waste or pollute it, there is less to share.

Watch for: Thinking only people change the environment. Fire, floods, disease and erosion change it too, so ask for one natural change and one caused by people.

Try this at home

Talk about one thing your family could do differently with water or waste. Then actually try it.

May and JunePulling the year together

What your child is learning

  • Reviewing every strand from September on
  • A cumulative check across the whole year
  • Extension work for those ready for it
  • Looking back at how much has changed since September

Words to know: review · evidence · conclusion

By the end of the unit: Explain the big ideas from every science unit this year and support a conclusion with evidence from an investigation.

Sample question: What was one investigation you did this year, and what evidence supported your conclusion?A strong answer: We tested which soil held the most water. Water drained through the sand quickly but stayed in the clay. Our measurements showed that, so our conclusion was that clay holds water best.

Watch for: Giving a conclusion with no evidence, like saying clay is best just because. Ask what they saw or measured that proves it.

Try this at home

Ask what they will remember most from science this year, and why that one.

A WORD YOUR CHILD WILL BRING HOME: CER

Twice this year, after the dissolving investigation and again after the plant investigation, your child writes up what they found using CER. Claim, what I think the answer is. Evidence, what I actually saw or measured. Reasoning, why that evidence supports the claim. If they mention CER at home, that is what it means, and asking them for the evidence behind a claim is exactly the right question.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

School alone will not get your child here. Science sticks when it is talked about outside the classroom, on a walk or at the kitchen table.

  • Name the simple machines and say what each one does
  • Explain what dissolves and what does not
  • Say how an adaptation helps an animal survive
  • Describe a life cycle and name an inherited trait
  • Trace a food chain from producer to decomposer
  • Explain the water cycle in their own words
  • Back up a claim with evidence they collected themselves

WHICH IS WHY THESE FIVE THINGS MATTER

  • Ask what they learned in science this week.
  • Ask how they know. Every time.
  • Let them explain something to you. Explaining it out loud is how it sticks.
  • Say you do not know when you do not, then look it up together.
  • Notice science outside: puddles drying, rust, ice melting, seeds sprouting.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

This year your child studies water, soil, animals and the way people affect all three. The Quran calls people khalifah, stewards placed on this earth and answerable for how it is treated, and the April unit asks exactly that question: what have people done to the air, the water and the habitats, and what can be done about it. Amanah, trust, also runs through every investigation: recording what you actually saw rather than what you hoped to see is a matter of honesty before it is a matter of science.

Questions are always welcome. Please speak to your child’s teacher or the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School · 703-910-7029

Grade 3 · Social Studies

Grade 3 Social Studies

The ancient world, and our own country, month by month

PLEASE READ THIS FIRST

This guide is a plan, not a promise. Grade 3 Social Studies meets three times a week, and most of the year is spent on five ancient cultures before turning to our own government in the spring. Each unit ends in a real project with something the class makes and shows. The months are approximate and the timing will change. Where your child is going by June will not.

Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Test and showcase dates live there, not on this sheet.

Late Aug & SeptThinking like a historian

What your child is learning

  • What historians and geographers actually do
  • Continents, oceans, and locating places on a map and globe
  • Using latitude and longitude to find a place
  • The class builds an atlas and teaches it to Grade 2

Words to know: historian · geographer · continent · ocean · equator ·

location

By the end of the unit: Locate the seven continents and five oceans on a map and globe, and use latitude and longitude to find a place.

Sample question: How do latitude and longitude help you find a place on a globe?A strong answer: Latitude lines run east and west and show how far north or south of the equator a place is. Longitude lines run north and south and show how far east or west. Where they cross is the spot.

Watch for: Mixing up latitude and longitude. A trick that sticks: latitude lines lie flat, like the rungs of a ladder, and lat sounds like ladder.

Try this at home

Find a country in the news on a map together. Ask which continent and which ocean is nearest.

OctoberAncient Egypt

What your child is learning

  • Where Egypt was, and why the Nile mattered so much
  • How Egyptians lived, what they believed, and what they built
  • Pyramids, hieroglyphics and the inventions they left behind
  • An engineering challenge judged by Grade 4

Words to know: Nile · pharaoh · pyramid · hieroglyphics · civilization

By the end of the month: Explain how the Nile River made life in Egypt possible, and describe contributions such as pyramids, hieroglyphics and papyrus.

Sample question: Why did almost all ancient Egyptians live close to the Nile River?A strong answer: Egypt is mostly desert. Every year the Nile flooded and left rich soil behind, so farmers could grow food. The river also gave water to drink and a way to travel and trade by boat.

Watch for: Thinking the Nile floods were a disaster. For Egypt the yearly flood was a gift, because it made farming possible in the middle of a desert.

Try this at home

Ask what the Nile gave the Egyptians. Almost everything about that civilization starts with the river.

NovemberAncient China

What your child is learning

  • The rivers and mountains that shaped ancient China
  • Chinese inventions and how they reached the rest of the world
  • Beliefs, writing, and the Great Wall
  • A Silk Road Marketplace families are welcome to visit

Words to know: Huang He · silk · dynasty · invention · trade route

By the end of the month: Explain how the Huang He and the land shaped ancient China, and describe Chinese contributions such as silk, paper and the Great Wall.

Sample question: Why did the ancient Chinese build the Great Wall?A strong answer: They built it to protect China from invaders coming from the north. Guards on the wall could watch for attackers and send signals, and it was built and rebuilt over hundreds of years.

Watch for: Mixing up which culture gave which invention, such as giving paper to Egypt. Egypt made papyrus from reeds, but China invented the paper we use today.

Try this at home

Look at labels at home and find where things were made. That is the Silk Road question in modern form.

DecemberAncient Greece

What your child is learning

  • Greek geography, city states and daily life
  • Where the idea of voting and democracy came from
  • Greek contributions in art, building and thinking
  • Starting a class constitution: how should we decide things?

Words to know: democracy · city state · citizen · assembly · contribution

By the end of the month: Explain how Greek geography led to separate city-states, and how Athens gave the world the idea of democracy.

Sample question: Why did ancient Greece have separate city-states instead of one big country?A strong answer: Greece has lots of mountains and islands, so it was hard to travel between places. Each community grew on its own with its own government. Athens became a democracy, where citizens voted on laws.

Watch for: Thinking everyone in Athens could vote. Only free men who were citizens could vote. Women, enslaved people and people from other places could not.

Try this at home

Let your child help decide something at home by a real vote. That is the whole unit in five minutes.

JanuaryAncient Rome

What your child is learning

  • How Rome grew from a city into an empire
  • Roman roads, aqueducts, law and government
  • What Rome borrowed from Greece and what it changed
  • Rewriting the class constitution the Roman way

Words to know: empire · republic · aqueduct · law · senate

By the end of the month: Explain how Rome grew into an empire, and describe Roman contributions such as roads, aqueducts, a republic and written laws.

Sample question: How was Rome's government like Greece's, and how was it different?A strong answer: Both gave citizens a say. In Athens, citizens voted on laws themselves. In the Roman Republic, citizens elected leaders to make decisions for them. That is more like our government today.

Watch for: Using republic and empire as if they mean the same thing. A republic has elected leaders, and an empire is ruled by one emperor. Rome was a republic first, then an empire.

Try this at home

Ask what Rome copied from Greece and what it did differently. Comparing is the skill all year.

FebruaryThe Empire of Mali

What your child is learning

  • Where Mali was, and how it grew rich from trade
  • Mansa Musa, and the journey that made him famous
  • Timbuktu, its libraries and its scholars
  • Gold, salt and the trade routes across the Sahara

Words to know: Mali · Mansa Musa · Timbuktu · Sahara · manuscript ·

trade

By the end of the month: Locate Mali in West Africa and explain how gold and salt trade across the Sahara made it rich and made Timbuktu a center of learning.

Sample question: Why was salt so valuable in the Empire of Mali?A strong answer: People need salt to stay healthy and to keep food from spoiling. Mali had lots of gold but little salt, so traders brought salt across the Sahara on camels. Because it was hard to get, it was worth a lot.

Watch for: Thinking Mali was poor or had no cities. Mali was one of the richest empires in the world, and Timbuktu had schools and libraries full of manuscripts.

Try this at home

If your family has West African heritage or hajj experience, the teacher would welcome hearing from you.

MarchMali, and comparing the cultures

What your child is learning

  • Building the Timbuktu Library as a class project
  • Putting all five ancient cultures side by side
  • What they had in common, and what made each one different
  • Writing about a cause and its effect

Words to know: compare · contrast · cause · effect · evidence

By the end of the month: Compare Egypt, China, Greece, Rome and Mali, and write about a cause and its effect using evidence.

Sample question: What is one cause and effect from the ancient cultures you studied?A strong answer: In Egypt, the Nile flooded every year. That was the cause. The effect was rich soil, so farmers could grow plenty of food and the civilization could grow.

Watch for: Mixing up cause and effect. The cause happens first and makes the effect happen. Listen for the words because and so to check the order.

Try this at home

Ask which of the five cultures they would most want to visit and why. The reason is what matters.

AprilOur own government

What your child is learning

  • The Ancient Cultures Museum, which families are invited to
  • The three branches of the United States government
  • What each branch does, and how they check each other
  • Who represents us, and which one to go to with a problem

Words to know: branch · legislative · executive · judicial · represent

By the end of the month: Name the three branches of the United States government, tell what each does, and explain how they check each other.

Sample question: What does each branch of the United States government do?A strong answer: The legislative branch, Congress, makes the laws. The executive branch, led by the President, carries out the laws. The judicial branch, the courts, decides what laws mean and whether they are fair.

Watch for: Thinking the President makes the laws. Congress writes and passes laws, and the President signs or vetoes them. Ask who writes a new law.

Try this at home

The Leader Lookup comes home this month. Sit with your child and work out who represents you.

MayBeing a citizen

What your child is learning

  • The rights every citizen has, and the responsibilities too
  • What good citizens do in a community
  • Writing a real proposal to make something better
  • The start of the economics unit

Words to know: rights · responsibility · community · proposal · volunteer

By the end of the month: Explain the rights and responsibilities of a citizen, and write a proposal that names a problem, a solution and who could help.

Sample question: What is one right and one responsibility you have as a citizen?A strong answer: One right is freedom of speech, so I can share my ideas. One responsibility is to obey the laws, like following traffic rules. Rights are freedoms we have, and responsibilities are things we should do.

Watch for: Mixing up rights and responsibilities. A right is a freedom you have, and a responsibility is something you should do. Ask which one helping clean a park is.

Try this at home

Ask what they would change about our community and how. Then ask who they would have to ask.

JuneResources, trade and choices

What your child is learning

  • Natural, human and capital resources
  • Why we cannot have everything, and how choices get made
  • Supply, demand and setting a price
  • The year ends with the WIS Trade Fair

Words to know: resources · scarcity · supply · demand · price · trade

By the end of the month: Name natural, human and capital resources, explain why scarcity forces choices, and use supply and demand to set a price.

Sample question: Lots of people want your bracelets, but you only made five. Should you raise or lower the price? Why?A strong answer: I could raise the price a little. The supply is small and the demand is big, so people will pay more. If nobody buys them at that price, I would lower it.

Watch for: Calling money a capital resource. Capital resources are things people make to produce goods, like a hammer, an oven or a computer.

Try this at home

Let them set a price for something and defend it. That is exactly what the Trade Fair asks of them.

THREE DAYS YOU ARE INVITED TO

Much of this year is built around projects the children present to a real audience, and families are welcome at three of them. The Silk Road Marketplace in November. The Ancient Cultures Museum in April, which includes the Timbuktu Library the class builds in March. The WIS Trade Fair in June, where children set prices and defend them. In September, the class also handed its finished atlas to Grade 2 and taught them to use it. Dates are confirmed on Class Dojo closer to the time. Coming makes a real difference to how seriously a nine year old takes the work.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

School alone will not get your child here. A child who talks about these cultures at home remembers them; a child who only meets them in class does not.

  • Locate places using a map, a globe and coordinates
  • Describe each of the five ancient cultures and where it was
  • Explain what each culture contributed that we still use
  • Compare two cultures and explain a cause and its effect
  • Name the three branches of government and what each does
  • Say what rights and responsibilities a citizen has
  • Explain scarcity, and defend a choice they have made

WHICH IS WHY THESE FIVE THINGS MATTER

  • Ask what they are building at the moment. The project is the spine of the year.
  • Ask how they know, not just what happened.
  • Look at maps together. Any map, any time.
  • Come to the showcases if you possibly can.
  • If it is getting hard, tell the teacher in October, not April.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Mali is not an add-on to this year, it is one of the five. Timbuktu held libraries and scholars when much of the world had neither, and your child spends March building that library and learning what was kept in it. Ilm, the pursuit of knowledge, has a place and a history, and it is one your child may not have expected to find in a Social Studies book. Adab sits alongside it: five cultures, five sets of beliefs, and the manners to study each one fairly.

Questions are always welcome. Please speak to your child’s teacher or the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School · 703-910-7029

Grade 4 · English

Grade 4 English

What your child will read and write this year, month by month

PLEASE READ THIS FIRST

Everything on this sheet is tentative. The months are approximate, a unit may run long because a class is enjoying it or short because a week was lost, and the order can shift. What does not change is this: every unit here will be taught, one way or another, before your child leaves Grade 4. If something arrives two weeks later than the sheet says, it is still coming.

Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Test, showcase and spelling dates live there, not on this sheet.

Late Aug & SeptPersonal narratives

What your child is learning

  • What makes a true story about your own life worth reading
  • Sensory details, dialogue, and putting events in order
  • Character traits, and cause and effect
  • The unit’s Memory Showcase is held in November

Words to know: memoir · sensory detail · dialogue · chronological · trait

By the end of the unit: Write a true story about their own life with events in order, sensory details and dialogue that show how people felt.

Sample question: In your personal narrative, how did you show the reader how you felt instead of just telling them?A strong answer: Instead of writing I was scared, I wrote that my hands were shaking and my heart was pounding. I also added what my mom said, so the reader can hear the moment.

Watch for: Stories that list everything from the whole day (and then, and then) instead of zooming in on one moment. Ask which single moment matters most.

Try this at home

Tell your child a story from your own childhood. That is the exact form they are learning to write.

OctoberThe Middle Ages

What your child is learning

  • Knights, castles and how the feudal system worked
  • Castle architecture and what daily life was really like
  • Cause and effect in a piece of history writing
  • Drafting a cause-and-effect essay

Words to know: feudal · knight · castle · cause · effect · evidence

By the end of the month: Explain how the feudal system worked and write a cause-and-effect essay that uses evidence from what they read.

Sample question: Why did lords build castles, and what happened because of them?A strong answer: Lords built castles to protect their land from attacks. Because the walls were thick and high, people could shelter inside during a raid, so the lord kept his land and his people safe.

Watch for: Mixing up cause and effect, naming what happened as the reason. Ask which came first; the cause always comes before the effect.

Try this at home

Ask what caused something and what happened because of it. That question runs through the whole unit.

NovemberFinishing the Middle Ages, then poetry

What your child is learning

  • The Memory Showcase from the first unit, on November 6
  • Finishing the Middle Ages with a Castle Gallery Walk
  • What poets do that prose writers do not
  • Simile, metaphor, rhythm and repetition
  • Reading and discussing real poems closely

Words to know: poem · stanza · simile · metaphor · rhythm · repetition

By the end of the month: Find a simile, a metaphor and repetition in a poem and explain the picture each one creates in the reader's mind.

Sample question: In a poem, what is the difference between a simile and a metaphor?A strong answer: A simile compares two things using like or as, such as the snow was like a blanket. A metaphor says one thing is another, the snow was a blanket. Both help you picture it.

Watch for: Calling every comparison a simile, even with no like or as. Ask them to point to the exact word that makes it a simile.

Try this at home

Read one short poem together and ask what picture it put in their head.

DecemberPoetry, then inventing

What your child is learning

  • Writing, revising and performing an original poem at a Poetry Café
  • How inventions actually get made, and who makes them
  • Researching a real inventor
  • Building an argument for an opinion essay

Words to know: revise · perform · invention · prototype · opinion

By the end of the month: Revise and perform an original poem, then begin researching a real inventor and how the invention was made.

Sample question: What did you change in your poem when you revised it, and why?A strong answer: I changed nice to golden and crunchy so the reader could picture the leaves. I also cut a line that did not fit the rhythm, so it sounds better read out loud.

Watch for: Treating revising as fixing spelling only. Revising means changing words, lines or order to make the writing better; fixing spelling is editing.

Try this at home

Ask to hear their poem before the Poetry Café. Reading it aloud twice at home makes the performance easier.

JanuaryEureka! Student inventor

What your child is learning

  • Pitching an idea and defending it
  • Writing an opinion essay with real reasons behind it
  • The unit ends with an Inventor’s Expo
  • Starting geology, and Greek word roots

Words to know: pitch · persuade · reason · evidence · root word

By the end of the month: Write an opinion essay that states a clear opinion and backs it with reasons and evidence, then pitch and defend an invention.

Sample question: What is your invention, and what is your best reason someone should use it?A strong answer: My invention is a backpack with a light inside so you can find things fast. My best reason is that kids waste time searching, and in my test it took half as long to find a pencil.

Watch for: Reasons that only repeat the opinion, like it is good because it is great. Ask how they know; a real reason has evidence behind it.

Try this at home

Let them convince you of something, then ask for the reasons. That is the essay in conversation form.

FebruaryGeology

What your child is learning

  • Plate tectonics, volcanoes and earthquakes
  • Greek and Latin roots inside long science words
  • Reading dense informational text and taking notes
  • The unit ends with an Earth Science Showcase

Words to know: tectonic · eruption · seismograph · root · prefix

By the end of the month: Use Greek and Latin roots to figure out long science words and take clear notes from informational text on volcanoes and earthquakes.

Sample question: What does seismograph mean, and how do the word parts help you figure it out?A strong answer: Seismo means shaking, like an earthquake, and graph means to write or record. So a seismograph is a machine that records the shaking of an earthquake.

Watch for: Copying whole sentences into notes instead of key words. Ask them to explain a note without looking; if they cannot, it was copied, not understood.

Try this at home

Break a long word into its parts with them. Seismograph, biographer, autograph all share pieces.

MarchThe road to independence

What your child is learning

  • Colonial America, taxation, and the Boston Tea Party
  • The Declaration of Independence and what it argued
  • The war, and the people on every side of it
  • Reading history and judging a source

Words to know: colony · taxation · declaration · liberty · source

By the end of the month: Explain what led to the Declaration of Independence and judge a source by asking who wrote it and why.

Sample question: Why were colonists so angry about taxes like the tax on tea?A strong answer: They had to pay taxes to Britain but had no one speaking for them in Parliament. They called it taxation without representation, so at the Boston Tea Party they dumped the tea into the harbor.

Watch for: Trusting every source equally. Ask who wrote it and which side they were on; a British soldier and a colonist describe the same event very differently.

Try this at home

Ask whose side the writer was on. Grade 4 is old enough for that question and it changes everything.

AprilA whole novel

What your child is learning

  • Reading From the Mixed-Up Files of Mrs. Basil E. Frankweiler
  • Character motivation, rising action and how a plot is built
  • Word Work: learning vocabulary from the book itself
  • A Heroes and Villains Gallery, and the unit ends with an Author’s Chair

Words to know: novel · motivation · plot · rising action · setting

By the end of the unit: Explain what drives a character's choices and trace how the rising action builds through a whole novel.

Sample question: Why does Claudia decide to run away to the museum?A strong answer: Claudia feels that nobody at home appreciates her and every day is the same. She picks the museum because it is comfortable and elegant, and she wants to come home feeling different.

Watch for: Retelling what happened instead of explaining why a character did it. Ask why, then ask which part of the book shows it.

Try this at home

Read a chapter alongside them or ask them to catch you up. A shared novel is the best talk of the year.

MayTales from around the world

What your child is learning

  • Folktales from Brazil, Argentina, Russia and the Arab world
  • What the same story becomes when a different people tells it
  • Reimagining a tale and writing their own version
  • A Storytelling Open Mic at the end of the month

Words to know: folktale · culture · retelling · theme · narrator

By the end of the month: Compare how one tale changes from culture to culture, name its theme, and write their own retelling.

Sample question: How can two folktales from different countries be the same story but still different?A strong answer: They have the same plot, like a small clever animal tricking a big one, but the setting, food and animals change to fit the people telling it. The theme, being clever beats being strong, stays the same.

Watch for: Confusing theme with plot. The plot is what happened and the theme is the lesson, said as a sentence like greed causes trouble, not a single word.

Try this at home

If your family knows a traditional tale, tell it. That is exactly what this unit is built on.

JuneResearch, and the year’s end

What your child is learning

  • Finishing the tales unit and the final assessment
  • A research project taken from question to presentation
  • Presenting to a real audience at the Research Expo
  • Looking back over a whole year of reading and writing

Words to know: research · source · present · portfolio · revise

By the end of the month: Take a research question from start to finish, using more than one trustworthy source, and present the findings to an audience.

Sample question: How did you decide which sources to trust for your research project?A strong answer: I used sources from experts, like a museum website and a library book, and checked that two sources agreed. I skipped a page with no author because I could not tell who wrote it.

Watch for: Copying sentences from a source word for word. Ask them to explain a fact in their own words and tell you where it came from.

Try this at home

Ask them to practice the Expo presentation on you. Saying it out loud twice beats saying it once.

NINE TIMES THE CLASS SHOWS ITS WORK

Almost every unit ends with the children presenting something finished rather than handing in a paper. The Memory Showcase in November, the Castle Gallery Walk in November, the Poetry Café in December, the Inventor’s Expo in January, the Earth Science Showcase in February, the Heroes and Villains Gallery in April, the Author’s Chair at the end of April, the Storytelling Open Mic in May, and the Research Expo in June. Dates are confirmed on Class Dojo closer to the time. A ten year old works differently when they know someone is coming.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

School alone will not get your child here. Twenty minutes of reading a day, and a conversation about it, is what turns a taught skill into an easy one.

  • Read a whole novel and talk about why characters act as they do
  • Support what they say about a text by quoting from it
  • Read dense informational text and take useful notes
  • Write a narrative, an opinion essay and a poem
  • Plan, draft, revise and publish a finished piece
  • Research a question using more than one source
  • Present their work out loud to an audience

WHICH IS WHY THESE FIVE THINGS MATTER

  • Read every day, even now they read alone. Twenty minutes is enough.
  • Ask why a character did something, then ask what in the book shows it.
  • Ask for the reasons behind an opinion, every time.
  • Ask to see the finished piece at the end of each unit.
  • If it is getting hard, tell the teacher in October, not April.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

This year asks your child to make a claim and then show where it came from, in every unit, whether the subject is a poem, a volcano or a revolution. Knowledge traced back to its source is how our tradition has always handled a claim, and amanah is being honest about that source even when a different answer would be more convenient. In May they study tales from Brazil, Argentina, Russia and the Arab world side by side, which asks something else of them: the adab to read each one on its own terms.

Questions are always welcome. Please speak to your child’s teacher or the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School · 703-910-7029

HOW TO PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Three or four words a night, not fifteen on Monday.
  • Say the word out loud while writing it. Silent copying does very little.
  • Cover the word, write it from memory, then check. That is the move that works.
  • Read the paragraph back aloud. Most mistakes are heard before they are seen.
  • For the seven definitions, let your child say the meaning before writing it.
  • Help with ideas for the paragraph, but let your child do the writing.

WHERE THE WORDS COME FROM

  • Amplify CKLA publishes spelling lists for Units 2, 5, 6 and 8 only.
  • Those lists are used exactly as published, and topped up to fifteen with words teaching the same pattern.
  • For the other units the list is written at school, from the letter patterns and the subject vocabulary of that week.
  • Six Tuesdays in the year have no school. In each case the list at home simply gets an extra week.

Questions are always welcome. Please speak to your child’s teacher or the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School · 703-910-7029
