Grade 4 · Mathematics

Grade 4 Mathematics

What your child will learn this year, month by month

PLEASE READ THIS FIRST

Everything on this sheet is tentative. Mathematics is 70 minutes every day, and a unit may run a week longer because a class needs it. What does not change is this: every topic here will be taught before your child leaves Grade 4. Homework goes home on Tuesday and is due the following Tuesday, five nights of about twenty minutes.

Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Test dates live there, not on this sheet.

Late Aug & SeptPlace value, and adding and subtracting

What your child is learning

  • Reading and writing numbers up to nine digits
  • Naming the place and the value of any digit
  • Comparing and ordering large numbers, including the not equal sign
  • Adding and subtracting to 1,000,000, estimating first every time

Words to know: place · value · period · round · estimate · sum · difference ·

regroup

By the end of the unit: Read, write, compare and round numbers up to nine digits, and add and subtract numbers up to 1,000,000, estimating first.

Sample question: What is 52,347 + 38,968? Estimate first.A strong answer: Estimate first: 52,000 + 39,000 = 91,000. Then add column by column, regrouping in the ones, tens, hundreds and thousands. I get 91,315, which is close to my estimate, so it makes sense.

Watch for: Subtracting the smaller digit from the larger in each column instead of regrouping, so 5,302 minus 1,478 becomes 4,176 instead of 3,824. An estimate of about 3,800 catches it.

Try this at home

Read big numbers aloud from signs, prices and odometers. Ask what the 8 is worth, not just what it is.

OctoberMultiplying by one digit

What your child is learning

  • Multiplying by multiples of 10, 100 and 1,000
  • Area models and partial products
  • The standard multiplication algorithm
  • Estimating a product before working it out

Words to know: factor · product · partial product · area model · multiple

By the end of the month: Multiply a number up to four digits by a one-digit number using partial products and the standard algorithm, estimating first.

Sample question: What is 3,746 × 6? Estimate first.A strong answer: Estimate: 4,000 × 6 = 24,000. Partial products: 3,000 × 6 = 18,000, 700 × 6 = 4,200, 40 × 6 = 240, 6 × 6 = 36. Adding gives 22,476, a bit under 24,000 because I rounded up.

Watch for: Adding the regrouped number before multiplying. In 47 × 6, multiply 4 × 6 = 24 and then add the 4, giving 282; adding first gives 482. The estimate of 300 catches it.

Try this at home

Five minutes of multiplication facts a night. This is the month it starts to matter and it does not stop mattering.

NovemberFactors, patterns, and two-digit multiplying

What your child is learning

  • All the factor pairs of a number, and the greatest common factor
  • Finding the rule in a pattern and extending it
  • Multiplying two two-digit numbers
  • Why the standard algorithm works, not just how

Words to know: factor pair · common factor · multiple · pattern · rule

By the end of the month: Find all the factor pairs of a number, extend a pattern using its rule, and multiply two two-digit numbers.

Sample question: What is 34 × 26? Show how you know.A strong answer: I broke it into parts: 30 × 20 = 600, 30 × 6 = 180, 4 × 20 = 80, 4 × 6 = 24. Adding gives 884. My estimate was 30 × 30 = 900, so 884 is reasonable.

Watch for: Forgetting the zero in the second row. In 34 × 26, the row for 20 × 34 must be 680, not 68. The estimate of about 900 catches it.

Try this at home

Ask what two numbers multiply to make 36, then ask for another pair. Factors, out loud, in the car.

DecemberDividing by one digit

What your child is learning

  • Estimating a quotient using compatible numbers
  • Partial quotients, then the standard algorithm
  • Checking a division by multiplying back
  • What a remainder means, and what to do with it

Words to know: dividend · divisor · quotient · remainder · inverse

By the end of the month: Divide a number up to four digits by a one-digit number, check by multiplying back, and decide what the remainder means.

Sample question: 437 students ride in vans that hold 6 each. How many vans are needed?A strong answer: 43 ÷ 6 is 7 with 1 left, then 17 ÷ 6 is 2 with 5 left, so 72 r 5. Check: 72 × 6 + 5 = 437. Those 5 students still need a ride, so 73 vans.

Watch for: Leaving a zero out of the quotient, so 624 ÷ 6 becomes 14 instead of 104. Multiplying back, 14 × 6 = 84, shows right away that it is wrong.

Try this at home

Share something unevenly and ask what the remainder means here. Sometimes you round up, sometimes you ignore it.

JanuaryMultistep problems, then fractions

What your child is learning

  • Writing an equation with an unknown to match a problem
  • Solving problems that need more than one step
  • Judging whether an answer is reasonable
  • Equivalent fractions, and comparing them

Words to know: equation · unknown · not equal · numerator · denominator ·

equivalent

By the end of the month: Write an equation with a letter for the unknown to solve a two-step problem, judge if the answer is reasonable, and find equivalent fractions.

Sample question: A pack has 3 rows of 8 stickers. You give away 9. Write an equation and solve it.A strong answer: 3 × 8 − 9 = s. First 3 × 8 = 24 stickers, then 24 − 9 = 15, so s = 15. It makes sense because I gave away less than half of 24.

Watch for: Making equivalent fractions by adding the same number to the top and bottom, so 2/3 becomes 3/4. Only multiplying or dividing both by the same number works: 2/3 = 4/6.

Try this at home

Ask how they know an answer is sensible before you ask whether it is right.

FebruaryFractions

What your child is learning

  • Comparing fractions using 0, one half and 1 as benchmarks
  • Adding and subtracting fractions with the same denominator
  • Mixed numbers, and regrouping with them
  • A whole number times a unit fraction

Words to know: benchmark · mixed number · simplify · unit fraction · justify

By the end of the month: Compare fractions using benchmarks, add and subtract fractions and mixed numbers with like denominators, and multiply a whole number by a unit fraction.

Sample question: What is 2 3/8 + 1 7/8?A strong answer: Add the wholes: 2 + 1 = 3. Add the eighths: 3/8 + 7/8 = 10/8, which is 1 2/8. So 3 + 1 2/8 = 4 2/8, which simplifies to 4 1/4.

Watch for: Adding the denominators too, so 3/8 + 2/8 becomes 5/16. Ask whether the pieces are still eighths; the size of the piece does not change when you add.

Try this at home

Cut food into equal parts and add them out loud. Three eighths and two eighths, said aloud, is the whole lesson.

MarchDecimals

What your child is learning

  • Decimals through thousandths, and what each digit is worth
  • Reading, writing and comparing decimals
  • Fractions and decimals as two ways of writing the same thing
  • Placing decimals on a number line

Words to know: tenths · hundredths · thousandths · equivalent · benchmark

By the end of the unit: Read, write, compare and order decimals through thousandths, and write a fraction as a decimal and place both on a number line.

Sample question: Order 0.6, 0.06 and 0.606 from least to greatest. Explain how you know.A strong answer: I wrote them all in thousandths: 0.600, 0.060 and 0.606. That is 600, 60 and 606 thousandths, so the order is 0.06, 0.6, 0.606.

Watch for: Thinking a longer decimal is always larger, so 0.45 seems bigger than 0.5. Writing 0.5 as 0.50 lets them compare hundredths to hundredths.

Try this at home

Read prices and measurements aloud as decimals. Ask which is larger, 0.5 or 0.45, and why.

AprilAdding decimals, then measuring

What your child is learning

  • Adding and subtracting decimals, lining up the point
  • Choosing the right unit for length, weight and volume
  • Elapsed time, across morning and afternoon
  • Area and perimeter of rectangles and squares

Words to know: decimal point · convert · elapsed time · area · perimeter

By the end of the unit: Add and subtract decimals, find elapsed time across noon, choose sensible units, and find the area and perimeter of rectangles.

Sample question: A game starts at 10:45 a.m. and ends at 1:20 p.m. How long did it last?A strong answer: From 10:45 to 12:45 is 2 hours. From 12:45 to 1:20 is 35 more minutes. So the game lasted 2 hours and 35 minutes.

Watch for: Mixing up area and perimeter. For a 6 foot by 4 foot rug, the perimeter is 20 feet around the edge and the area is 24 square feet inside. Ask which one needs square units.

Try this at home

Ask how long something took when it crossed noon. Measure a room and ask for both the area and the perimeter.

MayData, and shapes

What your child is learning

  • Asking a question, collecting data, and drawing a line graph
  • Reading a line graph and drawing a conclusion from it
  • Probability: impossible, unlikely, likely, certain
  • Lines, angles, and classifying quadrilaterals

Words to know: line graph · trend · probability · parallel · perpendicular ·

quadrilateral

By the end of the month: Collect data and draw a line graph, describe its trend, use probability words correctly, and classify lines, angles and quadrilaterals.

Sample question: A bag has 7 red marbles and 1 blue marble. Is pulling blue impossible, unlikely, likely or certain?A strong answer: Unlikely. Only 1 of the 8 marbles is blue, so it probably will not happen. It is not impossible, though, because there is one blue marble in the bag.

Watch for: Saying a square is not a rectangle. A rectangle only needs four right angles, so every square is also a rectangle, a parallelogram and a quadrilateral.

Try this at home

Look at any graph in the news together and ask what it shows and what it does not.

JuneSolid figures, then the year

What your child is learning

  • Faces, edges and vertices of solid figures
  • Comparing flat shapes with solid ones
  • A review of every strand from September on
  • The final assessment

Words to know: face · edge · vertex · prism · pyramid · review

By the end of the month: Describe solid figures by their faces, edges and vertices, and show what they have mastered across every strand of the year.

Sample question: How many faces, edges and vertices does a rectangular prism have?A strong answer: It has 6 faces, like a cereal box with a top, a bottom and four sides. It has 12 edges where the faces meet and 8 vertices, which are the corners.

Watch for: Counting only the faces they can see in a drawing, so a cube seems to have 3 faces instead of 6. Let them hold a real box and count.

Try this at home

Keep the facts going through the summer. Five minutes a day protects the whole year.

THE TWO HABITS THAT RUN ALL YEAR

The multiplication facts. Virginia asks Grade 4 students to recall every fact through twelve times twelve automatically by June, with the matching division facts. The class practices five minutes every day, and five minutes at home on top of that is the most useful thing you can do. A child still counting to find six times seven will struggle with division, fractions, area and decimals.

Estimate before you calculate. Virginia asks for an estimate first, then for it to be checked afterward. So when you help, ask roughly how much before any working out. It is not a shortcut, it is the thing being assessed.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

School alone will not get your child here. Five minutes of facts a day at home is what makes the rest of Grade 4 possible.

  • Read, write and compare numbers up to nine digits
  • Know every multiplication and division fact through 12 x 12
  • Multiply two-digit numbers and divide by a one-digit number
  • Add, subtract and compare fractions with the same denominator
  • Read, compare and add decimals through thousandths
  • Find area and perimeter, and work out elapsed time
  • Draw and read a line graph, and explain what it shows

WHICH IS WHY THESE FIVE THINGS MATTER

  • Five minutes of multiplication facts every single day.
  • Ask for an estimate before the real answer, every time.
  • Ask how they worked it out, not just the answer.
  • Ask them to explain why an answer is reasonable.
  • If it is getting hard, tell the teacher in October, not April.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Three of our core values sit inside an ordinary mathematics lesson. Amanah, trust, is honest work: checking your answer against your estimate and owning a mistake rather than quietly changing it. Hikmah, wisdom, is choosing the strategy that fits the numbers and knowing when an estimate is enough. Adab is listening to how a classmate solved it before saying how you did.

Questions are always welcome. Please speak to your child’s teacher or the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School · 703-910-7029

Grade 4 · Science

Grade 4 Science

What your child will learn this year, month by month

PLEASE READ THIS FIRST

Everything on this sheet is tentative. Science meets four periods a week, so a closure costs real teaching time and a unit may arrive a week or two later than shown. What does not change is this: every unit here will be taught, one way or another, before your child leaves Grade 4. There is a short check most weeks and a unit assessment at the end of each unit.

Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Test dates live there, not on this sheet.

Late Aug & SeptThe solar system

What your child is learning

  • Telling an observation from an inference
  • The eight planets in order, and what makes each one different
  • Rotation, spinning on an axis, versus revolution, orbiting the sun
  • Building a model, then saying what the model cannot show

Words to know: observation · inference · orbit · rotation · revolution ·

model

By the end of the unit: Tell an observation from an inference, name the eight planets in order, and explain the difference between rotation and revolution.

Sample question: What is the difference between Earth's rotation and its revolution?A strong answer: Rotation is Earth spinning on its axis, which takes about 24 hours and gives us day and night. Revolution is Earth traveling around the sun, which takes about one year.

Watch for: Mixing up rotation and revolution. A quick check: rotation makes the day, revolution makes the year.

Try this at home

Ask whether something is what they saw or what they worked out. That difference is the whole first unit.

OctoberEarth, moon and sun

What your child is learning

  • Why we have day and night, and why the sun does not move
  • Why we have seasons: the tilt, not the distance
  • The phases of the moon and why the moon appears to change
  • How the moon and sun together cause the tides

Words to know: axis · tilt · direct rays · moon phase · tide · tidal range

By the end of the month: Explain day and night, the seasons, the phases of the moon, and the tides using how Earth, the moon and the sun move.

Sample question: Why is it hot in summer and cold in winter?A strong answer: Earth is tilted on its axis. In summer our half tilts toward the sun, so we get more direct rays and longer days. In winter we tilt away, so the rays are more slanted.

Watch for: Saying seasons happen because Earth is closer to the sun in summer. Ask why Australia has summer during our winter; distance cannot explain that, but tilt can.

Try this at home

Look at the moon together for a week and ask what changed. The phases are easier seen than read about.

NovemberWeather

What your child is learning

  • Using a thermometer, barometer, rain gauge and wind vane
  • Clouds and air pressure, and predicting from them
  • Common weather versus extreme weather, and staying safe
  • What happens to an ecosystem when the weather changes

Words to know: pressure · cumulus · cirrus · forecast · drought · flooding

By the end of the month: Use weather tools to collect data, read clouds and air pressure to predict the weather, and explain how to stay safe in extreme weather.

Sample question: The barometer shows air pressure is dropping. What weather might be coming, and why?A strong answer: Falling air pressure usually means clouds and rain or storms are on the way. Rising pressure usually brings clear, dry weather. So I would bring an umbrella tomorrow.

Watch for: Mixing up the instruments. Ask what each one measures: thermometer, temperature; barometer, air pressure; rain gauge, rainfall; wind vane, wind direction.

Try this at home

Check the forecast together and then check whether it was right. Predicting and then testing is the skill.

DecemberWeather, climate and the ocean

What your child is learning

  • Weather is today, climate is the pattern over many years
  • What the ocean floor actually looks like
  • Salinity, and what makes ocean water move
  • How tides and currents carry water and materials

Words to know: climate · trend · continental shelf · trench · salinity ·

current

By the end of the month: Explain the difference between weather and climate, describe the ocean floor, and explain how salinity, tides and currents move ocean water.

Sample question: What makes ocean water move?A strong answer: Wind pushes the surface into waves and currents. The moon's pull causes the tides. Differences in temperature and saltiness move water too, because cold, salty water is heavier and sinks.

Watch for: Using weather and climate as if they mean the same thing. One cold day does not change the climate; climate is the pattern over many years.

Try this at home

Talk about the difference between today’s weather and what our winters are usually like. That is climate.

JanuaryOcean life, then Virginia

What your child is learning

  • Producers, consumers and decomposers in a marine food web
  • How the ocean works as one connected system
  • Virginia’s natural resources and its waterways
  • What a watershed is, and why everyone lives downstream

Words to know: plankton · food web · resource · watershed · runoff

By the end of the month: Build a marine food web with producers, consumers and decomposers, and explain how a watershed carries water and runoff to the Chesapeake Bay.

Sample question: How can trash on a street in our town end up in the Chesapeake Bay?A strong answer: Rain washes it into a storm drain that empties into a creek. The creek flows to a river like the Occoquan or the Potomac, and that river flows into the Chesapeake Bay. We all live in its watershed.

Watch for: Leaving producers or decomposers out of an ocean food web. Ask where the energy starts; the answer is producers like phytoplankton, the tiny plant-like plankton.

Try this at home

Find your nearest stream or river on a map and trace where it goes. It ends up in the Chesapeake.

FebruaryVirginia’s natural resources

What your child is learning

  • Plants and animals as resources, and what they do for us
  • Rocks, minerals and ores in everyday objects
  • Forests, soil and land, and how they connect
  • Designing something that reduces runoff or erosion

Words to know: ore · mineral · soil · stewardship · conservation

By the end of the month: Identify Virginia's natural resources, trace everyday objects back to them, and design a way to reduce runoff or erosion.

Sample question: How can planting trees and grass near a stream reduce erosion?A strong answer: Roots hold the soil in place, so rain does not wash it into the stream. The plants also slow the water and soak some of it up, so less runoff carries dirt and pollution.

Watch for: Thinking renewable means a resource can never run out. Trees are renewable, but forests can still disappear if we cut them faster than they regrow.

Try this at home

Pick up an object at home and ask what natural resource it came from. Almost everything traces back.

MarchHow plants live

What your child is learning

  • Photosynthesis: plants make food, they do not take it from soil
  • What roots, stems and leaves each do
  • Running an investigation on sunlight and plant growth
  • Flowers, pollination and how new plants are made

Words to know: photosynthesis · chlorophyll · root · stem · pollination

By the end of the month: Explain photosynthesis, describe what roots, stems, leaves and flowers do, and run a fair test on how sunlight affects plant growth.

Sample question: Where does a plant get its food?A strong answer: A plant makes its own food in its leaves through photosynthesis. Chlorophyll captures sunlight, and the plant uses it with water and carbon dioxide from the air to make sugar. Soil gives water and minerals, not food.

Watch for: Saying plants get their food from the soil through their roots. Roots take in water and minerals; the food itself is made in the leaves.

Try this at home

Ask where a plant gets its food. Most adults get this wrong too, so let them correct you.

AprilAnimals and ecosystems

What your child is learning

  • How an animal’s body parts help it survive
  • Ecosystems, populations and communities, and the difference
  • Food chains and food webs, and which way the arrows point
  • Habitat, where it lives, versus niche, what it does there

Words to know: population · community · producer · consumer · habitat ·

niche

By the end of the month: Describe populations, communities and ecosystems, explain habitat versus niche, and draw food chains and webs with the arrows pointing the right way.

Sample question: In a food chain of grass, rabbit and fox, which way do the arrows point and why?A strong answer: The arrows go from the grass to the rabbit to the fox. They show which way the energy flows, so each arrow points to the animal doing the eating.

Watch for: Drawing food chain arrows backward, from the eater to what is eaten. Remind them the arrow means gives energy to.

Try this at home

Ask what would happen if one animal disappeared from a food web. Then ask what else changes.

MaySorting, and what changes

What your child is learning

  • Classifying organisms and building a key others can use
  • Predicting what happens when one part of an ecosystem changes
  • Pulling together space, weather, ocean and resources
  • Cumulative checks across the whole year

Words to know: classify · dichotomous key · interdependence ·

disturbance

By the end of the month: Build a dichotomous key that others can follow, and predict how one change in an ecosystem affects the other living things in it.

Sample question: In a pond food web, what happens if all the frogs disappear?A strong answer: The insects frogs eat would increase because nothing is eating them. Snakes and herons that eat frogs would have less food, so their numbers might drop. One change spreads through the whole web.

Watch for: Key steps that use opinions like pretty or big, which others cannot follow. Each step should be a yes or no question about something you can see or measure.

Try this at home

Ask them to explain a food web to you and then change one thing in it. Explaining is where it lands.

JuneThe capstone

What your child is learning

  • Choosing a real environmental problem to work on
  • Designing a solution, testing it, and improving it
  • Presenting the capstone to an audience beyond the class
  • A science portfolio from the whole year

Words to know: design · criteria · evidence · revise · present

By the end of the month: Design, test and improve a solution to a real environmental problem, and present it with evidence to an audience.

Sample question: What problem did your capstone solve, and how did your test show whether it worked?A strong answer: We worked on soil washing off a slope. We tested a model with and without plants, and without plants much more soil washed away. Then we improved the design and tested it again.

Watch for: Changing more than one thing at a time in a test, so they cannot tell what made the difference. Ask what they changed and what they kept the same.

Try this at home

Ask them to practice the capstone presentation on you. Saying it out loud twice beats saying it once.

THE WEATHER LOG, AND THE CAPSTONE

Two things run longer than a single lesson. From late October your child keeps a weather log, recording the same measurements week after week including the weeks when nothing happens, because that is what makes a record trustworthy. And in June the year ends with a capstone: a real environmental problem your child chooses, designs a solution for, tests, and then presents to an audience beyond their own classroom. Ask about both.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

School alone will not get your child here. Grade 4 science is mostly about noticing, and the noticing has to happen outside the classroom too.

  • Explain day, night, seasons, moon phases and tides using a model
  • Read weather instruments, predict from the data, and tell weather from climate
  • Describe the ocean floor and what makes ocean water move
  • Name Virginia’s resources and explain what a watershed is
  • Explain photosynthesis, and what a root, stem and leaf do
  • Trace energy through a food web and predict what a change does

WHICH IS WHY THESE FIVE THINGS MATTER

  • Ask what they learned in science this week.
  • Ask how they know. Every time.
  • Let them explain something to you. Explaining it out loud is how it sticks.
  • Say you do not know when you do not, then find out together.
  • Look at the moon, the sky and the weather with them. It is the whole first half of the year.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

In October your child learns the phases of the moon and the cycle our own calendar is built on, so Ramadan and Eid arrive out of something they can now explain. Amanah shows up in the weather log: keeping an honest record week after week, including the dull weeks, is a trust before it is a science skill. And stewardship of land and water is treated as a responsibility to the people who come after us, not only the ones here now.

Questions are always welcome. Please speak to your child’s teacher or the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School · 703-910-7029

Grade 4 · Social Studies

Grade 4 Social Studies

Virginia Studies: the story of our own state

PLEASE READ THIS FIRST

This guide is a plan, not a promise. The months are approximate, and the order of the units may shift. Every topic here is a Virginia Studies standard and every one will be taught before your child leaves Grade 4.

Timing and detail will change, but where your child ends up in June will not. Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo, and test and assessment dates live there, not on this sheet.

SOME OF THIS YEAR IS HARD, AND WE WILL NOT SOFTEN IT

Three parts of this year are difficult: how enslavement became race-based by Virginia law, that the institution of slavery was the cause of the Civil War, and how Jim Crow removed rights that had been won. The standards name all of it plainly, so we teach it plainly. It falls around December, March and April, though those months may move. Ten year olds can hold this when the teaching is calm and factual. What they cannot hold is a vague version, because vagueness reads to a child as something hidden. If you would like to know more before it is taught, please ask.

Late Aug & SeptHistorians, and Virginia’s land

What your child is learning

  • What a historian does, and how to tell whether a source can be trusted
  • Locating Virginia and the five states that border it
  • Virginia’s five regions: Coastal Plain, Piedmont, Blue Ridge, Valley and Ridge, Appalachian Plateau
  • Why rivers and the Chesapeake Bay shaped where people settled

Words to know: primary source · region · Piedmont · Tidewater · fall line · Chesapeake

Bay

By the end of the unit: Locate Virginia and its neighbors, name and describe its five regions, and explain how rivers and the Chesapeake Bay shaped where people settled.

Sample question: Why did early towns in Virginia grow along rivers and the Chesapeake Bay?A strong answer: Rivers and the Bay gave people water, fish and a way to ship goods by boat. Ships could only sail up to the fall line, where waterfalls block the way, so towns grew there too.

Watch for: Mixing up a primary source, made at the time by someone who was there, with a secondary source written later. Ask whether the writer was actually there.

Try this at home

Name the region you live in and find it on a map. Ask what the land is like an hour east and an hour west.

OctoberVirginia’s Indigenous nations

What your child is learning

  • The people who lived here first, and how archaeologists know
  • Werowocomoco, and what artifacts tell us
  • The three language groups: Algonquian, Siouan and Iroquoian
  • Virginia’s Indigenous nations today, not only in the past

Words to know: Indigenous · archaeologist · artifact · Werowocomoco · Powhatan ·

Monacan

By the end of the month: Explain how archaeologists learn about the past, name the three language groups, and describe Virginia's Indigenous nations then and today.

Sample question: How do archaeologists know what life was like at Werowocomoco?A strong answer: They dig carefully and study artifacts like pottery, tools and the remains of houses. Each artifact is a clue, so they can figure out how people lived, cooked and traded there long ago.

Watch for: Talking about Virginia Indians only in the past tense. Virginia has eleven state-recognized tribes today, and seven of them are also federally recognized.

Try this at home

Ask what surprised them. Most children assume this story ended long ago, and it did not.

NovemberJamestown

What your child is learning

  • Why the English came, and why they chose that spot
  • The hardships, and how the colony survived
  • The role of the Powhatan in keeping the colonists alive
  • The year 1619: the first General Assembly, the arrival of Africans, and of women

Words to know: charter · colony · cash crop · tobacco · General Assembly · 1619

By the end of the month: Explain why the English settled at Jamestown, what nearly ended the colony, and why the year 1619 matters.

Sample question: Why did the Jamestown colony nearly fail?A strong answer: The settlers chose a swampy spot with bad water, so many got sick. Many did not want to farm, and food ran out. They survived with help from the Powhatan and later by growing tobacco to sell.

Watch for: Remembering only one event from 1619. Three things happened that year: the first General Assembly met, the first Africans arrived, and many more English women arrived.

Try this at home

Ask why the colony nearly failed. The answer is more interesting than the one most adults remember.

DecemberLife in the Virginia colony

What your child is learning

  • Farming, and why it shaped everything else
  • How Indigenous, European and African cultures all shaped colonial Virginia
  • The difference between an indentured servant and an enslaved person
  • How enslavement became race-based by law, and why the capital moved to Williamsburg

Words to know: agriculture · indentured servant · enslaved · law · Williamsburg · trade

By the end of the month: Explain how farming shaped colonial life, compare indentured servants with enslaved people, and explain why the capital moved to Williamsburg.

Sample question: How was an indentured servant different from an enslaved person?A strong answer: An indentured servant agreed to work for a set number of years, often to pay for the trip, and then was free. An enslaved person was held for life, and their children were enslaved too.

Watch for: Treating indentured servants and enslaved people as the same. Listen for the key difference: servitude ended after a set time, while slavery, made race-based by law, did not.

Try this at home

This is hard material. Ask what they learned and listen. See the note above.

JanuaryThe American Revolution

What your child is learning

  • What convinced Virginians to declare independence
  • Washington, Jefferson, Mason and Madison
  • James Armistead Lafayette, and the women, Indigenous people and free and enslaved Blacks who took part
  • Why the capital moved to Richmond, and why Yorktown mattered

Words to know: Declaration of Independence · principle · Yorktown · Richmond ·

patriot

By the end of the month: Explain why Virginians declared independence, describe the roles of key leaders and other Virginians, and explain why Yorktown mattered.

Sample question: Why was the Battle of Yorktown so important?A strong answer: At Yorktown, American and French forces trapped the British army, and it surrendered in 1781. That ended the major fighting, and soon Britain accepted that America was independent.

Watch for: Thinking only the famous leaders won independence. Ask about James Armistead Lafayette, an enslaved man whose spying helped win at Yorktown.

Try this at home

Ask who else was in the story besides the famous four. They will have a name you do not expect.

FebruaryA new nation

What your child is learning

  • The Virginia Declaration of Rights and the Statute for Religious Freedom
  • How Virginia’s documents shaped the Bill of Rights
  • How geography and new technology pushed people west
  • Nat Turner’s Rebellion, and what followed it

Words to know: Bill of Rights · religious freedom · constitution · turnpike · rebellion

By the end of the month: Explain how Virginia's Declaration of Rights and Statute for Religious Freedom shaped the Bill of Rights, and why people moved west.

Sample question: Why does the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom still matter today?A strong answer: Thomas Jefferson wrote it so people could worship as they choose and not be forced to support a state church. It helped shape the First Amendment, so everyone in America has religious freedom.

Watch for: Mixing up the Virginia Declaration of Rights, written by George Mason, with the Statute for Religious Freedom, written by Thomas Jefferson. Both shaped the Bill of Rights.

Try this at home

The Statute for Religious Freedom is worth reading a line of together. It is why a school like ours can exist.

MarchThe Civil War

What your child is learning

  • John Brown and Harpers Ferry
  • That the institution of slavery was the cause of the war
  • The Underground Railroad and Harriet Tubman
  • Why Virginia split, and how West Virginia came to exist

Words to know: secession · Union · Confederacy · Underground Railroad · West

Virginia

By the end of the month: Explain that slavery caused the Civil War, describe John Brown's raid and the Underground Railroad, and explain how West Virginia was formed.

Sample question: Why did Virginia split in two during the Civil War?A strong answer: Virginia seceded and joined the Confederacy, but many people in the northwestern counties disagreed. They stayed loyal to the Union and formed the new state of West Virginia in 1863.

Watch for: Giving a cause other than slavery for the war. The Virginia standards are clear that the institution of slavery was the cause; listen for that in their explanation.

Try this at home

Ask them to explain why the war started. The standard is clear about it and so is the class.

AprilAfter the war

What your child is learning

  • The Thirteenth, Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments
  • Freedmen’s Schools, and John Mercer Langston’s election to Congress
  • Plessy v. Ferguson, segregation and Jim Crow
  • Railroads, new industries, and Virginia’s growing cities

Words to know: amendment · Reconstruction · segregation · Jim Crow · railroad ·

urban

By the end of the month: Explain what the Reconstruction amendments did, how Jim Crow laws took rights away, and how railroads and industry grew Virginia's cities.

Sample question: What did the Thirteenth, Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments do?A strong answer: The Thirteenth ended slavery. The Fourteenth made formerly enslaved people citizens with equal protection of the law. The Fifteenth gave Black men the right to vote.

Watch for: Thinking rights, once won, stayed secure. Jim Crow laws and Plessy v. Ferguson took many back; ask what separate but equal really meant in practice.

Try this at home

This unit is about rights won and then taken back. Ask how that felt to the people it happened to.

MayThe World Wars, and Civil Rights

What your child is learning

  • What Virginians did at home and abroad in both world wars
  • Voting rights taken away, and how they were won back
  • Barbara Johns, who led a school strike at sixteen
  • Massive Resistance, and Virginians in Brown v. Board of Education

Words to know: veteran · Medal of Honor · desegregation · Massive Resistance ·

Barbara Johns

By the end of the month: Describe how Virginians served in both world wars, and explain how Barbara Johns, Brown v. Board and Massive Resistance shaped civil rights in Virginia.

Sample question: Why did Barbara Johns lead a strike at her school in 1951?A strong answer: Her school in Farmville was overcrowded and in poor shape, while the white school was much better. She led students out to demand a fair school, and their case became part of Brown v. Board of Education.

Watch for: Thinking schools desegregated right after Brown v. Board in 1954. Virginia leaders answered with Massive Resistance, and some schools closed rather than integrate.

Try this at home

Barbara Johns was sixteen. Ask what your child would do if their school were treated unfairly.

JuneVirginia then and now

What your child is learning

  • Why Virginia is called the Mother of Presidents
  • What Virginia makes and sells to the world today
  • A review of the whole year, from the land to the present
  • A final piece of work presented to an audience

Words to know: Mother of Presidents · export · global economy · innovation · industry

By the end of the month: Tell the story of Virginia from its land to today, explain why it is called the Mother of Presidents, and describe what it sells to the world.

Sample question: Why is Virginia called the Mother of Presidents?A strong answer: Eight presidents were born in Virginia, more than in any other state. They include George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, James Madison and James Monroe.

Watch for: Thinking Virginia's economy is still mostly tobacco farms. Today it also depends on technology, government work, shipping through the Port of Virginia, and many kinds of farming.

Try this at home

Ask them to tell you the story of Virginia from start to finish. That is exactly what June asks of them.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

School alone will not get your child here. This subject lives or dies on whether it gets talked about at home.

  • Name Virginia’s five regions and describe each one
  • Say who lived in Virginia first, and who lives here now
  • Explain why Jamestown nearly failed, and what 1619 changed
  • Explain what the Civil War was fought over
  • Describe what Reconstruction gave and what Jim Crow took back
  • Name Virginians who changed the law, and say how

WHICH IS WHY THESE FIVE THINGS MATTER

  • Ask what they learned in Social Studies this week.
  • Ask how they know, not just what happened.
  • Ask whose side the writer was on.
  • Take them somewhere in Virginia and name what you see.
  • If it is getting hard, tell the teacher early, not in April.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

History is told by someone, and how it is told is a matter of adab and amanah. This year your child learns that Virginia’s Indigenous nations were here first and are here still, that 1619 brought a representative assembly and the first enslaved Africans in the same year, and that rights can be granted by law and removed by law. Telling that story honestly is the same honesty we ask of them everywhere else.

This guide is a plan, not a promise. Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo.

Woodbridge Islamic School · 703-910-7029

Grade 5 · English

Grade 5 English

A family guide to the year: reading and writing, month by month

THIS PLAN IS TENTATIVE

This is a plan, not a promise. These are the overall topics for each month. Order and timing will change as the year goes on, and months are approximate. The goals for June stay the same. Anything that changes is emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Quiz and test dates are not printed here; they live there, where they stay current.

This guide covers Grade 5 English, both reading and writing. Your child works from Savvas myView Literacy, plus other selections and texts chosen by our own teachers at WIS. (Tentative: the full book list will be confirmed.)

SeptemberInformational text

What your child is learning

  • Reading: Call Me Joe, Paper Son, The Places Scientists Will Go and The Great Migration, for central idea, text features, text structure and point of view. Ibn Battuta read aloud.
  • Writing: a baseline sample, then short responses that state a central idea and back it with evidence from the text.
  • Handed in: two section quizzes, a spelling and vocabulary quiz, and a central idea response.

Words to know: central idea, text feature, text structure, summarize, point of view

By the end of the month: Name the central idea of an article and support it with two details, using text features and structure to find them.

Sample question: What is the central idea of The Great Migration, and which details prove it?A strong answer: The central idea is that millions of Black families moved from the South to Northern cities looking for a better life. One detail says they left to escape unfair laws, and another says Northern factories had jobs.

Watch for: Retelling every detail instead of naming the big idea. A summary gives the central idea and only the details that matter most; a retelling goes through everything in order. Keep summaries short.

Try this at home

Ask your child to tell you an article in three sentences. That is summarizing.

Late September and early OctoberPersonal narrative

What your child is learning

  • Reading: mentor narratives from Flying Lessons, read for how a writer holds one small moment still.
  • Writing: the full process on one small moment, plan, draft, peer review, revise, edit, publish. An Ibn Sina article rewritten in his own voice.
  • Handed in: the planning organizer, then the personal narrative essay, scored on the narrative rubric.

Words to know: small moment, sensory language, voice, sequence, revise

By the end of the unit: Write a personal narrative about one small moment, using sensory details and dialogue, and revise it to make it stronger.

Sample question: In your own narrative, how can you make one small moment feel big?A strong answer: Slow the moment down. Instead of writing “I scored a goal,” show the few seconds before the kick: the noise around you, how the ball felt, and what you were thinking, so a short moment fills the whole page.

Watch for: Writing a bed to bed story, from waking up to falling asleep. If the draft covers a whole day or trip, help your child pick the one minute that mattered most.

Try this at home

Ask for the story of one ordinary afternoon in detail. That is what the unit asks of them.

OctoberInformation and argument text

What your child is learning

  • Reading: How Scientists Study Ocean Life, From Far from Shore, Protecting Habitats, A Place for Frogs, and the argument Let Wild Animals Be Wild.
  • Skills: reading an infographic, drawing inferences, and naming an author’s purpose and organizational pattern.
  • Handed in: a text dependent response, a section quiz, and a graded class discussion.

Words to know: evidence, inference, infographic, author’s purpose, organization

By the end of the month: Draw an inference from an informational or argument text, name the author's purpose, and point to the sentence that proves it.

Sample question: In Let Wild Animals Be Wild, what does the author want you to believe, and how do you know?A strong answer: The author wants us to believe wild animals belong in their natural habitats, not as pets. I know because the author gives reasons and uses words like should, which shows the purpose is to persuade.

Watch for: Giving an inference with no proof. If your child says I just know, ask which words in the text led them there.

Try this at home

When your child states a fact, ask which sentence in the text says so.

NovemberResearch project and informational writing

What your child is learning

  • Project: contributions of the Muslim world. Each student takes one figure or contribution, researches it and presents it.
  • Writing: an informational piece of their own with headings and text features, from prewriting through publishing.
  • Handed in: a research checkpoint, a prewriting organizer, a draft conference and the published piece.

Words to know: research, source, heading, draft, revise, publish

By the end of the month: Research one contribution of the Muslim world and publish an informational piece with headings, text features and facts from trusted sources.

Sample question: Why did you add headings to your informational piece, and what does each one tell the reader?A strong answer: Headings split my piece into parts so a reader can find things fast. My piece on al-Khwarizmi has one heading for his life, one for algebra, and one for how we still use his ideas today.

Watch for: Copying sentences straight from a source. If the writing sounds too grown up or uses words your child cannot explain, ask them to say it in their own words.

Try this at home

Ask who your child chose for the project and why, then what they still cannot answer about them.

DecemberPoetry and figurative language

What your child is learning

  • Reading: A New Life in a New Land, A Poetry Machine, Perfect Inspiration and Rumi in translation, with poems compared across one theme.
  • Writing: original poems in several forms, acrostic, haiku and free verse.
  • Handed in: a figurative language check, a poetry analysis response, the poetry assessment, and a reading aloud at the Open Mic.

Words to know: imagery, metaphor, simile, stanza, rhyme, free verse

By the end of the month: Identify similes, metaphors and imagery in a poem, explain what they show, and write original poems in several forms.

Sample question: What is the difference between a simile and a metaphor? Give an example of each.A strong answer: A simile compares two things using like or as, such as the snow was like a blanket. A metaphor says one thing is another, such as the snow was a blanket. Both help you picture it.

Watch for: Calling every comparison a simile. If it uses like or as, it is a simile; if it says one thing is another, it is a metaphor. For haiku, count syllables on fingers: 5, 7, 5.

Try this at home

Ask to hear a poem read twice, once for the words and once for the sound.

JanuaryRealistic fiction

What your child is learning

  • Reading: Hatchet, Morning Serenade, Advice from Mr. Chan, How Many Pets, Snow Ball and The Proudest Blue.
  • Skills: character traits and motivation, dialogue, point of view, plot structure and theme.
  • Handed in: a trait evidence chart, a selection quiz, a scene rewritten from another point of view, a plot map, and their own realistic fiction story.

Words to know: character trait, motivation, conflict, plot, theme, dialogue

By the end of the month: Describe a character's traits and motivation with evidence, map a story's plot, and state its theme as a full sentence.

Sample question: In Hatchet, what does Brian want, and what stands in his way?A strong answer: Brian wants to survive and be rescued after the plane crash. Nature stands in his way: no food, bad weather, and only a hatchet. He learns that patience and not giving up keep him alive, which is the theme.

Watch for: Giving a one-word theme like courage. A theme is a full sentence lesson, such as never give up, even when things seem hopeless.

Try this at home

After a book or a show, ask what the character wanted and what stood in the way.

FebruaryBiography

What your child is learning

  • Reading: The Early Civil Rights Movement, The Underground Railroad, and The Amazing Discoveries of Ibn Sina as the anchor biography.
  • Skills: timelines, sequence, summarizing nonfiction, and the mark one person leaves on others.
  • Handed in: a timeline, a biography summary, a trait evidence chart and reading questions.

Words to know: biography, chronology, sequence, summary, impact

By the end of the month: Put the key events of a person's life in order on a timeline and summarize how that person affected others.

Sample question: What is one way Ibn Sina still affects people today?A strong answer: Ibn Sina wrote The Canon of Medicine, a huge book about diseases and cures. Doctors in the Middle East and Europe used it for hundreds of years, so his ideas helped shape modern medicine.

Watch for: Listing dates without saying why they matter. On the timeline, each event should have a short note on what changed because of it.

Try this at home

Ask who your child would write a biography about, and the one question they would ask that person.

MarchNonfiction, then historical fiction

What your child is learning

  • Reading: I Will Go West and How Volcanoes Work, and one real event told two different ways.
  • Writing: a historical fiction piece of their own, planned, drafted, revised and published.
  • Handed in: a fact versus fiction sort, a reading assessment, and a book report (tentative: details will be confirmed). School is closed for Eid al-Fitr in early March.

Words to know: historical fiction, fact, opinion, primary source, text structure

By the end of the month: Tell fact from fiction in historical writing and write a historical fiction story that blends real events with invented characters.

Sample question: In historical fiction, what can a writer make up, and what must stay true?A strong answer: The writer can invent characters, conversations and small events. The time period, real places and big historical events must stay true, like real dates and the tools people actually used back then.

Watch for: Mixing modern details into the past, like a phone in a covered wagon story. Ask your child how they checked that each object and job fit the time period.

Try this at home

Ask which parts of their story are real and which they invented. They should know the line.

AprilOpinion and argument writing

What your child is learning

  • Reading: You Are What You Eat, Saving Natural Habitats and Deforestation Must Be Controlled, read for claim, reasons and evidence.
  • Skills: counterclaims, transitions, introductions and conclusions, plus a structured class debate.
  • Handed in: a claim and evidence organizer, quick writes, the debate, and a published opinion essay.

Words to know: claim, reason, evidence, counterclaim, transition, conclusion

By the end of the month: Write an opinion essay with a clear claim, reasons backed by evidence, a counterclaim answered, and transitions linking the ideas.

Sample question: In Deforestation Must Be Controlled, what is the claim, and which reason supports it best?A strong answer: The claim is that people must limit cutting down forests. A strong reason is that forests are home to many animals, and when the trees are cut, those animals lose their habitats. The author backs this with facts.

Watch for: Confusing a reason with evidence. A reason says why; evidence is a fact, number or example that proves it. Because it is better is not evidence.

Try this at home

Let your child argue for something small at home, but require three reasons with evidence.

MayResearch skills

What your child is learning

  • Skills: writing a research question, judging whether a source can be trusted, note taking and paraphrasing.
  • Topic: one influential person of their choice, such as Malala Yousafzai, Ibn Battuta or Harriet Tubman.
  • Handed in: a research notebook check, a paraphrasing task and a source log.

Words to know: source, paraphrase, cite, plagiarism, outline

By the end of the month: Write a focused research question, judge whether a source can be trusted, and take notes in their own words with the source listed.

Sample question: How do you know a website about Harriet Tubman can be trusted?A strong answer: I check who made it, like a museum, a university or a government site. I look for an author and a date, and I check that other trusted sources say the same thing.

Watch for: Paraphrasing by swapping a few words for synonyms. Real paraphrasing means closing the source, writing the idea from memory, then checking it back.

Try this at home

Ask how they know a website can be trusted. Two reasons, not one.

Late May and JuneResearch project and presentation

What your child is learning

  • Work: notes pulled into one product, visuals designed, then rehearsal with a partner.
  • Presenting: speaking to the class, naming sources aloud, and taking questions from the audience.
  • Handed in: a product checkpoint, the presentation and product scored on rubrics, and a self reflection.
  • Grade 5 graduation is Saturday June 19.

Words to know: synthesize, visual, audience, rehearse, reflection

By the end of the unit: Combine research notes into one product, present it clearly to an audience, name sources aloud, and answer questions.

Sample question: What did you learn about your person, and where did that information come from?A strong answer: I learned Malala Yousafzai spoke up for girls' education in Pakistan and won the Nobel Peace Prize at seventeen. I found this in a biography from the school library and on the Nobel Prize website.

Watch for: Reading slides word for word with eyes on the screen. During home rehearsal, ask your child to tell you the main points without looking.

Try this at home

Let your child rehearse on you. Listen the whole way through, then ask one question.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Read a grade level text and explain its central idea using evidence from it.
  • Plan, revise and publish a narrative, an informational piece and an opinion essay.
  • Take notes from sources, paraphrase, and say where a fact came from.
  • Present to a group for several minutes, with visuals, and be understood.

Talking about this at home makes a real difference. Children who discuss their learning with family build these skills with more confidence.

SO HERE IS WHAT HELPS MOST AT HOME

  • Twenty minutes of reading every night.
  • Talk about the book rather than quizzing on it. One real question is enough.
  • Ask “where does it say that?” whenever your child tells you what a text meant.
  • Let your child read their writing aloud to you before they hand it in.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Reading and writing are how our students take hold of knowledge and pass it on, so this year is ilm in practice. Citing a source is taught as amanah, returning what belongs to someone else, with the isnad shown as an early and careful form of citation. Writing a counterclaim fairly and listening without interrupting are taught as adab. And when Ibn Sina and Rumi sit beside the American texts, our children see that these genres belong to their tradition too, Inshallah.

Questions are always welcome. Please reach out through Class Dojo or the office.

Grade 5 · Mathematics

Grade 5 Mathematics

A family guide to the year, month by month

THIS PLAN IS TENTATIVE

This is a plan, not a promise. These are the overall topics for each month. Order and timing will change as the year goes on, and months are approximate. A unit may run a week longer because a class needs it. What we plan for is this: every topic here is scheduled to be taught before your child leaves Grade 5. Anything that changes is emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Test dates are not printed here; they live there, where they stay current.

Homework goes home on Monday and is due the following Monday, five nights of about twenty minutes. There is a short graded check most weeks and a full period test every two weeks, so nothing is left to build up.

Late August and SeptemberPlace value, decimals and prime numbers

What your child is learning

  • Reading and writing decimals through thousandths.
  • Writing a fraction as a decimal, and a decimal as a fraction.
  • Comparing and ordering a set of fractions and decimals together.
  • Prime and composite numbers, and breaking a number into its prime factors.

Words to know: tenths, hundredths, thousandths, equivalent, prime, composite, factor, prime factorization

By the end of the unit: Read, write and compare decimals through thousandths, switch between fractions and decimals, and write a number as a product of primes.

Sample question: Which is greater, 0.45 or 3/8? Then write 36 as a product of prime numbers.A strong answer: 3/8 is 0.375. Comparing tenths, 4 tenths beats 3 tenths, so 0.45 is greater. For 36, I split it into 6 × 6, then each 6 into 2 × 3, so 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3.

Watch for: Thinking a longer decimal is bigger, so 0.125 seems greater than 0.5. Ask your child to add zeros: 0.500 compared with 0.125 makes it clear.

Try this at home

Read prices and measurements aloud. Ask what the 7 is worth, not just what it is. Ask whether a number is prime, out loud, in the car.

OctoberAdding and subtracting decimals, then multiplying big numbers

What your child is learning

  • Estimating first, then adding and subtracting decimals.
  • Lining up place value, not lining up digits.
  • Multiplying three digits by two digits.
  • Checking every answer against the estimate.

Words to know: estimate, sum, difference, factor, product, partial product

By the end of the unit: Estimate, then add and subtract decimals by lining up place values, and multiply a three-digit number by a two-digit number.

Sample question: What is 12.5 + 3.75? What is 214 × 36?A strong answer: Line up the decimal points: 12.50 + 3.75 = 16.25. For 214 × 36: 214 × 30 = 6,420 and 214 × 6 = 1,284, so 6,420 + 1,284 = 7,704. The estimate 200 × 40 = 8,000 is close.

Watch for: Lining up digits on the right instead of the decimal points, so 4.5 + 2.35 comes out as 2.80. The estimate, about 5 plus 2, shows the real answer is near 7.

Try this at home

Add up a receipt together before the total is read out. Quarter 1 exams are October 13 to 16.

NovemberMultiplying decimals

What your child is learning

  • Multiplying a decimal by a whole number, with models first.
  • Multiplying a decimal by a decimal.
  • Deciding where the decimal point goes, and why it goes there.
  • Starting division with two digit divisors.

Words to know: area model, partial product, distributive property, quotient

By the end of the unit: Multiply decimals by whole numbers and by decimals, using an estimate to decide where the decimal point belongs.

Sample question: What is 2.4 × 0.3, and how do you know where the decimal point goes?A strong answer: First 24 × 3 = 72. The factors have two decimal places in all, so the answer is 0.72. Check: three tenths of about 2 is about 0.6, so 0.72 makes sense.

Watch for: Expecting multiplication to always make a number bigger. Multiplying by a decimal less than 1, like 0.3, gives a smaller product. An answer of 7.2 here means the point is misplaced.

Try this at home

Ask roughly how much before they solve it. If the estimate and the answer are far apart, check both again.

DecemberDividing whole numbers and decimals

What your child is learning

  • Estimating a quotient using compatible numbers.
  • Dividing four digit numbers by two digit divisors.
  • What a remainder means in the actual problem.
  • Dividing decimals, and a semester review before the break.

Words to know: dividend, divisor, quotient, remainder, compatible numbers

By the end of the month: Divide four-digit numbers by two-digit divisors, divide decimals, and explain what a remainder means in a word problem.

Sample question: 158 students ride buses that hold 24 each. How many buses are needed?A strong answer: 24 × 6 = 144, and 158 minus 144 leaves 14, so 158 ÷ 24 is 6 remainder 14. Those 14 students still need seats, so we need 7 buses.

Watch for: Writing 6 R14 as the final answer without thinking about the story. Ask what the leftover means: here it is extra students, so the answer rounds up to 7.

Try this at home

Share something unevenly and ask what the remainder means here. Sometimes you round up, sometimes you ignore it.

JanuaryMid year exams, then order of operations

What your child is learning

  • A full review week, one day per strand, January 4 to 8.
  • Mid year exams, January 11 to 15.
  • The order of operations, and why everyone must use the same order.
  • Writing an expression to match a description, and saying which step comes first.

Words to know: order of operations, expression, parentheses, simplify

By the end of the month: Simplify expressions using the order of operations and write an expression that matches a word description.

Sample question: What is 20 ÷ (2 + 3) × 4 + 1?A strong answer: Parentheses first: 2 + 3 = 5. Then multiply and divide from left to right: 20 ÷ 5 = 4, then 4 × 4 = 16. Last, add: 16 + 1 = 17.

Watch for: Always multiplying before dividing. They go left to right together, so 20 ÷ 5 × 2 is 8, not 2. Ask your child which step they did first and why.

Try this at home

The review sheet comes home before each test. Work through it together rather than reading it.

FebruaryPatterns and letters, then fractions

What your child is learning

  • A letter or a box standing for a number we do not know yet.
  • Writing an equation from a real situation.
  • Finding a common denominator.
  • Adding and subtracting fractions and mixed numbers with different denominators.

Words to know: variable, equation, pattern, common denominator, simplest form, mixed number

By the end of the month: Write an equation with a variable from a real situation, and add and subtract fractions and mixed numbers with unlike denominators.

Sample question: What is 2 1/2 + 1 2/3?A strong answer: The common denominator is 6, so 1/2 = 3/6 and 2/3 = 4/6. Wholes: 2 + 1 = 3. Fractions: 3/6 + 4/6 = 7/6, which is 1 1/6. Total: 4 1/6. Estimate: 2.5 + 1.7 is about 4, so it fits.

Watch for: Adding tops and bottoms straight across, so 1/2 + 1/3 becomes 2/5. Ask: is 2/5 even bigger than 1/2? A sum cannot be smaller than one of its parts.

Try this at home

Halve and double recipes out loud. Ask which is bigger, three fourths or two thirds, and how they know.

MarchMultiplying by a fraction, then measuring

What your child is learning

  • School is closed March 1 to 12 for Eid al-Fitr.
  • Multiplying a whole number by a fraction, with models.
  • Choosing the right metric unit for length, mass and liquid volume.
  • Estimating and then measuring for real.

Words to know: millimeter, centimeter, meter, kilometer, gram, kilogram, milliliter, liter

By the end of the month: Multiply a whole number by a fraction using models, and choose sensible metric units to estimate and measure length, mass and liquid volume.

Sample question: What is 3/4 of 20? Would you measure a water bottle in milliliters or liters?A strong answer: 20 ÷ 4 = 5, so each fourth is 5, and three fourths is 3 × 5 = 15. A small water bottle holds about 500 milliliters, so milliliters fit best. A liter is more like a big juice bottle.

Watch for: Mixing up the size of metric units. 1 meter is 100 centimeters or 1,000 millimeters. If a pencil is recorded as 15 meters, the unit is wrong.

Try this at home

Measure things at home in centimeters and again in millimeters. Guess first, then check. Quarter 3 exams are March 30 to April 2.

AprilArea, volume, angles and triangles

What your child is learning

  • Finding the area of a right triangle, and where the formula comes from.
  • Volume of a box, built with cubes before any formula.
  • Deciding whether a problem wants perimeter, area or volume.
  • Measuring and drawing angles with a protractor.
  • Sorting triangles by their sides and by their angles.
  • The three angles in any triangle add up to 180 degrees, and using that to find a missing angle.

Words to know: area, volume, cubic units, right triangle, acute, obtuse, equilateral, isosceles, scalene

By the end of the month: Find the area of a right triangle and the volume of a box, measure angles with a protractor, classify triangles by sides and angles, and find a missing angle in a triangle.

Sample question: A box is 5 cm long, 3 cm wide and 4 cm tall. What is its volume?A strong answer: The bottom layer holds 5 × 3 = 15 cubes. There are 4 layers, so 15 × 4 = 60. The volume is 60 cubic centimeters.

Watch for: Reading the wrong scale on the protractor, so a 40° angle is called 140°. Ask first whether the angle is smaller or bigger than a square corner; that tells which number fits.

Try this at home

Ask which unit fits: is this a length, a surface or a space? A protractor for home costs about five dollars and is worth it.

MayData, averages and chance

What your child is learning

  • Asking a question, collecting the data, and showing it properly.
  • Line plots and stem and leaf plots.
  • Mean, median, mode and range, and what each one actually tells you.
  • Listing every possible outcome, and finding how likely one is.

Words to know: line plot, stem and leaf, mean, median, mode, range, outcome, sample space

By the end of the month: Show data in line plots and stem and leaf plots, and find and explain the mean, median, mode and range.

Sample question: Find the mean, median, mode and range of 4, 7, 7, 9, 13.A strong answer: Mean: 4 + 7 + 7 + 9 + 13 = 40, and 40 ÷ 5 = 8. Median: the middle number is 7. Mode: 7, since it appears twice. Range: 13 minus 4 = 9.

Watch for: Picking the median without putting the numbers in order first. Ask your child to rewrite the list from least to greatest before choosing the middle.

Try this at home

Find the average of anything: trip times, scores, ages at a family gathering. Ask whether the average is fair here.

JuneFinishing, and looking at Grade 6

What your child is learning

  • Probability and counting all the possibilities.
  • Final exams, June 7 to 11.
  • A first look at Grade 6 work, including the coordinate plane.
  • Grade 5 graduation is Saturday June 19.

Words to know: probability, tree diagram, coordinate plane, ordered pair

By the end of the month: List every possible outcome with a tree diagram or table, write a probability as a fraction, and plot ordered pairs on a coordinate plane.

Sample question: Flip a coin and spin a red, blue, green spinner. How many outcomes? What is the chance of heads and red?A strong answer: The coin has 2 outcomes and the spinner has 3, so the tree diagram shows 2 × 3 = 6 outcomes. Heads and red is just one of them, so the probability is 1/6.

Watch for: Switching the order in an ordered pair. The first number goes across, the second goes up. A memory trick: walk along the hall before you climb the stairs.

Try this at home

Keep the facts going through the summer. Five minutes a day helps keep the year's skills fresh.

THE TWO HABITS THAT RUN ALL YEAR

The facts. Grade 5 mathematics assumes every multiplication and division fact through twelve times twelve is instant. It is not taught again this year, it is used. A child still counting to find seven times eight will struggle with long division, with fractions and with decimals, and will run out of time in a test. Five minutes a night at home is the single most useful thing you can do. Estimate before you calculate. Virginia asks Grade 5 students to estimate first, then check the real answer against the estimate. So when you help, ask roughly how much before any calculating. It is not a shortcut, it is part of what is being graded.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Read, compare and order decimals through thousandths.
  • Say whether a number up to 100 is prime, and give its prime factors.
  • Add, subtract, multiply and divide decimals.
  • Multiply three digits by two digits, and divide by two digits.
  • Add and subtract fractions with different denominators.
  • Use the order of operations correctly.
  • Find the area of a right triangle and the volume of a box.
  • Measure an angle and find the missing angle in a triangle.
  • Find the mean, median, mode and range of a set of data.

Practice at home makes a real difference. Children who practice a little each week usually find these goals much easier.

WHICH IS WHY THESE FIVE THINGS MATTER

  • Five minutes of multiplication and division facts every single day.
  • Ask for an estimate before the real answer, every time.
  • Ask how they worked it out, not just what the answer is.
  • Do the review sheet with them the night before a test.
  • If it is getting hard, tell the teacher in October, not April.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Three of our core values sit inside an ordinary mathematics lesson. Amanah, trust, is honest work: weighing and measuring accurately, checking an answer against the estimate, and owning a mistake rather than quietly changing it. Hikmah, wisdom, is seeing the structure inside a number and choosing the strategy that fits it. Khidmah, service, is why we divide fairly and measure carefully in the first place, whether that is sharing food, figuring out zakat, or building something that has to stand up, Inshallah.

Questions are always welcome. Please reach out through Class Dojo or the office.

Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org | arsheen.sayeed@wischools.org
