Grade 5 · Science

Grade 5 Science

A family guide to the year, month by month

THIS PLAN IS TENTATIVE

This is a plan, not a promise. These are the overall topics for each month. Order and timing will change as the year goes on, and months are approximate. The goals for June stay the same. Anything that changes is emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Quiz and test dates are not printed here; they live there, where they stay current.

Your child works from Savvas Experience Science, Grade 5. Five topics Virginia requires are not in that book, so energy and force, electricity and magnetism, sound, light, and how Earth changes are taught from packets built by WIS.

Late August and SeptemberMatter

What your child is learning

  • Everything is made of atoms and particles too small to see, and the matter is still there even when you cannot see it.
  • Properties like mass, volume, magnetism and solubility. Mixtures and solutions, measured with balances and cylinders.

Words to know: matter, atom, particle, mass, volume, property, mixture, solution

By the end of the unit: Explain that all matter is made of tiny particles, measure mass and volume, and tell a mixture from a solution.

Sample question: Where does the sugar go when it dissolves in water?A strong answer: The sugar breaks into particles too small to see, and they spread out between the water particles. It is still there: the water tastes sweet, and if the water evaporates, the sugar is left behind.

Watch for: Saying the sugar disappeared or melted. Dissolving is not melting: melting turns a solid into a liquid, but dissolved sugar is spread out among the water particles, even in cold water. Ask how they could prove the sugar is still there.

Try this at home

Ask where the sugar goes when it dissolves in tea. That answer is the whole unit.

Late September and OctoberChanges in matter

What your child is learning

  • How adding or removing heat melts, freezes, evaporates and condenses matter.
  • The difference between a physical and a chemical change, and why the mass stays the same either way.

Words to know: solid, liquid, gas, evaporation, condensation, thermal energy, chemical change

By the end of the unit: Explain how adding or removing heat changes a state of matter, and tell a physical change from a chemical change.

Sample question: Why is melting ice a physical change, but baking a cake a chemical change?A strong answer: Melted ice is still water, and you can freeze it back into ice. Baking makes new substances, and you cannot turn a cake back into eggs and flour. In both changes, the total mass stays the same, as long as you count any gas that escapes into the air.

Watch for: Thinking the water on the outside of a cold glass leaked through. It is water vapor from the air condensing on the cold surface. Ask where the drops came from.

Try this at home

Cooking is the lab. Ask which changes in tonight’s dinner could be undone and which could not.

Late October and NovemberEnergy and force

What your child is learning

  • Forms of energy, how energy changes from one form into another, and that it is never lost.
  • Speed, direction, force and friction: why things move, and why they stop.

Words to know: energy, kinetic, force, motion, speed, collision, friction

By the end of the unit: Describe how energy changes form without being lost, and explain how force and friction change an object's speed and direction.

Sample question: Why does a ball rolling on carpet stop sooner than one rolling on tile?A strong answer: Carpet is rougher, so it makes more friction. Friction is a force that pushes against the motion and slows the ball. The ball's motion energy turns into heat and sound, so it stops sooner.

Watch for: Thinking energy gets used up and disappears. Listen for used up; the energy actually changes into another form, like heat or sound.

Try this at home

Ask why a ball rolling on carpet stops sooner than one rolling on tile.

Late November and early DecemberElectricity and magnetism

What your child is learning

  • Conductors, insulators, and building circuits that actually work.
  • Static electricity, and how a current running through a wire makes a magnet.

Words to know: circuit, conductor, insulator, current, static electricity, electromagnet

By the end of the unit: Build a complete circuit, sort materials into conductors and insulators, and explain how an electric current can make an electromagnet.

Sample question: Why does the light go off when you flip the switch?A strong answer: Flipping the switch opens the circuit and makes a gap in the path. Electric current needs a complete loop to flow, so with a gap, no current reaches the bulb and it goes dark.

Watch for: Drawing a circuit with one wire from the battery to the bulb. Current needs a closed loop, so ask your child to trace the path all the way back to the battery with a finger.

Try this at home

Ask your child to explain what happens when a light switch goes off. Listen for the word circuit.

December and JanuaryEarth’s systems

What your child is learning

  • The four systems, land, living things, air and water, and how each one acts on the others.
  • Where Earth’s water is, how little of it is fresh, and what a watershed is, including our own in Virginia.

Words to know: geosphere, biosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere, watershed, freshwater

By the end of the unit: Describe how land, living things, air and water affect each other, and explain where Earth's fresh water is and what a watershed is.

Sample question: Why do we need to protect fresh water if most of Earth is covered in water?A strong answer: About 97 percent of Earth's water is salty ocean water. Most of the fresh water is frozen in ice or underground, so only a tiny amount is in lakes and rivers we can use, and we have to keep that little bit clean.

Watch for: Thinking a watershed is a building or a shed. It is all the land that drains into one body of water. Our rain drains toward the Chesapeake Bay.

Try this at home

Follow the rain from your street. Ask where it goes and what it carries with it.

Late January and FebruaryHuman impact on Earth

What your child is learning

  • Renewable and nonrenewable resources, and what conserving them looks like at home and in a community.
  • Designing and defending a solution that protects a local resource.

Words to know: renewable, nonrenewable, natural resource, conservation, pollution

By the end of the unit: Sort resources as renewable or nonrenewable, and design a plan that conserves a local resource and defend it with evidence.

Sample question: Why is coal nonrenewable but wind renewable?A strong answer: Coal took millions of years to form, so once we burn it, it is gone for our lifetime. Wind keeps coming because the sun keeps heating the air, so we cannot use it up.

Watch for: Thinking anything natural must be renewable. Coal and oil are natural but take millions of years to form. Ask how long the resource takes to come back.

Try this at home

Pick one thing your family wastes and cut it for a week. Let your child keep the record.

Late February and MarchSound

What your child is learning

  • Sound as vibration, and as energy traveling through solids, liquids and gases.
  • Pitch and volume, tested by building a simple instrument. School is closed for Eid al-Fitr in early March.

Words to know: vibration, wave, medium, pitch, volume, frequency

By the end of the unit: Explain that sound is made by vibrations that travel as waves through solids, liquids and gases, and how pitch and volume change.

Sample question: Why does a short, tight rubber band make a higher sound than a long, loose one?A strong answer: A short, tight band vibrates faster. Faster vibrations mean a higher frequency, which we hear as a higher pitch. A long, loose band vibrates slower, so its pitch is lower.

Watch for: Mixing up pitch and volume. Pitch is high or low, like a whistle compared with a drum; volume is loud or soft. Listen for loud when your child means high.

Try this at home

Hum with a hand on your throat, then ask your child what exactly is moving.

Late March and early AprilLight

What your child is learning

  • Light as radiant energy, the visible spectrum, and why we see color.
  • Reflection, refraction, and materials that are transparent, translucent or opaque.

Words to know: radiant energy, spectrum, wavelength, reflection, refraction, opaque

By the end of the unit: Explain that light is radiant energy, describe reflection and refraction, and sort materials as transparent, translucent or opaque.

Sample question: Why does a spoon look broken in a glass of water?A strong answer: Light changes speed when it passes from water into air, so it bends. That bending is called refraction. It makes the part of the spoon underwater look shifted from the part above.

Watch for: Mixing up reflection and refraction. Reflection bounces light back, like a mirror; refraction bends it, like the spoon. Ask which one is happening and how they can tell.

Try this at home

Stand a spoon in a glass of water and ask why it looks broken.

AprilPatterns in space, a short review

What your child is learning

  • A short review of Grade 4 work, which the Virginia Grade 5 science test also covers.
  • Gravity, the sun as a star, and why other stars look dim from here.
  • Day and night, the seasons, and shadows, all explained by Earth turning and orbiting.

Words to know: gravity, star, rotation, revolution, orbit, axis, shadow

By the end of the unit: Explain day and night, the seasons and changing shadows using Earth's rotation, its orbit and its tilted axis, and describe the pull of gravity.

Sample question: Why do we have summer and winter?A strong answer: Earth's axis is tilted, and it stays tilted the same way as Earth travels around the sun each year. For part of the year, our half of Earth leans toward the sun, so sunlight hits more directly and days are longer: summer. Half a year later, on the other side of its path, our half leans away: winter.

Watch for: Thinking seasons happen because Earth gets closer to the sun. Earth is actually closest to the sun in early January, during our winter.

Try this at home

Look at the moon from the same window for a week. Ask what pattern your child notices.

Late April to mid MayHow Earth changes

What your child is learning

  • Earth’s layers, and the plates of its crust: how heat inside Earth slowly moves them, building mountains and causing earthquakes and volcanoes.
  • The rock cycle: how igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rock form and change from one kind into another.
  • Weathering, erosion and deposition: how water, wind and ice break rock down, carry the pieces away and drop them somewhere new.
  • Fossils, and what they show about how Earth and its living things have changed.

Words to know: crust, mantle, plate, rock cycle, weathering, erosion, deposition, fossil

By the end of the unit: Explain how Earth’s surface changes slowly through moving plates, the rock cycle, and weathering, erosion and deposition, and quickly through earthquakes and volcanoes, and say what fossils tell us.

Sample question: How can a river change the land?A strong answer: Moving water, and the sand it carries, wears rock down into smaller bits, which is weathering. It carries them downstream, which is erosion. Where the water slows down, it drops them, which is deposition. Over a long time a river can carve a valley in one place and build new land in another.

Watch for: Mixing up weathering and erosion. Weathering breaks the rock; erosion moves the pieces. Ask your child: did it break, or did it move?

Try this at home

After a heavy rain, look at where soil or gravel washed to on a sidewalk or driveway. Ask your child to name what happened: weathering, erosion or deposition.

Late May and JuneMatter and energy in ecosystems

What your child is learning

  • Where a plant’s material actually comes from: mostly air and water, not soil.
  • Food webs, producers, consumers and decomposers, and energy traced back to the sun.

Words to know: ecosystem, producer, consumer, decomposer, food web, photosynthesis

By the end of the unit: Explain that plants make food from air, water and sunlight, and trace energy through a food web from the sun to producers, consumers and decomposers.

Sample question: Where does a tree get the material to grow so big?A strong answer: Mostly from the air. The tree takes in carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil, and uses sunlight to turn them into sugar, which builds its wood and leaves. Soil adds only a little.

Watch for: Drawing food web arrows backward, from the fox to the rabbit. Arrows show where the energy goes, so they point toward the eater: grass to rabbit to fox.

Try this at home

At dinner, trace one food on the plate back to the sun. It is shorter than it sounds.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Explain that matter is made of particles, and that it is conserved when it changes.
  • Describe how energy changes form, and how force and friction change motion.
  • Build a working circuit and explain what makes it work.
  • Explain how Earth’s systems interact, and name one way to protect a local resource.
  • Explain how Earth’s surface changes over time through moving plates, the rock cycle, and weathering, erosion and deposition.
  • Explain day, night, the seasons and shadows using Earth’s motion.

Talking about this at home makes a real difference. Children who discuss their learning with family build these skills with more confidence.

SO HERE IS WHAT HELPS MOST AT HOME

  • Let your child answer the why question before you give the answer.
  • Ask for evidence: what did you see that makes you say that?
  • Cooking, weather and the night sky are free laboratories. Use them.
  • Make your child draw it. A labeled drawing shows what a sentence hides.
  • Let them be wrong out loud. Guessing then checking is how science works.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Science in Grade 5 is ilm at its most hands on: our students measure, test and explain a world made in due measure, as the Quran puts it. Precision in the invisible, particles, circuits, the courses of the sun and moon, is taken as a sign worth reflecting on, which is hikmah. The units on Earth’s systems and human impact rest on amanah and khidmah, the earth as a trust and waste as something we answer for, and the space unit gives us room to name the Muslim astronomers who mapped these same skies, Inshallah.

Questions are always welcome. Please reach out through Class Dojo or the office.

Grade 5 · Social Studies

Grade 5 Social Studies

A family guide to the year, month by month

THIS PLAN IS TENTATIVE

This is a plan, not a promise. These are the overall topics for each month. Order and timing will change as the year goes on, and months are approximate. The goals for June stay the same. Anything that changes is emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Quiz and test dates are not printed here; they live there, where they stay current.

Social Studies only. Your child works from myWorld Interactive: Building Our Country, plus two units written by our own teachers at WIS on topics the textbook does not cover. (Tentative: which two units will be confirmed.)

Late August and SeptemberMaps, and the first Americans

What your child is learning

  • Where North America sits among the continents and oceans, and the main regions of our country.
  • How to read a map: compass rose, scale, key, latitude and longitude. The 50 states.
  • The first Americans, the Cactus Hill site here in Virginia, and how land and climate shaped food, shelter and trade.

Words to know: continent, region, landform, migrate, artifact, culture

By the end of the unit: Locate continents, oceans and U.S. regions, use latitude and longitude, and explain how the first Americans adapted to their land and climate.

Sample question: How did the land and climate shape the way the first Americans lived?A strong answer: People used what was around them. In the Eastern Woodlands, the Iroquois built longhouses from trees and farmed corn. On the Great Plains, the Lakota hunted bison and lived in tipis they could move.

Watch for: Mixing up latitude and longitude. Latitude lines run east and west, like ladder rungs, and measure north or south. Longitude lines run from pole to pole.

Try this at home

Keep a map or a globe where the family sits. When a place comes up, ask your child to find it.

OctoberExplorers, then West Africa

What your child is learning

  • Why European countries sent ships out, and what stood in their way.
  • What the Dutch, English, French, Portuguese and Spanish claimed, and how the meeting of these worlds changed life on both sides of the Atlantic.
  • West Africa begins: the empires of Ghana, Mali and Songhai, and the gold and salt trade.

Words to know: navigation, expedition, colony, empire, trade route

By the end of the month: Explain why Europeans explored, what each country claimed, and how the gold and salt trade made Ghana, Mali and Songhai powerful.

Sample question: Why did European countries send explorers across the ocean?A strong answer: They wanted wealth, like gold and a faster trade route to Asia. They wanted to spread Christianity, and they competed with other countries for land and power. Tools like the compass and astrolabe made the trips possible.

Watch for: Thinking explorers found empty land. Millions of American Indians already lived there. Listen for discovered, and ask who was already living in that place.

Try this at home

Ask what your child would pack for a voyage with no map of where they are going, and why.

NovemberWest Africa, 1619, and the first colonies

What your child is learning

  • Mansa Musa, the libraries of Timbuktu, and griots who carried history by memory.
  • The Ndongo Kingdom, the Africans who arrived at Point Comfort in 1619, and the Transatlantic Slave Trade.
  • Jamestown, tobacco, the House of Burgesses, and why Virginia mattered.

Words to know: caravan, griot, triangular trade, charter, cash crop

By the end of the month: Explain Mali's wealth under Mansa Musa, the arrival of Africans at Point Comfort in 1619, and why Jamestown and the House of Burgesses mattered.

Sample question: Why was Jamestown important to the history of our country?A strong answer: Founded in 1607, Jamestown was the first permanent English settlement in North America. Tobacco became its cash crop, and the House of Burgesses, started in 1619, was the first elected lawmaking group in the colonies.

Watch for: Thinking the Africans who arrived in 1619 came by choice, like settlers. They were captured in the Ndongo Kingdom, in present day Angola, and forced here. Ask your child where they came from and how.

Try this at home

This is hard history and we teach it with care. Ask what surprised your child, and listen.

DecemberLife in the thirteen colonies

What your child is learning

  • New England, Middle and Southern colonies: the land, the work, and who settled where.
  • Daily life for farmers, artisans, merchants, women, servants, and enslaved and free Black people.
  • How the regions came to depend on one another and on Britain.

Words to know: artisan, barter, import, export, mercantilism

By the end of the month: Compare the New England, Middle and Southern colonies by land, climate and work, and explain how the regions traded and depended on each other.

Sample question: Why did large plantations grow in the Southern colonies but not in New England?A strong answer: The South had warm weather, a long growing season and rich soil, good for cash crops like tobacco and rice. New England had rocky soil and cold winters, so people fished, built ships and ran small farms.

Watch for: Mixing up the three regions. A quick check: New England, fishing and shipbuilding; Middle, the breadbasket with wheat; Southern, tobacco and rice. Ask which region each job belongs to.

Try this at home

Pick one colonial job at dinner and work out the day with no electricity or running water.

JanuaryThe road to revolution

What your child is learning

  • The colonial unit closes with its unit test.
  • The French and Indian War, the debt it left Britain, and taxes the colonists had no vote on.
  • Boycotts, the Boston Massacre, the Tea Party, and the First Continental Congress. Patriots and Loyalists.

Words to know: boycott, tariff, militia, patriot, loyalist

By the end of the month: Explain how the French and Indian War led to new British taxes and how colonists protested, and describe the Patriot and Loyalist sides.

Sample question: Why were the colonists so angry about taxes after the French and Indian War?A strong answer: Britain needed money to pay its war debts, so it taxed the colonists with laws like the Stamp Act. The colonists had no representatives in Parliament, so they said no taxation without representation.

Watch for: Thinking the colonists were angry only because taxes were high. The bigger issue was having no vote on them. Ask your child what the colonists wanted besides lower taxes.

Try this at home

Ask your child to argue the Loyalist side for two minutes, even though they disagree with it.

FebruaryIndependence, then a new government

What your child is learning

  • The Declaration of Independence, and George Mason and the Virginia Declaration of Rights.
  • The war, from Lexington and Concord to Yorktown, and the leaders on every side.
  • Why the first plan of government, the Articles of Confederation, did not hold.

Words to know: independence, treason, alliance, treaty, delegate

By the end of the month: Explain the main ideas of the Declaration of Independence, key events from Lexington and Concord to Yorktown, and why the Articles of Confederation failed.

Sample question: Why did the Articles of Confederation not work?A strong answer: The Articles made the national government too weak. Congress could not collect taxes, there was no president to enforce laws, and it could not control trade between states, so the country could not pay debts or act together.

Watch for: Thinking the Declaration of Independence started the war. Fighting began at Lexington and Concord in 1775, and the Declaration came a year later, in 1776. Ask for the order of events.

Try this at home

Read one sentence of the Declaration together and ask for it in your child’s own words.

MarchThe Constitution

What your child is learning

  • School is closed for Eid al-Fitr March 1 to 12, and Quarter 3 exams begin March 30, so this unit is short and may continue into April.
  • The Constitutional Convention, the bargains, and the Three-Fifths Compromise.
  • Why a Bill of Rights was added, and how three branches check one another.

Words to know: constitution, compromise, ratify, amendment, veto

By the end of the unit: Explain why the Constitution replaced the Articles, how the three branches check each other, and why the Bill of Rights was added.

Sample question: Why does the Constitution split power among three branches?A strong answer: So no one person or group gets too much power. Congress makes the laws, the president carries them out, and the courts decide what laws mean. Each branch can check the others, like the president vetoing a bill.

Watch for: Mixing up the branches' jobs. A quick check: legislative makes laws, executive carries them out, judicial decides what they mean. When the news comes on, ask which branch is acting.

Try this at home

When Congress, a court or the president is in the news, ask which branch that is.

AprilA young country grows

What your child is learning

  • The first presidents and the habits they set for everyone after them.
  • The Louisiana Purchase, Lewis and Clark, Sacagawea, the War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine.
  • The Indian Removal Act and the Trail of Tears. Frederick Douglass, Sojourner Truth, and the early fight for women to vote.

Words to know: cabinet, frontier, nationalism, reform, abolition, suffrage

By the end of the month: Describe how the country grew through the Louisiana Purchase and Lewis and Clark, and explain the Trail of Tears and the work of reformers.

Sample question: How did the Louisiana Purchase change the United States?A strong answer: In 1803, Thomas Jefferson bought the Louisiana Territory from France. It almost doubled the size of the country and gave us control of the Mississippi River and the port of New Orleans.

Watch for: Thinking Lewis and Clark went west to settle there. They were sent to explore and map the new land, with Sacagawea helping as a guide and interpreter. Ask what their mission was.

Try this at home

Ask your child to name one person from this month who spoke up when it cost them.

MayMoving west, then a nation divided

What your child is learning

  • Inventions that changed daily life: the cotton gin, reaper, steam engine, telegraph, canals and railroads.
  • Texas, Oregon, California and the Gold Rush, and who gained and who paid. School is closed for Eid al-Adha mid month.
  • The Civil War begins: slavery and its spread as the cause, and the states that left the Union.

Words to know: patent, migration, territory, annex, secession, Union, Confederacy

By the end of the month: Explain how inventions and westward expansion changed the country, and why disagreement over slavery led Southern states to secede.

Sample question: Why did Southern states leave the Union in 1860 and 1861?A strong answer: They feared the national government would stop slavery from spreading into new territories and, in time, end it. After Abraham Lincoln was elected in 1860, South Carolina seceded first, and other Southern states followed.

Watch for: Thinking the cotton gin reduced slavery. It made growing cotton more profitable, so slavery actually grew. Ask your child how one invention could make life worse for some people.

Try this at home

Ask which invention changed daily life most. Then disagree, and make your child defend it.

JuneThe Civil War, and the year in review

What your child is learning

  • The economies of North and South, the major battles, the Emancipation Proclamation and Appomattox.
  • Voices of the War: Robert Smalls, Harriet Tubman, Clara Barton and others beyond the textbook.
  • The final week builds a class timeline of 1607 to 1865.

Words to know: blockade, emancipation, siege, amendment, turning point

By the end of the month: Explain the major events and people of the Civil War through Appomattox, and place the year's key events from 1607 to 1865 in order.

Sample question: Why was the Emancipation Proclamation important?A strong answer: In 1863, Lincoln declared enslaved people in the Confederate states free. It made ending slavery a goal of the war and let Black soldiers join the Union army. Slavery fully ended with the 13th Amendment in 1865.

Watch for: Thinking the Emancipation Proclamation freed all enslaved people right away. It applied only to Confederate states; the 13th Amendment ended slavery everywhere. Ask which one ended it.

Try this at home

Ask your child to tell the whole year as five events, in order.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Tell the story from the first Americans to 1865, in order, in their own words.
  • Find the regions and 50 states on a blank map.
  • Explain the three branches and what each one does.
  • Read a map, a timeline or a short document and say what it shows.
  • Find evidence and defend an answer instead of guessing.

Talking about this at home makes a real difference. Children who discuss their learning with family build these skills with more confidence.

SO HERE IS WHAT HELPS MOST AT HOME

  • Ask what they learned today, then wait through the silence.
  • Fifteen minutes reading the chapter aloud beats an hour of rereading notes.
  • Keep a map or a globe where the family sits.
  • Name the branch of government behind one news story a week.
  • Let your child teach you the week’s words. Explaining is what makes it stick.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Grade 5 is the year our students learn the story of the country they are growing up in. We want them to know it well enough to belong to it, and honestly enough to tell the truth about it. That is ilm. Much of the year is about power, so amanah runs through it: leadership is a trust, and history records who kept it. Debating Patriots and Loyalists teaches adab, disagreeing without contempt. And in the kingdoms of West Africa and the faith of enslaved people, our children see their own tradition standing inside American history, Inshallah.

Questions are always welcome. Please reach out through Class Dojo or the office.

Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org | arsheen.sayeed@wischools.org

Grade 3 · Quran

Grade 3 Quran

Memorizing Al-Bayyinah to Ash-Shams, learning what each surah means, and reading all of Juz 1

TENTATIVE PLAN: SUBJECT TO CHANGE

This guide is a plan, not a promise. The months are approximate, and a surah may take longer than planned. Timing and detail will change.

The Grade 3 surah list is being revised. What is written here is what the class is doing right now, and the updated list will be sent to you once it is settled.

Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. This guide replaces any earlier Grade 3 Quran guide. It covers Quran only; Islamic Studies has its own family guide.

Late August to OctoberAl-Bayyinah, Al-Qadr, Al-Alaq

What your child is learning

  • Memorizing: Al-Bayyinah, then Al-Qadr, then Al-Alaq.
  • Understanding: The new words in the surah, what it means (tafsir), and the tajweed rules used to recite it.

Try this at home

Sit with your child for ten minutes each evening and listen to the surah they are working on.

November to DecemberAt-Tin, Ash-Sharh

What your child is learning

  • Memorizing: At-Tin, then Ash-Sharh.
  • Understanding: The new words in the surah, what it means (tafsir), and the tajweed rules used to recite it.

Try this at home

Ask your child to tell you, in their own words, what one ayah means.

January to FebruaryAd-Duha, Al-Layl ayat 1 to 10

What your child is learning

  • Memorizing: Ad-Duha, then the first ten ayat of Al-Layl.
  • Understanding: The new words in the surah, what it means (tafsir), and the tajweed rules used to recite it.

Try this at home

Play a recording of Ad-Duha in the car and recite along together.

March to MayAl-Layl ayat 11 to 21, Ash-Shams

What your child is learning

  • Memorizing: The rest of Al-Layl, then Ash-Shams.
  • Understanding: The new words in the surah, what it means (tafsir), and the tajweed rules used to recite it.

Try this at home

Take turns: you read one ayah and your child recites the next from memory.

May to JuneReview

What your child is learning

  • Review: All eight surahs of the year, so they are secure before Grade 4.
  • Grade 4 builds on this: Grade 4 opens with a review of Ad-Duha, Al-Layl and Ash-Shams.

Try this at home

Name any surah from the list below and ask your child to recite it for you.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

These goals follow the current surah list. If the list changes, we will send you the updated goals.

  • Recite all eight surahs from memory, from Al-Bayyinah to Ash-Shams.
  • Explain what each surah is about and know its key words.
  • Apply the tajweed rules learned in class.
  • Have read the whole of Juz 1 aloud.

Class lessons build the foundation, and a few minutes of practice at home each day helps memorization last.

HOW YOU GET THEM THERE

  • Ten minutes of recitation every day, not a long session once a week.
  • Listen while your child recites, even if you follow along from the mushaf.
  • Use the 4-6-6-4 steps at home, with the websites listed below.
  • Watch Class Dojo for any change to the plan.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

The Prophet, peace be upon him, taught that the best of us are those who learn the Quran and teach it. Every surah your child carries by heart is one they can pray with for the rest of their life.

HOW YOUR CHILD MEMORIZES IN CLASS: THE 4-6-6-4 METHOD

  1. Step 1, 4 times: read or listen. Read the new ayah from the mushaf, or listen to it.
  2. Step 2, 6 times: recite from memory. Say the ayah without looking.
  3. Step 3, 6 times: read or listen again. Back to the mushaf or the recording.
  4. Step 4, 4 times: recite from memory. Say it again without looking.

If your child gets stuck: pause the count, practice the word that was missed, then pick the count back up. Use the same four steps at home.

READING SKILLS IN CLASS

Every student works on Quran reading skills this year, to read and memorize with proper tajweed. Your child also reads the whole of Juz 1 aloud: Al-Fatihah and Al-Baqarah to ayah 141.

TO LISTEN AND READ AT HOME

  • Quran.com, read, listen and study
  • al-Muqri’, listen and recite
  • QuranWBW.com, word by word translation

THE GRADE 3 SURAHS THIS YEAR

  • 98 Al-Bayyinah, 8 ayat
  • 97 Al-Qadr, 5 ayat
  • 96 Al-Alaq, 19 ayat
  • 95 At-Tin, 8 ayat
  • 94 Ash-Sharh, 8 ayat
  • 93 Ad-Duha, 11 ayat
  • 92 Al-Layl, 21 ayat
  • 91 Ash-Shams, 15 ayat

Eight surahs, 95 ayat in all. The number beside each name is its place in the Quran. This is the current list and may be revised.

IF YOUR CHILD MOVES AHEAD

A child who finishes a surah early moves straight on to the next surah on the list, without waiting for the class. A child who finishes the whole Grade 3 list carries on into the Grade 4 surahs, beginning with Al-Balad. The teacher assigns surahs to children who move ahead, based on testing.

Questions about your child’s Quran progress? Message the teacher on Class Dojo or contact the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org

Grade 4 · Quran

Grade 4 Quran

Memorizing Al-Balad to Al-Mutaffifin, learning what each surah means, and reading all of Juz 2

TENTATIVE PLAN: SUBJECT TO CHANGE

This guide is a plan, not a promise. The months are approximate, and a surah may take longer than planned. Timing and detail may change, but the goals for June stay the same.

Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. This guide replaces any earlier Grade 4 Quran guide. It covers Quran only; Islamic Studies has its own family guide.

Late August to mid SeptemberReview: Ad-Duha, Al-Layl, Ash-Shams

What your child is learning

  • Review: The last three surahs from Grade 3, so the year starts on solid ground.
  • Understanding: Refreshing the meaning and tajweed of each.

Try this at home

Ask your child to recite Ad-Duha for you at dinner.

September to mid OctoberAl-Balad

What your child is learning

Try this at home

Listen to your child recite for ten minutes each evening.

Mid October to mid NovemberAl-Fajr

What your child is learning

  • Memorizing: Al-Fajr, 30 ayat.

Try this at home

Ask your child to explain what one ayah means in their own words.

Mid November to mid DecemberAl-Ghashiyah

What your child is learning

  • Memorizing: Al-Ghashiyah, 26 ayat.
  • Understanding: The new words in the surah, what it means (tafsir), and the tajweed rules used to recite it.

Try this at home

Play a recording of Al-Ghashiyah and recite along together.

JanuaryAl-A’la, At-Tariq

What your child is learning

  • Memorizing: Al-A’la, then At-Tariq: two shorter surahs in one month.
  • Understanding: The new words in the surah, what it means (tafsir), and the tajweed rules used to recite it.

Try this at home

Two surahs in a month is a quick pace. Check in every day this month.

February to MarchAl-Buruj, Al-Inshiqaq

What your child is learning

  • Memorizing: Al-Buruj, then Al-Inshiqaq.
  • Understanding: The new words in the surah, what it means (tafsir), and the tajweed rules used to recite it.

Try this at home

Keep practice going over the Eid al-Fitr break in early March.

April to MayAl-Mutaffifin

What your child is learning

  • Memorizing: Al-Mutaffifin, 36 ayat, the longest surah of the year.
  • Understanding: The new words in the surah, what it means (tafsir), and the tajweed rules used to recite it.

Try this at home

Take turns: you read one ayah and your child recites the next from memory.

JuneReview

What your child is learning

  • Review: All eight new surahs, plus Ad-Duha, Al-Layl and Ash-Shams from Grade 3.
  • Grade 5 builds on this: Grade 5 opens with a review of Al-Ghashiyah, Al-Buruj, Al-Inshiqaq and Al-Mutaffifin.

Try this at home

Name any surah from the list below and ask your child to recite it for you.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Recite Al-Balad through Al-Mutaffifin from memory, eight new surahs.
  • Still recite Ad-Duha, Al-Layl and Ash-Shams from Grade 3.
  • Explain what each surah is about and know its key words.
  • Have read the whole of Juz 2 aloud.

Class lessons build the foundation, and a few minutes of practice at home each day helps memorization last.

HOW YOU GET THEM THERE

  • Ten minutes of recitation every day, not a long session once a week.
  • Listen while your child recites, even if you follow along from the mushaf.
  • Use the 4-6-6-4 steps at home, with the websites listed below.
  • Watch Class Dojo for any change to the plan.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

The Prophet, peace be upon him, taught that the best of us are those who learn the Quran and teach it. Every surah your child carries by heart is one they can pray with for the rest of their life.

HOW YOUR CHILD MEMORIZES IN CLASS: THE 4-6-6-4 METHOD

  1. Step 1, 4 times: read or listen. Read the new ayah from the mushaf, or listen to it.
  2. Step 2, 6 times: recite from memory. Say the ayah without looking.
  3. Step 3, 6 times: read or listen again. Back to the mushaf or the recording.
  4. Step 4, 4 times: recite from memory. Say it again without looking.

If your child gets stuck: pause the count, practice the word that was missed, then pick the count back up. Use the same four steps at home.

READING SKILLS IN CLASS

Every student works on Quran reading skills this year, to read and memorize with proper tajweed. Your child also reads the whole of Juz 2 aloud: Al-Baqarah ayat 142 to 252.

TO LISTEN AND READ AT HOME

  • Quran.com, read, listen and study
  • al-Muqri’, listen and recite
  • QuranWBW.com, word by word translation

THE GRADE 4 SURAHS THIS YEAR

  • 90 Al-Balad, 20 ayat
  • 89 Al-Fajr, 30 ayat
  • 88 Al-Ghashiyah, 26 ayat
  • 87 Al-A’la, 19 ayat
  • 86 At-Tariq, 17 ayat
  • 85 Al-Buruj, 22 ayat
  • 84 Al-Inshiqaq, 25 ayat
  • 83 Al-Mutaffifin, 36 ayat

Eight new surahs, 195 ayat in all, after a review of three surahs from Grade 3.

IF YOUR CHILD MOVES AHEAD

A child who finishes a surah early moves straight on to the next surah on the list, without waiting for the class. A child who finishes the whole Grade 4 list carries on into the Grade 5 surahs, beginning with Al-Infitar. The teacher assigns surahs to children who move ahead, based on testing.

Questions about your child’s Quran progress? Message the teacher on Class Dojo or contact the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org

Grade 3 · Islamic Studies

Grade 3 Islamic Studies

What your child learns each month, and how you can help at home

THIS GUIDE IS A PLAN, NOT A PROMISE

Months are approximate. Timing and detail may change, but the goals for June stay the same. Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo, and exact test dates will be shared as they are set.

Islamic Studies meets twice a week and uses the Safar Grade 4 textbook. Quran is taught separately and has its own family guide.

Exam dates are tentative. Exams are planned for the school's exam weeks (October 13 to 16, January 11 to 15, March 30 to April 2 and June 7 to 11). Exact date TBD.

Late August and SeptemberReview, then what we believe

What your child is learning

  • Review of Grade 2: the pillars, wudu, salah and the prophets.
  • Beautiful Names of Allah and what each one teaches us.
  • The angels and their jobs.
  • Why Allah sent prophets, and their five qualities, such as truthful and trustworthy.

Words to know: Asma ul Husna, Jibril, sidq, amanah

Try this at home

Ask your child to tell you one Name of Allah and one thing it teaches us to do.

OctoberMiracles and the Last Day

What your child is learning

  • Miracles Allah gave the prophets, and how a miracle is different from a trick.
  • Signs of the Last Day, taught calmly: we get ready by doing good.
  • Quarter 1 exam, October 13 to 16.
  • The Day of Judgment and filling our scale with good deeds.

Words to know: mujizah, Mizan, Sirat

Try this at home

Name one good deed each evening that makes the scale heavy.

NovemberJannah, tawbah and cleanliness

What your child is learning

  • Jannah, and Allah’s mercy, with Jahannam taught gently.
  • Sins, shirk, and how to say sorry to Allah (tawbah).
  • Test on belief in mid November.
  • Keeping clean for salah, and the steps of wudu.

Words to know: shirk, tawbah, Astaghfirullah, taharah

Try this at home

Say Astaghfirullah together after a small mistake at home.

DecemberWudu, ghusl and tayammum

What your child is learning

  • The musts of wudu and what breaks it.
  • Ghusl: what it is, and that it is sunnah on Fridays and Eid.
  • Tayammum: cleaning with earth when there is no water.

Words to know: wudu, ghusl, tayammum

Try this at home

Watch your child make wudu and ask which steps are in the Quran.

JanuaryGetting ready for salah

What your child is learning

  • Why salah matters and its rewards.
  • Mid year exam, January 11 to 15.
  • The checks before salah and facing the qiblah.
  • The steps of two rakahs and the parts that must never be left out.

Words to know: qiblah, ruku, sujud, tashahhud

Try this at home

Pray two rakahs together and let your child lead the words aloud.

FebruarySalah check, then Ramadan

What your child is learning

  • Salah practice, the practical check, and a test in early February.
  • The Islamic calendar and its twelve months.
  • Fasting in Ramadan: why we fast and what breaks the fast.
  • A test on fasting and Ramadan in late February.
  • Laylat al Qadr, zakat al fitr, Eid, and a short family interview.

Words to know: Hijri, suhoor, iftar, zakat al fitr

Try this at home

Answer your child’s three interview questions about your own Ramadan.

MarchProphet Ibrahim

What your child is learning

  • School is closed early in the month for Eid al-Fitr.
  • Prophet Ibrahim searches for the truth and speaks kindly to his father.
  • Allah protects Ibrahim from the fire: trusting Allah.
  • Quarter 3 exam, March 30 to April 2.

Words to know: tawhid, tawakkul

Try this at home

Share a time you trusted Allah when something was hard.

AprilThe Kaaba, Dhul Qarnayn and the Companions

What your child is learning

  • Ibrahim and Ismail build the Kaaba.
  • Dhul Qarnayn, a fair king who thanked Allah.
  • The Companions of the Prophet, peace be upon him.
  • The Prophet’s life on a timeline, and sending salawat on him.

Words to know: Kaaba, Sahabah, salawat

Try this at home

Say the salawat together after salah.

MaySirah, then good character

What your child is learning

  • The Battle of the Trench: teamwork and patience.
  • The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah: Allah’s plan is best.
  • Eid al-Adha and Prophet Ibrahim, then a test in late May.
  • Good deeds Allah loves, and treating everyone as brothers and sisters.

Words to know: Khandaq, treaty, akhlaq

Try this at home

Help your child choose three character promises for their poster.

JuneReview and the final exam

What your child is learning

  • Final review.
  • Final exam, June 7 to 11.
  • Character promise presentations and a closing dua.

Try this at home

Keep one character promise going through the summer.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME, YOUR CHILD CAN

  • Explain what Muslims believe about Allah, the angels, the prophets and the Last Day.
  • Make wudu correctly and know when tayammum is allowed.
  • Pray two rakahs correctly and calmly, and know the parts that must never be missed.
  • Tell the stories of Ibrahim, Dhul Qarnayn, the Trench and Hudaybiyyah and what they teach.

Practice at home helps your child reach these goals.

HOW YOU GET THEM THERE

  • Pray together at home whenever you can.
  • Watch your child make wudu once a week.
  • Ask one question each week: What did you learn in Islamic Studies?
  • Help with the Ramadan family interview in February.
  • Make dua together, even a short one before bed.

HOW YOUR CHILD IS ASSESSED

  • Exams: Quarter 1 on October 13 to 16, Mid Year on January 11 to 15, Quarter 3 on March 30 to April 2, and the Final on June 7 to 11, in the school’s exam weeks. The teacher reads every question aloud.
  • Unit tests: mid November, early February, late February and late May, with a review lesson the class before.
  • Practical check: wudu and salah in early February.
  • Home projects: the Ramadan family interview and the character promise poster.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Islamic Studies is where belief turns into practice. This year your child learns who Allah is, how to get clean and pray correctly, and how the prophets and Companions trusted Allah. Inshallah, what your child learns in class becomes who they are at home.

Questions? Contact the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org

Grade 6 · English

Grade 6 English

What your child is reading and writing this year, and how you can help at home

PLEASE READ FIRST

This guide is a plan, not a promise. The months shown are approximate. Some topics will move, some will take longer than expected, and the order may change. What will not change is where your child is headed by June.

Test and assessment dates are not printed here because they shift; anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo.

Late August and SeptemberGrowing Up

What your child is learning

  • Reading: Two true life stories by Firoozeh Dumas and Walter Dean Myers, a poem about growing up, and short stories including “Eleven” by Sandra Cisneros. Also a short science article on what happens to the brain between eleven and fourteen. Your child also chooses a book of their own to read all year.
  • Writing and words: Planning and drafting a personal narrative about a moment that changed them. Nouns and pronouns. Word parts from Latin.
  • Handed in for a grade: A short weekly quiz, a test every two weeks, and the first draft of the personal narrative.

By the end of the unit: Draft a personal narrative about a moment that changed them, using vivid details, and identify how authors show a character growing up.

Sample question: In Eleven by Sandra Cisneros, why does Rachel say turning eleven does not make you feel eleven right away?A strong answer: Rachel says you are still all the ages before, like rings inside a tree. When the teacher embarrasses her about the red sweater, she cries like a three year old, which shows the younger ages are still inside her.

Watch for: A narrative that lists events in order without slowing down on the moment that mattered. Ask your child to point to the sentence where the change happens; it should have the most detail.

Try this at home

Ask your child which moment from their own life they chose to write about, and why that one.

OctoberGrowing Up, then Natural Allies

What your child is learning

  • Reading: Finishing the short stories, then moving into true accounts of people and animals, starting with Jane Goodall and the chimpanzees.
  • Writing and words: Finishing, correcting and publishing the personal narrative. Beginning to research a topic and judge whether a source can be trusted.
  • Handed in for a grade: The finished personal narrative, which is the first big piece of the year, during the Quarter 1 exam window.

By the end of the month: Publish a polished personal narrative, and decide whether a source is trustworthy by checking its author, date and purpose.

Sample question: How can you tell whether a website about chimpanzees is a source you can trust?A strong answer: I check who wrote it and whether they are an expert, like a scientist or a zoo. I look at the date, and whether it is trying to teach or sell something. Then I see if another good source agrees.

Watch for: Trusting a site because it looks professional or came up first in a search. Ask your child who wrote the source they are using; if they cannot find out, that is a warning sign.

Try this at home

Ask to read the finished narrative. Praise one specific sentence rather than saying it is good overall.

NovemberNatural Allies

What your child is learning

  • Reading: Three poems about cats, a fable from Kalila wa Dimna about a lion outwitted by a hare, and the true story of Bob Lemmons in “Black Cowboy, Wild Horses.” Why an author wrote something, and how they organized it.
  • Writing and words: Researching and drafting a report on what people can learn from animals. Pronouns and sentence structure.
  • Handed in for a grade: Weekly quizzes and tests every two weeks. Research notes and a first draft.

By the end of the month: Identify an author's purpose and text structure, and draft a research report using notes in their own words.

Sample question: In the fable from Kalila wa Dimna, how does the hare beat a lion who is so much stronger?A strong answer: The hare tells the lion another lion lives in a well. The lion looks in, sees his own reflection, thinks it is a rival, and jumps in. The lesson is that cleverness can beat strength.

Watch for: Research notes copied word for word from a source. Ask your child to explain a note without looking at it; if they cannot, they need to rewrite it in their own words.

Try this at home

Ask your child to tell you one thing they found in their research that surprised them.

DecemberNatural Allies, then Living With Technology

What your child is learning

  • Reading: Finishing the animals unit, then starting texts that argue about technology, including articles on privacy and fingerprint scanning.
  • Writing and words: Finishing the report, then giving a set of spoken instructions the class has to follow. Then learning how a written argument is built.
  • Handed in for a grade: The finished report and the spoken instructions that go with it.

By the end of the month: Finish an organized report, give clear spoken instructions, and identify the claim and evidence in a written argument.

Sample question: In an article about fingerprint scanning, what is the author's claim, and what evidence supports it?A strong answer: The claim is the author's main opinion, such as fingerprint scanners put privacy at risk. The evidence is the facts that back it up, like examples of stolen fingerprint data. Facts count more than feelings.

Watch for: Confusing the topic with the claim. Technology is a topic; a claim takes a side, such as schools should not collect fingerprints. Ask your child to say the author's claim in one sentence.

Try this at home

Over the break, ask what your child thinks about a piece of technology at home. Make them give you a reason.

JanuaryLiving With Technology

What your child is learning

  • Reading: Comparing an article and an argument on the same topic. A science fiction story by Arthur C. Clarke. An article about microchip implants, and one about social media influencers.
  • Writing and words: Drafting an argument essay with a clear claim and real evidence. Looking at videos and posts and asking who made them and what they want.
  • Handed in for a grade: A mid-year exam covering everything since September, during the school mid-year exam window.

By the end of the month: Draft an argument essay using CER (Claim, Evidence, Reasoning), and ask who made a media message and what it wants the viewer to do.

Sample question: Should kids your age follow social media influencers? Give a claim, evidence and reasoning.A strong answer: My claim is that kids should be careful. The article said many influencers are paid to promote products. That matters because a post that looks like an honest opinion may really be an ad.

Watch for: Evidence with no reasoning, where a fact is dropped in without explaining how it proves the claim. Ask your child, so what does that fact show? That answer is the reasoning.

Try this at home

Watch something together and ask your child who made it, who it is for, and what it is trying to get you to do.

FebruaryLiving With Technology, then Imagined Worlds

What your child is learning

  • Reading: Finishing the technology unit, then beginning the stage play of “A Wrinkle in Time.” Reading a play means working out character from dialogue alone.
  • Writing and words: Finishing and correcting the argument essay. Then reading parts aloud in class.
  • Handed in for a grade: The finished argument essay, plus a class debate. See the Ramadan note below.

By the end of the month: Complete a corrected argument essay, take part in a class debate, and work out a character's traits from dialogue in a play.

Sample question: In A Wrinkle in Time, what does Meg's dialogue show about her, even when no one describes her?A strong answer: Meg talks back and gets frustrated fast, which shows she is impatient and unsure of herself. But she keeps asking questions about her father, which shows she is loyal and does not give up.

Watch for: Describing a character with one word and no proof, like she is nice. Ask your child which line of dialogue shows it.

Try this at home

Ask your child to read one of their play parts aloud to you. Reading aloud builds confidence quickly.

MarchImagined Worlds

What your child is learning

  • Reading: Finishing “A Wrinkle in Time,” then a Japanese folk tale about a boy whose only talent is drawing cats, which everyone tells him is useless.
  • Writing and words: Beginning an original short story of their own, using characters from the play. Word origins.
  • Handed in for a grade: A quiz and discussion work. This is a light assessment month because of the Eid al-Fitr break.

By the end of the month: Explain how A Wrinkle in Time resolves, retell and interpret a folk tale's theme, and begin an original short story.

Sample question: In the folk tale about the boy who draws cats, why does his useless talent turn out to matter?A strong answer: Everyone tells him drawing cats is a waste of time. But at the temple, the cats he drew come alive and defeat the giant goblin rat. The theme is that a talent others overlook can still be valuable.

Watch for: Retelling the plot without stating a theme, or giving a one-word theme like friendship. A theme is a full sentence about life. Ask what the story teaches, not what it is about.

Try this at home

Ask your child to retell the folk tale, then ask what the boy was good at and why nobody valued it.

AprilImagined Worlds, then Extraordinary People

What your child is learning

  • Reading: Nonsense poetry, including “Jabberwocky,” and a science fiction story that jumps back in time. Then a new unit on ordinary people who did remarkable things.
  • Writing and words: Finishing the short story, then writing a second one to perform aloud. Verb tense.
  • Handed in for a grade: Their own short stories, during the Quarter 3 exam window and again at the end of April.

By the end of the month: Write and perform short stories with consistent verb tense, and explain how a writer creates meaning even from nonsense words.

Sample question: In Jabberwocky, how can you understand the poem when many of the words are made up?A strong answer: The grammar gives clues. In the vorpal blade, vorpal comes before a noun, so it describes the sword, probably as sharp or powerful. The sounds help too, so I can follow the battle even without real words.

Watch for: Verb tense shifting in the middle of their own stories, like he runs to the door and opened it. Have your child read a paragraph aloud and listen for the jump.

Try this at home

Ask who your child thinks is an extraordinary person and why. Push past famous names to someone they know.

MayExtraordinary People

What your child is learning

  • Reading: The whole class reads one book together, starting this month. See the box below. Alongside it, a short story about islanders crossing an ocean, a video about a blind mountain biker, a biography of Ada Lovelace, and an account of Sacagawea.
  • Writing and words: Choosing a research question about an extraordinary person and beginning the research paper that closes the year. Figurative language and tone.
  • Handed in for a grade: A test in mid May, plus ongoing reading journal entries on the book.

By the end of the month: Write a focused research question about an extraordinary person, and explain how figurative language shapes a text's tone.

Sample question: Why is Ada Lovelace called an extraordinary person?A strong answer: In the 1840s she wrote steps for a machine that had not been fully built yet, Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine. Many people call it the first computer program, and she imagined machines could do more than math.

Watch for: Research questions so broad they cannot be answered, like who was Ada Lovelace. A strong question asks how or why. Ask your child what exactly they are trying to find out.

Try this at home

Ask your child where they are in the book each week, and what they would have done in that situation.

JuneExtraordinary People

What your child is learning

  • Reading: Finishing the book in the first days of June, then looking back at everything read this year and how much their reading has changed since August.
  • Writing and words: Finishing the research paper, then writing and performing an advertisement for an extraordinary invention. An honest letter about their own growth as a reader and writer.
  • Handed in for a grade: The research paper in early June, and the end of year exam during the final exam week, June 7 to 11.

By the end of the month: Complete a research paper that cites sources, perform an original advertisement, and reflect honestly on their growth as a reader and writer.

Sample question: How has your writing changed since your personal narrative in September?A strong answer: In September I mostly told what happened. Now I can back up a claim with evidence and explain my reasoning. I also revise more, and I choose stronger words instead of my first ones.

Watch for: A reflection that just says I improved a lot. Ask for one specific example, a skill or a piece of work, that shows the change.

Try this at home

Ask your child to name one book they would read again, and help them pick one for the summer.

THE ONE BOOK THE WHOLE CLASS READS TOGETHER THIS YEAR

The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind, by William Kamkwamba and Bryan Mealer. Read in class from the first week of May, finishing on June 2. Six full lessons are given to the book itself.

A true story. William Kamkwamba was fourteen in Malawi when a famine forced him out of school. He taught himself physics from library books and built a windmill out of scrap to bring electricity and water to his village. Your child will read it alongside the classroom texts in the May and June rows above and keep a reading journal. It is also the most likely subject for the research paper that closes the year.

What to expect: the book describes real hunger and hardship during a famine. It is honest but not graphic, and it ends in hope. Please read a few pages yourself if you would like to know what your child is reading. Every student gets a copy from school. Reading is done mostly in class.

DURING RAMADAN

Ramadan is expected in February. Homework in English is reduced to reading only. One essay deadline is extended and one test is given as an open book take home paper. No student is penalized for needing the extra time, whether they are fasting or not.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Read a whole book on their own and stay with it to the end.
  • Say what a story or article is really about, and point to the exact lines that prove it.
  • Write a clear essay with a point of view and real evidence, then correct their own spelling and grammar before handing it in.
  • Tell the difference between a fact and a claim, and ask whether the evidence is enough.
  • Speak in a discussion or a debate without reading from a page.

School lessons alone will not get your child there. The reading and talking that happen at home are what make the difference.

THE FIVE THINGS THAT HELP MOST AT HOME

  • Twenty minutes of reading every night, including weekends. Any book they choose. This matters more than anything else on this page.
  • Ask what happened in the story today, then ask why it happened. The second question is the one that builds thinking.
  • Let them read to you out loud sometimes, even at this age. It builds confidence for presentations and debates.
  • Talk about the news, an advertisement or a video, and ask who made it and what they want you to believe.
  • When an essay is due, ask to see it the night before and have your child read it aloud to you. They will hear their own mistakes.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Grade 6 English is built around five values we return to all year. Ilm, the seeking of beneficial knowledge, runs through the research unit and through William Kamkwamba, who taught himself from library books when school was closed to him. Amanah, trust, shapes how we treat sources honestly and never pass off another writer’s words as our own. Adab, good conduct, is how we disagree in a debate: we argue the idea and never the person. Hikmah, wisdom, is why stories have carried teaching across generations. And Khidmah, service, is the question we close the year on: what will you do with what you have learned?

Questions about your child’s progress are always welcome. Please contact the school office and we will put you in touch with the Grade 6 English teacher. Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org

Grade 6 · Mathematics

Grade 6 Mathematics

A family guide to the year, month by month

THIS PLAN IS TENTATIVE

This is a plan, not a promise. These are the overall topics for each month. Order and timing will change as the year goes on, and months are approximate. The goals for June stay the same.

Anything that changes is emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. The test dates below are the plan as it stands today; when the calendar moves, the real dates are posted there.

Your child works from Savvas enVision Mathematics Virginia Grade 6. Everything taught this year comes from that book, so there is no separate packet to keep track of. Homework comes from the Student Edition.

Exam dates are tentative. Exams are planned for the school's exam weeks (October 13 to 16, January 11 to 15, March 30 to April 2 and June 7 to 11). Exact date TBD.

Late August and SeptemberFractions

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Multiplying fractions, dividing fractions by fractions, dividing mixed numbers, and multi-step problems with fractions and decimals.
  • Skills: The first week is routines and a baseline check, used to group and support. Ratios begin Sep 22.
  • Handed in: A short quiz most weeks, a test every other week, and the Topic 1 test on Sep 21.

Words to know: numerator, denominator, reciprocal, mixed number, quotient

By the end of the unit: Multiply and divide fractions and mixed numbers, and solve multi-step problems with fractions and decimals, checking that answers are reasonable.

Sample question: What is 2/3 ÷ 4/5?A strong answer: Dividing by a fraction is multiplying by its reciprocal, so 2/3 × 5/4 = 10/12, which simplifies to 5/6. Check: 5/6 × 4/5 = 20/30 = 2/3.

Watch for: Flipping the wrong fraction, giving 3/2 × 4/5 = 6/5. Also watch mixed numbers: they must be rewritten as improper fractions before multiplying or dividing.

Try this at home

Halve or triple a recipe together, and ask them to show their work rather than the answer.

OctoberRatio and rate

What your child is learning

  • Topics: What a ratio is, equivalent ratios, rates and unit rates, unit rates with fractions, and proportional relationships.
  • Skills: Reading ratio tables and graphs, and deciding whether two quantities are proportional.
  • Handed in: Weekly quizzes, the Topic 2 test, and the Quarter 1 exam in the school exam week, October 13 to 16.

Words to know: ratio, equivalent ratio, rate, unit rate, proportional

By the end of the month: Write equivalent ratios, find unit rates, and decide whether two quantities are proportional using tables and graphs.

Sample question: A 12-ounce bottle costs $3.00 and a 20-ounce bottle costs $4.40. Which is the better buy?A strong answer: Find the price per ounce. $3.00 ÷ 12 = $0.25 an ounce. $4.40 ÷ 20 = $0.22 an ounce. The 20-ounce bottle is the better buy because each ounce costs less.

Watch for: Mixing up the two unit rates. 12 ÷ 3 = 4 is ounces per dollar, where bigger is better; 3 ÷ 12 = $0.25 is dollars per ounce, where smaller is better. Ask what the unit rate means in words: dollars per ounce or ounces per dollar.

Try this at home

At the store, ask which size is the better buy and make your child prove it with the unit price.

NovemberPercents and exponents, then integers

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Percent as a comparison to 100, relating fractions, decimals and percents, percents above 100 and below 1, exponents and perfect squares. Then integers, opposites and absolute value.
  • Skills: This is no-calculator work. Percent and fraction equivalence is assessed without one.
  • Handed in: Weekly quizzes, the Topic 3 test on Nov 13, and a cumulative benchmark on Topics 1 to 3 on Nov 16.

Words to know: percent, equivalent, exponent, perfect square, integer, absolute value

By the end of the month: Move between fractions, decimals and percents without a calculator, evaluate exponents, and compare integers and find their absolute values.

Sample question: What is 0.8% of 500?A strong answer: 0.8% means 0.8 out of 100, which is 0.008. Then 0.008 × 500 = 4. Check: 1% of 500 is 5, and 0.8% is a little less than 1%, so 4 makes sense.

Watch for: Treating 0.8% as 0.8 or as 8%. Another common mix up: 5² means 5 × 5 = 25, not 5 × 2 = 10.

Try this at home

Ask what 0.8% of something is, not 8%. The difference between them is most of the unit.

DecemberInteger operations

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing integers, and one and two step problems that use them.
  • Skills: Integers are modeled with chips and number lines before any rule is given.
  • Handed in: Weekly quizzes and the Topic 4 test on Dec 17, then review days before the winter break.

Words to know: integer, opposite, negative, product, quotient

By the end of the month: Add, subtract, multiply and divide integers, and use them to solve one-step and two-step real-world problems.

Sample question: It was −4°F at night and 9°F at noon. How many degrees did the temperature rise?A strong answer: Change is the end minus the start: 9 minus (−4). Subtracting a negative is the same as adding, so 9 + 4 = 13. On a number line, it is 4 steps up to zero and 9 more, 13 degrees.

Watch for: Applying the multiplication sign rules to addition, like saying −5 + (−3) is positive because two negatives make a positive. That rule only works for multiplying and dividing.

Try this at home

Temperature and a bank balance are where negative numbers live. Ask for the change, not the value.

JanuaryEquations and inequalities

What your child is learning

  • Topics: What an equation and a solution are, properties of equality, writing and solving one-step equations, then writing inequalities and graphing their solutions.
  • Skills: Class returns Jan 4 with a retrieval day. This unit runs Jan 5 to Feb 1.
  • Handed in: Weekly quizzes, a test every other week, and the Semester 1 exam in the school exam week, January 11 to 15.

Words to know: equation, solution, variable, inverse operation, inequality

By the end of the month: Write and solve one-step equations, check solutions by substitution, and write and graph inequalities on a number line.

Sample question: Movie tickets cost $9 each and you have $45. Write and solve an equation for how many tickets you can buy.A strong answer: Let t be the number of tickets. 9t = 45. Divide both sides by 9 to undo the multiplying, so t = 5. Check: 9 × 5 = 45. I can buy 5 tickets.

Watch for: Doing the wrong inverse operation, such as subtracting 9 instead of dividing. Also watch inequality graphs: an open circle means the number itself is not included, a closed circle means it is.

Try this at home

Ask your child to write an equation for something real at home, then solve it. Writing it is the hard part.

FebruaryArea, perimeter and the coordinate plane

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Area and perimeter of parallelograms and triangles, plotting integers and polygons on the coordinate plane, distances on the plane, and congruence.
  • Skills: The Topic 5 test is Feb 1. Geometry then runs to the middle of March.
  • Handed in: Weekly quizzes and a test every other week, including the geometry mid-point check on Feb 12.

Words to know: parallelogram, area, perimeter, coordinate plane, quadrant, congruent

By the end of the month: Find the area of triangles and parallelograms, and plot points and find horizontal and vertical distances on the coordinate plane.

Sample question: A triangle has a base of 10 cm and a height of 6 cm. What is its area?A strong answer: Area of a triangle is 1/2 × base × height. So 1/2 × 10 × 6 = 30 square centimeters. Check: a 10 by 6 rectangle is 60, and the triangle is half of it.

Watch for: Using the slanted side instead of the straight up height, or forgetting the 1/2. Also check units: area is in square units, perimeter is not.

Try this at home

Measure a room together. Ask which measurement you need for paint and which for the trim.

MarchCircles, then the quarter benchmark

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Radius, diameter and chord, where pi comes from, and solving problems with the circumference and the area of a circle.
  • Skills: School is closed for Eid al-Fitr Mar 1 to 12. The geometry unit finishes Mar 17.
  • Handed in: The Topic 6 test on Mar 17, then the Quarter 3 exam in the school exam week, March 30 to April 2.

Words to know: radius, diameter, chord, pi, circumference

By the end of the month: Use radius, diameter and pi to find the circumference and area of a circle, and explain where pi comes from.

Sample question: A circular table is 10 inches across. About how far is it around, and what is its area?A strong answer: The diameter is 10, so the circumference is about 3.14 × 10 = 31.4 inches. The radius is 5, so the area is about 3.14 × 5 × 5 = 78.5 square inches.

Watch for: Using the diameter in the area formula, which gives 314 instead of 78.5. The area formula uses the radius, which is half the diameter, squared.

Try this at home

Measure round things at home and divide the distance around by the distance across. 3.14 turns up every time.

AprilReteach, then data and statistics

What your child is learning

  • Topics: The first week and a half is reteach and fluency on whatever the Quarter 3 exam flagged. Then statistical questions, good samples, circle graphs, and mean, median, mode and range.
  • Skills: Reading a circle graph and judging which graph best represents a set of data.
  • Handed in: Spiral review quizzes during the flex days, then weekly quizzes and the Topic 7 test on Apr 30.

Words to know: statistical question, sample, circle graph, mean, median, mode, range

By the end of the month: Find the mean, median, mode and range of a data set, and choose a graph that fairly represents the data.

Sample question: Find the mean and median of 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. What happens if you add 50?A strong answer: Mean: 40 ÷ 5 = 8. Median: the middle number, 8. Adding 50 gives 90 ÷ 6 = 15, so the mean jumps to 15, but the median only moves to 9, halfway between 8 and 10.

Watch for: Finding the median without putting the numbers in order first. Ask your child to list the numbers from least to greatest before choosing the middle one.

Try this at home

Work out the mean of something in your house, then ask what happens to it if you add one very large number.

MayPutting the year together

What your child is learning

  • Topics: What happens to the mean, median and mode when a data point is added, removed or changed. Then review across all seven topics.
  • Skills: A cumulative benchmark on Topics 1 to 7 runs May 3 to 5, followed by reteach and fluency days. School is closed for Eid al-Adha May 17 to 19.
  • Handed in: The cumulative benchmark, spiral review quizzes, and the start of year-end review on May 20.

Words to know: outlier, balance point, cumulative, review

By the end of the month: Predict how the mean, median and mode change when a data point is added, removed or changed, and apply skills from all seven topics.

Sample question: The data is 5, 7, 7, 9, 12. If the 12 changes to 22, what happens to the mean, median and mode?A strong answer: The sum goes from 40 to 50, so the mean rises from 8 to 10. The median is still 7 because the middle number did not change. The mode is still 7 because it appears twice.

Watch for: Thinking every measure changes when one value changes. An outlier pulls the mean a lot but barely moves the median. Ask which measure best describes data that has an outlier.

Try this at home

Ask your child which topic they would most want to redo. That is the one to practice.

JuneFinal exam, then the project

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Cumulative review across the year, then the enVision STEM project and Pick a Project.
  • Skills: The project asks students to use the year’s mathematics on a real problem rather than a worksheet.
  • Handed in: The final exam in the school exam week, June 7 to 11, the project, and a portfolio and reflection in the closing week. Last day Jun 17.

Words to know: cumulative, model, justify, reflection

By the end of the month: Apply the year's math to a real problem, choosing the right operations and justifying each step.

Sample question: A garden is 12 feet by 8 feet. Fencing costs $3.50 per foot. How much will fencing cost?A strong answer: Fencing goes around the edge, so I need perimeter: 12 + 8 + 12 + 8 = 40 feet. Then 40 × $3.50 = $140. Estimate: 40 × $3 = $120 and 40 × 50 cents = $20, so $140 checks out.

Watch for: Using area when the problem needs perimeter, which here gives 96 × $3.50. Ask whether the answer covers the inside of the shape or goes around its edge.

Try this at home

Ask what they can do now that they could not do in August, and make them show you one of them.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Multiply and divide fractions and integers accurately, and explain why the method works.
  • Move between a fraction, a decimal and a percent without hesitating.
  • Write and solve a one-step equation for a real situation, and graph an inequality.

Talking about this at home makes a real difference. Children who discuss their learning with family build these skills with more confidence.

SO HERE IS WHAT HELPS MOST AT HOME

  • Ask them to explain one problem to you. Explaining is where the gaps show.
  • Ten minutes of practice most nights beats an hour the night before a test.
  • Let them be wrong and work it back. Erasing the answer teaches nothing.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Mathematics is taught here as ilm, knowledge worth having for its own sake and for what it lets you do for others. Precision is a form of amanah: a measurement, a price or a share that is reported carelessly is a trust handled carelessly, and the Quran is direct about giving full measure. Our students are asked to justify answers rather than just produce them, which is where hikmah is practiced, and the geometry unit opens naturally onto the Islamic tradition of pattern, proportion and the mathematics that came with it, Inshallah.

HOW YOUR CHILD IS CHECKED THIS YEAR

A short quiz of ten to fifteen minutes most weeks, on that week’s lessons, and a test every other week. Some of those tests are the ones printed in the textbook; the rest are written here. On top of that there is an exam in each of the school's exam weeks: Quarter 1 (October 13 to 16), Semester 1 (January 11 to 15), Quarter 3 (March 30 to April 2) and the final (June 7 to 11), plus a cumulative check on all seven topics in early May.

Fractions, percents and integer work are assessed without a calculator, because Virginia assesses them that way. Exact quiz and test dates are posted on Class Dojo, since they move when the calendar moves.

Questions are always welcome. Please reach out through Class Dojo or the office. Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org | arsheen.sayeed@wischools.org
