Grade 6 · Science

Grade 6 Science

A family guide to the year, month by month

THIS PLAN IS TENTATIVE

This is a plan, not a promise. Nine units run across the year and the dates below are the plan as it stands. A unit may run long because a class needs it. What does not change is where your child lands in June. Anything that changes is emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo, and test dates live there rather than here.

Your child works from Savvas Experience Science. Grade 6 Science is not SOL tested in Virginia, but the Grade 8 science test covers middle school content cumulatively, so this year is tested two years from now.

Late August and SeptemberDoing science, then the solar system

What your child is learning

  • Fair tests: what you change, what you measure, what you hold still. Metric measuring, honest graphs, lab safety.
  • From September 10, the solar system: planets, gravity and orbits, and the astronomers who worked it out.
  • Ends with a scale model built to real distances, and a written defense of it.

Words to know: hypothesis, variable, control, evidence, orbit, gravity

By the end of the unit: Plan a fair test that changes only one variable, and explain why a true-scale model of the solar system is so spread out.

Sample question: In your plant experiment, what did you change, what did you measure, and what did you keep the same?A strong answer: I changed the amount of water. I measured how tall the plant grew in centimeters. I kept the same soil, pot, light and plant type, so the water is the only thing that could cause the difference.

Watch for: Changing two things at once, like more water and more sunlight together. Ask which single thing caused the result; if your child cannot say, the test was not fair.

Try this at home

Ask what your child changed and what they measured.

OctoberSun, Earth and Moon, then atoms begin

What your child is learning

  • Rotation, revolution, moon phases and eclipses. A moon phase journal is kept daily.
  • The 23.5 degree tilt, and why it makes seasons rather than distance from the sun.
  • Tides from real Chesapeake Bay data. Matter and atoms begins October 26.

Words to know: rotation, revolution, phase, eclipse, solstice, tide

By the end of the month: Explain how Earth's tilt causes seasons, why the moon shows phases, and how the moon's pull causes tides.

Sample question: Why is it hot in Virginia in July if Earth is not much closer to the sun then?A strong answer: Earth is tilted 23.5 degrees. In July our half leans toward the sun, so sunlight hits us more directly and days are longer. Earth is actually a little farther from the sun in July.

Watch for: Saying summer happens because Earth is closer to the sun, or that moon phases come from Earth's shadow. Earth's shadow only causes a lunar eclipse; phases come from how much of the lit half we see.

Try this at home

Look at the moon together at the same time for a week.

NovemberMatter and atoms

What your child is learning

  • Protons, neutrons and electrons, and what makes one element different from another.
  • The periodic table, chemical symbols, and reading a formula to count atoms.
  • Why a compound behaves nothing like the elements in it. Cumulative quizzes twice a week.

Words to know: atom, element, proton, neutron, electron, compound

By the end of the month: Name the parts of an atom, use the periodic table to identify elements, and count the atoms in a chemical formula.

Sample question: How many atoms are in one molecule of glucose, C6H12O6, and what elements are in it?A strong answer: There are three elements: carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. The small numbers tell how many of each: 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 6 oxygen. 6 + 12 + 6 = 24 atoms in all.

Watch for: Thinking the number of neutrons or electrons decides the element. Only the number of protons does. Also listen for counting a formula's letters instead of using the small numbers after them.

Try this at home

Ask your child to read a label and count the atoms in one formula.

DecemberMatter closes, energy opens

What your child is learning

  • Matter ends December 2: notation, then explaining why a substance behaves as it does.
  • From December 3, energy: where it comes from, the greenhouse effect, and radiation, conduction and convection.
  • Ends with an insulation challenge: build it, test it, graph it, defend it.

Words to know: energy, thermal energy, heat, radiation, conduction, convection

By the end of the month: Describe how thermal energy moves by radiation, conduction and convection, and test and defend which insulation keeps heat in best.

Sample question: Why does a metal spoon in hot soup get hot, but a wooden spoon stays cool?A strong answer: That is conduction. Metal is a good conductor, so heat travels quickly through it to my hand. Wood is an insulator, so heat moves through it very slowly.

Watch for: Saying cold moves into things, like cold getting into the house. Heat always moves from warmer to cooler. Ask your child to retell any example in terms of where the heat is going.

Try this at home

Ask which of the three ways heat moves is warming your house tonight.

JanuaryWater

What your child is learning

  • Why water dissolves so much, and why that matters for everything living.
  • Surface tension, why ice floats, and why water takes so much heat to warm.
  • Freeze and thaw weathering, and why the Bay moderates our weather.

Words to know: solvent, cohesion, surface tension, specific heat, density, weathering

By the end of the month: Explain why water dissolves so many substances, why ice floats, and how water's ability to hold heat moderates weather near the Bay.

Sample question: Why does ice float on a pond instead of sinking to the bottom?A strong answer: When water freezes, its molecules lock into an open pattern with more space between them. That makes ice less dense than liquid water, so it floats. The ice layer also protects fish living below.

Watch for: Mixing up density and weight, such as saying ice floats because it is lighter. A big iceberg is heavy; it floats because it is less dense than the same amount of water.

Try this at home

Float a paperclip on water at the sink.

FebruaryWater closes, the atmosphere opens

What your child is learning

  • Water ends February 5 with a portfolio: two properties, each investigated to your child’s own procedure.
  • From February 8, the atmosphere: what air is made of, its layers, and what makes wind.
  • A daily weather log begins, and a home built barometer is tracked for three weeks.

Words to know: atmosphere, air pressure, barometer, humidity, convection

By the end of the month: Present a water investigation they designed, then describe the layers of the atmosphere and explain how uneven heating and air pressure create wind.

Sample question: What makes the wind blow?A strong answer: The sun heats Earth unevenly. Warm air rises and leaves lower pressure behind, while cooler air sinks and makes higher pressure. Air moves from high pressure toward low pressure, and that moving air is wind.

Watch for: Getting the direction backward and saying air moves from low pressure to high pressure. Check the barometer log too: a falling reading should be linked to clouds or rain coming.

Try this at home

Ask for tomorrow’s forecast and the reason behind it.

MarchThe atmosphere and weather

What your child is learning

  • School is closed March 1 to 12 for Eid al-Fitr, so the unit splits and resumes March 15.
  • Fronts, high and low pressure, and reading a weather map.
  • Ends March 26 with a forecaster task and a recorded weather broadcast.

Words to know: front, high pressure, low pressure, forecast, anemometer

By the end of the month: Read a weather map, identify fronts and high and low pressure, and make a forecast backed by evidence.

Sample question: The barometer has been falling all day and a cold front is coming. What weather do you predict?A strong answer: Falling pressure means a low pressure system is moving in, which usually brings clouds and rain. As the cold front passes, I expect storms, then cooler, drier air and clearing skies behind it.

Watch for: Forecasts with no evidence, such as it will rain because it looks gray. Ask what the map or barometer showed; a strong forecast names a front or a pressure change.

Try this at home

Watch a forecast and ask what evidence the forecaster is using.

AprilWatersheds and the Chesapeake Bay

What your child is learning

  • What a watershed is, which one our school sits in, and how the Bay works as an estuary.
  • Runoff, impervious surfaces, and point versus nonpoint pollution.
  • A field study at a local stream or Bay site, with real water testing. This is the anchor assessment of the year.

Words to know: watershed, tributary, estuary, salinity, runoff, impervious surface

By the end of the month: Explain what a watershed is, trace how runoff reaches the Chesapeake Bay, and test and interpret real stream water data.

Sample question: Why does a parking lot cause more pollution in the Bay than a forest of the same size?A strong answer: A parking lot is an impervious surface, so rain cannot soak in. It runs off fast, carrying oil, trash and fertilizer into storm drains, then creeks, the Potomac River and the Bay. A forest soaks it up and filters it.

Watch for: Thinking storm drains go to a treatment plant. Most go straight to local creeks with no cleaning. Also watch for nonpoint pollution being confused with one single pipe or factory, which is point pollution.

Try this at home

Follow the rain from your street and ask where it ends up.

MayThe field report, then human impact

What your child is learning

  • The watershed unit ends May 3 with a written report and a public presentation.
  • From May 4, human impact: resources, conservation, and air and water quality.
  • The real tradeoffs between fossil, nuclear, solar, wind, hydro and geothermal energy. School is closed May 17 to 19 for Eid al-Adha.

Words to know: renewable, nonrenewable, conservation, sustainability, air quality index

By the end of the month: Present the watershed report clearly, then compare renewable and nonrenewable energy sources by their real costs and benefits.

Sample question: Why don't we just use solar power for everything?A strong answer: Solar is renewable and makes no air pollution while running, but it only works when the sun shines, so we need storage or other sources at night. Panels also take land and materials to build.

Watch for: Calling one energy source all good or all bad. Every source has tradeoffs, such as nuclear making no air pollution but leaving waste. Ask for one benefit and one cost of each.

Try this at home

Pick one thing your family uses a lot of and trace where it comes from.

JunePolicy, and the end of the year

What your child is learning

  • Ends June 4 with a policy task: a real Virginia issue, three stakeholder views, and a brief presented at a public forum. Letters go to real decision makers.
  • A year end cumulative assessment across everything since August. The last day of school is June 17.

Words to know: stakeholder, cost and benefit, policy, tradeoff

By the end of the month: Present a policy brief on a real Virginia issue that weighs several stakeholders' views and uses scientific evidence from the year.

Sample question: Should Virginia limit fertilizer use on lawns near the Bay? Who would agree and who would not?A strong answer: Watermen and fishing families might agree, because extra fertilizer feeds algae that use up oxygen and kill fish. Lawn care companies might disagree because of lost business. A fair policy could limit it only near streams.

Watch for: Arguments that only give opinions without evidence, or that ignore the other side. Ask your child to state the strongest point of a stakeholder they disagree with.

Try this at home

Ask your child to argue the side they disagree with.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Design a fair test, run it, and defend the design choices.
  • Explain moon phases, seasons and tides with a model, not a memorized sentence.
  • Read a chemical formula, count the atoms, and show that matter is conserved.
  • Read a weather map and forecast from it, with reasons.
  • Take a position on a real environmental issue and support it with evidence.

Classroom lessons alone will not get your child there. The children who can do all five talked about this at home.

SO HERE IS WHAT HELPS MOST AT HOME

  • Ask for the evidence, not the answer. What did you see that makes you say that?
  • Let your child be wrong out loud. Revising an explanation is the skill being taught.
  • Cooking, weather and the night sky are free laboratories. Use them.
  • Look at the science notebook weekly, not at report card time.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Grade 6 Science is ilm at its most practical. Recording what was actually observed, including the result that ruins your own hypothesis, is taught as sidq, so honesty is a laboratory habit before it is a moral lesson. The solar system unit names the Muslim astronomers who mapped these same skies. The watershed unit sets amanah beside the hima, the protected land our tradition set aside for the common good. The year closes on khalifah, responsibility given rather than power held, turned into a real letter to a real decision maker, Inshallah.

HOW YOUR CHILD IS GRADED, AND THE FIELD STUDY IN APRIL

Day to day there are exit tickets two or three times a week, a science notebook kept daily, and a one page investigation brief for every lab. Every unit then ends in a task rather than only a test: a scale model, an explainer for Grade 4, an insulated container, an investigation portfolio, a weather broadcast, a field report, a policy brief. These are scored 3 secure, 2 developing, 1 beginning, with a cumulative benchmark each quarter and a year end assessment in June.

One gate: the lab safety practical in early September must be passed before any lab work, and can be retaken.

The April field study is the anchor of the year: real data collected at a stream or Bay site, written up and presented publicly. Protect attendance for it.

Questions are always welcome. Please reach out through Class Dojo or the office. Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org | arsheen.sayeed@wischools.org

Grade 6 · Social Studies

Grade 6 Social Studies

A family guide to the year, month by month

THIS PLAN IS TENTATIVE

This is a plan, not a promise. These are the overall topics for each month. Order and timing will change as the year goes on, and months are approximate. The goals for June stay the same.

Anything that changes is emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. Quiz and test dates are not printed here; they live there, where they stay current.

Your child works from Savvas myWorld Interactive, Growth of Our Nation, plus four units written by our own teachers at WIS. (Tentative: unit topics will be confirmed.) Social Studies meets four periods a week, not daily.

Exam dates are tentative. Exams are planned for the school's exam weeks (October 13 to 16, January 11 to 15, March 30 to April 2 and June 7 to 11). Exact date TBD.

Late August and SeptemberReconstruction and the West

What your child is learning

  • Topics: How historians judge a source, and US geography. Reconstruction, the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments, and why it ended. Then the railroad, homesteading, and the Indigenous nations who resisted.
  • Doing: Timelines, an amendment triptych, an adaptation challenge, a resilience card.
  • Handed in: Three quizzes, the Unit 1 and Unit 2 tests, daily exit tickets.

Words to know: primary source, bias, Reconstruction, amendment, citizenship, treaty

By the end of the unit: Judge a source for bias, explain what the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments did, and describe how westward settlement affected Indigenous nations.

Sample question: Why is the 14th Amendment so important?A strong answer: It made everyone born or naturalized in the United States a citizen, including people who had been enslaved. It also promised equal protection of the laws, which people later used to fight segregation.

Watch for: Mixing up the three amendments. A simple check: the 13th ended slavery, the 14th gave citizenship and equal protection, and the 15th said voting could not be denied because of race.

Try this at home

Ask what the 14th Amendment says. It is the backbone of everything after it.

OctoberEmpire, then industry, cities and immigration

What your child is learning

  • Topics: The Spanish-American War, Roosevelt and the Panama Canal, finishing the chapter on empire. Then railroads and big business, Carnegie and Rockefeller, cities outgrowing their governments. Then immigration, Ellis Island and Angel Island, the Chinese Exclusion Act, settlement houses.
  • Doing: A Build a Corporation decision log, a World’s Fair exhibit card, a four part immigration portfolio.
  • Handed in: Two quizzes, the Unit 3 test, and the portfolio, which replaces a unit test.

Words to know: monopoly, trust, mass production, push factor, nativism, enclave

By the end of the month: Explain how the United States gained an overseas empire, how big business grew, and why immigrants came and how they were treated.

Sample question: Why did so many immigrants come to the United States around 1900?A strong answer: Push factors like poverty, hunger and persecution made them leave home. Pull factors like factory jobs, cheap land and freedom drew them here. Many arrived at Ellis Island or Angel Island.

Watch for: Mixing up push and pull factors. A push is something at home that makes people leave; a pull is something here that attracts them. Ask your child to sort one example of each.

Try this at home

If your family’s own arrival story is one you share, tell it this month.

NovemberThe Progressive Era, then Jim Crow

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Muckrakers, child labor, the Triangle Shirtwaist fire, unions, suffrage, and reforms that caused harm, including eugenics. Then how segregation was built into law.
  • Doing: A Seven Threads tracker, a Reform Report Card, a chart of how law and housing worked together.
  • Handed in: Two quizzes and the Unit 5 test.

Words to know: reform, muckraker, labor union, suffrage, Jim Crow, poll tax

By the end of the month: Explain what Progressive reformers changed and why, including reforms that caused harm, and describe how Jim Crow laws built segregation.

Sample question: How did muckrakers help change laws?A strong answer: Muckrakers were journalists who exposed problems. Upton Sinclair wrote about filthy meatpacking plants, and the public was so upset that Congress passed food safety laws in 1906.

Watch for: Thinking Jim Crow was just unwritten custom. It was written into state and local law, like poll taxes and literacy tests that kept Black citizens from voting.

Try this at home

Ask which reform from this month is still with us. There is more than one answer.

DecemberJim Crow and the Great Migration

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Plessy v. Ferguson, redlining, the Great Migration, the NAACP, Washington and Du Bois.
  • Doing: A Built to Last contribution on Black institutions.
  • Handed in: Two quizzes and the Unit 6 test. The last two days before the break are review.

Words to know: Plessy v. Ferguson, redlining, Great Migration

By the end of the month: Explain Plessy v. Ferguson and redlining, the causes of the Great Migration, and the different strategies of Washington and Du Bois.

Sample question: Why did about six million Black Americans leave the South in the Great Migration?A strong answer: They left to escape Jim Crow laws, violence and poor pay as sharecroppers. Northern and Western cities offered factory jobs, especially during World War I, and a chance at more freedom.

Watch for: Thinking the North had no discrimination. Migrants still faced redlining and segregated housing. Ask your child how redlining worked to check they see it reached outside the South.

Try this at home

Ask what the Great Migration was, and why six million people left.

JanuaryWorld War I

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Militarism, alliances and nationalism; trench warfare and new technology; why the United States entered; how the peace of 1919 made the next war likelier.
  • Doing: A technology impact table, and a treaty negotiation argued in role.
  • Handed in: Two quizzes and the Unit 8 test, with a causal chain from 1919 to 1939, and the mid-year exam in the school exam week, January 11 to 15.

Words to know: alliance, neutrality, trench warfare, armistice, reparations

By the end of the month: Explain the long and short term causes of World War I, why the United States entered, and how the 1919 peace treaty helped lead to World War II.

Sample question: How did one assassination turn into a world war?A strong answer: In 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary was shot. Because of alliances, when Austria-Hungary attacked Serbia, Russia, Germany, France and Britain were pulled in one after another. Militarism and nationalism made everyone ready to fight.

Watch for: Naming the assassination as the only cause. It was the spark; alliances, militarism, imperialism and nationalism were the fuel. Ask your child to name one long-term cause too.

Try this at home

Ask how one assassination became a world war. That answer is the whole unit.

FebruaryThe Twenties, then the Depression

What your child is learning

  • Topics: The consumer boom and buying on credit, the Red Scare, the migration north, the culture of the decade. Then the crash, the Dust Bowl and the New Deal.
  • Doing: A credit ledger, a six leaders placard, a Three Rs sort, Still Running Today.
  • Handed in: Two quizzes, the Unit 9 and Unit 10 tests.

Words to know: credit, speculation, Black Tuesday, Dust Bowl, New Deal, relief

By the end of the month: Explain how buying on credit and speculation helped cause the Great Depression, and how New Deal programs tried to bring relief, recovery and reform.

Sample question: How did buying on credit help cause the Great Depression?A strong answer: In the 1920s people bought cars, radios and stocks with borrowed money. When stock prices crashed in 1929, many could not pay their debts, banks failed, and people stopped spending, so businesses closed.

Watch for: Thinking the stock market crash alone caused the Depression. Bank failures, debt, the Dust Bowl and falling spending all made it worse. Ask what happened after the crash.

Try this at home

Ask which New Deal programs still run. Social Security is the one to reach.

March and early AprilWorld War II

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Appeasement, Pearl Harbor, the two theaters, D-Day, the Holocaust, and who fought. Class resumes March 15 after Eid al-Fitr.
  • Doing: A two theater map set, profiles of six groups who served, and a Holocaust reflection read but not graded.
  • Handed in: A quiz and the Unit 11 test, the largest of the year, at the close of the quarter.

Words to know: fascism, appeasement, blitzkrieg, Holocaust, D-Day, internment

By the end of the unit: Explain how World War II began for the United States, the major events in Europe and the Pacific, and the Holocaust.

Sample question: Why did the United States enter World War II?A strong answer: Japan attacked the American naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on December 7, 1941. The next day Congress declared war on Japan, and Germany and Italy then declared war on the United States.

Watch for: Mixing up the two theaters, such as placing D-Day in the Pacific. D-Day was in Europe, on the beaches of Normandy, France. Ask your child to sort events by Europe and Pacific.

Try this at home

The heaviest unit of the year. Ask what they studied and be ready to sit with it.

AprilThe Cold War, then Civil Rights

What your child is learning

  • Topics: How two allies became enemies; the UN, NATO, containment, the Berlin Airlift and the arms race. Then Brown v. Board.
  • Doing: A T chart comparing a command economy with a market one, and a decision log.
  • Handed in: Two quizzes and the Unit 12 test, with a map and a systems comparison.

Words to know: containment, iron curtain, NATO, arms race, desegregation

By the end of the month: Explain how the United States and Soviet Union went from allies to rivals, what containment meant, and why Brown v. Board mattered.

Sample question: What was the real difference between the American and Soviet economic systems?A strong answer: In the United States, people and businesses decided what to make and what to charge. In the Soviet Union, the government owned the factories and decided what was made, how much and for what price.

Watch for: Thinking the Cold War was a direct shooting war between the two countries. It was a rivalry fought through alliances, an arms race and conflicts elsewhere. Ask why it was called cold.

Try this at home

Ask for the real difference between the two systems, without using the labels.

MayCivil Rights and a changing America

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Boycotts, sit-ins, freedom rides, the Civil Rights and Voting Rights Acts, and what urban renewal did to neighborhoods.
  • Doing: A twelve names card, and an accessibility audit of a real building, written as a memo.
  • Handed in: Two quizzes and the Unit 13 test, in the short week back after Eid al-Adha.

Words to know: boycott, sit-in, nonviolent resistance, urban renewal, displacement

By the end of the month: Describe how the civil rights movement used nonviolent resistance, name the key laws it won, and explain how urban renewal displaced neighborhoods.

Sample question: Why did civil rights leaders choose nonviolent protest?A strong answer: Peaceful protests like the Montgomery bus boycott and the sit-ins showed the injustice clearly. When protesters were attacked on television, many Americans turned against segregation, which helped pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

Watch for: Mixing up the two laws. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned segregation in public places and job discrimination; the Voting Rights Act of 1965 protected the right to vote.

Try this at home

Ask who the twelve names are. They should get past the two everybody knows.

JuneA new millennium, then the capstone

What your child is learning

  • Topics: September 11 and how it changed law and public life; what is asked of a community associated with an attack it condemns; then science and globalization.
  • Doing: A Then and Now trade-off analysis, then the capstone argument on what changed most since 1865.
  • Handed in: The Unit 14 test, and the capstone scored on thesis, evidence and chronology.

Words to know: terrorism, civil liberties, globalization, thesis, evidence

By the end of the month: Explain how September 11 and globalization changed American life, and defend a thesis about the biggest change since 1865 with evidence and chronology.

Sample question: What is the single biggest change in America since 1865?A strong answer: I think it is civil rights. Before 1865, most Black Americans were enslaved. Then the 14th Amendment, Brown v. Board in 1954 and the Voting Rights Act in 1965 each widened equal rights under the law.

Watch for: A thesis with events listed out of order or no dates. Ask your child to put their three pieces of evidence on a timeline; the capstone is scored on chronology too.

Try this at home

Ask for the single biggest change since 1865, defended with three pieces of evidence.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Tell the story of the United States from 1865 to today, with the turning points in the right places.
  • Explain how an amendment, a law or a court case changed what citizenship meant.
  • Read a primary source and say who wrote it, when, and what they wanted from it.

Talking about this at home makes a real difference. Children who discuss their learning with family build these skills with more confidence.

SO HERE IS WHAT HELPS MOST AT HOME

  • Ask what they studied today, then ask who benefited and who paid.
  • Connect one news story a week to something they have studied.
  • Fifteen minutes reading the chapter aloud beats an hour of rereading notes before a test.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

This is a year of hard history, and our five values give our students somewhere to stand in it. Judging a source honestly is amanah, since a historian who misreports the past has broken a trust. Land held in covenant, wealth that carries obligation, and the duty owed to the oppressed run through the units on the West, on industry and on the World Wars, and the Farewell Sermon’s rejection of racial hierarchy stands beside Jim Crow and civil rights, Inshallah.

TOPICS WE TEACH WITH PARTICULAR CARE

Three parts of this year are heavy: Jim Crow and racial violence in November and December, the Holocaust in March, and September 11 in June. We teach them honestly rather than softening them, and build in time to talk about them.

No student is asked to speak for a group or to share a family migration story, and the written reflections in those units are read but not graded. Please contact the teacher beforehand if you would like to know what will be read.

Questions are always welcome. Please reach out through Class Dojo or the office. Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org | arsheen.sayeed@wischools.org

Grade 1 Quran meets four times a week. This guide is a plan, not a promise. The months are approximate, and a surah may take longer than planned. Timing and detail will change, but where your child is headed by June will not.

Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. This guide replaces any earlier Grade 1 Quran guide. It covers Quran only; Islamic Studies has its own family guide.

Late August to SeptemberAl-Fil

Try this at home

OctoberAl-Humazah

What your child is learning

  • Memorizing: Al-Humazah.
  • Understanding: The new words in the surah, what it means (tafsir), and the tajweed rules used to recite it.

Try this at home

Ask your child what Al-Humazah warns us about, in their own words.

NovemberAl-Asr

What your child is learning

  • Memorizing: Al-Asr.
  • Understanding: The new words in the surah, what it means (tafsir), and the tajweed rules used to recite it.

Try this at home

Play a recording of Al-Asr in the car and recite along together.

DecemberAt-Takathur

What your child is learning

  • Memorizing: At-Takathur.
  • Understanding: The new words in the surah, what it means (tafsir), and the tajweed rules used to recite it.

Try this at home

Once the surah is finished, listen to your child recite it from beginning to end without the mushaf.

JanuaryAl-Qari’ah

What your child is learning

  • Memorizing: Al-Qari’ah.
  • Understanding: The new words in the surah, what it means (tafsir), and the tajweed rules used to recite it.

Try this at home

Ask your child to explain what one ayah means in their own words.

FebruaryAl-Adiyat

What your child is learning

  • Memorizing: Al-Adiyat.
  • Understanding: The new words in the surah, what it means (tafsir), and the tajweed rules used to recite it.

Try this at home

Take turns: you read one ayah and your child recites the next from memory.

March to JuneQaidah, and Al-Kawthar, Al-Ma’un and Quraish

What your child is learning

  • Reading skills: Qaidah is the focus of these months, working through Levels 5 to 8.
  • Memorizing: Al-Kawthar, Al-Ma’un and Quraish. For most children these are new. A few began them at the end of Kindergarten, and for them this is review.
  • Review: All six surahs memorized this year, so they are secure before Grade 2.
  • Grade 2 builds on this: Grade 2 moves on to Az-Zalzalah.

Try this at home

Keep practice going over the Eid al-Fitr break in early March. Name any surah from the list below and ask your child to recite it for you.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Recite all nine surahs from memory, from Al-Kawthar to Al-Adiyat.
  • Explain what each surah is about and know its key words.
  • Apply the tajweed rules learned in class.
  • Complete Qaidah Levels 5 to 8.

School lessons alone will not get your child there. Daily practice at home is what makes memorization last.

HOW YOU GET THEM THERE

  • Ten minutes of recitation every day, not a long session once a week.
  • Listen while your child recites, even if you follow along from the mushaf.
  • Use the 4-6-6-4 steps at home, with the websites listed below.
  • Keep the earlier surahs in rotation so nothing is forgotten.
  • Watch Class Dojo for any change to the plan.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

The Prophet, peace be upon him, taught that the best of us are those who learn the Quran and teach it. Every surah your child carries by heart is one they can pray with for the rest of their life.

HOW YOUR CHILD MEMORIZES IN CLASS: THE 4-6-6-4 METHOD

  1. Step 1, 4 times: read or listen. Read the new ayah from the mushaf, or listen to it.
  2. Step 2, 6 times: recite from memory. Say the ayah without looking.
  3. Step 3, 6 times: read or listen again. Back to the mushaf or the recording.
  4. Step 4, 4 times: recite from memory. Say it again without looking.

If your child gets stuck: pause the count, practice the word that was missed, then pick the count back up. Use the same four steps at home.

READING SKILLS (QAIDA) IN CLASS

Your child works through Qaidah Levels 5 to 8 this year: the vowel marks and tanween, stretched sounds, sukun and shaddah, and reading two words together in one breath. Qaidah is the main focus from March to June.

TO LISTEN AND READ AT HOME

  • Quran.com, read, listen and study
  • al-Muqri’, listen and recite
  • QuranWBW.com, word by word translation

THE GRADE 1 SURAHS THIS YEAR

  • 108 Al-Kawthar, 3 ayat (March to June)
  • 107 Al-Ma’un, 7 ayat (March to June)
  • 106 Quraish, 4 ayat (March to June)
  • 105 Al-Fil, 5 ayat
  • 104 Al-Humazah, 9 ayat
  • 103 Al-Asr, 3 ayat
  • 102 At-Takathur, 8 ayat
  • 101 Al-Qari’ah, 11 ayat
  • 100 Al-Adiyat, 11 ayat

Nine surahs, 61 ayat in all. Al-Fil to Al-Adiyat are memorized from August to February. Al-Kawthar, Al-Ma’un and Quraish are memorized from March to June, alongside the Qaidah. The number beside each name is its place in the Quran.

IF YOUR CHILD MOVES AHEAD

A child who finishes a surah early moves straight on to the next surah on the list, without waiting for the class. A child who finishes the whole Grade 1 list carries on into the Grade 2 surahs, beginning with Az-Zalzalah. The teacher assigns surahs to children who move ahead, based on testing.

TENTATIVE PLAN: SUBJECT TO CHANGE

This guide is a plan, not a promise. The months are approximate, and a surah may take longer than planned. Timing and detail will change, but where your child is headed by June will not.

Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. This guide replaces any earlier Grade 6 Quran guide. It covers Quran only; Islamic Studies has its own family guide. Quran meets four times a week.

Late August to OctoberTwo groups: Al-A’la, Al-Ghashiyah, Al-Mulk

What your child is learning

  • Group 1: Memorizing Surah Al-A’la, then beginning Surah Al-Ghashiyah.
  • Group 2: Memorizing Surah Al-Mulk.
  • Everyone: The meaning of the ayat (tafsir) of Surah Al-Mulk and the tajweed rules used to recite them.

November to December 4Two groups: Al-Ghashiyah, At-Tariq, Al-Mulk

December 7 to March 15One class: Surah Al-Qalam

What your child is learning

  • The whole class together: Surah Al-Qalam. The groups end and every student works on the same surah.
  • Covering: Memorization, tajweed, tafsir, and recitation of each passage.
  • Note: Ramadan begins in February and the Eid al-Fitr break runs March 1 to 12, so the pace is lighter through those weeks.

Try this at home

Ten minutes every evening matters most in this stretch. Ask your child to recite the newest ayat, then one older page. During the break days, ask your child to memorize Surah Al-Mulk if they have not memorized it yet.

March 15 to June 1One class: Surah Al-Haqqah

What your child is learning

  • The whole class together: Surah Al-Haqqah, from Juz 29.
  • Covering: Memorization, tafsir, and recitation.
  • Everyone: Surah Al-Qalam stays in weekly review so it is not lost.

JuneReview

What your child is learning

  • Grade 7 builds on this: Grade 7 continues in Juz 29.

Try this at home

Name any surah from the list below and ask your child to recite it for you.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Recite Surah Al-Qalam from memory, applying the tajweed rules taught in class.
  • Recite Surah Al-Haqqah from memory and explain what it teaches.
  • Explain the meaning of the ayat memorized, not only the words.
  • Keep the fall surahs secure: Al-A’la, Al-Ghashiyah and At-Tariq 1 to 8 for Group 1, and Al-Mulk for Group 2.

School lessons alone will not get your child there. Daily practice at home is what makes memorization last.

HOW YOU GET THEM THERE

  • Ten minutes of recitation every day, not a long session once a week.
  • Listen while your child recites, even if you follow along from the mushaf.
  • Add one older page to every evening so nothing memorized is lost.
  • Prepare for the monthly assessment before the week it falls, not the night before.
  • Watch Class Dojo for any change to the plan.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

The Prophet, peace be upon him, taught that the best of us are those who learn the Quran and teach it. Every surah your child carries by heart is one they can pray with for the rest of their life.

HOW THE CLASS IS ORGANIZED THIS YEAR

  • Until December 4, two memorization groups. Students memorize in one of two groups, each moving at its own pace, with one translation lesson taken by the whole class together.
  • From December 7, one class together. The groups end. Every student works on the same surah, and memorization, tajweed, tafsir and recitation are taught together.
  • All year, monthly assessments. Your child is assessed about once a month on what has been memorized, and is expected to keep earlier surahs ready, not only the newest ayat.

If your child falls behind: tell the teacher on Class Dojo rather than waiting for the assessment. A shorter daily portion, kept every day, catches a student up faster than a long weekend session.

DATES THAT AFFECT THE PACE

Quarter 2 ends January 15. Ramadan begins in February and the Eid al-Fitr break runs March 1 to 12. Quarter 3 ends April 9. The last day of school is June 17.

TO LISTEN AND READ AT HOME

  • Quran.com, read, listen and study
  • al-Muqri’, listen and recite
  • QuranWBW.com, word by word translation

THE GRADE 6 SURAHS THIS YEAR

  • 87 Surah Al-A’la, 19 ayat, Group 1, late August to October
  • 88 Surah Al-Ghashiyah, 26 ayat, Group 1, October to November
  • 86 Surah At-Tariq, ayat 1 to 8, Group 1, late November to December 4
  • 67 Surah Al-Mulk, 30 ayat, Group 2, late August to December 4
  • 68 Surah Al-Qalam, 52 ayat, whole class, December 7 to March 15
  • 69 Surah Al-Haqqah, 52 ayat, whole class, March 15 to June 1

The number beside each name is its place in the Quran. Surah Al-Qalam and Surah Al-Haqqah are memorized by the whole class, so every student finishes the year with both.

IF YOUR CHILD MOVES AHEAD

A student who finishes ahead of the class is given the next surah by the teacher, based on testing, rather than waiting. Extension surahs this year are Surah Al-Mursalat, and the last ten surahs of Juz 30 for students still building fluency.

Questions about your child’s Quran progress? Message the teacher on Class Dojo or contact the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org

Grade 4 · Islamic Studies

Grade 4 Islamic Studies

What your child learns each month, and how you can help at home

THIS GUIDE IS A PLAN, NOT A PROMISE

Months are approximate. Timing and detail may change, but the goals for June stay the same. Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo, and exact test dates will be shared as they are set.

Islamic Studies meets twice a week and uses the Safar Grade 5 textbook. Quran is taught separately and has its own family guide.

Exam dates are tentative. Exams are planned for the school's exam weeks (October 13 to 16, January 11 to 15, March 30 to April 2 and June 7 to 11). Exact date TBD.

Late August and SeptemberBack to basics, then Knowing Allah

What your child is learning

  • Review of Grade 3: belief, wudu, salah and the prophets.
  • The Names of Allah and what each one teaches us to do.
  • The angels, the revealed books, and why the Quran is protected.
  • Prophets and messengers, and why no prophet comes after Muhammad, peace be upon him.

Words to know: Asma ul Husna, Zabur, Injil, rasul, Seal of the Prophets

Try this at home

Ask your child to teach you one Name of Allah and one thing it tells us to do.

OctoberThe Hereafter

What your child is learning

  • Signs of the Last Day, taught calmly.
  • What happens after death, and good deeds that keep going.
  • The stages of the Day of Judgment.
  • Quarter 1 exam, October 13 to 16.

Words to know: barzakh, Mizan, Sirat, sadaqah jariyah

Try this at home

Choose one ongoing good deed as a family, such as giving regularly to a water or masjid project.

NovemberJannah, then Purification

What your child is learning

  • Jannah and Jahannam, and Allah’s generosity.
  • Test on belief and the Hereafter in early November.
  • The five kinds of rulings: fard, sunnah, allowed, disliked, forbidden.
  • Wudu: the musts, the sunnahs, what breaks it, and ghusl.

Words to know: fard, sunnah, makruh, haram, wudu

Try this at home

Watch your child make wudu and ask them to point out one must and one sunnah.

DecemberTayammum and prayer times

What your child is learning

  • Tayammum: when it is allowed and how to do it.
  • Wudu and tayammum practical check, then a unit test.
  • The times of the five prayers and how the sun sets them.
  • Times when voluntary prayer is not allowed.

Words to know: tayammum, Asr, sunrise, midday

Try this at home

Look at your masjid’s prayer schedule together and find today’s Asr time.

JanuarySunnah prayers and Salah

What your child is learning

  • The sunnah prayers and Witr.
  • Mid year exam, January 11 to 15.
  • The musts of salah, and what to do if something is forgotten.
  • Covering for salah, and what breaks salah.

Words to know: Witr, sujud as sahw, awrah

Try this at home

Pray the two sunnah rakahs before Fajr together on a weekend morning.

FebruarySalah every day, then Ramadan

What your child is learning

  • How to keep focus in salah, and a one week salah tracker at home.
  • Salah practical check and unit test in early February.
  • Fasting: who fasts, what breaks the fast, Laylat al Qadr, zakat al fitr and Eid, with a test in late February.
  • A Ramadan Plan with four family goals.

Words to know: khushu, suhoor, iftar, zakat al fitr

Try this at home

Sign the Ramadan Plan and help your child keep one goal.

MarchProphets Ayyub and Yunus

What your child is learning

  • School is closed early in the month for Eid al-Fitr.
  • Prophet Ayyub and patience in hard times.
  • Prophet Yunus and his dua in the darkness.
  • Quarter 3 exam, March 30 to April 2.

Words to know: sabr, tawbah, dua

Try this at home

Learn the dua of Prophet Yunus together: La ilaha illa Anta, subhanaka, inni kuntu minaz zalimin.

AprilProphet Dawud and the Sirah

What your child is learning

  • Talut's small army that obeyed and trusted Allah, and how young Dawud bravely defeated Jalut.
  • Prophet Dawud’s gifts, worship and dhikr.
  • The Prophet’s letters to kings, and the questions Heraclius asked.
  • The Conquest of Makkah.

Words to know: dhikr, dawah, Fath Makkah

Try this at home

After salah, say Subhanallah, Alhamdulillah and Allahu Akbar 33 times each, counting on fingers together.

MayMercy and good character

What your child is learning

  • The Prophet’s forgiveness at the Conquest of Makkah.
  • Test on the prophets and the Sirah in early May.
  • Good character, and four problems of the heart: arrogance, envy, backbiting and showing off.
  • A two week Character Habit Tracker, signed by you each week.

Words to know: akhlaq, hasad, ghibah

Try this at home

Notice your child practicing their chosen habit and tell them you saw it.

JuneReview and the final exam

What your child is learning

  • Year review.
  • Final practical check: wudu and salah.
  • Final exam, June 7 to 11.
  • Sharing the Character Habit Tracker.

Try this at home

Keep the salah tracker going through the summer.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME, YOUR CHILD CAN

  • Explain the six pillars of Iman and why Muhammad, peace be upon him, is the last prophet.
  • Make wudu and tayammum correctly and know what breaks wudu.
  • Pray on time, add the sunnah prayers and Witr, and know what breaks salah.
  • Tell the stories of Ayyub, Yunus, Dawud and the Conquest of Makkah and what they teach.

Practice at home helps your child reach these goals.

HOW YOU GET THEM THERE

  • Pray together at home whenever you can.
  • Watch your child make wudu once a week.
  • Ask one question each week: What did you learn in Islamic Studies?
  • Sign the salah tracker, the Ramadan Plan and the Character Habit Tracker when they come home.
  • Make dua together, even a short one before bed.

HOW YOUR CHILD IS ASSESSED

  • Exams: Quarter 1 on October 13 to 16, Mid Year on January 11 to 15, Quarter 3 on March 30 to April 2, and the Final on June 7 to 11, all in the school’s exam weeks.
  • Unit tests: early November, December, February, late February and early May, with a review lesson the class before.
  • Practical checks: wudu and tayammum in December; salah in February, and wudu and salah in early June.
  • Home projects: the salah tracker, the Ramadan Plan and the Character Habit Tracker.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Islamic Studies is where belief turns into practice. This year your child learns who Allah is, what waits after this life, how to pray well, and how the prophets stayed patient and merciful. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said he was sent to perfect good character. Inshallah, what your child learns in class becomes who they are at home.

Questions? Contact the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org

Grade 5 · Islamic Studies

Grade 5 Islamic Studies

What your child learns each month, and how you can help at home

THIS PLAN IS TENTATIVE

This is a plan, not a promise. Months are approximate and timing may change, but the year's learning goals stay the same. Any changes, including test dates, will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo.

This year your child learns from Islamic Studies Textbook 6. Quarter 1, August 24 to October 23, was a review of topics from earlier grades. Textbook 6 begins with Quarter 2 on October 26. Where Muslims follow different valid practices, we teach one clear way at school and respect what families practice at home. Class meets three times a week. This guide covers Islamic Studies only; Quran has its own guide.

Late August to mid SeptemberQuarter 1 review: knowing Allah

What your child is learning

  • The Names of Allah and what each Name teaches us to do
  • The angels and their duties, and the books Allah revealed, including the four named in the Quran (Tawrah, Zabur, Injil and Quran)
  • Prophets and messengers, nabi and rasul, and why Muhammad, peace be upon him, is the last prophet
  • Unit 1 test on Wednesday, September 16

Words to know: nabi, rasul, Jibril, Zabur

Try this at home

Ask your child to name three angels and the duty of each one.

Mid September to October 23Quarter 1 review: the Hereafter

What your child is learning

  • The minor and major signs of the Last Day, taught calmly
  • Death, the grave and barzakh, and preparing for the journey of the soul
  • The Day of Judgment: the resurrection, the scales and the records of deeds, the bridge and intercession
  • Paradise, Hell and Allah's mercy, and living for the Hereafter
  • Unit 2 test on Monday, October 19, then the Quarter 1 Islamic Studies exam on Wednesday, October 21
  • Quarter 1 project: the class Tawhid Wall Display, where each child makes a card with a fact and an ayah or hadith

Words to know: barzakh, mizan, sirat, Jannah

Try this at home

Talk about one good deed that keeps helping a person after they die, such as ongoing charity.

Late October and NovemberTextbook 6: prophets of Bani Isra'il

What your child is learning

  • Textbook 6 begins October 26: the prophets sent to Bani Isra'il, the descendants of Prophet Yaqub
  • Prophet Yaqub and his last advice to his children
  • Prophet Sulayman: the ant, the trial of the horses and remembering to say Inshallah, and his letter to the Queen of Saba
  • Unit test and a Prophetic Hall display before Thanksgiving

Words to know: Bani Isra'il, sabr, shukr

Try this at home

Ask your child to retell the story of Sulayman and the ant.

DecemberTextbook 6: purification

What your child is learning

  • Wudu in depth: what is required, the washing described in the Quran, the sunnah acts and what breaks it
  • Tayammum: when it is allowed and how to do it
  • Taharah Teacher project: teaching wudu to a younger child; unit test

Words to know: taharah, wudu, tayammum

Try this at home

Let your child teach wudu to a younger family member.

JanuaryTextbook 6: fasting

What your child is learning

  • Why we fast and what breaks the fast
  • Making up missed fasts; mid year exams January 11 to 15, with the Islamic Studies midterm that week
  • Getting ready for Ramadan (expected around February 8, depending on moon sighting): a Ramadan plan and a unit test

Words to know: siyam, qada, taqwa

Try this at home

Make a family plan for Ramadan together.

FebruaryTextbook 6: salah

What your child is learning

  • The adhan and iqamah: their story, words and meaning
  • The main parts of salah, and salah as our link with Allah
  • Praying on time, making up missed prayers, and fixing mistakes with sujud al sahw

Words to know: adhan, iqamah, qada, sujud al sahw

Try this at home

Answer the adhan together when you hear it.

MarchTextbook 6: salah, then the funeral prayer

What your child is learning

  • School is closed March 1 to 12 for the end of Ramadan and Eid al-Fitr (Eid is expected around March 9 or 10, depending on moon sighting)
  • The meaning of the words we say in salah, and focus in salah after Ramadan; unit test
  • What Muslims do when someone dies, the four takbirs of the funeral prayer and the dua for the deceased; unit test

Words to know: khushu, janazah

Try this at home

Talk about why we pray for those who have passed away.

AprilTextbook 6: the Prophet's last years

What your child is learning

  • Quarter 3 exam in the school exam week, March 30 to April 2; exact date TBD
  • The Battle of Hunayn and the lessons of Hunayn and Taif
  • The Farewell Pilgrimage and Sermon; unit test
  • Year review begins: belief, the Quran and the prophets

Words to know: Hunayn, Taif, Farewell Sermon

Try this at home

Ask your child what the Farewell Sermon teaches about equality.

MayReview and practicals

What your child is learning

  • Review of purity and salah
  • A short, simple lesson on cleanliness and growing up, taught to girls and boys separately
  • School is closed May 17 to 19 for Eid al-Adha
  • Practicals: wudu and salah

Words to know: review, practical

Try this at home

Help your child make a study plan for June.

JunePracticals and the final exam

What your child is learning

  • Practicals: the funeral prayer, the adhan and recitation
  • Final review, then the final exam in the school exam week, June 7 to 11; exact date TBD
  • Grade 5 graduation is Saturday June 19

Words to know: practical

Try this at home

Practice a full salah at home with your child.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME, YOUR CHILD SHOULD BE ABLE TO

Practicing at home helps your child remember and use what they learn in class.

  • Explain the beliefs reviewed in Quarter 1: the Names of Allah, the angels, the revealed books, the prophets and the Last Day
  • Retell the stories of Yaqub and Sulayman
  • Make wudu correctly and know when tayammum is allowed
  • Know the basic rules of fasting and making up missed fasts
  • Pray salah correctly and fix a mistake with sujud al sahw
  • Know the steps of the funeral prayer

WHAT HELPS MOST AT HOME

  • Pray together at home when you can
  • Check the weekly homework (two or three questions)
  • Ask your child what they learned this week
  • Talk about the stories of the prophets

HOW YOUR CHILD IS GRADED

  • A short quiz every other Tuesday, and a test at the end of each unit on that unit only
  • Four exams that cover several units: Quarter 1 (Islamic Studies exam on October 21), the midterm (January 11 to 15), Quarter 3 (March 30 to April 2) and the final (June 7 to 11); exact dates after Quarter 1 TBD
  • Practicals in late May and early June: wudu, salah, the funeral prayer, the adhan and recitation
  • Homework once a week: given on Monday, due the next Monday
  • Report card: quizzes, exams and projects 50 percent; classwork 25 percent; homework 25 percent

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Islamic Studies helps your child know Allah, love the Prophet, peace be upon him, and practice their worship with confidence. What we learn in class grows when it is lived at home.

Questions? Contact the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org | arsheen.sayeed@wischools.org

Grade 6 · Islamic Studies

Grade 6 Islamic Studies

What your child learns each month, and how you can help at home

THIS PLAN IS TENTATIVE

This is a plan, not a promise. Months are approximate and timing may change, but the year's learning goals stay the same. Any changes, including test dates, will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo.

This year your child learns from Islamic Studies Textbook 7. Quarter 1, August 24 to October 23, was a review of topics from earlier grades. Textbook 7 begins with Quarter 2 on October 26. Where Muslims follow different valid practices, we teach one clear way at school and respect what families practice at home. Class meets three times a week. This guide covers Islamic Studies only; Quran has its own guide.

Late August and SeptemberQuarter 1: review

What your child is learning

  • A look back at Grade 5, then who Allah is and why He created us
  • Tawhid, which WIS teaches in three parts, a framework many scholars use; shirk and how to stay away from it
  • Seeing Allah in Jannah (Quran 75:22 to 23), described in hadith as the greatest joy of Jannah; unit test in mid September

Words to know: tawhid, shirk, ibadah

Try this at home

Ask your child to explain in their own words why believing in one God matters.

Late September and OctoberQuarter 1: review

What your child is learning

  • The virtues of the Quran, its manners, and a daily reading plan
  • The Prophet, peace be upon him, as our role model, and why we follow the Sunnah
  • Halal and haram: why Allah forbids some things, harmful substances, reading ingredient lists. Quarter 1 Islamic Studies exam on Thursday, October 22

Words to know: sunnah, halal, haram

Try this at home

Read an ingredient list together. Talk about what to look for, and what to do when it is unclear, such as checking for halal certification or asking someone knowledgeable.

Late October and NovemberTextbook 7: prayer in depth, then fasting

What your child is learning

  • Textbook 7 begins October 26: arriving late to a congregation, doubts in prayer, and sujud al sahw
  • Praying while traveling, ill or in danger
  • Jumuah: its meaning, the khutbah and its manners
  • A salah practical check and a unit test in mid November
  • Fasting: its purpose, requirements and what breaks it, begun before Thanksgiving

Words to know: sujud al sahw, qasr, Jumuah, khutbah

Try this at home

Ask your child how salah changes when someone is traveling or ill.

DecemberTextbook 7: zakah and sadaqah

What your child is learning

  • Itikaf, Eid and zakat al fitr
  • Zakah: who pays, on what wealth, and who receives it
  • Sadaqah, then a unit test in mid December
  • How Islamic rulings are reached, begun before winter break

Try this at home

Talk about how your family gives zakat al fitr before Eid.

JanuaryTextbook 7: how scholars reach rulings

What your child is learning

  • The Quran, the Sunnah, scholarly agreement and analogy
  • Why qualified scholars differ, and respecting those differences
  • Majority opinion, the schools of thought, and the goals of Islamic law; unit test
  • Mid year exams, January 11 to 15; exact date TBD

Words to know: ijma, qiyas, madhhab, maqasid

Try this at home

Ask your child why respected scholars can reach different answers to the same question.

FebruaryTextbook 7: seerah and the prophets, during Ramadan

What your child is learning

  • The Prophet's life: a timeline and its turning points
  • Prophet Yusuf: trial, integrity and forgiveness
  • Zakariyya, Yahya, Maryam and Isa, peace be upon them
  • The ten Companions promised Paradise, and Muslim civilization
  • Ramadan is expected to begin around February 8, depending on moon sighting

At iftar, ask your child to share one story about a Companion.

MarchTextbook 7: history, then the Quran and the heart

What your child is learning

  • School is closed March 1 to 12 for the end of Ramadan and Eid al-Fitr (Eid is expected around March 9 or 10, depending on moon sighting)
  • Seerah and history review, then a unit test
  • The Quran as the Creator's guide
  • The journey of the soul, and nourishing the heart

Try this at home

Ask your child what nourishes the heart, and pick one habit to try as a family.

AprilTextbook 7: fitrah and Muslim life today

What your child is learning

  • Quarter 3 exam in the school exam week, March 30 to April 2; exact date TBD
  • Fitrah: the inner compass
  • The Quran and Sunnah as guiding lights
  • Manners online and offline, and checking information before sharing it
  • Confident Muslim identity and prophetic daily habits, then a unit test at the end of April

Before sharing a message or video, ask your child how they would check that it is true.

MayYear review

What your child is learning

  • A full year review
  • A short, simple lesson on cleanliness and growing up, taught to girls and boys separately
  • School is closed May 17 to 19 for Eid al-Adha

Words to know: review

Try this at home

Help your child make a study plan for June.

JuneThe final exam and the year's close

What your child is learning

  • Final exam in the school exam week, June 7 to 11; exact date TBD
  • The final days, chosen by the teacher

Try this at home

Ask your child which topic this year they would most like to learn more about.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME, YOUR CHILD SHOULD BE ABLE TO

Practicing at home helps your child remember and use what they learn in class.

  • Explain tawhid and why it matters
  • Read an ingredient list and know when to check further
  • Explain how salah changes when traveling or ill, and fix a mistake with sujud al sahw
  • Explain who must pay zakah and who receives it
  • Explain why qualified scholars can differ, and respect those differences
  • Retell the turning points of the Prophet's life and the story of Prophet Yusuf

WHAT HELPS MOST AT HOME

  • Pray together at home when you can
  • Check the weekly homework (two or three questions)
  • Ask your child what they learned this week
  • Talk about the stories of the prophets

  • A short quiz every other Tuesday, and a test at the end of each unit on that unit only
  • Four exams that cover several units: Quarter 1 (Islamic Studies exam on October 22), the midterm (January 11 to 15), Quarter 3 (March 30 to April 2) and the final (June 7 to 11); exact dates after Quarter 1 TBD

  • Homework once a week, due the next week

Grade 1 · Islamic Studies

Grade 1 Islamic Studies

What your child learns this year, and how you can help at home

PLEASE READ

This guide is a plan, not a promise. Months are approximate. Timing and detail may change, but the goals for June stay the same. Anything that changes, and all check dates, will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo.

Islamic Studies meets twice a week. Quran is taught separately and has its own Grade 1 Quran family guide.

Each unit is marked by area: Aqidah, what we believe; Fiqh, how we worship and live; Prophets, stories of the prophets; Seerah, the life of the Prophet, peace be upon him.

Late August to mid SeptemberReview: what we learned in Kindergarten

What your child is learning

  • The Shahadah and the five pillars of Islam.
  • The names of the five daily prayers.
  • The steps of wudu, in order.
  • A prophet story from Kindergarten, retold in their own words.

Words to know: Shahadah, salah, wudu

Try this at home

Count the five pillars on five fingers together, then the five prayers on the other hand.

Mid September to early OctoberFiqh: good manners

What your child is learning

  • Good manners (adab) in class, and the Islamic reason behind each rule.
  • Saying Salam and Bismillah.

Words to know: adab, Salam, Bismillah

Try this at home

Greet your child with Assalamu alaikum every morning and wait for the full reply.

OctoberAqidah: knowing Allah

What your child is learning

  • What Bismillah means and when we say it.
  • Five names of Allah: Ar-Rahman, Ar-Raheem, Al-Malik, As-Salam, As-Samee.

Words to know: Ar-Rahman, Ar-Raheem, As-Samee, dua

Try this at home

Before meals, ask: What does Bismillah mean?

Late October to early DecemberAqidah: our deen, the pillars and our beliefs

What your child is learning

  • The story of the angel Jibril visiting the Prophet, peace be upon him.
  • The Five Pillars of Islam and the six pillars of faith.
  • The four books Allah named in the Quran, good deeds, and Jannah.

Words to know: Shahadah, Salah, Zakah, Sawm, Hajj, Iman, Ihsan

Try this at home

Count the Five Pillars on your fingers together at bedtime.

December to early JanuaryFiqh: good character and being clean

What your child is learning

  • Kind words and choosing good friends.
  • Staying clean as part of faith.
  • Bathroom manners and the two bathroom duas.

Words to know: character, Jazakallahu Khairan, Ghufranak

Try this at home

Say Jazakallahu Khairan whenever your child helps you, and let them say it back.

Mid to late JanuaryFiqh: wudu

What your child is learning

  • When we need wudu, and the steps in order.
  • What breaks wudu, and the dua after wudu.

Words to know: wudu, rinse, elbow, ankle

Try this at home

Let your child make wudu next to you before one prayer each day.

February to late MarchFiqh: salah

What your child is learning

  • The five daily prayers and their times.
  • Each position of salah and what we say in it.
  • Praying 2 rakah, then learning which prayers are longer.
  • A week of salah practice after the Eid break, then the salah check the week of March 22.

Words to know: Fajr, Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib, Isha, ruku, sujud

Try this at home

Invite your child to pray one prayer a day beside you. The salah chart comes home in March.

Late March to AprilProphets: Adam and Nuh

What your child is learning

  • How Allah made Adam, and why Shaytan refused out of pride.
  • Adam and Hawwa saying sorry to Allah, and a gentle lesson on jealousy.
  • Prophet Nuh, the ark, and never giving up.

Words to know: tawbah, pride, jealous, sabr

Try this at home

Ask your child to retell the story of the ark to a younger sibling or grandparent.

Late April and MaySeerah: the life of the Prophet, peace be upon him

What your child is learning

  • The Year of the Elephant and Surah Al-Fil.
  • Haleemah, the trip to Sham, and why he was called Al-Ameen.
  • Cave Hira, Khadijah the first Muslim, and how Umar became Muslim.

Words to know: Makkah, Kaaba, Al-Ameen, Iqra

Try this at home

Ask: What does Al-Ameen mean? Talk about one way your child can be trustworthy.

JuneSeerah: the Hijrah and the year in review

What your child is learning

  • The hard years in Makkah and the Hijrah to Madinah.
  • The first masjid, then a review of the whole year and a final spoken check.

Words to know: Hijrah, Madinah, masjid

Try this at home

Learn the dua Rabbi zidni ilma (My Lord, increase me in knowledge) together.

HOW YOUR CHILD IS CHECKED

There are no big written tests in Grade 1 Islamic Studies. Children show what they know by saying, showing and doing.

  • A short check ends each unit, eight across the year. The teacher reads every question aloud; children circle, match or answer out loud.
  • Your child shows wudu in late January and prays 2 rakah for the teacher the week of March 22, after a week of practice back from the Eid break.
  • A final spoken check in June covers the Shahadah, the pillars, wudu, the prayers and one story of the Prophet, peace be upon him.
  • Between checks, the teacher records each child as Not Yet, Developing or Secure in each area, so growth is tracked all year.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME, YOUR CHILD SHOULD

  • Say the Shahadah, the Five Pillars and the six pillars of faith.
  • Name five names of Allah and what they mean.
  • Make wudu in order and pray 2 rakah.
  • Say the bathroom duas and use kind words.
  • Retell stories of Adam, Nuh and the Prophet, peace be upon him.

Practice at home helps your child reach these goals.

THE HABITS THAT GET THEM THERE

  • Make wudu and pray together, even one prayer a day.
  • Say Bismillah and Salam out loud at home.
  • Ask one question about the week’s lesson at dinner.
  • Retell a prophet story at bedtime.
  • Praise good manners when you see them.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Islamic Studies is where your child learns who Allah is, how to worship Him, and how to live with the character of the Prophet, peace be upon him. We teach with Ilm, Amanah, Adab, Hikmah and Khidmah, and we follow the practice agreed by the majority of scholars, kept simple for young children. What they learn in class grows when they see it lived at home.

Questions? Message your child’s teacher on Class Dojo. Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org

Grade 2 · Islamic Studies

Grade 2 Islamic Studies

What your child learns each month, and how you can help at home

THIS GUIDE IS A PLAN, NOT A PROMISE

Months are approximate. Timing and detail will change, but where your child ends up in June will not. Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo, and test and assessment dates live there, not on this sheet.

Islamic Studies meets twice a week and uses Safar Islamic Studies Textbook 3. Quran is taught separately and has its own family guide.

Each unit is marked by area: Aqidah, what we believe; Fiqh, how we worship and live; Prophets, stories of the prophets; Seerah, the life of the Prophet, peace be upon him.

Late August and SeptemberAqidah: review, then knowing Allah

What your child is learning

  • Review of Grade 1: the pillars of Islam and Iman, and wudu.
  • A short spoken check on names and manners.
  • Five Names of Allah, such as Al-Khaliq, the Creator, and Ar-Razzaq, the Provider.
  • Noticing Allah’s Names in our day.

Words to know: Al-Khaliq, Ar-Razzaq

Try this at home

At dinner, ask: What did Allah provide for us today?

OctoberAqidah: angels, books and prophets

What your child is learning

  • Who the angels are, and four angels and their jobs.
  • The four books of Allah.
  • Why the Quran is special and protected.
  • Believing in Allah’s prophets.

Words to know: malaikah, Tawrah, Zabur, Injil, Quran

Try this at home

Ask your child which angel brought the Quran, and who it was brought to.

NovemberAqidah and Fiqh: the Hereafter, then cleanliness

What your child is learning

  • What happens after we die, taught gently.
  • The path to Jannah and the good deeds that lead there.
  • Cleanliness is part of faith.
  • Clean clothes and clean places for salah.

Words to know: Jannah, Akhirah, taharah

Try this at home

Check together that the family prayer space is clean.

DecemberFiqh: cleanliness and wudu

What your child is learning

  • Bathroom manners and staying clean.
  • Wudu practice.

Words to know: istinja, wudu

Try this at home

Practice bathroom manners and the du’a for entering and leaving.

JanuaryFiqh: salah

What your child is learning

  • Why we pray.
  • The five prayers and how many rakahs each has.
  • Praying two rakahs, then three rakahs for Maghrib.
  • What breaks salah.
  • Practicing salah until it is calm and correct.

Words to know: rakah, Fajr, Maghrib, Isha

Try this at home

Pray Maghrib together and count the rakahs out loud afterward.

FebruaryProphets: prophets of the past and the Cave

What your child is learning

  • Stories of prophets sent to earlier nations, such as Hud and Salih.
  • Prophet Shuayb and honesty in buying and selling.
  • The Companions of the Cave and being brave for Allah.
  • Comparing the stories and their lessons.

Words to know: Madyan, Ashab al Kahf

Try this at home

Ask your child to retell the story of the Companions of the Cave.

MarchSeerah begins

What your child is learning

  • School is closed early in the month for Eid al-Fitr.
  • The Prophet, peace be upon him, invites people to Islam openly.
  • The Night Journey, al Isra.

Words to know: dawah, al Isra

Try this at home

Ask your child what the Prophet saw on the Night Journey.

AprilSeerah and Fiqh: from Makkah to Uhud, then manners

What your child is learning

  • Events of the Prophet’s life up to the Battle of Uhud.
  • The lesson of obeying instructions at Uhud.
  • A Sirah timeline review.
  • Manners of eating and drinking.

Words to know: Uhud, Sirah, adab

Try this at home

Say Bismillah before eating and Alhamdulillah after, together.

MayFiqh: manners and halal food

What your child is learning

  • Manners in the masjid.
  • Screens, games and using time well.
  • Halal and haram food, and reading food labels.
  • Good character around food.

Words to know: halal, haram, adab

Try this at home

Read a snack label together and look for ingredients to check.

JuneYear review

What your child is learning

  • Review of the year.
  • End of year checks.
  • Celebrating what we learned.

Try this at home

Keep one good manner from this year going all summer.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME, YOUR CHILD CAN

  • Name the pillars of Islam and Iman and five Names of Allah.
  • Keep clean, use good bathroom manners and make wudu.
  • Pray two and three rakah prayers and know what breaks salah.
  • Retell stories of earlier prophets and the Prophet’s life up to Uhud.
  • Show good manners at meals, in the masjid and with screens, and choose halal food.

Two lessons a week at school will not get your child there on their own.

HOW YOU GET THEM THERE

  • Pray together at home whenever you can.
  • Say the du’as for eating, the bathroom and sleeping together.
  • Ask one question each week: What did you learn in Islamic Studies?
  • Read a story from the unit with your child.
  • Set simple screen time limits together.

HOW YOUR CHILD IS ASSESSED

  • Checks: a short check at the end of units, many of them spoken rather than written.
  • Salah: your child practices two and three rakah prayers with the teacher watching and helping.
  • Portfolio: posters and class work collected across the year.
  • Dates: any test or check dates are posted on Class Dojo.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Islamic Studies helps your child love Allah and live as a Muslim every day. This year your child learns about Allah’s Names, the unseen world, how to stay clean and pray, and the stories of the prophets. Inshallah, the manners learned in class become habits at home.

Questions? Contact the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org
