Grade 7 · Mathematics

Grade 7 Mathematics

What your child learns and is assessed on, month by month

PLEASE READ

This guide is a plan, not a promise. Months are approximate and the test dates shown are the plan as it stands; timing and detail may change, but the goals for June stay the same. Real test dates and anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo.

Grade 7 uses the Savvas enVision Mathematics Virginia Grade 7 textbook.

Exam dates are tentative. Exams are planned for the school's exam weeks (October 13 to 16, January 11 to 15, March 30 to April 2 and June 7 to 11). Exact date TBD.

Late August to SeptemberLaunch and Topic 1: Rational Numbers

What your child is learning

  • Learning: Routines and a starting diagnostic; ordering, adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing positive and negative numbers, fractions and decimals.
  • Practice: A short quiz each week on that week’s lessons.
  • Assessed: Topic 1 checkpoint Tue Sep 8; Topic 1 test Mon Sep 21.

By the end of the unit: Add, subtract, multiply and divide positive and negative fractions and decimals, and order them on a number line.

Sample question: What is -3/4 + 1/2? What is -2.5 × (-4)?A strong answer: For -3/4 + 1/2, I rewrite 1/2 as 2/4, so -3/4 + 2/4 = -1/4. It is negative because the negative part is bigger. For -2.5 × (-4), negative times negative is positive, so it is 10.

Watch for: Mixing up sign rules, such as saying -3 + (-5) is positive 8 because two negatives make a positive. That rule is for multiplying and dividing, not adding. The answer is -8.

Try this at home

Use a thermometer or bank balance to talk about positive and negative numbers.

OctoberTopic 2: Expressions, Equations and Inequalities

What your child is learning

  • Learning: Order of operations; writing and evaluating expressions; solving two step equations and inequalities.
  • Practice: Modeling word problems with equations.
  • Assessed: Topic 2 checkpoint Wed Oct 7; Quarter 1 exam in the school exam week, Oct 13 to 16; Topic 2 test Thu Oct 22.

By the end of the month: Write and solve two-step equations and inequalities from word problems, and check each answer by substituting it back in.

Sample question: 3 books and a $5 pen cost $20. Each book costs the same. How much is one book?A strong answer: The equation is 3b + 5 = 20. Subtract 5 from both sides: 3b = 15. Divide by 3: b = 5. Each book is $5. Check: 3 × 5 + 5 = 20.

Watch for: Forgetting to flip the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative. For -2x is greater than 8, the answer is x is less than -4, not greater.

Try this at home

Ask your child to turn a real situation (“3 books and a $5 pen cost $20”) into an equation.

NovemberTopic 3: Proportional Relationships

What your child is learning

  • Learning: Equivalent ratios; converting customary and metric units; estimating and finding percents.
  • Practice: Unit conversions and percent problems from real life.
  • Assessed: Topic 3 checkpoint Wed Nov 4; Topic 3 test Tue Nov 24; Topics 1 to 3 benchmark Mon Nov 30.

By the end of the month: Use ratios and proportions to convert units and solve percent problems such as tax, tip and discount.

Sample question: A $40 jacket is 15 percent off. What is the sale price?A strong answer: 15 percent of 40 is 0.15 × 40 = 6, so the discount is $6 and the price is 40 minus 6, or $34. Check: 10 percent is $4 and 5 percent is $2, so $6 off makes sense.

Watch for: Converting units the wrong way, such as dividing instead of multiplying to change 3 feet to inches. Ask: should the number get bigger or smaller? 3 feet is 36 inches.

Try this at home

Compare unit prices at the grocery store to find the better deal.

DecemberTopic 4: Proportions, Slope and Geometry

What your child is learning

  • Learning: Slope as a rate; y = mx; properties of quadrilaterals; similar shapes and scale drawings.
  • Practice: Graphing proportional relationships.
  • Assessed: Topic 4 checkpoint Thu Dec 10.

By the end of the month: Find slope as a rate of change, graph y = mx, and use scale factors to find real lengths from scale drawings.

Sample question: A map scale says 1 inch = 25 miles. Two towns are 3.5 inches apart. How far apart are they?A strong answer: Each inch is 25 miles, so I multiply 3.5 × 25. 3 × 25 = 75 and 0.5 × 25 = 12.5, so it is 87.5 miles. Check: 4 inches would be 100 miles, so a bit less makes sense.

Watch for: Writing slope upside down, as run over rise. Slope is the change in y over the change in x; for y = 3x, each 1 step right goes 3 steps up.

Try this at home

Look at a map scale together and work out a real distance.

JanuaryTopic 4 finish, Topic 5: Data and Probability

What your child is learning

  • Learning: Dilations on the coordinate plane; likelihood, theoretical and experimental probability; histograms.
  • Practice: Running probability experiments.
  • Assessed: Topic 4 test Fri Jan 8; Semester 1 exam in the school exam week, Jan 11 to 15; Topic 5 checkpoint Wed Jan 20.

By the end of the month: Find theoretical and experimental probability, explain why they can differ, and draw dilations on the coordinate plane.

Sample question: A bag has 3 red and 5 blue marbles. What is the probability of picking red?A strong answer: There are 3 + 5 = 8 marbles and 3 are red, so the probability is 3/8, which is 0.375 or about 38 percent. That is less than one half, which makes sense because there are fewer red marbles.

Watch for: Expecting an experiment to match the prediction exactly. Getting 13 heads in 20 flips is normal; results tend to get closer to one half over many more trials.

Try this at home

Flip a coin 20 times and compare the results with what probability predicts.

FebruaryTopics 5 and 6: Samples, Surface Area and Volume

What your child is learning

  • Learning: Populations, samples and inferences; nets of solid figures; surface area of prisms and cylinders; volume of cylinders.
  • Practice: Measuring real boxes and cans.
  • Assessed: Topic 5 test Thu Feb 4; Topic 6 checkpoint Tue Feb 16; Topic 6 test Thu Feb 25. Ramadan: homework kept light.

By the end of the month: Use nets to find the surface area of prisms and cylinders, find the volume of a cylinder, and make inferences from a random sample.

Sample question: A can has a radius of 3 cm and a height of 10 cm. What is its volume? Use 3.14 for pi.A strong answer: Volume of a cylinder is pi × r² × h, so 3.14 × 9 × 10 = 282.6 cubic centimeters. Check: 3 × 9 × 10 = 270, so about 280 makes sense.

Watch for: Mixing up surface area and volume. Surface area covers the outside in square units; volume fills the inside in cubic units. A missing or wrong unit label is the clue.

Try this at home

Measure a cereal box and a can at home and find how much each holds.

MarchReteach and Fluency

What your child is learning

  • Learning: After the Eid break, review and reteaching of the skills the Topic 6 test showed were weakest.
  • Practice: Weekly spiral review quizzes on those skills.
  • Assessed: Spiral review quizzes, then the Quarter 3 exam in the school exam week, Mar 30 to Apr 2.

By the end of the month: Solve problems on the year's weakest skills more accurately, especially surface area and volume, and be ready for the Quarter 3 exam.

Sample question: A box is 8 in by 5 in by 2 in. What is its surface area?A strong answer: There are three pairs of faces: 8 × 5 = 40, 8 × 2 = 16, and 5 × 2 = 10. That adds to 66. Each face has a match, so I double it: 132 square inches.

Watch for: Counting each face only once and forgetting the matching opposite face, which gives half the surface area. Ask your child to point to all six faces on a real box.

Try this at home

Ask your child which topic was hardest this year and practice it together.

AprilReteach finish, Topic 7: Square Roots and Scientific Notation

What your child is learning

  • Learning: Square roots and perfect squares; powers of 10; writing and computing with numbers in scientific notation.
  • Practice: Very large and very small numbers from science.
  • Assessed: Topic 7 checkpoint Tue Apr 20; Topic 7 test Thu Apr 29.

By the end of the month: Find square roots of perfect squares, and write and compute with very large and very small numbers in scientific notation.

Sample question: Write 93,000,000 miles, the distance to the sun, in scientific notation. What is the square root of 144?A strong answer: I move the decimal 7 places left to get 9.3, so it is 9.3 × 10⁷ miles. The square root of 144 is 12, because 12 × 12 = 144.

Watch for: Writing a first number outside 1 to 10, like 93 × 10⁶. It has the right value but is not scientific notation; the first number must be at least 1 and less than 10.

Try this at home

Find the distance to the sun or the size of a cell and write it in scientific notation.

MayYear Benchmark and Review

What your child is learning

  • Learning: A full year benchmark, reteaching, then year end review of every topic.
  • Practice: Mixed review problems across the year.
  • Assessed: Topics 1 to 7 benchmark Apr 30 to May 4; weekly spiral review quizzes. No homework over the Eid break.

By the end of the month: Solve mixed problems from all seven topics and choose the right strategy without being told which topic a problem comes from.

Sample question: A $24 shirt has 5 percent sales tax. What is the total? Then solve 2x + 7 = 19.A strong answer: Tax is 0.05 × 24 = $1.20, so the total is $25.20. For 2x + 7 = 19, subtract 7 to get 2x = 12, then divide by 2, so x = 6. Check: 2 × 6 + 7 = 19.

Watch for: Memorizing formulas without knowing when to use them. When going over the study sheet, ask your child to name one problem each formula solves.

Try this at home

Help your child make a one page study sheet of the year’s key formulas.

JuneFinal Exam and Year End

What your child is learning

  • Learning: A STEM project and a portfolio of the year’s best work.
  • Practice: Explaining reasoning in the portfolio reflection.
  • Assessed: Final exam in the school exam week, Jun 7 to 11; STEM project.

By the end of the month: Explain mathematical reasoning clearly in writing, and use the year's skills in a STEM project and a portfolio reflection.

Sample question: In your STEM project, what math did you use, and how did you check your answer was reasonable?A strong answer: We designed a box to hold the most cereal with the least cardboard, so we used volume and surface area. I estimated with rounded numbers first, and my exact answer was close to my estimate.

Watch for: Reviewing for the final by only rereading notes. Working a few problems from each topic without looking at examples shows what your child truly remembers.

Try this at home

Read your child’s portfolio reflection and celebrate their growth.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Compute fluently with positive and negative numbers, fractions and decimals.
  • Solve two step equations and inequalities.
  • Solve unit conversion and percent problems.
  • Graph proportional relationships and explain slope as a rate.
  • Find surface area and volume of prisms and cylinders.
  • Use probability, samples and scientific notation.

Regular practice and talking about math at home make a real difference alongside class lessons.

HOW TO GET THERE AT HOME

  • Ten to fifteen minutes of math practice every school night.
  • Ask your child to explain a problem to you, not just give the answer.
  • Keep practicing multiplication and fraction facts; they speed up everything else.
  • Check Class Dojo each week for test dates and missing work.
  • Encourage mistakes as learning: ask what went wrong and try again.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Mathematics is a trust (amanah): honest measurement and fair dealing are commanded in the Quran (“And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with an even balance,” Surah Al-Isra 17:35, Sahih International translation). Students see math in Muslim life, from calculating zakat at 2.5 percent to finding the qibla direction, and in the legacy of al-Khwarizmi, whose work gave algebra its name.

HOW MATH CLASS WORKS AND HOW GRADES ARE MADE

  • A typical class: a warm up, the new enVision lesson, practice with a partner, then independent practice and a quick check.
  • Weekly quiz: a short 10 to 15 minute quiz each week on that week’s lessons, given at the start of class.
  • Tests: a test at least every other week: a mid topic checkpoint and a topic test for each of the seven topics, plus quarter benchmarks, a Semester 1 exam and a final exam. No quiz or test in a two day week.
  • Extra help: skills the class scores below 70 percent on are retaught the next week. A student below 60 percent gets small group support, and families are contacted if it happens twice in a row.

Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org | Questions: contact your child’s math teacher through Class Dojo

Grade 8 · Mathematics

Grade 8 Mathematics

What your child learns and is assessed on, month by month

PLEASE READ

This guide is a plan, not a promise. Months and test timing shown here are the plan as it stands; timing and detail may change, but the goals for June stay the same. Real test dates and anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo.

Grade 8 uses the Savvas enVision Mathematics Virginia Grade 8 textbook and prepares students for Algebra 1.

Exam dates are tentative. Exams are planned for the school's exam weeks (October 13 to 16, January 11 to 15, March 30 to April 2 and June 7 to 11). Exact date TBD.

Late August to SeptemberTopic 1: Real Numbers and Percents

What your child is learning

  • Learning: Rational and irrational numbers, square roots, ordering real numbers on a number line; the percent equation, percent increase and decrease, markup and discount.
  • Practice: Daily warm ups and number talks to build mental math.
  • Assessed: A mid topic checkpoint and the Topic 1 test in mid September.

By the end of the unit: Classify and order real numbers, estimate square roots, and solve percent increase, decrease, markup and discount problems.

Sample question: A $60 game is 25 percent off. What is the sale price? Is √50 rational?A strong answer: 25 percent is one fourth, and one fourth of 60 is 15, so the price is $45. √50 is irrational because 50 is not a perfect square. It is between 7 and 8, about 7.1.

Watch for: Finding percent change from the wrong starting number. A price going from $40 to $50 is a 25 percent increase, because the $10 change is compared to the original $40.

Try this at home

When shopping, ask your child to work out a 25 percent discount before you reach the register.

OctoberTopics 2 and 3: Expressions, Equations and Inequalities

What your child is learning

  • Learning: Writing, simplifying, expanding and factoring expressions; solving equations with variables on both sides; multistep inequalities.
  • Practice: Checking answers by substituting them back in.
  • Assessed: Topic 2 test in early October; Quarter 1 exam in the school exam week, October 13 to 16; Topic 3 test in late October.

By the end of the month: Simplify, expand and factor expressions, solve equations with variables on both sides, and solve and graph multistep inequalities.

Sample question: Solve 5x + 3 = 2x + 18, and check your answer.A strong answer: Subtract 2x from both sides: 3x + 3 = 18. Subtract 3: 3x = 15. Divide by 3: x = 5. Check: 5 × 5 + 3 = 28 and 2 × 5 + 18 = 28. Both sides match.

Watch for: Distributing to only the first term, writing 3(x + 4) as 3x + 4 instead of 3x + 12. Substituting the answer back in catches this right away.

Try this at home

Ask your child to explain one equation from homework to you step by step.

NovemberTopic 4: Functions and Linear Relationships

What your child is learning

  • Learning: What makes a relation a function; domain and range; slope and the y intercept.
  • Practice: Reading tables, graphs and equations as three views of the same pattern.
  • Assessed: A mid topic checkpoint.

By the end of the month: Decide whether a relation is a function, name its domain and range, and find slope and y-intercept from tables, graphs and equations.

Sample question: A phone plan costs $20 a month plus $5 per gigabyte. What are the slope and y-intercept, and what do they mean?A strong answer: The equation is y = 5x + 20. The slope is 5, meaning each gigabyte adds $5. The y-intercept is 20, the $20 you pay even with zero gigabytes.

Watch for: Thinking a relation is not a function when two inputs share an output. That is fine; it fails only when one input has two outputs, like x = 2 going to both 3 and 7.

Try this at home

Track a family cost that grows steadily (a phone plan or gas) and ask what the slope means.

DecemberTopic 4 finish, Topic 5 begins

What your child is learning

  • Learning: y = mx + b; scatter plots and lines of best fit; the Pythagorean Theorem begins.
  • Practice: Collecting and graphing real data.
  • Assessed: Topic 4 test in early December.

By the end of the month: Write and graph y = mx + b, draw a line of best fit on a scatter plot, and begin using the Pythagorean Theorem.

Sample question: A screen is 12 inches wide and 9 inches tall. How long is its diagonal?A strong answer: Using a² + b² = c², 12² + 9² = 144 + 81 = 225. The square root of 225 is 15, so the diagonal is 15 inches. Check: 15 is longer than either side, as it must be.

Watch for: Drawing a line of best fit through just the first and last points. A good line follows the overall trend, with about as many points above it as below it.

Try this at home

Measure a TV or tablet screen and use the Pythagorean Theorem to check its diagonal.

JanuaryTopics 5 and 6: Pythagorean Theorem and Geometry

What your child is learning

  • Learning: The Pythagorean Theorem and its converse, distance on the coordinate plane; angle pairs, and area and perimeter of composite shapes.
  • Practice: Drawing and labeling diagrams before solving.
  • Assessed: Topic 5 test in early January; mid-year exam in the school exam week, January 11 to 15.

By the end of the month: Use the Pythagorean Theorem and its converse, find distance on the coordinate plane, and use angle pairs to find missing angles.

Sample question: Two angles are supplementary and one is 115°. What is the other? Is a 6, 8, 11 triangle a right triangle?A strong answer: Supplementary angles add to 180°, so 180 minus 115 is 65°. For the triangle, 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100, but 11² = 121. They do not match, so it is not a right triangle.

Watch for: Forgetting the last square root, so c² = 100 becomes c = 100 instead of 10. Also watch for a leg used as c; c is always the longest side.

Try this at home

Find vertical and supplementary angles at a street intersection or in a window frame.

FebruaryTopic 6 finish, Topic 7 begins

What your child is learning

  • Learning: Translations and reflections on the coordinate plane; surface area and volume of pyramids and cones; probability begins.
  • Practice: Hands on models of 3D figures.
  • Assessed: Topic 6 test in early February. Ramadan: homework kept light.

By the end of the month: Translate and reflect figures on the coordinate plane, and find the surface area and volume of pyramids and cones.

Sample question: A cone has a radius of 3 cm and a height of 8 cm. What is its volume? Use 3.14 for pi.A strong answer: Volume of a cone is 1/3 × pi × r² × h, so 1/3 × 3.14 × 9 × 8 = 3.14 × 24 = 75.36 cubic centimeters. That is one third of a cylinder the same size.

Watch for: Forgetting the 1/3 in cone and pyramid volume, which makes the answer three times too big. A cone holds one third of a matching cylinder.

Try this at home

Estimate how much water an ice cream cone holds, then compute its volume together.

MarchTopic 7: Probability and Statistics

What your child is learning

  • Learning: Independent and dependent events, compound probability, box plots, comparing two groups using data.
  • Practice: Running simple experiments and recording results.
  • Assessed: Topic 7 test in mid March, after the Eid break, then the Quarter 3 exam in the school exam week, March 30 to April 2.

By the end of the month: Find probabilities of independent and dependent events, and compare two data sets using box plots, medians and spread.

Sample question: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue marbles. You pick two without putting the first back. What is the chance both are red?A strong answer: First pick: 4/10. One red is gone, so the second pick is 3/9. Multiply: 4/10 × 3/9 = 12/90 = 2/15, about 13 percent. That makes sense since red is the smaller group.

Watch for: Treating dependent events as independent, such as using 4/10 twice when the first marble is not replaced. Ask: did anything change after the first pick?

Try this at home

Play a dice or card game and ask your child the probability of the next outcome.

AprilSpiral Review and Projects

What your child is learning

  • Learning: Every topic from the year reviewed in cycles, with targeted help where the exams showed gaps.
  • Practice: Real world performance tasks that combine several skills.
  • Assessed: End of year performance tasks begin.

By the end of the month: Combine skills from several topics to solve real-world performance tasks and explain each step clearly.

Sample question: An $80 jacket is marked up 20 percent, then put on sale for 20 percent off. Is the final price $80?A strong answer: No. The markup makes it 80 × 1.2 = $96. Then 20 percent of $96 is $19.20, so the final price is $76.80. The discount comes off a bigger number, so it removes more than the markup added.

Watch for: Freezing on multistep problems because no single topic is named. Ask your child to say first what the problem wants, then which skill fits each step.

Try this at home

Ask your child which topic from the year still feels hardest, and practice it together for ten minutes.

MayReview and Algebra 1 Readiness

What your child is learning

  • Learning: Continued spiral review and the skills needed for Algebra 1 next year.
  • Practice: Multistep problems in real contexts.
  • Assessed: Performance tasks. No homework over the Eid break.

By the end of the month: Solve multistep real-world problems with equations, functions and percents, showing the skills needed for Algebra 1.

Sample question: A trip is 270 miles, the car gets 30 miles per gallon, and gas is $3.20 a gallon. What will gas cost?A strong answer: 270 ÷ 30 = 9 gallons. Then 9 × 3.20 = $28.80. Check: 10 gallons would be $32, so a little less makes sense.

Watch for: Sign slips when distributing a negative, such as writing -2(x + 3) as -2x + 6 instead of -2x minus 6. Algebra 1 depends on these steps being automatic.

Try this at home

Plan a family budget or trip together and let your child do the math.

JuneYear End

What your child is learning

  • Learning: Final review of all standards.
  • Practice: Showing work and explaining reasoning.
  • Assessed: The Year End Review Assessment in the school's final exam week, June 7 to 11, used to help show readiness for Algebra 1.
  • Grade 8 graduation: Saturday, June 19. Attendance is required.

By the end of the month: Show work and explain reasoning across all Grade 8 standards on the Year End Review Assessment, building the skills needed for Algebra 1.

Sample question: Solve 3(x + 2) = 4x + 1 and explain each step.A strong answer: Distribute: 3x + 6 = 4x + 1. Subtract 3x from both sides: 6 = x + 1. Subtract 1: x = 5. Check: 3(5 + 2) = 21 and 4 × 5 + 1 = 21. Both match.

Watch for: Writing only answers. Without steps a small slip cannot be found, so ask your child to explain one problem aloud as if teaching it to you.

Try this at home

Celebrate your child’s growth and ask what math skill they are proudest of.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Work confidently with real numbers, percents and square roots.
  • Solve multistep equations and inequalities.
  • Graph and explain linear functions and slope.
  • Use the Pythagorean Theorem and find area, surface area and volume.
  • Find probabilities and read box plots and scatter plots.
  • Build the skills needed for Algebra 1.

Regular practice and talking about math at home make a real difference alongside class lessons.

HOW TO GET THERE AT HOME

  • Ten to fifteen minutes of math practice every school night.
  • Ask your child to explain a problem to you, not just give the answer.
  • Keep practicing multiplication and fraction facts; they speed up everything else.
  • Check Class Dojo each week for test dates and missing work.
  • Encourage mistakes as learning: ask what went wrong and try again.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Mathematics is a trust (amanah): honest measurement and fair dealing are commanded in the Quran (“And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with an even balance,” Surah Al-Isra 17:35, Sahih International translation). Students see math in Muslim life, from calculating zakat at 2.5 percent to finding the qibla direction, and in the legacy of al-Khwarizmi, whose work gave algebra its name.

HOW MATH CLASS WORKS AND HOW GRADES ARE MADE

  • A typical class: a warm up or number talk, the new lesson, practice with a partner, then independent practice and a quick check before leaving.
  • Checkpoints: a short mid topic quiz about halfway through each topic, counted as a practice grade, so gaps are caught before the test.
  • Tests: a test and a performance task at the end of each of the seven topics, plus cumulative exams in the school's exam weeks: October 13 to 16, January 11 to 15, and March 30 to April 2.
  • Second chance: a student who scores below 70 percent on a topic test gets extra help and a retake within the next topic.
  • Year end: performance tasks in April and May, and a Year End Review Assessment in the final exam week, June 7 to 11, that helps show readiness for Algebra 1.

Grades 7 and 8 · English

Grades 7 and 8 English

What your child reads, writes and hands in, month by month

PLEASE READ

This guide is a plan, not a promise. Months are approximate, and timing and detail will change, but the June destination will not. Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo, and that is where test dates live.

Grades 7 and 8 learn together in one class: both read the same texts, and Grade 8 students complete deeper tasks and extra exam questions. Every text has been reviewed by WIS, and some textbook selections have been replaced with WIS readings.

Late August to SeptemberUnit 1: Crossing Generations

What your child is learning

  • Reading: A short story about a young basketball player and an older mentor; an article on disappearing languages; a memoir by Maya Angelou about meeting her mother.
  • Writing: A true personal narrative about learning from someone of another generation.
  • Handed in: The personal narrative draft; Unit Exams every two weeks.

By the end of the unit: Write a true personal narrative with a clear beginning, middle and end that shows a lesson learned from someone of another generation.

Sample question: What lesson does your personal narrative show, and which moment in the story shows it best?A strong answer: My narrative shows that patience matters. My grandmother taught me to bake bread, and the best moment is when my first loaf failed and she said to try again. That scene shows the lesson instead of just telling it.

Watch for: Stating the lesson in one line at the end instead of showing it through a scene with dialogue and detail. Ask: which moment in your story shows this?

Try this at home

Ask your child to interview a grandparent or elder about one lesson they learned young.

OctoberUnit 1 finish, Unit 2 begins

What your child is learning

  • Reading: Three family poems; space settlement artwork; “Dark They Were, and Golden-Eyed,” a science fiction story set on Mars.
  • Writing: A Tribute Letter to someone from another generation; the final personal narrative.
  • Handed in: The narrative and letter; Quarter 1 English exam in mid October.

By the end of the month: Write a tribute letter and a final personal narrative, and explain how a story's setting changes its characters.

Sample question: In Dark They Were, and Golden-Eyed, how does Mars change the Bittering family?A strong answer: Little by little their eyes turn golden, their skin darkens, and they start using Martian words. Mr. Bittering fights it at first, but by the end the family forgets Earth and moves to the hills. The setting changes who they are.

Watch for: Retelling the plot instead of explaining it. If an answer only lists events, ask: why does that detail matter, and what does it show?

Try this at home

Ask who they chose for the Tribute Letter and why.

NovemberUnit 2: Living Among the Stars

What your child is learning

  • Reading: The same Mars story as a radio script; a science article on Japan’s Moon and Mars research.
  • Writing: An editorial answering “Is space exploration important?”
  • Handed in: The editorial draft; a Unit Exam about every two weeks.

By the end of the month: Write an editorial that states a clear claim about space exploration and supports it with evidence and reasoning.

Sample question: Is space exploration important? Give your claim, one piece of evidence, and your reasoning.A strong answer: Yes, it is important. The article on Japan's Moon and Mars research shows that space programs push countries to build new technology. That matters because tools first made for space often end up helping people on Earth.

Watch for: Giving opinions with no evidence, or quoting evidence without explaining it. Each reason in the editorial needs a fact from a text and a sentence explaining why it matters.

Try this at home

At dinner, ask: should people ever live on Mars? Ask for one reason and one piece of evidence.

DecemberUnit 2 finish, Unit 3 begins

What your child is learning

  • Reading: Two opposing arguments about space; “The Three Questions” (a Tolstoy retelling); “Thank You, M’am” by Langston Hughes.
  • Writing: The final editorial; journal entries from two characters’ points of view.
  • Handed in: The editorial and a class debate.

By the end of the month: Explain how an author develops a theme, and write journal entries that show two characters' different points of view.

Sample question: What are the three answers in The Three Questions, and what theme do they teach?A strong answer: The most important time is now, the most important person is the one you are with, and the most important thing is to do good for that person. The theme is to pay attention to the present and help whoever is in front of you.

Watch for: Writing both journal entries in the same voice. In Thank You, M'am, Roger and Mrs. Jones see that night very differently, so each entry should show only what that character knows and feels.

Try this at home

Ask your child to explain the three answers in “The Three Questions.”

JanuaryUnit 3: Transformations

What your child is learning

  • Reading: An article on how learning changes the brain; three short poems about change.
  • Writing: Begin an original short story about a character who changes.
  • Handed in: The short story plan; Mid-Year English exam in mid January.

By the end of the month: Plan a short story with a character who clearly changes, and connect the article and poems to the idea of transformation.

Sample question: How does learning change the brain, according to the article?A strong answer: When you practice something new, the connections between brain cells, called neurons, get stronger. So the brain actually changes a little each time we learn. That means getting better comes from repeated practice, not just talent.

Watch for: A character who changes for no reason. Ask your child what event causes the change; a strong story shows the cause, not just a different ending.

Try this at home

Ask what their story’s character is like at the start and at the end.

FebruaryUnit 3 finish, Unit 4 and Animal Farm begin

What your child is learning

  • Reading: An article on bees in the city; Animal Farm, Chapters 1 to 4, one a week (see the box below).
  • Writing: Finish the short story; write and perform a short play adapted from a story or poem.
  • Handed in: The final short story and the play performance. Ramadan: homework kept light.

By the end of the month: Finish and revise an original short story, perform a short play adaptation, and summarize Animal Farm, Chapters 1 to 4.

Sample question: In Animal Farm, what was Old Major's dream, and why did the animals rebel?A strong answer: Old Major dreamed of a world without humans, where animals kept what they worked for. The animals were hungry and overworked, and when Mr. Jones forgot to feed them, they drove him off the farm.

Watch for: Reading Animal Farm as just an animal story. Ask who the pigs might stand for; noticing that the book is about people and power is the start of understanding it.

Try this at home

Ask your child to perform their play scene for the family.

MarchUnit 4: Learning From Nature

What your child is learning

  • Reading: Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring; two Native American stories about the sun; a poem about caring for the earth; an article on buildings inspired by nature.
  • Writing: Short responses and an allegory chart for Animal Farm.
  • Handed in: Animal Farm Chapters 5 to 7, one a week once school reopens after the Eid break. No reading over the break.

By the end of the month: Explain what an allegory is and match Animal Farm characters and events to the real history they stand for.

Sample question: What is an allegory, and who might Napoleon stand for in Animal Farm?A strong answer: An allegory is a story where characters and events stand for real people and ideas. Napoleon stands for Joseph Stalin, because he chases out his rival Snowball and uses his dogs to rule by fear.

Watch for: Mixing up Snowball and Napoleon after Chapter 5. If your child says Snowball is still on the farm, they have missed the chapter where the dogs chase him away.

Try this at home

Read a chapter of Animal Farm aloud together, or listen to the audio.

AprilUnit 4 finish

What your child is learning

  • Reading: A Japanese story about a hole that swallows everything people throw away; Animal Farm, Chapters 8 to 10, one a week.
  • Writing: An essay on how Animal Farm shows power and propaganda.
  • Handed in: Quarter 3 English exam in the school exam week, March 30 to April 2; the Animal Farm essay at the end of April.

By the end of the month: Write an essay explaining how Animal Farm shows power and propaganda, supported by quotations from the book.

Sample question: How does Squealer use propaganda to keep the animals loyal?A strong answer: Squealer twists facts and reads out made up numbers to prove life is better. The pigs even secretly change the Seven Commandments, so the animals doubt their own memory. Since they cannot prove him wrong, they keep obeying.

Watch for: Quoting the book without explaining it. After each quotation, the essay should say how it shows power or propaganda. Look for the word because.

Try this at home

Ask which character in Animal Farm reminds them of something in the news, and why.

MayUnit 5: Facing Adversity

What your child is learning

  • Reading: The Dust Bowl in nonfiction and in a diary; an article on accessibility; “The Circuit,” a story of a migrant family.
  • Writing: An informational essay about how people overcome challenges.
  • Handed in: The informational essay. No homework over the Eid break.

By the end of the month: Write an informational essay that explains how people overcome challenges, using facts from more than one text.

Sample question: In The Circuit, why does the ending hurt so much?A strong answer: Panchito finally feels at home at school, and Mr. Lema offers to teach him the trumpet. Then he comes home and sees the boxes packed for another move. The ending shows his hope being taken away again.

Watch for: Mixing opinion into an informational essay. Sentences that start with I think belong in an editorial; here each paragraph should explain using facts from the texts.

Try this at home

Share a hard time your family came through and how you kept going.

JuneUnit 5 finish and year end

What your child is learning

  • Reading: An interview with an astronaut who was rejected eleven times; a poem and a short prose piece about trees and strength.
  • Writing: Biographical profiles; a Letter of Encouragement; an end of year reflection.
  • Handed in: The profiles and letter; Final English exam in the school exam week, June 7 to 11.

By the end of the month: Write a biographical profile and a letter of encouragement, and reflect on their growth as a reader and writer this year.

Sample question: What does the astronaut's story of being rejected eleven times teach about facing adversity?A strong answer: It teaches that rejection is not the end. He kept building new skills each time he was turned down, and on the twelfth try he was chosen. Persistence and learning from each no got him there.

Watch for: A reflection that lists activities instead of showing growth. Ask your child for one thing they could not do in August that they can do now, with an example.

Try this at home

Read your child’s reflection letter and tell them one way you saw them grow.

OUR ONE NOVEL: ANIMAL FARM BY GEORGE ORWELL (FEBRUARY TO APRIL)

  • What it is: a short novel in which farm animals take over their farm, and the pigs slowly become the cruel masters they replaced. It is an allegory, a simple story that stands for real events in history.
  • How it is read: one chapter a week at home, ten chapters from February to April with a pause over the Eid break (an audio version is available), then discussed in class with a chart tracking what each animal stands for.
  • Handled with care: some chapters include the animals’ executions, the pigs drinking, and a raven used to mock how rulers misuse religion. Teachers present these as warnings about corrupt power.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Explain a text’s theme or central idea with evidence.
  • Write a clear narrative, argument, short story and informational essay.
  • Evaluate an argument and answer the other side respectfully.
  • Explain how Animal Farm uses a simple story to show how power corrupts.
  • Present to the class with confidence.

School lessons alone will not get your child here; reading and talking at home will.

HOW TO GET THERE AT HOME

  • Twenty minutes of reading every day, in any book.
  • Ask one question a day about what they read.
  • Have your child read their writing aloud to you before it is handed in.
  • Check Class Dojo each week for exam dates and missing work.
  • Keep a quiet place and time for homework.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Every text is chosen or replaced to fit our values. Students practice birr al walidayn as they write about elders, amanah as caretakers of the earth, sabr in the stories of people who overcame hardship, honest speech against propaganda in Animal Farm, and the adab of disagreeing respectfully in debate.

HOW GRADES ARE MADE THIS YEAR

A Unit Exam about every two weeks with a review day the day before, one quiz in each week without an exam, and major writing scored Secure, Developing or Beginning.

Grades 7 and 8 · World History

Grades 7 and 8 World History

What your child studies and hands in, month by month

PLEASE READ

This guide is a plan, not a promise. Months are approximate, and timing and detail may change, but the goals for June stay the same. Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo, and that is where test dates live.

Grades 7 and 8 learn World History together in one class, using the Savvas World History textbook alongside WIS lessons that go deeper into Islamic history.

Exam dates are tentative. Exams are planned for the school's exam weeks (October 13 to 16, January 11 to 15, March 30 to April 2 and June 7 to 11). Exact date TBD.

Late August to SeptemberOrigins to Egypt

What your child is learning

  • Studying: How the first civilizations began; Mesopotamia, the Assyrians, Persians and Phoenicians; ancient Egypt and Kush along the Nile.
  • Skills: Reading primary sources, starting with the Epic of Gilgamesh and an inscription of Ramses II.
  • Handed in: Topic 1, 2 and 3 tests.

By the end of the unit: Explain how rivers helped the first civilizations grow, and read a primary source such as the Epic of Gilgamesh for clues about its time.

Sample question: Why did ancient Egypt grow along the Nile when most of the land around it was desert?A strong answer: The Nile flooded every year and left rich silt for farming. It also gave water and a road for trade boats. With extra food, some people could become builders, scribes and priests, so a civilization grew.

Watch for: Mixing up early civilizations, such as placing Gilgamesh or cuneiform in Egypt. Mesopotamia lies between the Tigris and Euphrates; Egypt is on the Nile and used hieroglyphics.

Try this at home

Ask your child how the Nile shaped Egyptian life, and how the Quran describes Musa and Firawn.

OctoberIndia and China

What your child is learning

  • Studying: The Indus Valley, the Maurya and Gupta empires, the Asoka edicts; early China and the Han dynasty.
  • Skills: Maps and geography; judging a leader’s legacy.
  • Handed in: Topic 4 and 5 tests; the Quarter 1 checkpoint in the school exam week, October 13 to 16.

By the end of the month: Describe the Indus Valley, Maurya, Gupta and Han civilizations, locate them on a map, and judge a leader's legacy using evidence.

Sample question: How did Asoka change after the battle of Kalinga, and how do his edicts show it?A strong answer: After seeing how many people died at Kalinga, Asoka turned away from war. His edicts, carved on rocks and pillars, told people to be kind, tell the truth and respect other faiths. They show he wanted to rule fairly.

Watch for: Calling a ruler simply good or bad. For a legacy question, ask for one achievement and one cost with evidence, like Shi Huangdi uniting China but using forced labor for his walls.

Try this at home

Find India and China on a map together and trace the Silk Road.

NovemberAncient Greece and Rome

What your child is learning

  • Studying: Athens and Sparta, Greek learning and Alexander; how the Roman Republic governed and why it struggled.
  • Skills: Comparing kinds of government; working with documents.
  • Handed in: Topic 6 and 7 tests and short projects.

By the end of the month: Compare Athenian democracy, Spartan rule and the Roman Republic, and explain why the Republic struggled.

Sample question: How was the Roman Republic set up so that no one person held too much power?A strong answer: Romans elected two consuls who served only one year and could block each other. The Senate advised them, and tribunes could veto laws that hurt the plebeians. Power was shared and checked.

Watch for: Thinking Athenian democracy included everyone. Only free adult male citizens could vote; women, enslaved people and foreigners could not. Ask your child who was left out.

Try this at home

Talk about shura: how does your family make a big decision together?

DecemberRome, Byzantium and Medieval Europe

What your child is learning

  • Studying: The Roman and Byzantine empires; feudal Europe; the Crusades, the Magna Carta and eight centuries of Muslim Spain (al-Andalus).
  • Skills: Cause and effect; seeing events from more than one side.
  • Handed in: Topic 8, 9 and 10 tests.

By the end of the month: Explain the causes and effects of feudalism, the Crusades and the Magna Carta, and describe events from more than one point of view.

Sample question: Who was Salahuddin al-Ayyubi, and why is 1187 remembered?A strong answer: He was the Muslim leader who united Egypt and Syria. In 1187 he won at Hattin and took back Jerusalem. Unlike the Crusaders in 1099, he spared the people of the city, so he is remembered for mercy in victory.

Watch for: Seeing the Crusades from one side only. Ask how a Muslim, a Christian and a Jewish resident of Jerusalem might each describe the same event.

Try this at home

Ask your child who Salahuddin al-Ayyubi was and what he did in 1187.

JanuaryWorld Religions and the Semester Exam

What your child is learning

  • Studying: Judaism, Hinduism, Buddhism, Chinese belief systems and Christianity, taught with accuracy and adab while holding firmly to tawhid (see the box below).
  • Skills: Building and defending a comparison chart.
  • Handed in: The Semester 1 Midterm in the school exam week, January 11 to 15; the World Religions assessment.

By the end of the month: Describe the main beliefs of Judaism, Hinduism, Buddhism, Chinese belief systems and Christianity accurately, and compare them in a chart.

Sample question: How is studying another religion as a historian different from believing in it?A strong answer: A historian describes what a faith teaches, using accurate sources and respectful words. That does not mean accepting it. As Muslims we hold firmly to tawhid, and the Quran says there is no compulsion in religion.

Watch for: Mixing up terms across faiths, such as karma, Torah and the Eightfold Path. Ask your child to place each word under the right religion on their comparison chart.

Try this at home

Ask what the Quran teaches about Isa (AS) and about kindness to People of the Book.

FebruaryThe Islamic World, our flagship unit

What your child is learning

  • Studying: The Seerah, the Rightly Guided Caliphs, the Umayyads and Abbasids, the Golden Age of scholars and sciences, Islamic art and architecture, Ibn Khaldun.
  • Skills: Primary sources and a group project on the growth of Muslim empires.
  • Handed in: Mid-unit and Topic 11 tests; Ramadan Legacy Week project and service work.

By the end of the month: Trace the growth of the Muslim world from the Seerah through the Abbasids, and explain what the Golden Age gave to science and learning.

Sample question: Why did Baghdad become a world center of learning under the Abbasids?A strong answer: The Abbasids supported the House of Wisdom, Bayt al-Hikmah, where scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian books. Paper made books cheaper, and the call to seek knowledge drove scholars like al-Khwarizmi to make new discoveries.

Watch for: Blending the caliphates together. The Rashidun ruled mainly from Madinah, the Umayyads from Damascus, and the Abbasids from Baghdad. A quick timeline keeps them in order.

Try this at home

Share a favorite story of a Muslim scholar or scientist with your child.

MarchEast Asia and the Americas

What your child is learning

  • Studying: Tang, Song, Mongol and Ming China; Japan; how Islam reached Southeast Asia through trade; the Maya, Aztec and Inca.
  • Skills: Using maps and comparing civilizations.
  • Handed in: Topic 12 and 13 tests. No homework over the Eid break.

By the end of the month: Compare the civilizations of East Asia and the Americas, and explain how trade and contact spread ideas and faith.

Sample question: How did Islam reach Southeast Asia without armies?A strong answer: Muslim merchants sailed to ports like Malacca to trade spices. People saw they were honest and fair in business, and some rulers and traders accepted Islam. It spread along the trade routes.

Watch for: Mixing up the Maya, Aztec and Inca. A quick check: Maya in southern Mexico and Central America, Aztec in central Mexico at Tenochtitlan, Inca in the Andes of South America.

Try this at home

Ask your child about Zheng He, the Muslim admiral of Ming China.

AprilAfrica, the Renaissance and Muslim Empires

What your child is learning

  • Studying: Ghana, Mali and Songhai, Mansa Musa’s hajj, the manuscripts of Timbuktu, Ibn Battuta; the Renaissance and Reformation; the Ottomans begin.
  • Skills: Tracing how knowledge moved from the Muslim world into Europe.
  • Handed in: Topic 14 and 15 tests; the Quarter 3 checkpoint in the school exam week, March 30 to April 2.

By the end of the month: Explain how trade across the Sahara built Ghana, Mali and Songhai, and how knowledge from the Muslim world helped spark the Renaissance.

Sample question: Why was Mansa Musa's hajj in 1324 so famous?A strong answer: He traveled to Makkah with thousands of people and so much gold that he gave it away in Cairo, and gold lost value there. The journey put Mali on European maps and showed how rich West Africa was.

Watch for: Thinking the Renaissance came only from ancient Greece and Rome. Ask how Greek books and Arabic science reached Europe; the answer runs through al-Andalus and Sicily.

Try this at home

Look at a map of Ibn Battuta’s travels together.

MayGreat Muslim Empires and Global Convergence

What your child is learning

  • Studying: The Ottomans, Safavids and Mughals; European voyages, global trade and the Atlantic slave trade, including enslaved African Muslims in the Americas.
  • Skills: An Empire Portfolio project and a presentation.
  • Handed in: The Empire Portfolio and Unit and Topic 16 tests. Capstone project begins after the Eid break.

By the end of the month: Compare how the Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal empires ruled diverse peoples, and explain how global trade and the Atlantic slave trade changed the world.

Sample question: Why did the Ottoman capture of Constantinople in 1453 matter?A strong answer: Sultan Mehmed II, called al-Fatih, ended the Byzantine Empire and made the city, later Istanbul, his capital. The Ottomans then controlled key routes between Europe and Asia and taxed the trade, one more reason Europeans wanted sea routes of their own.

Watch for: Mixing up which empire built what. The Blue Mosque is Ottoman in Istanbul, the Taj Mahal is Mughal in India, and the great square of Isfahan is Safavid in Iran.

Try this at home

Ask which empires built the Taj Mahal and the Blue Mosque, and why they chose beauty.

JuneCapstone and Final Exam

What your child is learning

  • Studying: The Capstone, The Legacy of Islamic Civilization: each student researches, writes and presents a legacy.
  • Skills: Asking historical questions, judging sources, writing a claim, presenting like a historian.
  • Handed in: Four Capstone checkpoints, the Capstone Showcase, and the Final Exam in the school exam week, June 7 to 11.

By the end of the month: Research a legacy of Islamic civilization, write a clear claim backed by carefully judged sources, and present it like a historian.

Sample question: What is your Capstone claim, and why should we trust your best source?A strong answer: My claim is that Ibn al-Haytham helped create the experimental method. My best source is a university article that quotes his Book of Optics, so it is based on evidence and not just opinion.

Watch for: A Capstone that only lists facts about a person or invention. Ask your child what that legacy changed for people today; that answer is the claim.

Try this at home

Come to the Capstone Showcase if families are invited, and ask your child to rehearse for you.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Place the major civilizations from ancient times to about 1600 on a map and a timeline.
  • Explain what made an empire rise, last or fall.
  • Read a primary source and ask who wrote it and why.
  • Explain the contributions of Islamic civilization to the world.
  • Research, write and present a historical claim with evidence.

Reading and talking at home make a real difference alongside class lessons.

HOW TO GET THERE AT HOME

  • Ask your child to teach you one thing from each lesson.
  • Review key vocabulary with them before each test.
  • Keep a world map at home and use it when history comes up.
  • Check Class Dojo each week for test dates and missing work.
  • Share family stories of history, travel and faith.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

History is studied as a trust (amanah) and as seeking knowledge. Each unit connects to the Quran and our heritage: Nuh (AS) beside the Gilgamesh flood, Musa (AS) and Firawn, shura beside the Athenian assembly, Fatima al-Fihri and al-Qarawiyyin, Salahuddin’s mercy, Mansa Musa’s hajj, and the Golden Age of Muslim scholars. The year ends with Rabbi zidni ilma: the course ends, but the journey of knowledge does not.

TAUGHT WITH PARTICULAR CARE, AND HOW GRADES ARE MADE

  • World religions (January): students learn what Jews, Hindus, Buddhists, followers of Chinese traditions and Christians believe, accurately and with adab, guided by “no compulsion in religion” (2:256) and holding firmly to tawhid. No student is asked to take part in any other faith’s practice.
  • Hard history: the Crusades, conquest of the Americas and the Atlantic slave trade are taught honestly and calmly, with attention to the Muslims whose stories are often left out.
  • How grades are made: a test at the end of each topic with a review day first, a checkpoint in the Quarter 1 and Quarter 3 exam weeks, a Semester 1 Midterm in the mid-year exam week, a Final Exam in the final exam week, and the Capstone project graded in four checkpoints and a final Showcase.

Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org | Questions: contact your child’s World History teacher through Class Dojo

Grades 7 and 8 · Islamic Studies

Grades 7 and 8 Islamic Studies

What your child learns each month, and how you can help at home

THIS GUIDE IS A PLAN, NOT A PROMISE

Months are approximate. Timing and detail may change, but the goals for June stay the same. Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo, and exact test dates will be shared as they are set.

Islamic Studies meets three times a week, on Monday, Tuesday and Thursday, using the Safar Learn About Islam Textbook 7. Quran is taught separately and has its own family guide.

Exam dates are tentative. Exams are planned for the school's exam weeks (October 13 to 16, January 11 to 15, March 30 to April 2 and June 7 to 11). Exact date TBD.

SeptemberBelief: Iman and Qadar

What your child is learning

  • Islam as a complete way of life, and the Five Pillars.
  • The Hadith of Jibril: Islam, iman, ihsan and the six pillars of iman.
  • Qadar: Allah’s decree, our choices, and staying strong in hard times.
  • Evidence for faith and answering questions with confidence.

Words to know: iman, ihsan, qadar

Try this at home

Share a time something did not go to plan and how trusting Allah helped.

OctoberBelief in daily life, then Purification and Prayer

What your child is learning

  • Unit test on belief in early October.
  • Wudu in detail, and why respected scholars sometimes differ.
  • Wudu practical check in mid October.
  • The qiblah, joining a congregation, arriving late, doubts, and sujud al sahw.

Words to know: fard, sunnah, jamaah, sujud al sahw

Try this at home

Pray in congregation at home and let your child explain how to join a prayer late.

NovemberPrayer in hard situations, then Fasting

What your child is learning

  • Praying while traveling, ill or in danger.
  • Jumuah: its meaning, the khutbah and its manners.
  • Salah practical check and unit test in mid November.
  • Fasting: its purpose, requirements and what breaks it.

Words to know: qasr, khutbah, taqwa

Try this at home

Go to Jumuah together when you can and talk about the khutbah afterward.

DecemberZakah and Sadaqah

What your child is learning

  • Itikaf, Eid and zakat al fitr.
  • Zakah: who pays, on what wealth, and who receives it.
  • Sadaqah, then a unit test in mid December.
  • How Islamic rulings are reached, begun before winter break.

Words to know: nisab, hawl, sadaqah

Try this at home

Work out zakah together on a made up amount of savings.

JanuaryHow scholars reach rulings

What your child is learning

  • The Quran, the Sunnah, scholarly agreement and analogy.
  • Why qualified scholars differ, and respecting those differences.
  • Majority opinion, the schools of thought, and the goals of Islamic law.
  • Mid-year exam in the school exam week, January 11 to 15, then a unit test in late January.

Words to know: usul al fiqh, ijma, qiyas, maqasid

Try this at home

Talk about how your family respects Muslims who practice a detail differently.

FebruarySeerah and the prophets, during Ramadan

What your child is learning

  • The Prophet’s life: a timeline and its turning points.
  • Prophet Yusuf: trial, integrity and forgiveness.
  • Zakariyya, Yahya, Maryam and Isa, peace be upon them.
  • The ten Companions promised Paradise, and Muslim civilization.

Words to know: Sahabah, sabr, amanah

Try this at home

Read the story of Prophet Yusuf in translation together during Ramadan.

MarchHistory, then the Quran and the heart

What your child is learning

  • School is closed early in the month for Eid al-Fitr.
  • Seerah and history review, then a unit test in mid March.
  • The Quran as the Creator’s guide.
  • The journey of the soul, and nourishing the heart.

Words to know: tazkiyah, qalb, dhikr

Try this at home

Take five quiet minutes a day to read and reflect on a few ayat together.

AprilFitrah and Muslim life today

What your child is learning

  • Fitrah: the inner compass.
  • The Quran and Sunnah as guiding lights.
  • Manners online and offline, and checking information before sharing it.
  • Confident Muslim identity and prophetic daily habits, then a unit test at the end of April.

Words to know: fitrah, adab

Try this at home

Agree on a family rule to check a news story or video before sharing it.

MayYear review

What your child is learning

  • Full year review.
  • A short, simple lesson on cleanliness and growing up, taught to girls and boys separately. The school will contact you beforehand.

Words to know: review

Try this at home

Help your child make a study plan for the final assessment.

JuneThe final assessment, then Teacher’s Choice

What your child is learning

  • The Comprehensive Final Assessment in the school's final exam week, June 7 to 11.
  • The final days, chosen by the teacher: community sharing, a preview of next year, portfolios, or reteaching.

Try this at home

Keep one prophetic daily habit going through the summer.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME, YOUR CHILD CAN

  • Explain the pillars of iman, qadar, and why they believe with confidence.
  • Make wudu and pray correctly, including when traveling, ill, late or unsure.
  • Explain how zakah and fasting work and calculate zakah on a simple example.
  • Explain why scholars differ and treat different practices with respect.
  • Retell the lives of the prophets and Companions studied and use prophetic habits online and offline.

Practice at home helps your child reach these goals.

HOW YOU GET THEM THERE

  • Pray together at home and go to Jumuah when you can.
  • Check the weekly homework and talk about the questions.
  • Ask one question each week: What did you learn in Islamic Studies?
  • Discuss real situations: travel prayers, zakah, news you see online.

HOW YOUR CHILD IS ASSESSED

  • Quizzes: every other Tuesday.
  • Unit tests: early October, mid November, mid December, mid to late January, mid March and end of April.
  • Practical checks: wudu in mid October and salah in mid November.
  • Mid-year exam: in the school exam week, January 11 to 15.
  • Final: the Comprehensive Final Assessment in the final exam week, June 7 to 11.
  • Homework: two or three questions each week, given on Monday or Tuesday and due the next Monday or Tuesday.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Grades 7 and 8 are when belief meets real life. Your child learns not only what Islam teaches but why, how scholars reach rulings, and how to live with confidence as a Muslim at school, online and at home. Inshallah, they leave the year able to explain their faith and carry it themselves.

Questions? Contact the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org

Grades 7 and 8 · English

Grades 7 and 8 English

What your child reads, writes and hands in, month by month

PLEASE READ

This guide is a plan, not a promise. Months are approximate, and timing and detail will change, but the June destination will not. Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo, and that is where test dates live.

Grades 7 and 8 learn together in one class: both read the same texts, and Grade 8 students complete deeper tasks and extra exam questions. Every text has been reviewed by WIS, and some textbook selections have been replaced with WIS readings.

Late August to SeptemberUnit 1: Crossing Generations

What your child is learning

  • Reading: A short story about a young basketball player and an older mentor; an article on disappearing languages; a memoir by Maya Angelou about meeting her mother.
  • Writing: A true personal narrative about learning from someone of another generation.
  • Handed in: The personal narrative draft; Unit Exams every two weeks.

By the end of the unit: Write a true personal narrative with a clear beginning, middle and end that shows a lesson learned from someone of another generation.

Sample question: What lesson does your personal narrative show, and which moment in the story shows it best?A strong answer: My narrative shows that patience matters. My grandmother taught me to bake bread, and the best moment is when my first loaf failed and she said to try again. That scene shows the lesson instead of just telling it.

Watch for: Stating the lesson in one line at the end instead of showing it through a scene with dialogue and detail. Ask: which moment in your story shows this?

Try this at home

Ask your child to interview a grandparent or elder about one lesson they learned young.

OctoberUnit 1 finish, Unit 2 begins

What your child is learning

  • Reading: Three family poems; space settlement artwork; “Dark They Were, and Golden-Eyed,” a science fiction story set on Mars.
  • Writing: A Tribute Letter to someone from another generation; the final personal narrative.
  • Handed in: The narrative and letter; Quarter 1 English exam in mid October.

By the end of the month: Write a tribute letter and a final personal narrative, and explain how a story's setting changes its characters.

Sample question: In Dark They Were, and Golden-Eyed, how does Mars change the Bittering family?A strong answer: Little by little their eyes turn golden, their skin darkens, and they start using Martian words. Mr. Bittering fights it at first, but by the end the family forgets Earth and moves to the hills. The setting changes who they are.

Watch for: Retelling the plot instead of explaining it. If an answer only lists events, ask: why does that detail matter, and what does it show?

Try this at home

Ask who they chose for the Tribute Letter and why.

NovemberUnit 2: Living Among the Stars

What your child is learning

  • Reading: The same Mars story as a radio script; a science article on Japan’s Moon and Mars research.
  • Writing: An editorial answering “Is space exploration important?”
  • Handed in: The editorial draft; a Unit Exam about every two weeks.

By the end of the month: Write an editorial that states a clear claim about space exploration and supports it with evidence and reasoning.

Sample question: Is space exploration important? Give your claim, one piece of evidence, and your reasoning.A strong answer: Yes, it is important. The article on Japan's Moon and Mars research shows that space programs push countries to build new technology. That matters because tools first made for space often end up helping people on Earth.

Watch for: Giving opinions with no evidence, or quoting evidence without explaining it. Each reason in the editorial needs a fact from a text and a sentence explaining why it matters.

Try this at home

At dinner, ask: should people ever live on Mars? Ask for one reason and one piece of evidence.

DecemberUnit 2 finish, Unit 3 begins

What your child is learning

  • Reading: Two opposing arguments about space; “The Three Questions” (a Tolstoy retelling); “Thank You, M’am” by Langston Hughes.
  • Writing: The final editorial; journal entries from two characters’ points of view.
  • Handed in: The editorial and a class debate.

By the end of the month: Explain how an author develops a theme, and write journal entries that show two characters' different points of view.

Sample question: What are the three answers in The Three Questions, and what theme do they teach?A strong answer: The most important time is now, the most important person is the one you are with, and the most important thing is to do good for that person. The theme is to pay attention to the present and help whoever is in front of you.

Watch for: Writing both journal entries in the same voice. In Thank You, M'am, Roger and Mrs. Jones see that night very differently, so each entry should show only what that character knows and feels.

Try this at home

Ask your child to explain the three answers in “The Three Questions.”

JanuaryUnit 3: Transformations

What your child is learning

  • Reading: An article on how learning changes the brain; three short poems about change.
  • Writing: Begin an original short story about a character who changes.
  • Handed in: The short story plan; Mid-Year English exam in mid January.

By the end of the month: Plan a short story with a character who clearly changes, and connect the article and poems to the idea of transformation.

Sample question: How does learning change the brain, according to the article?A strong answer: When you practice something new, the connections between brain cells, called neurons, get stronger. So the brain actually changes a little each time we learn. That means getting better comes from repeated practice, not just talent.

Watch for: A character who changes for no reason. Ask your child what event causes the change; a strong story shows the cause, not just a different ending.

Try this at home

Ask what their story’s character is like at the start and at the end.

FebruaryUnit 3 finish, Unit 4 and Animal Farm begin

What your child is learning

  • Reading: An article on bees in the city; Animal Farm, Chapters 1 to 4, one a week (see the box below).
  • Writing: Finish the short story; write and perform a short play adapted from a story or poem.
  • Handed in: The final short story and the play performance. Ramadan: homework kept light.

By the end of the month: Finish and revise an original short story, perform a short play adaptation, and summarize Animal Farm, Chapters 1 to 4.

Sample question: In Animal Farm, what was Old Major's dream, and why did the animals rebel?A strong answer: Old Major dreamed of a world without humans, where animals kept what they worked for. The animals were hungry and overworked, and when Mr. Jones forgot to feed them, they drove him off the farm.

Watch for: Reading Animal Farm as just an animal story. Ask who the pigs might stand for; noticing that the book is about people and power is the start of understanding it.

Try this at home

Ask your child to perform their play scene for the family.

MarchUnit 4: Learning From Nature

What your child is learning

  • Reading: Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring; two Native American stories about the sun; a poem about caring for the earth; an article on buildings inspired by nature.
  • Writing: Short responses and an allegory chart for Animal Farm.
  • Handed in: Animal Farm Chapters 5 to 7, one a week once school reopens after the Eid break. No reading over the break.

By the end of the month: Explain what an allegory is and match Animal Farm characters and events to the real history they stand for.

Sample question: What is an allegory, and who might Napoleon stand for in Animal Farm?A strong answer: An allegory is a story where characters and events stand for real people and ideas. Napoleon stands for Joseph Stalin, because he chases out his rival Snowball and uses his dogs to rule by fear.

Watch for: Mixing up Snowball and Napoleon after Chapter 5. If your child says Snowball is still on the farm, they have missed the chapter where the dogs chase him away.

Try this at home

Read a chapter of Animal Farm aloud together, or listen to the audio.

AprilUnit 4 finish

What your child is learning

  • Reading: A Japanese story about a hole that swallows everything people throw away; Animal Farm, Chapters 8 to 10, one a week.
  • Writing: An essay on how Animal Farm shows power and propaganda.
  • Handed in: Quarter 3 English exam in the school exam week, March 30 to April 2; the Animal Farm essay at the end of April.

By the end of the month: Write an essay explaining how Animal Farm shows power and propaganda, supported by quotations from the book.

Sample question: How does Squealer use propaganda to keep the animals loyal?A strong answer: Squealer twists facts and reads out made up numbers to prove life is better. The pigs even secretly change the Seven Commandments, so the animals doubt their own memory. Since they cannot prove him wrong, they keep obeying.

Watch for: Quoting the book without explaining it. After each quotation, the essay should say how it shows power or propaganda. Look for the word because.

Try this at home

Ask which character in Animal Farm reminds them of something in the news, and why.

MayUnit 5: Facing Adversity

What your child is learning

  • Reading: The Dust Bowl in nonfiction and in a diary; an article on accessibility; “The Circuit,” a story of a migrant family.
  • Writing: An informational essay about how people overcome challenges.
  • Handed in: The informational essay. No homework over the Eid break.

By the end of the month: Write an informational essay that explains how people overcome challenges, using facts from more than one text.

Sample question: In The Circuit, why does the ending hurt so much?A strong answer: Panchito finally feels at home at school, and Mr. Lema offers to teach him the trumpet. Then he comes home and sees the boxes packed for another move. The ending shows his hope being taken away again.

Watch for: Mixing opinion into an informational essay. Sentences that start with I think belong in an editorial; here each paragraph should explain using facts from the texts.

Try this at home

Share a hard time your family came through and how you kept going.

JuneUnit 5 finish and year end

What your child is learning

  • Reading: An interview with an astronaut who was rejected eleven times; a poem and a short prose piece about trees and strength.
  • Writing: Biographical profiles; a Letter of Encouragement; an end of year reflection.
  • Handed in: The profiles and letter; Final English exam in the school exam week, June 7 to 11.
  • Grade 8 graduation: Saturday, June 19. Attendance is required.

By the end of the month: Write a biographical profile and a letter of encouragement, and reflect on their growth as a reader and writer this year.

Sample question: What does the astronaut's story of being rejected eleven times teach about facing adversity?A strong answer: It teaches that rejection is not the end. He kept building new skills each time he was turned down, and on the twelfth try he was chosen. Persistence and learning from each no got him there.

Watch for: A reflection that lists activities instead of showing growth. Ask your child for one thing they could not do in August that they can do now, with an example.

Try this at home

Read your child’s reflection letter and tell them one way you saw them grow.

OUR ONE NOVEL: ANIMAL FARM BY GEORGE ORWELL (FEBRUARY TO APRIL)

  • What it is: a short novel in which farm animals take over their farm, and the pigs slowly become the cruel masters they replaced. It is an allegory, a simple story that stands for real events in history.
  • How it is read: one chapter a week at home, ten chapters from February to April with a pause over the Eid break (an audio version is available), then discussed in class with a chart tracking what each animal stands for.
  • Handled with care: some chapters include the animals’ executions, the pigs drinking, and a raven used to mock how rulers misuse religion. Teachers present these as warnings about corrupt power.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Explain a text’s theme or central idea with evidence.
  • Write a clear narrative, argument, short story and informational essay.
  • Evaluate an argument and answer the other side respectfully.
  • Explain how Animal Farm uses a simple story to show how power corrupts.
  • Present to the class with confidence.

School lessons alone will not get your child here; reading and talking at home will.

HOW TO GET THERE AT HOME

  • Twenty minutes of reading every day, in any book.
  • Ask one question a day about what they read.
  • Have your child read their writing aloud to you before it is handed in.
  • Check Class Dojo each week for exam dates and missing work.
  • Keep a quiet place and time for homework.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Every text is chosen or replaced to fit our values. Students practice birr al walidayn as they write about elders, amanah as caretakers of the earth, sabr in the stories of people who overcame hardship, honest speech against propaganda in Animal Farm, and the adab of disagreeing respectfully in debate.

HOW GRADES ARE MADE THIS YEAR

A Unit Exam about every two weeks with a review day the day before, one quiz in each week without an exam, and major writing scored Secure, Developing or Beginning.

Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org | Questions: contact your child’s English teacher through Class Dojo
