Grades 7 and 8 · World History

Grades 7 and 8 World History

What your child studies and hands in, month by month

PLEASE READ

This guide is a plan, not a promise. Months are approximate, and timing and detail will change, but the June destination will not. Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo, and that is where test dates live.

Grades 7 and 8 learn World History together in one class, using the Savvas World History textbook alongside WIS lessons that go deeper into Islamic history.

Exam dates are tentative. Exams are planned for the school's exam weeks (October 13 to 16, January 11 to 15, March 30 to April 2 and June 7 to 11). Exact date TBD.

Late August to SeptemberOrigins to Egypt

What your child is learning

  • Studying: How the first civilizations began; Mesopotamia, the Assyrians, Persians and Phoenicians; ancient Egypt and Kush along the Nile.
  • Skills: Reading primary sources, starting with the Epic of Gilgamesh and an inscription of Ramses II.
  • Handed in: Topic 1, 2 and 3 tests.

By the end of the unit: Explain how rivers helped the first civilizations grow, and read a primary source such as the Epic of Gilgamesh for clues about its time.

Sample question: Why did ancient Egypt grow along the Nile when most of the land around it was desert?A strong answer: The Nile flooded every year and left rich silt for farming. It also gave water and a road for trade boats. With extra food, some people could become builders, scribes and priests, so a civilization grew.

Watch for: Mixing up early civilizations, such as placing Gilgamesh or cuneiform in Egypt. Mesopotamia lies between the Tigris and Euphrates; Egypt is on the Nile and used hieroglyphics.

Try this at home

Ask your child how the Nile shaped Egyptian life, and how the Quran describes Musa and Firawn.

OctoberIndia and China

What your child is learning

  • Studying: The Indus Valley, the Maurya and Gupta empires, the Asoka edicts; early China and the Han dynasty.
  • Skills: Maps and geography; judging a leader’s legacy.
  • Handed in: Topic 4 and 5 tests; the Quarter 1 checkpoint in the school exam week, October 13 to 16.

By the end of the month: Describe the Indus Valley, Maurya, Gupta and Han civilizations, locate them on a map, and judge a leader's legacy using evidence.

Sample question: How did Asoka change after the battle of Kalinga, and how do his edicts show it?A strong answer: After seeing how many people died at Kalinga, Asoka turned away from war. His edicts, carved on rocks and pillars, told people to be kind, tell the truth and respect other faiths. They show he wanted to rule fairly.

Watch for: Calling a ruler simply good or bad. For a legacy question, ask for one achievement and one cost with evidence, like Shi Huangdi uniting China but using forced labor for his walls.

Try this at home

Find India and China on a map together and trace the Silk Road.

NovemberAncient Greece and Rome

What your child is learning

  • Studying: Athens and Sparta, Greek learning and Alexander; how the Roman Republic governed and why it struggled.
  • Skills: Comparing kinds of government; working with documents.
  • Handed in: Topic 6 and 7 tests and short projects.

By the end of the month: Compare Athenian democracy, Spartan rule and the Roman Republic, and explain why the Republic struggled.

Sample question: How was the Roman Republic set up so that no one person held too much power?A strong answer: Romans elected two consuls who served only one year and could block each other. The Senate advised them, and tribunes could veto laws that hurt the plebeians. Power was shared and checked.

Watch for: Thinking Athenian democracy included everyone. Only free adult male citizens could vote; women, enslaved people and foreigners could not. Ask your child who was left out.

Try this at home

Talk about shura: how does your family make a big decision together?

DecemberRome, Byzantium and Medieval Europe

What your child is learning

  • Studying: The Roman and Byzantine empires; feudal Europe; the Crusades, the Magna Carta and eight centuries of Muslim Spain (al-Andalus).
  • Skills: Cause and effect; seeing events from more than one side.
  • Handed in: Topic 8, 9 and 10 tests.

By the end of the month: Explain the causes and effects of feudalism, the Crusades and the Magna Carta, and describe events from more than one point of view.

Sample question: Who was Salahuddin al-Ayyubi, and why is 1187 remembered?A strong answer: He was the Muslim leader who united Egypt and Syria. In 1187 he won at Hattin and took back Jerusalem. Unlike the Crusaders in 1099, he spared the people of the city, so he is remembered for mercy in victory.

Watch for: Seeing the Crusades from one side only. Ask how a Muslim, a Christian and a Jewish resident of Jerusalem might each describe the same event.

Try this at home

Ask your child who Salahuddin al-Ayyubi was and what he did in 1187.

JanuaryWorld Religions and the Semester Exam

What your child is learning

  • Studying: Judaism, Hinduism, Buddhism, Chinese belief systems and Christianity, taught with accuracy and adab while holding firmly to tawhid (see the box below).
  • Skills: Building and defending a comparison chart.
  • Handed in: The Semester 1 Midterm in the school exam week, January 11 to 15; the World Religions assessment.

By the end of the month: Describe the main beliefs of Judaism, Hinduism, Buddhism, Chinese belief systems and Christianity accurately, and compare them in a chart.

Sample question: How is studying another religion as a historian different from believing in it?A strong answer: A historian describes what a faith teaches, using accurate sources and respectful words. That does not mean accepting it. As Muslims we hold firmly to tawhid, and the Quran says there is no compulsion in religion.

Watch for: Mixing up terms across faiths, such as karma, Torah and the Eightfold Path. Ask your child to place each word under the right religion on their comparison chart.

Try this at home

Ask what the Quran teaches about Isa (AS) and about kindness to People of the Book.

FebruaryThe Islamic World, our flagship unit

What your child is learning

  • Studying: The Seerah, the Rightly Guided Caliphs, the Umayyads and Abbasids, the Golden Age of scholars and sciences, Islamic art and architecture, Ibn Khaldun.
  • Skills: Primary sources and a group project on the growth of Muslim empires.
  • Handed in: Mid-unit and Topic 11 tests; Ramadan Legacy Week project and service work.

By the end of the month: Trace the growth of the Muslim world from the Seerah through the Abbasids, and explain what the Golden Age gave to science and learning.

Sample question: Why did Baghdad become a world center of learning under the Abbasids?A strong answer: The Abbasids supported the House of Wisdom, Bayt al-Hikmah, where scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian books. Paper made books cheaper, and the call to seek knowledge drove scholars like al-Khwarizmi to make new discoveries.

Watch for: Blending the caliphates together. The Rashidun ruled mainly from Madinah, the Umayyads from Damascus, and the Abbasids from Baghdad. A quick timeline keeps them in order.

Try this at home

Share a favorite story of a Muslim scholar or scientist with your child.

MarchEast Asia and the Americas

What your child is learning

  • Studying: Tang, Song, Mongol and Ming China; Japan; how Islam reached Southeast Asia through trade; the Maya, Aztec and Inca.
  • Skills: Using maps and comparing civilizations.
  • Handed in: Topic 12 and 13 tests. No homework over the Eid break.

By the end of the month: Compare the civilizations of East Asia and the Americas, and explain how trade and contact spread ideas and faith.

Sample question: How did Islam reach Southeast Asia without armies?A strong answer: Muslim merchants sailed to ports like Malacca to trade spices. People saw they were honest and fair in business, and some rulers and traders accepted Islam. It spread along the trade routes.

Watch for: Mixing up the Maya, Aztec and Inca. A quick check: Maya in southern Mexico and Central America, Aztec in central Mexico at Tenochtitlan, Inca in the Andes of South America.

Try this at home

Ask your child about Zheng He, the Muslim admiral of Ming China.

AprilAfrica, the Renaissance and Muslim Empires

What your child is learning

  • Studying: Ghana, Mali and Songhai, Mansa Musa’s hajj, the manuscripts of Timbuktu, Ibn Battuta; the Renaissance and Reformation; the Ottomans begin.
  • Skills: Tracing how knowledge moved from the Muslim world into Europe.
  • Handed in: Topic 14 and 15 tests; the Quarter 3 checkpoint in the school exam week, March 30 to April 2.

By the end of the month: Explain how trade across the Sahara built Ghana, Mali and Songhai, and how knowledge from the Muslim world helped spark the Renaissance.

Sample question: Why was Mansa Musa's hajj in 1324 so famous?A strong answer: He traveled to Makkah with thousands of people and so much gold that he gave it away in Cairo, and gold lost value there. The journey put Mali on European maps and showed how rich West Africa was.

Watch for: Thinking the Renaissance came only from ancient Greece and Rome. Ask how Greek books and Arabic science reached Europe; the answer runs through al-Andalus and Sicily.

Try this at home

Look at a map of Ibn Battuta’s travels together.

MayGreat Muslim Empires and Global Convergence

What your child is learning

  • Studying: The Ottomans, Safavids and Mughals; European voyages, global trade and the Atlantic slave trade, including enslaved African Muslims in the Americas.
  • Skills: An Empire Portfolio project and a presentation.
  • Handed in: The Empire Portfolio and Unit and Topic 16 tests. Capstone project begins after the Eid break.

By the end of the month: Compare how the Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal empires ruled diverse peoples, and explain how global trade and the Atlantic slave trade changed the world.

Sample question: Why did the Ottoman capture of Constantinople in 1453 matter?A strong answer: Sultan Mehmed II, called al-Fatih, ended the Byzantine Empire and made the city, later Istanbul, his capital. The Ottomans then controlled trade between Europe and Asia, which pushed Europeans to look for sea routes.

Watch for: Mixing up which empire built what. The Blue Mosque is Ottoman in Istanbul, the Taj Mahal is Mughal in India, and the great square of Isfahan is Safavid in Iran.

Try this at home

Ask which empires built the Taj Mahal and the Blue Mosque, and why they chose beauty.

JuneCapstone and Final Exam

What your child is learning

  • Studying: The Capstone, The Legacy of Islamic Civilization: each student researches, writes and presents a legacy.
  • Skills: Asking historical questions, judging sources, writing a claim, presenting like a historian.
  • Handed in: Four Capstone checkpoints, the Capstone Showcase, and the Final Exam in the school exam week, June 7 to 11.
  • Grade 8 graduation: Saturday, June 19. Attendance is required.

By the end of the month: Research a legacy of Islamic civilization, write a clear claim backed by carefully judged sources, and present it like a historian.

Sample question: What is your Capstone claim, and why should we trust your best source?A strong answer: My claim is that Ibn al-Haytham helped create the experimental method. My best source is a university article that quotes his Book of Optics, so it is based on evidence and not just opinion.

Watch for: A Capstone that only lists facts about a person or invention. Ask your child what that legacy changed for people today; that answer is the claim.

Try this at home

Come to the Capstone Showcase if families are invited, and ask your child to rehearse for you.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Place the major civilizations from ancient times to about 1600 on a map and a timeline.
  • Explain what made an empire rise, last or fall.
  • Read a primary source and ask who wrote it and why.
  • Explain the contributions of Islamic civilization to the world.
  • Research, write and present a historical claim with evidence.

School lessons alone will not get your child here; reading and talking at home will.

HOW TO GET THERE AT HOME

  • Ask your child to teach you one thing from each lesson.
  • Review key vocabulary with them before each test.
  • Keep a world map at home and use it when history comes up.
  • Check Class Dojo each week for test dates and missing work.
  • Share family stories of history, travel and faith.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

History is studied as a trust (amanah) and as seeking knowledge. Each unit connects to the Quran and our heritage: Nuh (AS) beside the Gilgamesh flood, Musa (AS) and Firawn, shura beside the Athenian assembly, Fatima al-Fihri and al-Qarawiyyin, Salahuddin’s mercy, Mansa Musa’s hajj, and the Golden Age of Muslim scholars. The year ends with Rabbi zidni ilma: the course ends, but the journey of knowledge does not.

TAUGHT WITH PARTICULAR CARE, AND HOW GRADES ARE MADE

  • World religions (January): students learn what Jews, Hindus, Buddhists, followers of Chinese traditions and Christians believe, accurately and with adab, guided by “no compulsion in religion” (2:256) and holding firmly to tawhid. No student is asked to take part in any other faith’s practice.
  • Hard history: the Crusades, conquest of the Americas and the Atlantic slave trade are taught honestly and calmly, with attention to the Muslims whose stories are often left out.
  • How grades are made: a test at the end of each topic with a review day first, a checkpoint in the Quarter 1 and Quarter 3 exam weeks, a Semester 1 Midterm in the mid-year exam week, a Final Exam in the final exam week, and the Capstone project graded in four checkpoints and a final Showcase.

Grades 7 and 8 · Islamic Studies

Grades 7 and 8 Islamic Studies

What your child learns each month, and how you can help at home

THIS GUIDE IS A PLAN, NOT A PROMISE

Months are approximate. Timing and detail will change, but where your child ends up in June will not. Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo, and test and assessment dates live there, not on this sheet.

Islamic Studies meets three times a week, on Monday, Tuesday and Thursday, using the Safar Learn About Islam Textbook 7. Quran is taught separately and has its own family guide.

Exam dates are tentative. Exams are planned for the school's exam weeks (October 13 to 16, January 11 to 15, March 30 to April 2 and June 7 to 11). Exact date TBD.

SeptemberBelief: Iman and Qadar

What your child is learning

  • Islam as a complete way of life, and the Five Pillars.
  • The Hadith of Jibril: Islam, iman, ihsan and the six pillars of iman.
  • Qadar: Allah’s decree, our choices, and staying strong in hard times.
  • Evidence for faith and answering questions with confidence.

Words to know: iman, ihsan, qadar

Try this at home

Share a time something did not go to plan and how trusting Allah helped.

OctoberBelief in daily life, then Purification and Prayer

What your child is learning

  • Unit test on belief in early October.
  • Wudu in detail, and why respected scholars sometimes differ.
  • Wudu practical check in mid October.
  • The qiblah, joining a congregation, arriving late, doubts, and sujud al sahw.

Words to know: fard, sunnah, jamaah, sujud al sahw

Try this at home

Pray in congregation at home and let your child explain how to join a prayer late.

NovemberPrayer in hard situations, then Fasting

What your child is learning

  • Praying while traveling, ill or in danger.
  • Jumuah: its meaning, the khutbah and its manners.
  • Salah practical check and unit test in mid November.
  • Fasting: its purpose, requirements and what breaks it.

Words to know: qasr, khutbah, taqwa

Try this at home

Go to Jumuah together when you can and talk about the khutbah afterward.

DecemberZakah and Sadaqah

What your child is learning

  • Itikaf, Eid and zakat al fitr.
  • Zakah: who pays, on what wealth, and who receives it.
  • Sadaqah, then a unit test in mid December.
  • How Islamic rulings are reached, begun before winter break.

Words to know: nisab, hawl, sadaqah

Try this at home

Work out zakah together on a made up amount of savings.

JanuaryHow scholars reach rulings

What your child is learning

  • The Quran, the Sunnah, scholarly agreement and analogy.
  • Why qualified scholars differ, and respecting those differences.
  • Majority opinion, the schools of thought, and the goals of Islamic law.
  • Mid-year exam in the school exam week, January 11 to 15, then a unit test in late January.

Words to know: usul al fiqh, ijma, qiyas, maqasid

Try this at home

Talk about how your family respects Muslims who practice a detail differently.

FebruarySeerah and the prophets, during Ramadan

What your child is learning

  • The Prophet’s life: a timeline and its turning points.
  • Prophet Yusuf: trial, integrity and forgiveness.
  • Zakariyya, Yahya, Maryam and Isa, peace be upon them.
  • The ten Companions promised Paradise, and Muslim civilization.

Words to know: Sahabah, sabr, amanah

Try this at home

Read the story of Prophet Yusuf in translation together during Ramadan.

MarchHistory, then the Quran and the heart

What your child is learning

  • School is closed early in the month for Eid al-Fitr.
  • Seerah and history review, then a unit test in mid March.
  • The Quran as the Creator’s guide.
  • The journey of the soul, and nourishing the heart.

Words to know: tazkiyah, qalb, dhikr

Try this at home

Take five quiet minutes a day to read and reflect on a few ayat together.

AprilFitrah and Muslim life today

What your child is learning

  • Fitrah: the inner compass.
  • The Quran and Sunnah as guiding lights.
  • Manners online and offline, and checking information before sharing it.
  • Confident Muslim identity and prophetic daily habits, then a unit test at the end of April.

Words to know: fitrah, adab

Try this at home

Agree on a family rule to check a news story or video before sharing it.

MayYear review, then separate sessions

What your child is learning

  • Full year review.
  • Separate girls and boys sessions begin in mid May on growing up, ghusl, modesty and boundaries. The school will contact you before these sessions.

Words to know: bulugh, ghusl, haya

Try this at home

Be ready for questions about growing up and answer them openly and privately at home.

JuneSeparate sessions finish, the final assessment, then Teacher’s Choice

What your child is learning

  • The separate sessions close in early June with anonymous questions answered.
  • The Comprehensive Final Assessment in the school's final exam week, June 7 to 11.
  • The final days, chosen by the teacher: community sharing, a preview of next year, portfolios, or reteaching.
  • Grade 8 graduation: Saturday, June 19. Attendance is required.

Try this at home

Keep one prophetic daily habit going through the summer.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME, YOUR CHILD CAN

  • Explain the pillars of iman, qadar, and why they believe with confidence.
  • Make wudu and pray correctly, including when traveling, ill, late or unsure.
  • Explain how zakah and fasting work and calculate zakah on a simple example.
  • Explain why scholars differ and treat different practices with respect.
  • Retell the lives of the prophets and Companions studied and use prophetic habits online and offline.

Three lessons a week at school will not get your child there on their own.

HOW YOU GET THEM THERE

  • Pray together at home and go to Jumuah when you can.
  • Check the weekly homework and talk about the questions.
  • Ask one question each week: What did you learn in Islamic Studies?
  • Discuss real situations: travel prayers, zakah, news you see online.
  • Answer questions about growing up openly, in the privacy of home.

HOW YOUR CHILD IS ASSESSED

  • Quizzes: every second Tuesday.
  • Unit tests: early October, mid November, mid December, mid to late January, mid March and end of April.
  • Practical checks: wudu in mid October and salah in mid November.
  • Mid-year exam: in the school exam week, January 11 to 15.
  • Final: the Comprehensive Final Assessment in the final exam week, June 7 to 11.
  • Homework: two or three questions each week, given on Monday or Tuesday and due the next Monday or Tuesday.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

Grades 7 and 8 are when belief meets real life. Your child learns not only what Islam teaches but why, how scholars reach rulings, and how to live with confidence as a Muslim at school, online and at home. Inshallah, they leave the year able to explain their faith and carry it themselves.

Questions? Contact the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org

Grades 7 and 8 · Physical Science

Grades 7 and 8 Physical Science

A family guide to the year, month by month

THIS PLAN IS TENTATIVE

This is a plan, not a promise. These are the overall topics for each month. Order and timing will change as the year goes on, and months are approximate. The goals for June stay the same.

Anything that changes is emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. The test dates below are the plan as it stands today; when the calendar moves, the real dates are posted there.

Physical Science is one class for Grades 7 and 8 and meets five periods a week. Your child works from Savvas Experience Science with laboratory work built around it, following the Virginia Physical Science standards.

Exam dates are tentative. Exams are planned for the school's exam weeks (October 13 to 16, January 11 to 15, March 30 to April 2 and June 7 to 11). Exact date TBD.

Late August and SeptemberDoing science, then atoms

What your child is learning

  • Topics: How a result is made trustworthy: variables, repeated trials, measurement and graphing. Then the atom, its particles, and how the model was rebuilt as new evidence arrived.
  • In the lab: A measurement carousel, an investigation showing how a single trial misleads, a design challenge, and a gold foil simulation.
  • Handed in: The lab safety practical in early September, which must be passed before any Unit 2 lab work, and a design-and-test task.

Words to know: variable, control, trial, accuracy, precision, atom, proton, neutron, electron, isotope

By the end of the unit: Design a fair test that changes one variable, run repeated trials, and describe the parts of an atom and how the atomic model changed.

Sample question: Why is one trial not enough in an experiment?A strong answer: One trial could be off because of a mistake or bad luck. If I repeat it several times and the results agree, I can trust them more. I can also average them to get a better answer.

Watch for: Mixing up accuracy and precision. Precise means results are close to each other; accurate means close to the true value. Results can be precise and still wrong.

Try this at home

Ask why one trial is not enough. If your child can explain that, the first unit has landed.

OctoberStates of matter, then the periodic table

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Why a gas fills its container and a solid does not, what temperature measures, then reading the periodic table and predicting what an element will do from its position.
  • In the lab: Particle motion simulations, pressure demonstrations, and a mystery element sort where students build their own table before seeing the real one.
  • Handed in: A model evaluation task and the Unit 2 assessment, then an element prediction task. Quarter 1 closes Oct 23.

Words to know: kinetic molecular theory, group, family, period, valence electron, metal, metalloid, nonmetal

By the end of the month: Explain states of matter using particle motion, and use an element's group and period to predict how it behaves.

Sample question: Why does a gas fill its whole container while a solid keeps its shape?A strong answer: Gas particles move fast and are far apart, so they spread out until they fill the space. Solid particles are packed tightly and only vibrate in place, so a solid keeps its shape.

Watch for: Mixing up groups and periods. Groups are columns, and elements in a group behave alike; periods are rows. Sodium and chlorine sit in the same row but act nothing alike.

Try this at home

Point at anything in the kitchen and ask which elements are in it, then where they sit on the table.

NovemberProperties, changes and bonding

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Identifying a substance from properties that do not depend on how much you have, telling a physical change from a chemical one, and why ionic and covalent bonds form.
  • In the lab: A density column and unknown identification lab, and ionic and covalent samples compared by conductivity and melting point.
  • Handed in: Classification checks with evidence required, and bond-type predictions.

Words to know: density, solubility, physical change, chemical change, ion, ionic bond, covalent bond

By the end of the month: Identify a substance by density and other properties, tell physical from chemical changes, and predict whether a bond is ionic or covalent.

Sample question: Is cooking an egg a physical or a chemical change? How do you know?A strong answer: It is a chemical change. Heat changes the proteins into a new substance, the egg turns solid and white, and you cannot turn it back into a raw egg. A new substance formed.

Watch for: Calling melting or dissolving a chemical change because it looks different. If the substance is still the same, like ice to water or sugar in tea, it is a physical change.

Try this at home

Ask whether cooking an egg is a physical or a chemical change, and make them defend the answer.

DecemberConservation of matter

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Why a chemical equation has to balance, and why nothing is created or destroyed when atoms rearrange.
  • In the lab: Baking soda and vinegar in a sealed bag, massed before and after, then a closed-system reaction the students design themselves.
  • Handed in: Balancing practice sets twice a week, the conservation investigation, an unknown substance identification report, and the Unit 4 assessment.

Words to know: reactant, product, coefficient, balanced equation, conservation of matter

By the end of the month: Balance simple chemical equations and use measured mass to show that matter is conserved in a reaction.

Sample question: Balance this: H₂ + O₂ makes H₂O. Why must it balance?A strong answer: There are 2 oxygen atoms on the left and 1 on the right, so I write 2H₂O. Now there are 4 hydrogens on the right, so I write 2H₂. So 2H₂ + O₂ makes 2H₂O. Atoms rearrange; none are created or destroyed.

Watch for: Changing the small subscripts to balance, like writing H₂O₂. That makes a different substance. Only the big numbers in front, the coefficients, can change.

Try this at home

Ask where the mass went when something burned or dissolved. That question is the whole unit.

JanuaryWork, force and motion

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Speed, velocity and acceleration, reading motion graphs, balanced and unbalanced forces, and Newton’s three laws.
  • In the lab: Ramp and cart timing with repeated trials, a collision safety design challenge, and balloon rocket demonstrations.
  • Handed in: Weekly calculation sets on force, mass and acceleration, then the motion investigation with graphs. Quarter 2 closes Jan 15.

Words to know: velocity, acceleration, net force, inertia, friction, work, power, newton

By the end of the month: Calculate speed and acceleration, read motion graphs, and use Newton's three laws to explain how forces change motion.

Sample question: A net force of 12 newtons pushes a 3 kg cart. What is its acceleration?A strong answer: Newton's second law says force equals mass times acceleration, so acceleration is force divided by mass. 12 ÷ 3 = 4, so it is 4 meters per second squared. Check: 3 × 4 = 12.

Watch for: Thinking a moving object needs a force to keep moving. Without friction it would keep going; that is inertia, the first law. Listen for the idea that motion simply runs out.

Try this at home

In the car, ask why a passenger lurches forward when you brake. The answer is the first law.

FebruaryMotion assessed, then energy

What your child is learning

  • Topics: The motion unit closes in the first week, then forms of energy, energy transformation, and why energy is conserved but not always usable.
  • In the lab: Pendulum and roller coaster energy tracking, and a lab where students find the kinetic energy relationship from their own data.
  • Handed in: The Unit 5 assessment on Feb 5, then weekly energy calculations.

Words to know: kinetic energy, potential energy, efficiency, waste heat, conduction, convection, radiation

By the end of the month: Calculate kinetic energy, track energy as it changes form, and explain why energy is conserved but not all of it is usable.

Sample question: On a roller coaster, where is potential energy greatest, and where is kinetic energy greatest?A strong answer: Potential energy is greatest at the top of the highest hill, where the car is highest. As it drops, potential turns into kinetic, so kinetic is greatest at the bottom where it moves fastest. Some becomes heat from friction.

Watch for: Saying energy is used up or lost. It is never destroyed; it changes form, often into waste heat. Ask your child where the missing energy went.

Try this at home

Ask where the energy goes in a device at home that gets warm. Warm usually means wasted.

MarchEnergy and how we use it

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Energy sources, renewable and nonrenewable, compared on real cost data, and where energy becomes unusable.
  • In the lab: Students analyze a real device, diagram every transformation, and propose an efficiency improvement.
  • Handed in: The energy systems task and the Unit 6 assessment. School is closed for Eid al-Fitr Mar 1 to 12.

Words to know: renewable, nonrenewable, efficiency, transformation, joule

By the end of the month: Compare renewable and nonrenewable energy sources using real cost data, and trace every energy transformation in a device.

Sample question: A bulb uses 100 joules and gives off 20 joules of light. What is its efficiency, and where did the rest go?A strong answer: Efficiency is useful energy out divided by energy in, so 20 ÷ 100 = 0.2, or 20 percent. The other 80 joules became heat, which is why the bulb gets warm.

Watch for: Thinking renewable means free or perfect. Solar and wind still cost money to build and depend on the weather; strong answers weigh cost, supply and pollution.

Try this at home

Look at the electricity bill together. It is a measurement of energy, and your child can now read it.

AprilWaves and light

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Wavelength, frequency and amplitude, longitudinal and transverse waves, why sound needs a medium, then reflection, refraction and interference.
  • In the lab: Slinky and rope waves side by side, a ripple tank, a sound-in-a-vacuum demonstration, and prism stations.
  • Handed in: The wave investigation, measuring wave properties in two different media and explaining the difference. Quarter 3 closes Apr 9.

Words to know: wavelength, frequency, amplitude, medium, reflection, refraction, interference

By the end of the month: Describe waves by wavelength, frequency and amplitude, and explain reflection, refraction and why sound needs a medium.

Sample question: Why can sound travel through air but not through outer space?A strong answer: Sound is a longitudinal wave that moves when particles bump into each other. Space is nearly empty, so there is nothing to carry the vibration. Light can cross space because it does not need a medium.

Watch for: Mixing up frequency and amplitude in sound. Higher frequency means higher pitch; bigger amplitude means louder. Ask what changes when a song gets louder compared with higher.

Try this at home

Ask why you can hear around a corner but not see around one. Both are waves.

MayThe spectrum, then electricity

What your child is learning

  • Topics: The electromagnetic spectrum from radio to gamma and what each region is used for, then static electricity, conductors and insulators.
  • In the lab: Static electricity stations, then circuit building with bulbs, batteries and switches, including deliberate fault-finding.
  • Handed in: The spectrum application report on one technology that uses a region of the spectrum. The waves unit closes May 11.

Words to know: electromagnetic spectrum, infrared, ultraviolet, charge, conductor, insulator, current, voltage

By the end of the month: Order the electromagnetic spectrum from radio to gamma with a use for each region, and explain charge, conductors and insulators.

Sample question: Which part of the spectrum does a microwave oven use, a TV remote, and a cell phone?A strong answer: The microwave oven uses microwaves, the remote uses infrared, and the phone uses radio waves to send signals. They are all the same kind of wave, just with different wavelengths.

Watch for: Thinking all radiation is dangerous. Radio waves and visible light are safe in daily use; it is high energy ultraviolet, X rays and gamma rays that can damage cells.

Try this at home

Ask what part of the spectrum the microwave, the remote and the phone each use.

JuneCircuits, magnets, and the close

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Series and parallel circuits, resistance and Ohm’s law, magnetic fields, and how they give us motors and generators.
  • In the lab: Magnetic field mapping with iron filings, and an electromagnet challenge students test and improve.
  • Handed in: The circuit design task, the electromagnet challenge, and a cumulative assessment in the final exam week, June 7 to 11.

Words to know: series circuit, parallel circuit, resistance, Ohm’s law, magnetic field, electromagnet

By the end of the month: Build series and parallel circuits, use Ohm's law to find current, voltage or resistance, and explain how an electromagnet works.

Sample question: A 9 volt battery is connected to a 3 ohm resistor. What is the current?A strong answer: Ohm's law says voltage equals current times resistance, so current is voltage divided by resistance. 9 ÷ 3 = 3 amps. Check: 3 amps × 3 ohms = 9 volts.

Watch for: Mixing up series and parallel. In series there is one path, so one blown bulb breaks the whole circuit; in parallel each bulb has its own path. Ask your child to trace the path.

Try this at home

Ask why one blown bulb can kill a string of lights but not a room of them. That is series and parallel.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Design an investigation with repeated trials, and say why one trial is not evidence.
  • Explain motion with Newton’s laws and calculate speed, acceleration and energy from their own data.

Talking about this at home makes a real difference. Children who discuss their learning with family build these skills with more confidence.

SO HERE IS WHAT HELPS MOST AT HOME

  • Ask for evidence: what did you measure that makes you say that?
  • Let them predict before they check. That order is what makes it science.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

This course asks students to settle questions by measurement rather than intuition, which is ilm in its plainest form. Recording the trial that contradicts your own hypothesis is honesty, and the class rule on data rests on that rather than on a school rule. Conservation of matter and the study of energy are taught with balance and the prohibition of waste in view: once a student can calculate the energy a device throws away, wasting it stops being an abstraction, Inshallah.

HOW YOUR CHILD IS CHECKED, AND ONE THING TO WATCH FOR

Day to day: exit tickets two or three times a week, a daily science notebook, and an investigation brief for every lab. Each unit ends with a task rather than only a test, scored 3 secure, 2 developing, 1 beginning. Quarter exams fall in the school's exam weeks: Oct 13 to 16, Jan 11 to 15, Mar 30 to Apr 2, and Jun 7 to 11.

The one to watch: the lab safety practical in early September. A student must pass it before doing lab work in the next unit, and anyone who does not pass simply retests. Much of this course is hands on, with chemicals, heat and electrical equipment, so please go through it with your child when it comes home.

Questions are always welcome. Please reach out through Class Dojo or the office. Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org | arsheen.sayeed@wischools.org

Grades 7 and 8 · Quran

Grades 7 and 8 Quran

Reviewing Al-Bayyinah to An-Naba, then memorizing Ar-Rahman, Al-Waqi’ah and Ya-Sin with tafsir and tajweed

TENTATIVE PLAN: SUBJECT TO CHANGE

This guide is a plan, not a promise. The months are approximate, and a surah may take longer than planned. Timing and detail will change, but where your child is headed by June will not.

Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. This guide replaces any earlier Grades 7 and 8 Quran guide. Grades 7 and 8 learn Quran together, in separate classes for boys and girls, and both classes follow this plan. The one difference is in the fall, when the girls’ class also studied Surah Al-Jinn. Islamic Studies has its own family guide.

Late August to OctoberReview: Al-Bayyinah to An-Naba. Girls also: Al-Jinn

What your child is learning

  • Review: Surahs from Al-Bayyinah to An-Naba, all from Juz 30. The teacher assigns each student the surahs to review, based on what that student needs.
  • Recitation: Reciting each assigned surah to the teacher with correct tajweed.
  • Girls’ class: Also studied Surah Al-Jinn for its translation, meaning and tafsir.
  • Boys’ class: The review surahs only.

Try this at home

Ask which surahs your child has been assigned, and listen to one of them each evening.

November to JanuaryAr-Rahman

What your child is learning

  • Every student: The whole class works on the same surah together, with no separate levels.
  • Memorizing: Ar-Rahman, 78 ayat, from Juz 27.
  • Understanding: The tafsir of the surah, its new words, and the tajweed rules used to recite it.
  • Recitation: Reciting it properly with the teacher.

Try this at home

Ask your child what the repeated ayah of Ar-Rahman asks, and what it means for your family.

January or February to MarchAl-Waqi’ah

What your child is learning

  • Every student: The whole class works on the same surah together, with no separate levels.
  • Memorizing: Al-Waqi’ah, 96 ayat, from Juz 27. It begins in January or February, depending on when the class finishes Ar-Rahman.
  • Understanding: The tafsir of the surah, its new words, and the tajweed rules used to recite it.
  • Recitation: Reciting it properly with the teacher.

Try this at home

Ramadan falls in February and school is closed for Eid al-Fitr in early March. Keep daily practice going.

April to MayYa-Sin

What your child is learning

  • Every student: The whole class works on the same surah together, with no separate levels.
  • Memorizing: Ya-Sin, 83 ayat. It begins in Juz 22 and finishes in Juz 23.
  • Understanding: The tafsir of the surah, its new words, and the tajweed rules used to recite it.
  • Recitation: Reciting it properly with the teacher.

Try this at home

Take turns: you read one ayah and your child recites the next from memory.

JuneReview

What your child is learning

  • Review: Ar-Rahman, Al-Waqi’ah and Ya-Sin, so all three are secure before the summer.

Try this at home

Ask your child to recite any of the three surahs for you in one sitting.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Recite Ar-Rahman, Al-Waqi’ah and Ya-Sin from memory.
  • Explain what each surah is about, using its tafsir and key words.
  • Apply the tajweed rules learned in class.
  • Keep the assigned review surahs from Al-Bayyinah to An-Naba strong.

School lessons alone will not get your child there. Daily practice at home is what makes memorization last.

HOW YOU GET THEM THERE

  • Ten minutes of recitation every day, not a long session once a week.
  • Listen while your child recites, even if you follow along from the mushaf.
  • Use the 4-6-6-4 steps at home, with the websites listed below.
  • Watch Class Dojo for any change to the plan.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

The Prophet, peace be upon him, taught that the best of us are those who learn the Quran and teach it. Ar-Rahman, Al-Waqi’ah and Ya-Sin are surahs many families recite often, and knowing their meaning turns memorization into reflection.

HOW YOUR CHILD MEMORIZES IN CLASS: THE 4-6-6-4 METHOD

  1. Step 1, 4 times: read or listen. Read the new ayah from the mushaf, or listen to it.
  2. Step 2, 6 times: recite from memory. Say the ayah without looking.
  3. Step 3, 6 times: read or listen again. Back to the mushaf or the recording.
  4. Step 4, 4 times: recite from memory. Say it again without looking.

If your child gets stuck: pause the count, practice the word that was missed, then pick the count back up. Use the same four steps at home.

READING SKILLS IN CLASS

Every student works on Quran reading skills this year, so they can read and memorize the Quran with proper tajweed.

TO LISTEN AND READ AT HOME

  • Quran.com, read, listen and study
  • al-Muqri’, listen and recite
  • QuranWBW.com, word by word translation

THE GRADES 7 AND 8 SURAHS THIS YEAR

  • 98 to 78, Al-Bayyinah to An-Naba, Juz 30, review, assigned by the teacher
  • 72 Al-Jinn, Juz 29, 28 ayat, girls’ class, translation, meaning and tafsir, late August to October
  • 55 Ar-Rahman, Juz 27, 78 ayat
  • 56 Al-Waqi’ah, Juz 27, 96 ayat
  • 36 Ya-Sin, Juz 22 and 23, 83 ayat

Three surahs, 257 ayat in all, after a review assigned to each student. The number beside each name is its place in the Quran, and the Juz is the part of the Quran where it is found.

IF YOUR CHILD MOVES AHEAD

A student who finishes a surah early moves straight on to the next surah on the list, without waiting for the class. A student who finishes all three surahs is given more to memorize by the teacher. The teacher assigns surahs to students who move ahead, based on testing.

Questions about your child’s Quran progress? Message the teacher on Class Dojo or contact the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org

Grades 7 and 8 · Physical Science

Grades 7 and 8 Physical Science

A family guide to the year, month by month

THIS PLAN IS TENTATIVE

This is a plan, not a promise. These are the overall topics for each month. Order and timing will change as the year goes on, and months are approximate. Where your child lands in June does not change.

Anything that changes is emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. The test dates below are the plan as it stands today; when the calendar moves, the real dates are posted there.

Physical Science is one class for Grades 7 and 8 and meets five periods a week. Your child works from Savvas Experience Science with laboratory work built around it, following the Virginia Physical Science standards.

Exam dates are tentative. Exams are planned for the school's exam weeks (October 13 to 16, January 11 to 15, March 30 to April 2 and June 7 to 11). Exact date TBD.

Late August and SeptemberDoing science, then atoms

What your child is learning

  • Topics: How a result is made trustworthy: variables, repeated trials, measurement and graphing. Then the atom, its particles, and how the model was rebuilt as new evidence arrived.
  • In the lab: A measurement carousel, an investigation showing how a single trial misleads, a design challenge, and a gold foil simulation.
  • Handed in: The lab safety practical in early September, which must be passed before any Unit 2 lab work, and a design-and-test task.

Words to know: variable, control, trial, accuracy, precision, atom, proton, neutron, electron, isotope

By the end of the unit: Design a fair test that changes one variable, run repeated trials, and describe the parts of an atom and how the atomic model changed.

Sample question: Why is one trial not enough in an experiment?A strong answer: One trial could be off because of a mistake or bad luck. If I repeat it several times and the results agree, I can trust them more. I can also average them to get a better answer.

Watch for: Mixing up accuracy and precision. Precise means results are close to each other; accurate means close to the true value. Results can be precise and still wrong.

Try this at home

Ask why one trial is not enough. If your child can explain that, the first unit has landed.

OctoberStates of matter, then the periodic table

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Why a gas fills its container and a solid does not, what temperature measures, then reading the periodic table and predicting what an element will do from its position.
  • In the lab: Particle motion simulations, pressure demonstrations, and a mystery element sort where students build their own table before seeing the real one.
  • Handed in: A model evaluation task and the Unit 2 assessment, then an element prediction task. Quarter 1 closes Oct 23.

Words to know: kinetic molecular theory, group, family, period, valence electron, metal, metalloid, nonmetal

By the end of the month: Explain states of matter using particle motion, and use an element's group and period to predict how it behaves.

Sample question: Why does a gas fill its whole container while a solid keeps its shape?A strong answer: Gas particles move fast and are far apart, so they spread out until they fill the space. Solid particles are packed tightly and only vibrate in place, so a solid keeps its shape.

Watch for: Mixing up groups and periods. Groups are columns, and elements in a group behave alike; periods are rows. Sodium and magnesium sit side by side but do not act alike.

Try this at home

Point at anything in the kitchen and ask which elements are in it, then where they sit on the table.

NovemberProperties, changes and bonding

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Identifying a substance from properties that do not depend on how much you have, telling a physical change from a chemical one, and why ionic and covalent bonds form.
  • In the lab: A density column and unknown identification lab, and ionic and covalent samples compared by conductivity and melting point.
  • Handed in: Classification checks with evidence required, and bond-type predictions.

Words to know: density, solubility, physical change, chemical change, ion, ionic bond, covalent bond

By the end of the month: Identify a substance by density and other properties, tell physical from chemical changes, and predict whether a bond is ionic or covalent.

Sample question: Is cooking an egg a physical or a chemical change? How do you know?A strong answer: It is a chemical change. Heat changes the proteins into a new substance, the egg turns solid and white, and you cannot turn it back into a raw egg. A new substance formed.

Watch for: Calling melting or dissolving a chemical change because it looks different. If the substance is still the same, like ice to water or sugar in tea, it is a physical change.

Try this at home

Ask whether cooking an egg is a physical or a chemical change, and make them defend the answer.

DecemberConservation of matter

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Why a chemical equation has to balance, and why nothing is created or destroyed when atoms rearrange.
  • In the lab: Baking soda and vinegar in a sealed bag, massed before and after, then a closed-system reaction the students design themselves.
  • Handed in: Balancing practice sets twice a week, the conservation investigation, an unknown substance identification report, and the Unit 4 assessment.

Words to know: reactant, product, coefficient, balanced equation, conservation of matter

By the end of the month: Balance simple chemical equations and use measured mass to show that matter is conserved in a reaction.

Sample question: Balance this: H₂ + O₂ makes H₂O. Why must it balance?A strong answer: There are 2 oxygen atoms on the left and 1 on the right, so I write 2H₂O. Now there are 4 hydrogens on the right, so I write 2H₂. So 2H₂ + O₂ makes 2H₂O. Atoms rearrange; none are created or destroyed.

Watch for: Changing the small subscripts to balance, like writing H₂O₂. That makes a different substance. Only the big numbers in front, the coefficients, can change.

Try this at home

Ask where the mass went when something burned or dissolved. That question is the whole unit.

JanuaryWork, force and motion

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Speed, velocity and acceleration, reading motion graphs, balanced and unbalanced forces, and Newton’s three laws.
  • In the lab: Ramp and cart timing with repeated trials, a collision safety design challenge, and balloon rocket demonstrations.
  • Handed in: Weekly calculation sets on force, mass and acceleration, then the motion investigation with graphs. Quarter 2 closes Jan 15.

Words to know: velocity, acceleration, net force, inertia, friction, work, power, newton

By the end of the month: Calculate speed and acceleration, read motion graphs, and use Newton's three laws to explain how forces change motion.

Sample question: A net force of 12 newtons pushes a 3 kg cart. What is its acceleration?A strong answer: Newton's second law says force equals mass times acceleration, so acceleration is force divided by mass. 12 ÷ 3 = 4, so it is 4 meters per second squared. Check: 3 × 4 = 12.

Watch for: Thinking a moving object needs a force to keep moving. Without friction it would keep going; that is inertia, the first law. Listen for the idea that motion simply runs out.

Try this at home

In the car, ask why a passenger lurches forward when you brake. The answer is the first law.

FebruaryMotion assessed, then energy

What your child is learning

  • Topics: The motion unit closes in the first week, then forms of energy, energy transformation, and why energy is conserved but not always usable.
  • In the lab: Pendulum and roller coaster energy tracking, and a lab where students find the kinetic energy relationship from their own data.
  • Handed in: The Unit 5 assessment on Feb 5, then weekly energy calculations.

Words to know: kinetic energy, potential energy, efficiency, waste heat, conduction, convection, radiation

By the end of the month: Calculate kinetic energy, track energy as it changes form, and explain why energy is conserved but not all of it is usable.

Sample question: On a roller coaster, where is potential energy greatest, and where is kinetic energy greatest?A strong answer: Potential energy is greatest at the top of the highest hill, where the car is highest. As it drops, potential turns into kinetic, so kinetic is greatest at the bottom where it moves fastest. Some becomes heat from friction.

Watch for: Saying energy is used up or lost. It is never destroyed; it changes form, often into waste heat. Ask your child where the missing energy went.

Try this at home

Ask where the energy goes in a device at home that gets warm. Warm usually means wasted.

MarchEnergy and how we use it

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Energy sources, renewable and nonrenewable, compared on real cost data, and where energy becomes unusable.
  • In the lab: Students analyze a real device, diagram every transformation, and propose an efficiency improvement.
  • Handed in: The energy systems task and the Unit 6 assessment. School is closed for Eid al-Fitr Mar 1 to 12.

Words to know: renewable, nonrenewable, efficiency, transformation, joule

By the end of the month: Compare renewable and nonrenewable energy sources using real cost data, and trace every energy transformation in a device.

Sample question: A bulb uses 100 joules and gives off 20 joules of light. What is its efficiency, and where did the rest go?A strong answer: Efficiency is useful energy out divided by energy in, so 20 ÷ 100 = 0.2, or 20 percent. The other 80 joules became heat, which is why the bulb gets warm.

Watch for: Thinking renewable means free or perfect. Solar and wind still cost money to build and depend on the weather; strong answers weigh cost, supply and pollution.

Try this at home

Look at the electricity bill together. It is a measurement of energy, and your child can now read it.

AprilWaves and light

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Wavelength, frequency and amplitude, longitudinal and transverse waves, why sound needs a medium, then reflection, refraction and interference.
  • In the lab: Slinky and rope waves side by side, a ripple tank, a sound-in-a-vacuum demonstration, and prism stations.
  • Handed in: The wave investigation, measuring wave properties in two different media and explaining the difference. Quarter 3 closes Apr 9.

Words to know: wavelength, frequency, amplitude, medium, reflection, refraction, interference

By the end of the month: Describe waves by wavelength, frequency and amplitude, and explain reflection, refraction and why sound needs a medium.

Sample question: Why can sound travel through air but not through outer space?A strong answer: Sound is a longitudinal wave that moves when particles bump into each other. Space is nearly empty, so there is nothing to carry the vibration. Light can cross space because it does not need a medium.

Watch for: Mixing up frequency and amplitude in sound. Higher frequency means higher pitch; bigger amplitude means louder. Ask what changes when a song gets louder compared with higher.

Try this at home

Ask why you can hear around a corner but not see around one. Both are waves.

MayThe spectrum, then electricity

What your child is learning

  • Topics: The electromagnetic spectrum from radio to gamma and what each region is used for, then static electricity, conductors and insulators.
  • In the lab: Static electricity stations, then circuit building with bulbs, batteries and switches, including deliberate fault-finding.
  • Handed in: The spectrum application report on one technology that uses a region of the spectrum. The waves unit closes May 11.

Words to know: electromagnetic spectrum, infrared, ultraviolet, charge, conductor, insulator, current, voltage

By the end of the month: Order the electromagnetic spectrum from radio to gamma with a use for each region, and explain charge, conductors and insulators.

Sample question: Which part of the spectrum does a microwave oven use, a TV remote, and a cell phone?A strong answer: The microwave oven uses microwaves, the remote uses infrared, and the phone uses radio waves to send signals. They are all the same kind of wave, just with different wavelengths.

Watch for: Thinking all radiation is dangerous. Radio waves and visible light are safe in daily use; it is high energy ultraviolet, X rays and gamma rays that can damage cells.

Try this at home

Ask what part of the spectrum the microwave, the remote and the phone each use.

JuneCircuits, magnets, and the close

What your child is learning

  • Topics: Series and parallel circuits, resistance and Ohm’s law, magnetic fields, and how they give us motors and generators.
  • In the lab: Magnetic field mapping with iron filings, and an electromagnet challenge students test and improve.
  • Handed in: The circuit design task, the electromagnet challenge, and a cumulative assessment in the final exam week, June 7 to 11.
  • Grade 8 graduation: Saturday, June 19. Attendance is required.

Words to know: series circuit, parallel circuit, resistance, Ohm’s law, magnetic field, electromagnet

By the end of the month: Build series and parallel circuits, use Ohm's law to find current, voltage or resistance, and explain how an electromagnet works.

Sample question: A 9 volt battery is connected to a 3 ohm resistor. What is the current?A strong answer: Ohm's law says voltage equals current times resistance, so current is voltage divided by resistance. 9 ÷ 3 = 3 amps. Check: 3 amps × 3 ohms = 9 volts.

Watch for: Mixing up series and parallel. In series there is one path, so one blown bulb breaks the whole circuit; in parallel each bulb has its own path. Ask your child to trace the path.

Try this at home

Ask why one blown bulb can kill a string of lights but not a room of them. That is series and parallel.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Design an investigation with repeated trials, and say why one trial is not evidence.
  • Explain motion with Newton’s laws and calculate speed, acceleration and energy from their own data.

Classroom lessons alone will not get your child there. The children who can do both are the ones who talked about this at home.

SO HERE IS WHAT HELPS MOST AT HOME

  • Ask for evidence: what did you measure that makes you say that?
  • Let them predict before they check. That order is what makes it science.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

This course asks students to settle questions by measurement rather than intuition, which is ilm in its plainest form. Recording the trial that contradicts your own hypothesis is honesty, and the class rule on data rests on that rather than on a school rule. Conservation of matter and the study of energy are taught with balance and the prohibition of waste in view: once a student can calculate the energy a device throws away, wasting it stops being an abstraction, Inshallah.

HOW YOUR CHILD IS CHECKED, AND ONE THING TO WATCH FOR

Day to day: exit tickets two or three times a week, a daily science notebook, and an investigation brief for every lab. Each unit ends with a task rather than only a test, scored 3 secure, 2 developing, 1 beginning. Quarter exams fall in the school's exam weeks: Oct 13 to 16, Jan 11 to 15, Mar 30 to Apr 2, and Jun 7 to 11.

The one to watch: the lab safety practical in early September. A student must pass it before doing lab work in the next unit, and anyone who does not pass simply retests. Much of this course is hands on, with chemicals, heat and electrical equipment, so please go through it with your child when it comes home.

Questions are always welcome. Please reach out through Class Dojo or the office. Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org | arsheen.sayeed@wischools.org

Grades 7 and 8 · Quran

Grades 7 and 8 Quran

Reviewing Al-Bayyinah to An-Naba, then memorizing Ar-Rahman, Al-Waqi’ah and Ya-Sin with tafsir and tajweed

TENTATIVE PLAN: SUBJECT TO CHANGE

This guide is a plan, not a promise. The months are approximate, and a surah may take longer than planned. Timing and detail will change, but where your child is headed by June will not.

Anything that changes will be emailed to you or posted on Class Dojo. This guide replaces any earlier Grades 7 and 8 Quran guide. Grades 7 and 8 learn Quran together, in separate classes for boys and girls, and both classes follow this plan. The one difference is in the fall, when the girls’ class also studied Surah Al-Jinn. Islamic Studies has its own family guide.

Late August to OctoberReview: Al-Bayyinah to An-Naba. Girls also: Al-Jinn

What your child is learning

  • Review: Surahs from Al-Bayyinah to An-Naba, all from Juz 30. The teacher assigns each student the surahs to review, based on what that student needs.
  • Recitation: Reciting each assigned surah to the teacher with correct tajweed.
  • Girls’ class: Also studied Surah Al-Jinn for its translation, meaning and tafsir.
  • Boys’ class: The review surahs only.

Try this at home

Ask which surahs your child has been assigned, and listen to one of them each evening.

November to JanuaryAr-Rahman

What your child is learning

  • Every student: The whole class works on the same surah together, with no separate levels.
  • Memorizing: Ar-Rahman, 78 ayat, from Juz 27.
  • Understanding: The tafsir of the surah, its new words, and the tajweed rules used to recite it.
  • Recitation: Reciting it properly with the teacher.

Try this at home

Ask your child what the repeated ayah of Ar-Rahman asks, and what it means for your family.

January or February to MarchAl-Waqi’ah

What your child is learning

  • Every student: The whole class works on the same surah together, with no separate levels.
  • Memorizing: Al-Waqi’ah, 96 ayat, from Juz 27. It begins in January or February, depending on when the class finishes Ar-Rahman.
  • Understanding: The tafsir of the surah, its new words, and the tajweed rules used to recite it.
  • Recitation: Reciting it properly with the teacher.

Try this at home

Ramadan falls in February and school is closed for Eid al-Fitr in early March. Keep daily practice going.

April to MayYa-Sin

What your child is learning

  • Every student: The whole class works on the same surah together, with no separate levels.
  • Memorizing: Ya-Sin, 83 ayat. It begins in Juz 22 and finishes in Juz 23.
  • Understanding: The tafsir of the surah, its new words, and the tajweed rules used to recite it.
  • Recitation: Reciting it properly with the teacher.

Try this at home

Take turns: you read one ayah and your child recites the next from memory.

JuneReview

What your child is learning

  • Review: Ar-Rahman, Al-Waqi’ah and Ya-Sin, so all three are secure before the summer.
  • Grade 8 graduation: Saturday, June 19. Attendance is required.

Try this at home

Ask your child to recite any of the three surahs for you in one sitting.

BY JUNE, WITH PRACTICE AT HOME

  • Recite Ar-Rahman, Al-Waqi’ah and Ya-Sin from memory.
  • Explain what each surah is about, using its tafsir and key words.
  • Apply the tajweed rules learned in class.
  • Keep the assigned review surahs from Al-Bayyinah to An-Naba strong.

School lessons alone will not get your child there. Daily practice at home is what makes memorization last.

HOW YOU GET THEM THERE

  • Ten minutes of recitation every day, not a long session once a week.
  • Listen while your child recites, even if you follow along from the mushaf.
  • Use the 4-6-6-4 steps at home, with the websites listed below.
  • Watch Class Dojo for any change to the plan.

OUR CONNECTION TO THIS WORK

The Prophet, peace be upon him, taught that the best of us are those who learn the Quran and teach it. Ar-Rahman, Al-Waqi’ah and Ya-Sin are surahs many families recite often, and knowing their meaning turns memorization into reflection.

HOW YOUR CHILD MEMORIZES IN CLASS: THE 4-6-6-4 METHOD

  1. Step 1, 4 times: read or listen. Read the new ayah from the mushaf, or listen to it.
  2. Step 2, 6 times: recite from memory. Say the ayah without looking.
  3. Step 3, 6 times: read or listen again. Back to the mushaf or the recording.
  4. Step 4, 4 times: recite from memory. Say it again without looking.

If your child gets stuck: pause the count, practice the word that was missed, then pick the count back up. Use the same four steps at home.

READING SKILLS IN CLASS

Every student works on Quran reading skills this year, so they can read and memorize the Quran with proper tajweed.

TO LISTEN AND READ AT HOME

  • Quran.com, read, listen and study
  • al-Muqri’, listen and recite
  • QuranWBW.com, word by word translation

THE GRADES 7 AND 8 SURAHS THIS YEAR

  • 98 to 78, Al-Bayyinah to An-Naba, Juz 30, review, assigned by the teacher
  • 72 Al-Jinn, Juz 29, 28 ayat, girls’ class, translation, meaning and tafsir, late August to October
  • 55 Ar-Rahman, Juz 27, 78 ayat
  • 56 Al-Waqi’ah, Juz 27, 96 ayat
  • 36 Ya-Sin, Juz 22 and 23, 83 ayat

Three surahs, 257 ayat in all, after a review assigned to each student. The number beside each name is its place in the Quran, and the Juz is the part of the Quran where it is found.

IF YOUR CHILD MOVES AHEAD

A student who finishes a surah early moves straight on to the next surah on the list, without waiting for the class. A student who finishes all three surahs is given more to memorize by the teacher. The teacher assigns surahs to students who move ahead, based on testing.

Questions about your child’s Quran progress? Message the teacher on Class Dojo or contact the school office. Woodbridge Islamic School | 13385 Minnieville Road, Woodbridge, VA 22192 | 703-910-7029 | wischools.org

Reading list

Books to read at home

Recommended by the Islamic Schools League of America, sorted by reading level

Please read a book yourself before your child does. These titles are recommended by the Islamic Schools League of America, not selected by Woodbridge Islamic School, and only you can judge whether a book fits your family and your values.

ISLA chose every title here twice over: once for being genuinely well written, and once for what it puts in front of a Muslim child. The ratings and the original summaries are largely the work of Dr. Freda Crane Shamma.

These are not our curriculum books. They are for home, the library, car rides and the long weeks of summer. ISLA’s high school level is left out, so what is here is for Kindergarten through Grade 8.

ISLA publishes a short description of each book alongside its list. You can read the full annotated version at the Islamic Schools League of America.

What the stars mean

★
Worth reading, and nothing in it cuts against Islamic values.
★★
Worth reading, and it carries an Islamic value of its own.
★★★
The top rating. Excellent writing, with Islamic values running all through it.
